name: Study Guide
text: 1 | Page Study Guide for course MED210: Neuroscience I Dr Course coordinator: Dr. Hanaa Mahmoud Nagdy Lecturer of Internal Medicine Contact information: hm_nagdy@aast.edu 2 | Page INTRODUCTION TO MEDICAL PROFESSION YEAR 1 SEMESTER 1 STUDY GUIDE IN THIS Guide: • Welcome Note P. 3 • Educational Opportunities P.4-7 • Timetable P. 8-14 • Assessment P.15-17 • Learning Resources P. 18-19 3 | Page Dear students Welcome to Medical School. We hope you enjoy your 5 years' journey of becoming a physician. Here in the sixth course" Neurosciences I”, you will learn how to integrate smoothly between basic medical and clinical sciences, in a manner that will help you rationalize the clinical importance of the topics your study in the pre-clerkship phase. It consists of an extensive and in-depth study of the anatomical and functional aspects of central nervous system in order to understand the human brain & behavior. The aim of this course is to help you be acquainted with the gross and microscopic structural features of the brain, brain stem, basal ganglia and spinal cord. You will discover the miraculous physiology of synapses, neurotransmitters and mechanisms of neuronal excitation as well as the structure and functions of different receptors during neuronal excitation. You will discover the mechanisms and pathways of sensory inputs in the nervous system. You will explore the structure and functions of motor system and how can you maintain your posture. You will be surprised a lot about neuronal plasticity and memory types. You will realize the structure of skin and how you can feel pain. You will explore treatment of various cerebral dysfunctions such as Alzheimer's disease, Parkinson's disease and the uses of anti-seizure drugs in different clinical scenarios. We hope you enjoy your sixth block in your enjoyable long-life medical knowledge. 4 | Page IN THIS SECTION: • The different Course Themes • The Course Objectives • Different Teaching and Learning Methods EDUCATIONAL OPPORTUNITIES 5 | Page Through reviewing the following table, you will understand the Four major themes in Neuroscience I course and how these themes are related to the course objectives. You will also know which teaching method will be used to cover each theme. It is important for you to review the course objectives at the beginning of each week. Educational Strategy (Interactive Lecturing- Practical- Problem Based Learning- Tutorial- skills Sessions- self-directed learning- E-learning) Course Theme Course objectives Theme 1: General Organization of Head & Neck & CNS 1. Describe the different bones bounding the cranial cavity and the meninges. 2. Compare the basic organization of the peripheral and central nervous systems in relation to their primary functions. 3. Discriminate the activation and inhibition mechanism of action of different neurotransmitters on human body 4. Describe the triangles of the neck in relevance to their related structures, boundaries, and contents. 5. Appraise the anatomical-clinical importance of different structures of the neck. 6. Appraise the importance of identifying the level of termination of the spinal cord to different clinical disorders. 7 Appraise the congenital anomalies affecting the head & neck relative to their development. Theme 2: The Somatosensory System 8. Classify the receptors according to their structure and function with emphasis on skin structure and its receptors. 9. Appraise neurotransmission and the excitatory and inhibitory postsynaptic potential. 10.Differentiate sub-modalities of sensations in relation to somato-tropic map. EDUCATIONAL OPPORTUNITIES 6 | Page 11. Deduce types of pain, pathways for pain sensation and mechanisms of hypoalgesia and hyperalgesia. 12. Discuss spinal cord role in the gating of nociceptive transmission and the role of endorphins in central control of pain. 13. Determine principles of pain management, categories of analgesics and classification of opiate and non- opiate analgesics. Theme3: Motor Control: Cerebrum, Brain stem & Spinal cord 14. Appraise the functional and clinical correlation of different sulci & gyri and cortical areas. 15. Interpret the functional relation of different parts of the brain & spinal cord to its vascular supply. 16. Correlate microstructure of the cerebral cortex to its function 17. Define Brodmann areas for motor control and its clinical relevance to cortical injuries. 18. Deduce the causes and risk factors for different types of cerebral strokes and the patterns of brain damage caused by head injury. 19. Define the neuronal plasticity as a mechanism of memory, types of memory and the characteristics of each type. 20. Outline cortical areas for speech control and main types of aphasia. 21. Classify cranial nerves according to their function and clinical importance and the different functional components of their nuclei. 22. Delineate the neural pathways for monosynaptic& polysynaptic spinal cord reflexes. 23. Categorize neuronal circuits of spinal reflexes, types of motor units and the role of muscle tone in maintaining posture Theme 4: Motor Modulation: The Basal Ganglia 24. Distinguish between upper and lower motor neuron and the interconnections between them in health and disease. 25. Classify types of neuroglia according to their sites and function and components of the blood brain barrier. 26. Differentiate between types of white matter of the brain, the importance of internal capsule and relevant clinical conditions. 7 | Page 27. Describe the organization, connections and neurotransmitters of the basal ganglia and its related clinical disorders. 28. Compare neurodegenerative diseases to demyelinating CNS disorders (Alzheimer disease and multiple sclerosis) as regards etiology, pathogenesis and clinical presentation 29. Deduce the treatment of various cerebral dysfunction such as Alzheimer's and Parkinson's diseases, chronic pain and anti-seizure drugs. 30. Appraise the importance of micro and macro nutrients to neuronal function in health and disease. Practical 31. Identify the anatomical structure of the skull, cranial cavity, triangles of the neck, vertebrae, brain, dural folds and spinal cord.) 32. Identify microscopically the layers of cerebrum, types of neurons, the skin and skin appendages. 33. Distinguish principles of safe prescription and OTC prescribed medications Assignment 2 concept map of 2 cases in the opening sessions 8 | Page IN THIS SECTION: • Topic covered in each week • Course Timetable BLOCK TIMETABLE 9 | Page Week 1: (Covered lectures L1-L6, Practical 1,2) Day Session 1 9-11 Session 2 11-1 Session 3 1-3 Sat 1-10 Sun 2-10 L1: Cranial Cavity L2: understanding CNS function PBL 1 opening session (clinical 1) Hall 102 8 think tanks Mon 3-10 L3: Neurotransmitters L4: Anterior triangle practical: Cranial cavity Medical profession 3/ Research 3 (L1 &2) Hall 102 2 Labs (Anatomy) 2-103/2-105 Tues. 4-10 L5: Posterior angle L6: Anatomy of vertebrae & spinal cords Clinical skills (1) Hall 102 Skill lab 4-103/4-105 Wed 5- 10 L7: Development of H&N L8: Somatic sensory system Practical: Brain parts Clinical skills (2) Thu 6-10 Hall 102 Lab 4-101 / 4-201 Lab Skill lab 4-103/4-105 Fri 7-10 Week 1 Timetable 10 | Page Week 2: (Covered lectures L7-L14, Practical 3,4,5) Day Session 1 9-11 Session 2 11-1 Session 3 1-3 Sat 8-10 Sun 9-10 L9: Skin & its receptors L10: Physiological function of receptors & sensory coding Practical: Ant, Post triangle Clinical skills (3) Hall 102 2 Labs (Anatomy) Skill lab 4-103/4-105 Mon 10-10 L11: Ascending pathways & Somatosensory cortex I L12: Pain sources & transduction of painful stimuli - pain pathways Practical: Vertebrae Medical profession 3/ Research 3 (L3 &4) Hall 102 2 Labs (Anatomy) Lab 206 Lab 401 2-103/2-105 Tues 11-10 L13: Central control of pain L14: Analgesics Tutorial: Overview of sensory structural consideration & function (anatomy& physiology) Clinical skills (4) Hall 102 228 / 4-302 Skill lab 4-103/4-105 Wed 12-10 Practical: N

What is the location and functions of paracentral lobule? - Location: Around the central sulcus on the medial surface of the brain. - Function: Contains the lower limb, perineum primary motor and somatosensory cortical function regions. Q: Which gyri are concerned for olfaction on the inferior surface of the brain? 1- Parahypocampus 2- Uncus 3- Olfactory gyrus Q: A 45-year-old farmer complains of headaches. Neurologic examination reveals mild hemiparesis on the right side. The lesion is most likely in which of the following cortices? Frontal Insular Occipital Parietal Temporal Q: A An 80-year-old microbiologist has a cerebral infarction. His speech is limited, he cannot write but does respond to questions by shaking his head, and he has lower facial weakness on the right side. The lesion is most likely in the: left frontal lobe left parietal lobe left temporal lobe right frontal lobe right parietal lobe Q: A Ophthalmic Artery Anterior Cerebral Artery Middle Cerebral Artery Anterior C horoidal Artery Posterior Communicating Artery What are the branches of internal carotid artery? Branches of internal carotid artery 18 19 It consists of: Two vertebral arteries. 2. Basilar artery (single). 3. Posterior cerebral artery (two). What are the arteries forming the Vertebro -basilar system? Vertebro -basilar system Dear students & A 60-year-old hypertensive man complains of numbness and weakness in his left leg and foot. Which of the following arteries’ occlusion can account for this complaint? Anterior cerebral Anterior choroidal Interior carotid Middle cerebral Posterior cerebral Q: A Which of the following arteries, on occlusion, can result in Broca aphasia? Posterior choroidal Anterior choroidal Anterior cerebral Middle cerebral Basilar Q: D Your patient presents with signs of a stroke. Based on the angiograph and the patient's balance impairments, you suspect that the right posterior inferior cerebellar artery was occluded; this artery is a direct branch of which of the following arteries? Basilar Vertebral Internal carotid Posterior cerebral Superior cerebella Q: B 24 What are the branches of the Vertebral artery? Branches: 1. Anterior spinal artery; the 2 Ars unite together to form a single trunk which runs in the anterior median fissure of the spinal cord. 2. Posterior spinal artery ; two arteries, each one arises from the corresponding vertebral artery. Each artery divides into two longitudinal branches which descend on each side of the posterior root of the spinal nerves. 3. Posterior inferior cerebellar artery (PICA) is a tortuous artery and is the largest branch of the vertebral artery. 4. Medullary branches; to supply the medulla oblongata. What is the artery related to the anterior surface of pons? Mention its branches. 26 Basilar artery Origin: At the lower border of pons by the union of the 2 vertebral arteries. Course & relations: It passes on the front of the pons in the midline (pontine sulcus, groove for basilar artery). Termination: Bifurcates into the 2 posterior cerebral arteries. Branches: 1. Anterior inferior cerebellar artery , supplies also the cerebellar tonsil. 2. Superior cerebellar artery 3. Pontine branches 4. Labyrinthine (internal auditory) artery 5. Posterior cerebral artery (terminal branches) What are the arteries forming the circle of Willis? 27 Hemiplegia and sensory deficit on the right side of the body may be caused by infarction in the territory of the: left middle cerebral artery right anterior cerebral artery left posterior cerebral artery left superior cerebellar artery anterior communicating artery Q: A Students’ learning outcomes At the end of this session, the student will be able to: Correlate the different functional areas of the cerebral cortex with the cortical lobes, gyri& sulci. Appraise the distribution of carotid system & vertebrobasilar system. Differentiate between the territory of each artery in the anterior and posterior circulation of the brain. Appraise the clinical application of blood supply of the brain. text: 1. Name one function of the Premotor area. Answer: planning gross movements that are already learned. State the types of explicit memory? Answer: semantic and episodic memories Enumerate the different layers of the cerebral cortex Answer: I. The molecular layer (plexiform layer) II. The external granular layer III. The external pyramidal cell layer IV. The internal granular layer V. The internal pyramidal cell layer (ganglionic layer) VI. The polymorphic layer (multiform layer) Describe cells of Marinotti and mention its site in the cerebral cortex Answer: They are multipolar neurons that are most densely located within the deepest layer of the cortex. Their numerous axons and dendrites course towards the surface of the cortex. Compare dynamic and static stretch reflex regarding stimulus and response? Answer: Dynamic: stimulus: sudden stretch/ Response: rapid strong contraction (tendon jerk) Static: Stimulus: maintained stretch/ Response: sustained contraction (muscle tone) Define innervation ratio and classify motor unit according to innervation ratio? Answer: Innervation ratio: is the number of muscle fibers innervated by a single motor neuron. Small Innervation ratio: have few no. of muscle fibers Large Innervation ratio: large no. of muscle fibers Define the area involved in understanding the meaning of the spoken words? Answer: Auditory association area (area 22) OR Wernicke’s area Define the gyrus that lies below the cingulate sulcus and state its function. Answer: Cingulate gyrus lies below cingulate sulcus. Answer: 1- Olfactory 2- Optic 3- Vestibulocochlear Indicate the diagnostic microscopic feature of Ischemic infarct 18 hours after arterial occlusion? text: Practical brain stem white matter External Features of the Medulla Oblongata The groove between the pyramid and the olive is called anterolateral sulcus and it gives exit for the rootlets of the hypoglossal nerve. The groove lateral to the olive is called posterolateral sulcus. It gives exit to the rootlets of the glossopharyngeal, vagus and cranial accessory nerves . External Features of the Medulla Oblongata Dorsal surface : It is divided into: open medulla (cranial) closed medulla (caudal). Dorsal surface of medulla oblongata (closed ) Posterior median sulcus The longitudinal elevation lateral to the posteromedian sulcus is called gracile fasciculus as it overlies the gracile tract. The upper end of the gracile fasciculus expands to form the gracile tubercle which overlies the gracile nucleus. elevation lateral to the gracile fasciculus is called cuneate fasciculus as it overlies the cuneate tract. The upper end of the cuneate fasciculus expands to form the cuneate tubercle which overlies the cuneate nucleus. The ridge lateral to the cuneate tubercle is the inferior cerebellar peduncle. External Features of the Pons The ventral surface presents the following features : It is convex from side to side Laterally it is continuous with the middle cerebellar peduncle A median groove called basilar groove as it lodges the basilar artery. Cranial nerves related to pons (5-8) Trigeminal nerve: emerges from the middle part of the pons at its junction with the middle cerebellar peduncle. Abducent nerve: emerges between pons and the pyramid. The facial and vestibulo -cochlear N: emerge at the lower border of the pons, between it and the medulla. Note : Cranial nerves VII and VIII exit at the cerebellopontomedullary angle. What are the cranial nerves related to pons ? What are the cranial nerves related to pons ? Dear students & External Features of the Pons The dorsal surface presents the following features : Separated from open medulla by an imaginary line Form the cranial 2/3rd of the floor of the 4th ventricle . External Features of the midbrain The midbrain presents a narrow lumen called cerebral aqueduct (aqueduct of sylvius ) . A coronal plane passing through the cerebral aqueduct divides the midbrain into two divisions: A. Cerebral Peduncle B. Tectum External Features of the midbrain The ventral surface presents the following features : Cerebral peduncles: formed of a large column of fibers (crus cerebri )on either side. interpeduncular fossa : depression between the 2 Cerebral peduncles. Occulomotor (3rd): emerge from medial aspect of Cerebral peduncles . External Features of the midbrain The dorsal surface presents the following features : 4 elevations/colliculi: • Two superior colliculi: concerned with visual reflexes . • Two inferior colliculi: forms part of auditory reflexes . Each colliculus gives rise to a brachium from its lateral side : The superior brachium connects the superior colliculus with the lateral geniculate body. The inferior brachium connects the inferior colliculus with the medial geniculate body. External Features of the midbrain Dorsal surface : Marked by Trochlear (4th)Nerve: The only cranial nerve emerging from dorsal surface of brain stem (the rest were from the ventral). name: Notes: Part II peripheral receptors
ref: file:MED 210 L 9 part II peripheral receptors 23-24.pdf
text: 1 Specialized peripheral receptors What is a receptor? It is the specialized sensory nerve ending that is adapted to receive and respond to different stimuli. They are distributed in different regions in the body, for example; muscles, tendons, skin, fascia, and joint capsules, with skin representing the richest site with receptors. Classifications of receptors Functional according to types of stimuli 1. Mechanoreceptors They respond to mechanical stimuli (touch, stretch, vibrations, and pressure) that may affect the receptor directly or indirectly through the surrounding tissues. For example; Meissner’s and Pacinian corpuscles, Merkel’s disks, muscle spindles and Golgi tendon organs. 2. Nociceptors; pain receptors that respond to painful stimuli. 3. Thermoreceptors; Respond to cold or hot stimuli. 4. Other receptors; Photoreceptors (rods & cones), gustatory cells in taste buds of the tongue and olfactory cells in olfactory epithelium of the nose. Structural according to presence or absence of a connective tissue (CT) capsule 1- Encapsulated (CT capsule) Meissner’s and Pacinian corpuscles are in the skin. Muscle spindles and Golgi tendon organs are found in skeletal muscles. 2- Non- Encapsulated (no CT capsule) Free nerve endings (nociceptors & thermoreceptors) and Merkel’s disks in the skin. Receptors of the skin (Fig. 1) Encapsulated Non- Encapsulated Type Meissner’s corpuscles Pacinian corpuscles Merkel’s disks Free nerve endings (nociceptors & thermoreceptors) Site Dermal papillae Deep in dermis & hypodermis Stratum basale • Nociceptors; Epidermis • Thermoreceptors; Epidermis & dermal epidermal junction Structure Axon has a spiral course • Axon has an axial course, ends & by a Ends by flat expanded • Nociceptors; ramify (branches) freely in between the epidermis L9 Part II Microstructure of the Peripheral Receptors ILOs • Correlate structure & site of different skin sensory nerve endings to their specific function. • Correlate microstructure of the muscle spindle & Golgi tendon organs to their functions. 2 between modified Schwann cells terminal bulb. • Concentric collagen fibers, Schwann cells & fibroblasts disk-like part in contact with basal surface of Merkel’s cell cells till granular cells layer. • Thermoreceptors; Penetrate the basal lamina & also gives branches parallel to the dermal epidermal junction Function Fine touch (velocity) Vibrations, deep pressure Slow adapting to pressure • Nociceptors; painful stimuli • Thermoreceptors; Cold or hot stimuli Pathway of sensations transmitted from skin receptors (extra knowledge) (Fig 2) 1- Sensory receptor: Action potential is generated in the axon hillock close to the sensory nerve ending. 2- Pseudo unipolar neurons: central process synapses with sensory neurons in the spinal cord. Encapsulated receptors in the skeletal muscle (Fig 3) 1- Muscle spindle • Function: Muscle spindles continuously monitor the length and the changes in length of the muscle. When muscle is stretched, it normally undergoes reflex contraction, or stretch reflex. • Site: Between skeletal muscle fibers near the tendon. • Structure: Well-developed CT capsule that separates intrafusal (modified muscle fibers) from extrafusal fibers (skeletal muscle fibers). Core contains two types of intrafusal fibers. A- Nuclear chain; They are cylindrical and uniform in shape. The nuclei are arranged in one row. B- Nuclear bag are of two subtypes; dynamic and static. They have a swollen middle part that contains randomly aggregated nuclei. 1 2 3 Figure (1): Skin receptors Figure (2): Pathway of sensations transmitted from skin receptors 3 • Both types of intrafusal fibers lack myofibrils at their central (non- contractile central parts). However, the peripheral portions contain myofibrils, thus they are contractile. Innervation: a. Gamma efferent (Motor axons) that supply the peripheral zones of intrafusal fibers; to maintain intrafusal fibers stretched and sensitive. b. Primary (Ia) afferent sensory axons that end by annulo spiral sensory nerve endings on all types of intrafusal fibers. c. Secondary II afferent sensory axons that end by flower spray sensory nerve endings on static type of nuclear bag fibers and nuclear chain. • Mode of stimulation of the sensory nerve endings Group Ia and group II fibers both respond to a stretching of the muscle at a constant rate. Only group Ia fibers, however, respond to a change in the rate of stretching. 2- Golgi tendon organs (GTO) • Function: Golgi tendon organs monitor the intensity (force) of muscle contraction. When a muscle undergoes strenuous contraction, GTO induce reflex muscle relaxation to protect the muscle, bone and tendons. • Site: At the junction between a muscle with its tendon and are positioned in series with the muscle fibers • Structure: Formed of wavy collagen fibers and the continuation of a nonmyelinated type Ib sensory axon that ramifies as free nerve endings in spaces between the collagen fibers. • Mode of stimulation: When the muscle contracts, it places tensile forces on the collagen fibers, straightening them, with a consequent compression and stimulation of the entwined nerve endings. name: Notes: Part I Histology of the skin
ref: file:Med 210 L9 Part I Histology of the skin 2023-24.pdf
text: 1 The integ ument, composed of skin and its appendages -the sweat glands, sebaceous glands, hair, and nails-is the largest organ of the body, constituting 16% of body weight Functions of the skin: Besides providing a cover for the underlying soft tissues, skin performs many additional functions, including (1) protection against injury, bacterial invasion (2) regulation of body temperature; (3) reception of continual sensations from the environment (e.g., touch, temperature, and pain); (4) excretion from sweat glands; and (5) absorption of ultraviolet radiation from the sun for the synthesis of vitamin D. Layers of the skin (Fig 1): 1- Epidermis; the superficial layer that is formed of keratini zed stratifie d squamous epithelium. 2- Dermis; the underlying connective tissue layer, which is subdivided into: a- A superficial layer, the papillary layer that is formed of loose CT and elastic fibers. It is highly vascular and rich in immune cells. b- A deeper layer, the reticular layer that is composed of dense irregular CT. • The interface between the epidermis and the dermis is formed by raised ridges of the dermis, called dermal papillae that interdigitate with epidermal ridges. (WHY?) L 9 (Part I) Histology of the skin ILOs: 1- Correlate structure of skin layers to their function. 2- Differentiate layers of keratinocytes on morphological & structural basis. 3- Differentiate between different types of non-keratinocytes. 4- Differentiate between microstructure of the skin layers. 5- Classify sensory nerve endings on histological basis. 6- Correlate structure & site of different skin sensory nerve endings to their specific function 7- Correlate microstructure of the muscle spindle to its function Figure (1): Layers of the skin. Keratinocytes & Non-keratinocytes 2 N.B. The hypodermis, a loose connective tissue containing varying amount s of fat and it is not part of the skin. It has a role as thermal insulator and maintains regular shape of skin. Types of skin: 1- Thick skin; covers the palms and soles. 2- Thin skin; covers most of the body surface. Type of skin Thick skin Thin skin 1. Stratum corneum Thick layer Thin layer 2. Stratum lucidum Present only in thick skin absent 3. Sweat glands More Few 4. Hair follicles& sebaceous glands Absent Present Cells of the epidermis are of two types: I- Keratinocytes; they are capable of keratin synthesis and co nstitute the largest cell population of the epidermis. II- Non-keratinocytes; not capable of keratin synthesis and they are distributed within the epidermis. I- Keratinocytes are represented in five different morphological layers (strata), as following from the basal to the superficial layers (Fig 1): 1- Stratum basale; a single layer of cuboidal or low columnar cells. The cells are capable of mitosis, thus responsible for renewal and regeneration of the epidermis. The epidermis is in a continuous state of slo ughing and regeneration, a process that takes 20-30 days. 2- Stratum spinosum ; It is the thickest layer of epidermis , whose keratinocytes are polyhedral in shape with multiple short processes (spines), which interdigitate with one another by forming intercell ular bridges and connected by desmosomes. The cytoplasm show m embrane-coating lamellar granules that contain lipid material . These cells are mitotically active, thus share in epidermis regeneration. 3- Stratum granulosum; A layer three to five cell layers th ick; these keratinocytes still retain nuclei; cells c ontain large, coarse keratohyaline granules as well as membrane-coating granules. The contents of lamellar granules are released in between cells of this layer, coating the cell membranes by a lipid rich coat forming the skin-water barrier. 4- Stratum lucidum ; present in thick skin only . The cells are without nuclei or organelles and contain densely packed keratin filaments. 3 5- Stratum corneum (horny layer ); numerous layers of dead flattened keratinized cells, keratinocytes, without nuclei and organelles (squamo us, or horny cells) that will be sloughed off (desquamated). NB; Keratinocytes undergo morphological changes as the cells move towards the surface, where they become flatter and contain more keratin. II- Non-keratinocytes (Fig 2) Type of cell Melanocytes Langerhans’ cells Merkel’scells Layer Stratum basale & have processes that extend into stratum spinosum • Stratum spinosum & can extend to granulosum by multiple cell processes. • They are motile cells. Stratum basale Function Synthesis & storage of melanin granules in melanosomes that are transferred to the surrounding keratinocytes (Fig 1B). • Antigen presenting cells that have an immunological function, where they endocytose foreign antigen & present them to immune cells in the dermis. • They are also involved in hypersensitivity reactions. • Sensory nerves traverse the basal lamina to approximate the Merkel cells, thus forming Merkel cell-neurite complexes. • These complexes function as mechanoreceptors Figure (2): Non-keratinocytes

section: PBL 1 - Theme 2: The Somatosensory System
name: Notes: The somatic sensory system. Structure of the neuron
ref: file:MED 210 L 8 The somatic sensory system. Structure of the neuron 23-24 Final.pdf
text: 1 The nervous tissue is one of the four primary basic tissues of the human body. The components of the nervous tissue It consists of two types of cells: 1- Neurons: They are the structural and functional unit of the nervous tissue. 2- Neuroglia: They are the supportive cells of the nervous tissue. The functions of neurons: 1- Excitability: as they respond to environmental changes by g eneration of action potential and transmission of nerve impulse. 2- Conductivity: as they are capable of propagati ngt he nerve impulse to other neurons, or to effector organs that produce an action (muscles and glands). The modes of neuron stimulation 1- Direct response to a stimulus, for example light falling on the photoreceptor of the retina. 2- Chemically; through neurotransmitters released at synapses (junctions between neurons or neuron & effector organs). 3- Electrical; through gap junctions between adjacent neurons. The structure of the neuron • Neurons come in many different shapes and sizes but in their most basic form consist of t wo elements: the cell body ( soma, perikaryon ) and the neuron processes (neurites) including the dendrites and the axon (Fig. 1). 1. A cell body (soma , perikaryon): It contains the nucleus and other intracellular organelles that are concerned particularly with protein synthesis and secretory processes. • The nucleus : It is large, euchromatic with prominent nucleolus, indicating active synthetic activity of the neuron. • Nissl bodies (granules): These are basophilic granules that are observed scattered within the cytoplasm on light microscopic examination and they represent aggregates of ribosomes (polysomes) and rough endoplasmic reticulum that are observed by electron microscopic examination. These are essential for protein synthesis, which include the neuron cytoskeleton and the neurotransmitters. • Well-developed Golgi complex that is responsible for the packaging of neurotransmitter substances in secretory vesicles, which are transported along the axon till its termination. • Abundant mitochondria. • The cytoskeleton of the neuron (neurofibrils): - It includes three types: Microtubules (MT), n eurofilaments (intermediate filaments) and microfilaments (actin). - Function: Support of the neuron and plays an essential role in axonal transport. L8 Somatic sensory system: Structure of neurons and nerve endings ILOs • Correlate structure of different parts of the neuron to its role in nerve impulse transmission. • Identify types of neurons on morphological basis. • Appraise the functional classification of receptors. 2 Axonal transport It occurs in two directions (Fig 2): a. Anterograde: It is the transport (for example of mitochondria & neurotransmitter vesicles ) away from the cell body. It occurs in association with motor protein Kinesin. b. Retrograde: It is the transport of molecules for recycling ( for example the receptors) towards the cell body. It occurs in association with motor protein Dyenin. 2. The neuron processes (neurites) (Fig 1): a. The axon: - A single process extending from the cell body to the target cell. - The length of the a xon varies, as it may be short extending just for a few millimeters to a nearby cell or, it may be long extending for several meters as in the case of the motor neurons supplying the muscles away from the spinal cord. - It arises from the axon hillock (site where the action potential is generated). The impulse is then conducted through the axon away from the perikaryonwhich terminates at a synapse. - The axon has no branches except at axon termination forming the terminal arborizations, and it may give off collaterals along its course. - The axoplasm (cytoplasm): It contains few organelles; (n eurofibrils, vesicles and mitochondria). Nissl bodies are absent. - The axolemma (cell membrane) may be surrounded by sheaths according to the type of nerve fiber (myelin sheath and/or neurilemma). b. The dendrites: - Short, highly branched processes originate from any part of the cell body. - The dendrites are usually multiple as in multipolar neurons but it may be single as in bipolar neurons. - They conduct the impulse towards the cell body. The axon The dendrite Origin Arises from axon hillock. Arises from any part of the cell body. Direction of the impulse Conducts nerve impulse away from the cell body. Conducts nerve impulse toward the cell body. Figure (1): Structure of the neuron Figure (2): Axonal transport 3 Number Always single. Usually multiple as in multipolar neurons. It may be single as in bipolar neurons. Length Long Short Branching Limited Numerous Organelles Contains few organelles (neurofibrils, vesicles and mitochondria) . Nissl granules are absent. Contains most of the organelles as in the perikaryon except Golgi. Nissl granules are present. Sheaths It may be surrounded by sheaths. It is not surrounded by sheaths. Distribution of nerve cell bodies within the nervous system 1- Central nervous system (CNS): consists of the brain and spinal cord. The cell bodies of neurons are present in the grey matter, while the axons are present in the white matter. 2- Peripheral nervous system (PNS): formed of peripheral nerves and ganglia, and nerve endings. The cell bodies of the neurons are present in the ganglia, while the axons form the peripheral nerves. Classification of neurons I-Functionally: 1. Sensory neurons: where impulses are carried from receptors to the CNS. 2. Motor neurons: where impulses are carried from CNS to the effector organs e.g. muscle s or glands. 3. Interneurons: act as a link between sensory and motor neurons. They are present in CNS only. II-Morphologically: Neurons are classified according to the number of their processes into: 1. Multipolar: most common type in the body, example: a. Pyramidal cells: present in cerebral cortex (brain). b. Purkinje cells: presentin the cerebellar cortex of the cerebellum. 2. Pseudo-unipolar: It h as a single pro cess that divides into central and peripheral divisions. Present in the dorsal root ganglion (outside the CNS). 3. Bipolar: It has two processes, an axon and a dendrite (example in the retina). The synapse • It is the area of contact between two neurons or a neuron and an effector organ. Types of synapses • Chemical: Most of the synapses are chemical synapses that depend on the release of neurotransmitters. 4 • Electrical: In an electrical synapse, the two cells are connected by gap junctions. Parts of the chemical synapse (Fig 4) 1- Presynaptic terminal: - It is the axon terminal of the presynaptic neuron. The axon terminal contains many mitochondria and neurotransmitter vesicles. 2- Synaptic cleft: - It is the space between the presynaptic and the postsynaptic neuron. - Neurotransmitters are released from neurotransmitter vesicles by exocytosis into the synaptic cleft, with the help of calcium ions. - The synaptic cleft contains enzymes that get rid of excess neurotransmitters. 3- Post synaptic membrane: - The postsynaptic membrane of postsynaptic neuron that contains numerous receptors for the neurotransmitters. Nerve endings: - The axons end at a synapse by a nerve ending. Types of nerve endings: 1- Motor nerve ending: the axon terminals establish a synapse with an effector organ (muscle or gland). 2- Sensory nerve ending: the axon terminals end in the periphery of the body; skin, joints, muscle & some viscera. They transmit information from the periphery of the body to the CNS. Figure (3): Morphological Types of neurons Figure (4) Parts of the chemical synapse

section: PBL 1 - Theme 1: General Organization of Head and Neck & CNS
name: Notes: Understanding CNS function
text: Page 1 of 6 2 Introduction to Neuroscience ILOs By the end of this lecture, students will be able to 1. Describe basic organization of the peripheral versus central nervous systems. 2. Appraise the primary functions of their different parts 3. Interpret the multiple levels of function seen in the nervous system 4. Describe the different dermatomes. Everything we do, every thought we've ever had, is produced by the human brain. But exactly how it operates remains one of the biggest unsolved mysteries, and it seems the more we probe its secrets, the more surprises we find. Neil deGrasse Tyson The nervous system is what enables us to perceive and interact with our environment. The bra in regulates voluntary and involuntary function, enables us to be alert and responsive, and enables us to respond physically and emotionally to the world. It is an information -processing system that regulates all the physiological functions of the organism. The nervous system has many functions as: • Propagate sensory information (APs) from eyes, skin, blood vessels, ears, digestive tract, joints, muscles, lungs… to the CNS • Integration. Brain and spinal cord process sensory input and initiate responses • Motor output: effector (to produce a motor response) • Mental activity. Consciousness, thinking, memory, emotion Anatomical Organization of the Nervous System • Central nervous system (CNS) • the brain • the spinal cord • Peripheral nervous system (PNS) • Nerves that connect the CNS and other locations of the body (cranial and spinal nerves) • Neurons propagate APs towards and away from the CNS • Ganglions (group of neuronal somas) The CNS can be divided into five major areas: (1) telencephalon, (2) cerebellum, (3) diencephalon, (4) brainstem and (5) spinal cord. Each of these areas has symmetric right and left sides. The BRAIN consists of many parts that function as an integrated whole. The major parts of the brain are the medulla, pons, and midbrain (collectively called the brainstem), the cerebellum, the hypothalamus, the thalamus, basal ganglia and the cerebrum Page 2 of 6 Cerebral Cortex (Cerebrum) Largest portion of the brain , 4 main lobes (frontal, parietal, temporal and occipital) . The surface of the cortex is highly convoluted and is s ub- divided into fissures (deep grooves), gyri (elevated folds) and sulci (shallow grooves between folds). The folds massively increase the surface area of the cortex. Some Functional Areas of Cerebral Cortex • Motor areas: initiate action potential for skeletal muscle contraction (voluntary movement) (pre -central gyrus of the frontal lobe) • Sensory areas: perceive sensory information from the skin, muscles and joints (post-central gyrus of parietal lobe) • Integrative areas: areas function in learning, motivation, memory • Areas for language and speech Lateralization of the Cerebral Cortex. Fig. 1: Cerebral Cortex The cortex is divided anatomically into right and left hemispheres, connected in the middle by the corpus callosum. Right Side controls left side of the body & vice-versa Left Hemisphere Functions (dominant) Language, analytical and rational thinking reasoning, mathematical calculations Right Hemisphere Functions Processing music, drawing, assembling puzzles, spatial navigation Diencephalon: This brain region consists of the thalamus, the subthalamus, and the hypothalamus, each with a very different function. Thalamus • Major relaying center for both sensory (afferent) and motor (efferent) information as it passes between the brain and the PNS. • Divided into several sub-nuclei that have reciprocal connections with the cortex Fig. 2: Diencephalon • Can be divided into three functional relay groups: SPECIFIC, ASSOCIATION AND DIFFUSE NUCLEI Page 3 of 6 Hypothalamus Group of nuclei forms the floor and lower walls of the third ventricle , concerned with homeostasis and control of different body systems. Functions include the following: Control of the autonomic nervous system , Control of emotional responses , Regulation of body temperature, Regulation of hunger and thirst sensations , Control of behavior , Regulation of sleep - wake cycles, Control of the endocrine system, Formation of memory The Limbic System • Location: Medial aspect of cerebral hemispheres • Composed of: – Septal nuclei, cingulate gyrus, and hippocampal formation, Part of the amygdala – concerned with; control of emotion, regulation of autonomic function, motivation, memory, feeding, sexual behavior. Basal ganglia The basal ganglia are a group of large subcortical nuclei found in the forebrain. They are located above and anterior to the thalamus . The basal ganglia are concerned with the initiation and maintenance of actions and are involved in decision-making about what the body is going to do next. The Cerebellum Little brain This brain region lies immediately dorsal to the brainstem. Has an important role in coordination of voluntary movements. Functionally, the cerebellum can be divided into three parts , the vestibulocerebellum (also called the archicerebellum) is the oldest of these three parts, followed by the spinocerebellum (also called the paleocerebellum) and then by the cerebro - cerebellum (also called the neocerebellum). Fig. 3: Cerebellum Page 4 of 6 Brainstem These relay information to and from the periphery to higher centres such as the cortex and cerebellum. The brainstem also receives direct input from the cranial nerves. It Comprised of midbrain, pons and the medulla oblongata. MIDBRAIN • The midbrain is short • Cranial nerve III,IV emerge from mid brain • Has a role in wakefulness and sleep • Concerned with righting reflexes. • The dorsal surface of the mid - brain is called the tectum and has two paired swellings, the inferior and superior colliculi, which are involved in auditory and visual reflexes. PONS • Located between the midbrain and medulla oblongata • Contains the nuclei of cranial nerves V, VI, and VII,VIII • There are two respiratory center that work with those in the medulla to produce a normal breathing rhythm • The pons is sharply demarcated both rostrally and caudally from the other parts of the brainstem MEDULLA OBLONGATA • On the ventral surface of the medulla are the pyramids that contain descending motor fibres from the cerebral cortex • Control involuntary activity as breathing, heart rate • The lower four cranial nerves nuclei emerge from the medulla Reticular Formation Large masses of neurons scattered within the brain stem. Concerned with adjustment of reflex es, contains many areas for regulation of heart rate, blood pressure. Modify pain through raphe nucleus which secrets serotonin and has a role in Regulation of sleep Spinal Cord • The spinal cord is attached to the brain and extends to the lumbar region of th e vertebral column • The adult spinal cord is only about (46cm) long and extends from the foramen magnum to the level of the L2 vertebra. • The spinal cord receives input from the periphery, relays it to the brain and sends response signals back to the periphery. • The spinal cord consists of grey matter and white matter, like the brain (except that in the spinal cord the white matter is on the outside) • Functions include: – integration reflex action Page 5 of 6 • Withdrawal reflex in response to pain • Walking movements. • Reflexes that stiffen the legs to support the body against gravity. • Reflexes that control local blood vessels, gastrointestinal movements. • Dorsal (posterior) horns (left and right) – sensory neurons enter the cord on the dorsal aspect where they synapse with interneurons or motor neurons – extend into dorsal roots and ganglia • Ventral (anterior) horns (left and right) – motor neurons exits the cord on the ventral aspect where they control effectors (muscle or glands) • Dorsal and ventral roots merge together to form spinal nerves • The spinal cord narrows at its caudal end to form the CONUS MEDULLARIS, and beyond this point the spinal canal is filled only with spinal

section: PBL 2 - Theme 3: Motor Control: Cerebrum, Brain Stem & Spinal Cord
name: Notes L18
text: Page 1 of 4 18 Organization and function of motor and association cortex ILOs By the end of this lecture, students will be able to: 1. Identify Brodmann areas for motor control. 2. Understand the function of each area in motor function 3. Recognize the different manifestation of lesions in cortical areas. 4. Compare between motor cortex and premotor cortex in motor control 5. Describe the functions of the prefrontal association cortex. 6. Identify thalamo-cortical projection Introduction Most “voluntary” movements initiated by the cerebral cortex are achieved when the cortex activates “patterns” of function stored in lower brain areas —the cord, brain stem, basal ganglia, and cerebellum. These lower centers, in turn, send specific control signals to the muscles. For a few types of movements, however, the cortex has almost a direct pathway to the anterior motor neurons of the cord, bypassing some motor centers on the way. This is especially true for control of the fine dexterous movements of the fingers and hands. The motor cortex consists of three reciprocally interconnected regions: 1. Primary motor cortex (MI), 2. Secondary association areas: a) Premotor (PM) area b) Supplementary motor area (medial premotor,or SMA) Primary motor cortex (MI) Site : The MI cortex, located in the precentral gyrus.(figure 1) Representation and characters: Has a topographical representation of the body surface, with the head, lips and hands represented laterally, and the legs and feet medially similar to the primary somatosensory cortex. The precentral gyrus of the left hemisphere sends motor output to the right side of the body, In this region, the more complex the movement of a particular body part, the more motor cortex is devoted to it. Thus, the lips, Figure 1:Functional areas of the motor cortex viewed from the lateral and medial surfaces Page 2 of 4 tongue, and hands, which we use to explore and communicate, have distorted representations due to the variety and complexity of the movements.(Figure 2) Function: Involved in the voluntary control of movements, by carrying the motor command to the LMNs. Has main role in control of fine precise movements which are executed by distal parts of the body Figure 2: Homuncular map of the body surface in MI The PM area Function: is involved in planning movements that involve external sensory cues. Activity in PM cells is temporally linked to movements. Here, cells are active when there is an intention to make a movement rather than during the movement. The PM area is about six times larger than MI, and receives a rich sensory input (tactile and visuospatial) from the parietal lobe. It deals with learned motor activities of a complex and sequential nature, by coordinating contractions of specific groups of muscles; for example, it is active during writing. Has a role in control of gross movements(figure2, 3A). The SMA Function: The SMA is also involved in planning movements, but is concerned with internally generated commands or cues. Its cells are active while an intended movement is being thought about. The SMA is crucial for the performance of complicated tasks involving both sides of the body, e.g. two-handed tasks such as typing. (figure 2,3B) This area contains motor maps for postures, and its efferents generally terminate bilaterally and innervate the truncal musculature for postural stabilization. Lesion: Damage to the PM or SMA results in apraxia. Apraxia is the loss of ability to carry out familiar learned purposeful movements, in the absence of sensory or motor impairment. Patients with apraxia have normal reflexes and tone, and no muscle weakness, but they have difficulty in performing complex motor tas ks such as brushing their hair, cleaning their teeth, or dressing themselves. The frontal eye field region The frontal eye field region of the motor cortex controls voluntary scanning movements of the eyes, such as during reading. This region has connec tions with the superior colliculus and the gaze centres located in the paramedian pontine reticular formation. (figure 3A) Function: Stimulation of this region causes conjugate deviation of the eyes towards the opposite side to the stimulation. Lesion: Damage to this region induces a transient conjugate deviation of the eyes towards the side of the lesion. Page 3 of 4 The prefrontal cortex The prefrontal cortex relays input from the limbic system to the motor cortex, about the desired goal of the movement. The MI cortex is involved in a motor loop with the cerebellum, while the SMA forms a loop with the basal ganglia. These loops allow the cortex to recruit and coordinate specific motor programs. (figure 3) Prefrontal association area receives, analyses, and integrates signals from both motor and sensory cortex as well as from subcortical structures. It is divided into the dorsolateral prefrontal cortex (Executive functions) and the ventromedial prefrontal cortex (orbitofrontal cortex) (Controlling behavior). Functions of dorsolateral prefrontal cortex 1. Shares with the motor cortex in planning complex pattern of voluntary movements. 2. Provides the ability to concentrate and promotes attention. 3. Mediates working memory. 4. Controls the ability to follow and obey rules. 5. Controls creativity and learning. Functions of ventromedial prefrontal cortex 1. Plays a role in motivation. 2. Regulates emotions and impulsive behavior. 3. Involved in social decision-making. All the association areas feed into the higher-order motor areas, which then project to the primary motor cortex, which ultimately exerts control over the motor neurons.(Figure 4) Figure 4: interconnections of primary, higher-order and association cortices used in processing a sensory stimulus to produce a behavioral response. Figure 3:Functional anatomy of specific cortical areas on the lateral surface(A)and medial surface (B) of the brain. A B Page 4 of 4 Thalamocortical projection The thalamus is a sensory relay station and is important in motor control. Deep within the brain is the diencephalon, a midline structure that forms the walls of the third ventricular cavity, one of the spaces through which CSF flows. The diencephalon consists of two main parts, the thalamus and the hypothalamus. The thalamus serves as a “relay station” for preliminary processing of sensory input. All sensory input synapses in the thalamus on its way to the cortex. The thalamus screens out insignificant signals and routes the important sensory impulses to appropriate areas of the somatosensory cortex, as well as to other regions of the brain. The thalamus also plays an important role in motor control. It receives input from different motor region, and project to a specific cortical region Thalamus is also involved in arousal, regulating the level of cortical excitability, and controlling of behaviour.

text: Page 1 of 4 21 Cortical areas of speech ILOs By the end of this lecture, students will be able to: 1. Identify cortical areas for speech control. 2. 2. Explain the role of each area in speech Processing &Comprehension 3. Define aphasia. 4. Categorize main types of aphasia Introduction The comprehension and production of language are complex tasks involving many areas of the brain in both hemispheres. Language is a complex form of communication in which WRITTEN or SPOKEN words symbolize objects and convey ideas. The areas of the brain dedicated to language are highly lateralized. In almost all right-handed people (~98%) and most left-handed people (~70%), the main centers for language are in the left hemisphere. The location of the language areas defines the dominant hemisphere: handedness may or may not be correlated with language. The right (or non -dominant) hemisphere is thought to contribute more t o the melody ( prosody), rhythm, emotional expression, and accent in language. The primary brain areas concerned with language are located along and near the Sylvian fissure (lateral cerebral sulcus) of the categorical hemisphere. Areas involved in language processing I. Non-language areas 1. Auditory areas (Concerned with spoken speech) • Primary auditory area 41, 42 • Auditory association area 22 2. Visual areas (Concerned with written speech) • Primary visual area 17 • Visual association area (18,19) II. Language areas 1. Wernicke's area Location: Large area in “the posterior part of auditory association area” (area 22 on the left hemisphere) in the posterior part of the superior temporal gyrus. After the interpretation of auditory or visually presented words, the word meanings are fed into Wernicke's area. Functions: 1. Understanding auditory and visual information (both spoken and written language). 2. Word recognition 3. Understanding thoughts, 2. Broca’s area (area 44,45) Area 44: Located in posterior part of the inferior left frontal gyrus. It is part of a network used in combining sounds into words and words into sentences for language production. Area 45 The information in this area is stored, and at needed times projected to the motor cortex to initiate the needed movements of muscles. Located in anterior part of the left inferior frontal gyrus. Page 2 of 4 5. Arrange words into coherent sentences. 6. Analysis of sounds (associating sound with concept) for comprehension of words both spoken and written. 7. involved in transforming the visual impression of letters (graphemes) into mental representations of speech sounds (phonemes). ▪ It processes the grammatical structure of sentences and the proper use of grammatical vocabulary and verbs. ▪ It is not directly involved in meaning. 3. Inferior parietal lobule (area 39 and area 40) Angular gyrus (area 39) Location: In the posterior parietal lobule (posterior to Wernick’s area and anterior to the visual occipital areas (areas 17, 18, and 19). Functions: • Translation of written words into sounds, • important in writing words that are not phonetic e.g circuit. Supramarginal gyrus (area 40) Location: Arches over the end of the Lateral sulcus adjacent to the inferior portion of the somatosensory cortex. Functions: • Involved in correlation of sounds and letters. • Associating letters with sounds.Acts as short term auditory memory, to remember how to sound words . Arcuate fasciculus: The arcuate fasciculus connects these two areas of the cortex . Having such a connection is logical, because we want to produce words (Broca) that make sense (Wernicke) and, similarly, understand language input and respond. The arcuate fasciculus is thought to be a connection that monitors speech and facilitates the repetition of words . Figure 1:Cortical pathways for understanding language Page 3 of 4 Basic circuit for understanding spoken language(Figure 1) 1. When a person hears a sentence, this is transmitted via the auditory apparatus to the primary auditory cortex in the temporal lobe. 2. This then connects to Wernicke’s area (in the temporal lobe), which decodes the language into meaning. 3. If the sentence is to be repeated, or replied to, the information must be transmitted forwards to Broca’s area (expressive speech) in the frontal lobe (via the arcuate fasciculus). 4. Broca’s area then produces speech via the motor programs of the motor cortex, which activate the tongue and laryngeal muscles. Basic circuit for understanding written speech (Figure 1) 1. Visual input is transmitted to the visual cortex (areas 17–19) in the occipital lobe. 2. Input from the visual association area is sent to the left angular gyrus, where the objects are recognized and named. 3. Input then goes to Wernicke’s area, where words are assembled into sentences, and the appropriate messages are sent via the arcuate and superior longitudinal fasciculi to Broca’s area. 4. Broca’s area activates motor programs in the primary motor cortex that elicit speech via appropriate brainstem centers and muscles of the tongue and larynx. Effects of damage to specific cortical areas When the language areas are damaged, the resultant clinical syndrome is called aphasia(without speech). Aphasias are abnormalities of language functions that are not due to defects of vision or hearing or to motor paralysis. They are caused by lesions in the categorical hemisphere • Receptive aphasia: Wernicke’s aphasia: Damage to the Wernicke area leads to receptive or sensory aphasia. Patients with Wernicke’s aphasia have no difficulty with syntax, grammar, or the structure of words, and their speech appears to be fluent and to reta in melody and rhythm , they may talk excessively . Because these patients cannot understand the language they are hearing (or seeing), the content of their speech is markedly full of mistakes . They might use the wrong word to describe something, create new word. • Broca aphasia: Damage to Broca area leads to expressive or productive or (non-fluent aphasia): in this type of aphasia, Speech is slow, and words are hard to come by. Patients with severe damage to this area are limited to two or three words with which to express the whole range of meaning and emotio n. Has difficulty with syntax and grammar; word/phrase repetition. Speech is, ungrammatical but meaningful, speech understanding may be intact (grammar conveys meaning). • Conduction aphasia: Damage to the arcuate fasciculus leads to conduction aphasia, in which the connection between Wernicke ’s (language comprehension) and Broca (language production) areas is lost. The hallmark of conduction aphasia is the inability to repeat words. Comprehension and the expression of language are intact , but patients cannot transfer the understood word to Broca area to be expressed. When asked to repeat the word “milk,” for example, they might say, “the white stuff.” • Alexia (inability to read) damage to Angular gyrus: with agraphia (inability to write), but the patient can comprehend speech and speak normally. Page 4 of 4 When a lesion damages the angular gyrus in the categorical hemisphere without affecting Wernicke ’s or Broca ’s areas, there is no difficulty with speech or the understanding of auditory information; instead there is trouble understanding written language or pictures, because visual information is not processed and transmitted to Wernicke’s area. The result is a condition called anomic aphasia.

text: 1 What are Neuroglia? They are the supporting cells of the nervous system . They make up about half the brain mass. These cells have a number of functions, which include structural and metabolic support, immune functions and electrical insulation of axons. Classification of neuroglia I. Neuroglia in CNS (Fig 1) Include astrocytes, oligodendrocytes, microglia (microglial cells), and ependymal cells. II. Neuroglia in PNS Schwann cells. Neuroglia in CNS 1- Astrocytes In the CNS, the most common glial cells are astrocytes. They can be distinguished from neurons by the presence of a specific protein, glial fibrillary acidic protein. Origin: The precursors of astrocytes are radial glial cells which, during early development, span the cerebral cortex, forming scaffolding for the migration of new nerve cells to their destinations. Structure: They are l arge, stellate cells. They have multiple radiating processes that surro und neurons, capillaries and the ependymal cells lining the ventricles. Types: (Fig 2) a. Protoplasmic astrocytes they are found mainly in the grey matter and have many short branching processes. b. Fibrous astrocytes they present mainly in the white matter of the CNS and have long unbranched processes. Functions: 1. Share in formation of blood–brain barrier (BBB) The BBB is a b arrier that prevents blood borne compounds from entering the brain, unless specifically transported. It is formed from endothelial cells, which make up the continuous capillaries of the brain. These are surrounded by a layer of basement membrane, which itself is covered by a layer consisting of the endfeet of astrocytes (Fig. 3). These do not touch the L27 Neuroglia and myelination ILOs 1. Classify types of neuroglia according to their sites. 2. Distinguish the structural adaptation of each to its specific function. 3. Specify components of the blood brain barrier. 4. Differentiate between process of myelination in CNS & PNS. Figure (1): Neuroglia in CNS Figure (2): Types of astrocytes CNS 2 endothelial cells but are important in producing factors that induce specific characteristics in the endothelial cells. These characteristics include high transendothelial resistance which is due to the length and complexity of th e tight junctions between the endothelial cells. There are also very few pores, either small or large, that cross the endothelium, and transcytosis is limited. 2. Regulation of K+ levels in extracellular medium around neurons 3. Storage of glycogen that can be supplied to neurons, in the form of lactate, when required 4. Controlling distribution of neurotransmitters released by neurons by restricting diffusion and by transporting neurotransmitters into the astrocyte, where they can be metabolized or recycled. 5. Astrocytes have recently been shown to play a potentially more active role in signaling. Astrocytes are linked to each other by gap junctions, through which small molecules can diffuse. When stimulated by neurotransmitters, they show changes in intracellular le vels of Ca2+ ions, which spread between astrocytes as waves. Gap junctions also occur between astrocytes and neurons, and could modulate the behavior of the neurons by allowing the passage of Ca2+ between them. 2- Oligodendrocytes:  One of the neuroglia of the CNS  Large cells with few processes  They are responsible for the process of MYELINATION in the CNS ( a single oligodendrocyte may wrap several axons with segments of myelin Fig 1) 3- Microglaia: Microglial cells are small cells of the CNS with long spiny processes. During development, they release growth factors and also act as macrophages, removing debris produced by the programmed cell death which occurs on a large scale at this time. In the adult, they are normally relatively inactive. However, in the presence of almost any type of injury or insult to the nervous system, they revert to the role of phagocytotic macrophages, when they are said to be reactive. 4- Ependymal cells: (Fig 4) • simple epithelial cells with numerou s microvilli and one or two cilia on their apical surface • Their basolateral surface is in contact with astrocytic processes line the ventricles are not connected by tight junctions Figure (4): Ependymal cells 3 Neuroglia in PNS Schwann cells One of the neuroglia of the PNS They are flattened cells whose cytoplasm contains a flattened nucleus Functions: 1. Important for the process of MYELINATION (Fig 5) (myelinate a single axon, and the cell body is closely apposed to the myelin sheath). Schwann cell envelops the axon, rotates several times wrapping its plasma membrane around it forming myelin sheath. The Schwann cell cytoplasm is forced from between the membranes forming together with the nucleus the neurilemmal sheath. Interruptions occur in the myelin sheath at regular inter vals along the length of the axon, exposing the axon; these interruptions are called nodes of Ranvier . Each node indicates an interface between the myelin sheaths of two different Schwann cells located along the axon. The outer portion of Schwann cel ls is covered by a basal lamina that dips into the nodes of Ranvier, covering the overlapped areas of the myelin sheath lamellae of adjacent Schwann cells. Note; Not all axons are myelinated, and this can be seen in the brain and spinal cord as grey matter, which consists of cell bodies and unmyelinated axons, as opposed to white matter, which consists of axons, most of which are myelinated. Dendrites are never myelinated. 2. Role in regeneration of peripheral axons following injury. In order for a peripheral nerve to regrow, the tip of the axon must make contact with a Schwann cell. This stimulates mitosis in the Schwann cell, which then extends processes towards the growth cone of the axon. The axon regrows at between 2 and 5 mm per day along the Schwann cells, which remyelinate the new axon. Figure (5): Schwann cells 4 Note; Damaged neurones in the CNS do not seem to regenerate successfully, because CNS glial cells release factors that specifically inhibit axon growth.

text: Page 1 of 5 L 15 ANATOMY OF CEREBRUM ILOs By the end of this session, the student should be able to: 1. Relate the different parts of cerebrum to its position inside the cranial cavity. 2. Describe general features of the cerebral hemisphere: surfaces, borders and lobes. 3. Correlate the different sulci and gyri of the cerebral cortex to their function. 4. Appraise the different cortical areas relevant to their clinical application Cortical lobes: • There are four lobes of the brain: the occipital (vision), temporal (hearing), parietal (sensory) and frontal (motor) lobes. • There is one other lobe that can’t be seen from the outside of the brain: the limbic lobe. • The corpus callosum connects the two cortical hemispheres. Lobes of the cerebrum General features: • Each cerebral hemispheres has three surfaces, and three poles. • The surfaces are superolateral, medial and inferior. • The poles are frontal, occipital and temporal. Page 2 of 5 Different surfaces of cerebrum Surface features: sulci and gyri: The surface of the cortex is highly convoluted and is subdivided into fissures (deep grooves), gyri (elevated folds; and sulci ; shallow grooves between folds). • The longitudinal fissure separates the two cortical hemispheres. • The lateral fissure (of Sylvius) separates the temporal lobe from the parietal and frontal lobes. • The central sulcus separates the frontal and parietal lobes. • The parieto-occipital sulcus separates parietal and occipital lobes. Cerebral lobes and main sulci separating them Page 3 of 5 • On the lateral surface of the hemispheres, the boundaries between parietal, occipital and temporal lobes are established by continuing the line of the parieto -occipital sulcus downwards and the line of the posterior ramus of lateral fissure backwards to meet this line. Superolateral surface of the cerebrum: Central sulcus • The central sulcus marks the position of two important functional areas: primary somatosensory cortex posterior in the postcentral gyrus and primary motor cortex anterior to this sulcus in the precentral gyrus. Both areas control the opposite side of the body. • It lies between two parallel sulci (pre- and post- central sulci). Lateral Sulcus • The stem appear s on the inferior surface and runs to the lateral surface where it gives; anterior horizontal, anterior ascending (or superior) and posterior rami. • It is a deep sulcus, where the cortex invaginates the lateral surface to give deep gray matter called the “insula” which is hidden inside. • Motor speech centre (Broca’s area) lies around the ascending and horizontal rami of lateral sulcus. Central and lateral sulcus on inferior and superolateral surfaces of cerebrum Broca’s area between ascending and horizontal rami of lateral sulcus Page 4 of 5 Medial surface of the cerebrum: Cingulate gyrus: • The cingulate sulcus follows the curvature of the corpus callosum, extending through both the frontal and parietal lobes. • Below this sulcus is the cingulate gyrus (functionally associated with the limbic lobe). • This cingulate sulcus terminates by passing upwards to form a sulcus that continues onto the lateral surface as the postcentral sulcus . • The central sulcus is the sulcus anterior to this sulcus (on the lateral surface). • The gyrus in between these two sulci is the postcentral gyrus, which contains the primary somatosensory cortex which control the opposite side of the body. Para central lobule: • Anterior to the point where the cingulate sulcus crosses (to the lateral surface of the brain) is the paracentral lob ule, which contains the lower limb, perineum primary motor and somatosensory cortical function regions controlling the opposite side of the body. Medial surface of cerebrum Calcarine sulcus: The calcarine sulcus is located at the caudal end of the medial surfa ce of the brain. It separates the occipital lobe into two parts associated with vision: 1) lingual gyrus (inferior part) 2) cuneus (superior part) which lies posterior to parieto-occipital sulcus. Medial frontal gyrus: Medial frontal gyrus is a part of the frontal lobe that lies in front of the cingulate sulcus. Functionally, it is considered as part of the prefrontal area responsible for behavior, attention and concentration. Inferior surface of the cerebrum: The inferior surface of the cerebral hemisphere is divided by the stem of lateral sulcus into an orbital part and a tentorial part. • On the inferior surface of the temporal lobe, the most medial gyrus is the parahippocampal gyrus, which expands at its anterior end to form the uncus. They are medial to collateral sulcus. • These are concerned with the olfactory (smell) system and memory. Page 5 of 5 Inferior surface of cerebrum • In the orbitofrontal cortex (the part that sits above the orbit in the skull) is located the olfactory gyrus. These structures form part of the limbic system, which is involved in emotional processing and perception ادراك. Clinical notes: • Lesions of the primary motor cortex in one hemisphere result in paralysis of the contralateral extremities. • Lesions involving the calcarine sulcus result in a loss of vision in the opposite visual field.

text: Page 1 of 6 22 Brain Stem Anatomy ILOs At the end of this session, the student will be able to: 1. Correlate the external features of the brain stem to its internal structure. 2. Classify cranial nerves according to their function. 3. Differentiate between the deep origin of the different cranial nerves (nuclei), and their functional components. 4. Appraise the clinical importance of the different functional components of nuclei. Brain stem: It is a part of CNS present in posterior cranial fossa. Parts: Mid brain Pons Medulla Brain stem is connected to cerebellum by three peduncles. Functions of the Brain Stem: 1. Pathway of tracts between cerebral cortex & spinal cord (ascending and descending tracts). 2. Site of origin of nuclei of cranial nerves (from 3rd to 12th). 3. Site of emergence of cranial nerves (from 3rd to 12th). 4. Contains reticular formation: control of level of consciousness, regulation of cardiovascular & respiratory systems. Cranial nerves: 1- Olfactory nerve 2- Optic nerve 3- Oculomotor nerve 4- Trochlear nerve 5- Trigeminal nerve 6- Abducens nerve 7- Facial nerve 8- Vestibulocochlear nerve 9- Glossopharyngeal nerve 10- Vagus nerve 11- Accessory nerve 12- Hypoglossal nerve Page 2 of 6 1- External Features of the Medulla Oblongata: A- ventral surface: - Anteromedian fissure: • Continuation of Anteromedian fissure of spinal cord. • Divides the medulla into 2 halves. • Its lower part is marked by decussation of pyramidal (corticospinal) Fibers. - Pyramid: • An elevation, lies on either (lateral) side of Anteromedian fissure • Produced by corticospinal tract (pyramidal tract) -Olive: • An elevation, lies lateral to the pyramid. • Produced by inferior olivary nucleus. Cranial nerves related to medulla (9-12): The groove between the pyramid and the olive is called anterolateral sulcus and it gives exit for the rootlets of the hypoglossal nerve. The groove lateral to the olive is called posterolateral sulcus. It gives exit to the rootlets of the glossopharyngeal, vagus and cranial accessory nerves. B- Dorsal surface: It is divided into: open medulla (cranial) closed medulla (caudal). The open and closed medulla, due to the emergence of the central canal from the spinal cord opening into the fourth ventricle. The point at which this occurs is called the Obex. Dorsal surface (closed medulla): form lower part of floor of fourth ventricle. Posterior median sulcus. The longitudinal elevation lateral to the posteromedian sulcus is called gracile fasciculus as it overlies the gracile tract. The upper end of the gracile fasciculus expands to form the gracile tubercle which overlies the gracile nucleus. Elevation lateral to the gracile fasciculus is called cuneate fasciculus as it overlies the cuneate tract. The upper end of the cuneate fasciculus expands to form the cuneate tubercle which overlies the cuneate nucleus. The ridge lateral to the cuneate tubercle is the inferior cerebellar peduncle. Page 3 of 6 2 - External Features of the Pons: A. The ventral surface: It is convex from side to side Laterally it is continuous with the middle cerebellar peduncle. A median groove called basilar groove as it lodges the basilar artery. Cranial nerves related to pons (5-8): Trigeminal nerve: emerges from the middle part of the pons at its junction with the middle cerebellar peduncle. Abducent nerve: emerges at the lower border of the pons, between it and the pyramid. The facial and vestibulo-cochlear N: emerge at the lower border of the pons, between it and the medulla. Cranial nerves VII and VIII exit at the cerebellopontomedullary angle. B. The dorsal surface: Separated from open medulla by an imaginary line Form the cranial 2/3rd of the floor of the 4th ventricle. 2- External Features of the midbrain The midbrain presents a narrow lumen called cerebral aqueduct (aqueduct of sylvius). A coronal plane passing through the cerebral aqueduct divides the midbrain into two divisions: A. Cerebral Peduncle B. Tectum The ventral surface presents the following features: Cerebral peduncles: formed of a large column of fibers (crus cerebri) on either side. interpeduncular fossa: depression between the 2 Cerebral peduncles. Occulomotor (3rd): emerge from medial aspect of Cerebral peduncles. A. The dorsal surface presents the following features: 4 elevations/colliculi: • Two superior colliculi: concerned with visual reflexes. • Two inferior colliculi: forms part of auditory reflexes. Page 4 of 6 Each colliculus gives rise to a brachium from its lateral side: • The superior brachium connects the superior colliculus with the lateral geniculate body. • The inferior brachium connects the inferior colliculus with the medial geniculate body. Dorsal surface marked by Trochlear (4th) Nerve: The only cranial nerve emerging from dorsal surface of brain stem. blood supply of brain stem: the entire brainstem derives its blood supply from the posterior - vertebral-basilar Medulla: two vertebral arteries Pons: the basilar artery. Midbrain: posterior cerebral arteries. Branches from the three main arteries, the vertebral, basilar and posterior cerebral, supply both the dorsal and ventral surfaces of the brainstem. Clinical correlation: 1- Brainstem death: In brainstem death, spontaneous breath ceases and there is a loss of reflexes. Cardiovascular function can be artificially maintained for a short while but will eventually deteriorate due to loss of function of the brainstem regulatory centers in the medulla. 2- Compression injuries of the brainstem by cerebellar or cortical herniation are often fatal. Functional classification and deep origin of the cranial nerves Page 5 of 6 Cranial nerve nuclei of Occulomotor nerve: Oculomotor nucleus (GSE) Edinger-wesphal nucleus (GVE) Cranial nerve nuclei of Trochlear nerve: Trochlear nucleus (GSE). Cranial nerve nuclei of Abducent nerve: Abducent nucleus (GSE) Cranial nerve nuclei of Facial nerve Motor facial nucleus (SVE) Superior salivary nucleus (GVE) Solitary nucleus (GVA, SVA) Page 6 of 6 Cranial nerve nuclei of Vestibulocochlear nerve Cochlear nucleus (SSA) Vestibular nucleus (SSA) Cranial nerve nuclei of Glossopharyngeal nerve Nucleus ambiguus (SVE)+10+11 Inferior salivary nucleus (GVE) Solitary nucleus (GVA, SVA) Cranial nerve nuclei of Vagus nerve Nucleus ambiguus (SVE) Dorsal vagal nucleus (GVE) Solitary nucleus (GVA, SVA) Cranial part: from nucleus ambiguus (SVE) Spinal part: from upper 5 or 6 spinal segments (GSE) Cranial nerve nuclei of Hypoglossal nerve: hypoglossal nucleus (GSE)

text: Anatomy of the Posterior triangle of the neck Dr. Basma Mady Faculty of Medicine; Alexandria University 1 Dear students 2 & Transfer Goal Appraise the boundaries and contents of the posterior triangle and correlate them with different clinical conditions related to them. 3 Students’ learning outcomes At the end of this session, the students will be able to: Appraise the importance of sternocleidomastoid muscle for identifying the different structures of the neck. Differentiate between the different layers of the fascia of the neck. Differentiate between different boundaries of the posterior triangle. Appraise the structures forming the roof and the floor of the posterior triangle. Correlate the boundaries & contents of the posterior triangle to their clinical importance. 4 Sternocleidomastoid (Sternomastoid) muscle The sternocleidomastoid muscle divides the neck into anterior and posterior triangles. When it contracts, it appears as an oblique band crossing the side of the neck from the sternoclavicular joint to the mastoid process of the skull. 5 Sternomastoid Origin  Anterior surface of the sternum and medial one- third of the clavicle . Insertion  Lateral surface of the mastoid process of the skull. Nerve supply  Spinal Accessory nerve [XI] 6 Sternomastoid 7 8 Action of Sternomastoid Individually it will: Tilt the head toward the shoulder on the same side (i.e., lateral flexion of the neck) Rotating head to turn the face superiorly to the opposite side . 9 Action of Sternomastoid Both muscles  draw the head forward (i.e., anterior flexion of the neck). 10 Clinical correlates Clinical correlates Torticollis it means spasm of the sternomastoid muscle, which is a painful condition and leads to abnormal head posture. 12 13 Clinical correlates The carotid pulse It is palpated along the anterior border of the sternomastoid muscle. 14 15 Fascia of the neck 16 Fascia of the neck Platysma Muscle It is a broad thin superficial muscle which lies anteriorly in the neck in the superficial cervical fascia. Innervation  facial nerve 17 18 19 20 Deep cervical fascia The deep cervical fascia is organized into several layers: 21 22 Deep cervical fascia 23 Deep cervical fascia Investing Layer  surrounds all the structures in the neck. It divides where it meets the trapezius and sternomastoid muscles and surrounds them. 24 Deep cervical fascia Pretracheal Layer  It is situated in the anterior neck. Thyroid gland and infrahyoid muscles are enclosed by the pretracheal fascia. The thyroid gland and all thyroid swellings move with the swallowing/deglutition. 25 Deep cervical fascia Prevertebral Layer  surrounds the vertebral column and its associated muscles. Carotid Sheath  encloses the neurovascular bundle of the neck. 26 The posterior triangle of the neck A: sternomastoid B: Trapezius C : posterior triangle D: anterior triangle Boundaries: Anteriorly  sternomastoid muscle. Posteriorly  trapezius muscle. Apex  the occipital bone at attachments of 2 muscles. Base  the middle 1/3 of the clavicle. 27 Roof Skin, Superficial cervical fascia, The investing layer of the cervical fascia  surrounds the sternocleidomastoid and the trapezius muscles as it passes through the region. 28 Floor It is formed by a muscular floor covered by a fascia : Prevertebral layer of the cervical fascia. Muscles from superior to inferior: Splenius capitis Levator scapulae Scalene muscles 29 30 31 Contents: Muscle  inferior belly of omohyoid. Nerves: Spinal accessory nerve, Posterior branches from the cervical plexus of nerves, Trunks of the brachial plexus. Vessels: External jugular vein, Subclavian artery (3 rd part) and some branches, Subclavian vein 32 33 34 Clinical correlates C linical correlates Injury to the spinal accessory nerve due to trauma in the posterior triangle,  paralysis of the trapezius muscle. 36 37 Summary or take-home message The sternocleidomastoid muscle divides the neck into anterior and posterior triangles. Mastering the anatomy of the fascia of the neck is important to understand swallowing mechanism in addition to different surgical appreoaches . The posterior triangle of the neck is an important area containing many vital structures. 38 Drake RL, Vogl AL, Mitchell AWM. Gray’s anatomy for students. 4 th ed. Elsevier. 2020 : 1012-20. 39 Dear Student: Don’t forget to complete your KWL chart And reflect on your learning experience by writing down what do you learnt from the lecture (3 points at least) 40 41
