text: Page 1 of 5 L 28 White Matter& Internal Capsule ILOs By the end of this lecture, students will be able to 1. Differentiate between the different types of white matter of the brain. 2. Relate the different parts of corpus callosum to their location. 3. Appraise the importance of internal capsule relative to its contents. 4. Correlate the anatomy of corpus callosum & internal capsule to relevant clinical conditions. The white matter of the brain is divided into: Association fibers; Commissural fibers; Projection fibers I.Association fibers: (Fig. 1) Connect 2 areas on the same side of the cerebral hemisphere, includes: A. Short association fibers: connecting adjacent gyri together. B. Long association fibers II. Commissural fibers: (Fig. 2) These connect between 2 same areas on both sides of the cerebral hemispheres. The brain houses two minds, not one, but they only orchestrate into a single personality if the two cerebral hemispheres communicate& exchange information, as by the commissural fibers. Thus, consciousness is controlled by both hemispheres, and there is a crossing over of functions so that one never normally experiences a dissociation of information. Fig. 1: Association fibers Fig. 2: Commissural fibers Page 2 of 5 Types of Commissural Fibers: 1. Anterior commissure: It connects olfactory structures of both sides (olfactory bulb; anterior perforated substance). (Fig. 3) 2. Posterior commissure: it is present just above the upper end of the cerebral aqueduct. It connects visual structures on both sides. (Fig. 3) 3. Hippocampal commissure (or commissure of the fornix): these fibers connect the hippocampus with its fellow of the opposite side. (Fig. 4) 4. Corpus callosum: It is the greatest commissure. It is divided into: ❑ Rostrum, is the thin part of the anterior end of the corpus callosum, ❑ Genu, the curved anterior end of the corpus callosum, ❑ Body, arches posteriorly and ends as the splenium. ❑ Splenium. Parts of Corpus Callosum: (Fig. 5 A& B) • Rostrum: Connects between the orbital surface of the frontal lobes on both sides. • Genu: Connects the anterior part of the frontal lobes on both sides. The fibers of the genu radiate forwards towards the frontal poles forming the forceps minor. • Body: Connects between the posterior part of the frontal lobe and anterior part of the parietal lobe on both sides. • Splenium: Connects between the posterior part of the parietal lobe, temporal lobe and occipital lobe on both sides. These fibers pass either: • Lateral to the posterior horn of the lateral ventricle and are called tapetum. • Medial to the posterior horn of the lateral ventricle and are called forceps major. Fig. 3: Anterior & Posterior commissures Fig. 4: Hippocampal commissure Page 3 of 5 Split-brain’ syndrome: (Fig. 6) ‘Splitting’ the brain, by sectioning the corpus callosum, and thereby disconnecting the hemispheres, was used by surgeons to treat chronic intractable forms of epilepsy. To the casual observer, the split-brain patients appeared normal, and their seizures disappeared. However, psychological testing revealed that if the patient held up an object like a comb in the left hand, they could not say what it was. When it was transferred to the right hand, the patient had no trouble at all to identity it. The same happened with words. If a card with a printed word like ‘ring’ was visible only in the patient’s left visual field, they could not read it, yet vision in the left eye was fine. When the word was in the right field, the patient immediately recognized it. Fig 5; A: Parts of corpus callosum in sagittal section Fig 5; B: Parts of corpus callosum in horizontal section Fig.6: Split- brain’ syndrome Page 4 of 5 III. Projection fibers: These are fibers passing from or to the cerebral cortex; thus, they are subdivided into: A. Ascending fibers B. Descending fibers e.g. for the projection fibers is the Internal Capsule. (Fig. 7: A, B, C) INTERNAL CAPSULE: (Fig. 7: A) The internal capsule is composed of all the fibers, afferent and efferent, which go to, or come from, the cerebral cortex. It has anterior limb, genu, & posterior limb (Fig. 7: B) Fibers of the internal capsule: (Fig. 7: C) A. Anterior limb: 1. Frontopontine fibers. 2. Anterior thalamic radiation. B. Genu: Corticobulbar fibers. C. Posterior limb: Subdivided into: I. Thalamolentiform part: Lies between the lentiform nucleus and the thalamus; contains: 1. Parietopontine fibers. 2. Superior thalamic radiation. 3. Corticospinal tract. 4. Corticorubral. 5. Corticostriate. II. Retrolentifrom part: Extends caudally behind the lentiform nucleus; contains: 1. Occipitopontine fibers. 2. Posterior thalamic radiation including optic radiation. III. Sublentifrom part: Passing beneath the lentiform nucleus; contains: 1. Tempropontine fibers. 2. Inferior thalamic radiation including auditory radiation. Fig. 7: A Fig. 7: B Fig. 7: C Page 5 of 5 Blood supply of Internal Capsule: Both anterior and posterior limbs are supplied primarily by branches of the middle cerebral artery. In addition, each part of the internal capsule receives another arterial branch: • The anterior cerebral artery supplies the anteromedial parts of the anterior limb. • The genu receives direct branches from the internal carotid artery. • The ventral portion of the posterior limb and its entire retrolenticular part are supplied by branches of the anterior choroid artery. CLINICAL CORRELATION: Infarction of the internal capsule: (Fig. 8) Most frequently results from occlusion of the lenticulostriate branches of the middle cerebral artery and results in the following contralateral conditions: • Anesthesia • Hemiparesis (with the Babinski sign) • Lower facial weakness Fig. 8: Infarction of the internal capsule

section: PBL 2 - Theme 4: Motor Modulation -The Basal Ganglia
name: L29-Notes
text: 1 Basal ganglia A journey into the deep nuclei Learning objectives: ➢ Describe the organization of the basal ganglia and their connections with other central nervous system regions. ➢ Understand Circuits and neurotransmitters of basal ganglia ➢ Describe the main symptoms and diseases associated with dysfunction of the basal ganglia, and their pathophysiology. ➢ Describe the role of the basal ganglia in the motor regulation The basal ganglia: structure and organization The basal ganglia consist of five subcortical interconnected nuclei that are involved in the initiation and execution of movement. This system receives inputs from wide areas of the cerebral cortex and returns it, via the thalamus, to the cortex . They are : 1. The caudate nucleus 2. The putamen nucleus The caudate nucleus and the putamen are two nuclei that are interconnected and form the striatum. The striatum receives afferents from the neocortex, the thalamus and the substantia nigra. 3. The globus pallidus. The globus pallidus has an internal (or medial) a nd an external (or lateral) division. It receives projections from the striatum and the subthalamic nucleus. It is the discharging center of the Basal ganglia. The major output of the basal ganglia projects from the globus pallidus (internal division) to thalamic nuclei (in particular, the ventral anterior, ventral lateral nuclei), which project to motor and prefrontal cortical areas. 4. The subthalamic nucleus 5. The substantia nigra The substantia nigra can be subdivided into substantia nigra pars compacta and substantia nigra pars reticulata. The pars compacta contains dopaminergic neurones that project to the striatum. Figure 1 nuclei of the basal ganglia 2 Circuits and neurotransmitters One of the principal roles of the basal ganglia in motor control is to function in association with the corticospinal system to control complex patterns of motor activity. 1. the direct pathway : The direct pathway starts from the cortex and projects to the striatum (caudate nucleus and putamen) with excitatory glutamatergic (glu) neurons. The neurons from the striatum, which are inhibitory GABAergic, send their axons to the medial (internal) globus pallidus and substantia nigra, pars reticulata (SNr). The neurons from the internal globus pallidus and SNr send their axons to the thalamus, and they are also inhibitory. 2. The indirect pathway: This pathway begins (like the direct pathway) from the cortex, projecting to the striatum. Instead of sending axons directly to the GPi , they inhibits the external globus pallidus. The neurons from the GPe send inhibitory fibers to the subthalamic nucleus that causes disinhibition of the subthalamus. From the subthalamic nucleus, neurons excite the GPi/SNr and then continue as the direct pathway with GABAergic inhibitory neurons to the thalamus and glutamate excitatory efferents to the cortex. The final result of this pathway is a decreased activity of the c ortical motor neurons and consequential suppression of the extemporaneous movement. In summary, when a given motor pattern is computed by the cerebral cortex, it is first conveyed to the basal ganglia via glutamatergic projections to the striatum, with the purpose of releasing the intended movement and suppressing the unintended ones. Figure 2; circuits connecting the motor cortex with the basal ganglia Green arrows: excitatory; red arrows :inhibitory 3 Substantia Nigra An important pathway in the modulation of the direct and indirect pathways is the dopaminergic, nigrostriatal projection from the substantia nigra to the striatum.Stimulation of Dopamine (D1) receptors, depolarizes and stimulates direct pathway striatal neurons. While, stimulation of dopamine (D2) receptors, hyperpolarizes and inhibits the indirect pathway striatal neurons. The nigrostriatal pathway thus has the dual effect of exciting the direct pathway while inhibiting the indirect pathway. Functions of the basal ganglia Motor functions: 1. They are involved in the planning of voluntary movement. (discharge before movement begins ). Caudate circuits 2. Executing pattern of learned acts. Putamen circuit. 3. They inhibit and suppress unwanted motor activity through the indirect circuit. 4. C. striatum share in learning and storing automatic subconscious movements Therefore, Inactivate caudate – cannot learn new sequences. While, inactivate putamen – cannot execute previously learned sequences Disorders of movement in Basal ganglia disease 1. Hyperkinetic: Excessive abnormal movement i.e. chorea, athetosis, ballism. (excess direct- insufficient indirect) 2. Hypokinetic: Slow movements (akinesia, bradykinesia) (insufficient direct-excessive indirect) Lesions: ✓ Lesion in the globus pallidus frequently → spontaneous and often continuous slow writhing movements of a hand, an arm, the neck, or the face. called athetosis. ✓ Lesion in the subthalamus → sudden flailing intense and violent movements of an entire limb, called hemiballismus. ✓ Multiple small lesions in the putamen → Rapid involuntary “ dancing” movements called chorea. ✓ Lesions of the substantia nigra → the common and extremely severe disease of rigidity, akinesia, and tremors known as Parkinson’s disease. Parkinson’s disease Pathophysiology: The pathological hallmark of PD is the degeneration of the nigrostriatal dopaminergic pathway. Nigrostriatal dopaminergic neurones are tonically active and exert a modulatory 4 influence on the striatum and the striatonigral and striatopallidal efferent pathways, through D1 and D2 receptors, respectively. Symptoms: 1. tremor The most prominent symptom is the resting tremor of the extremities that almost always accompanies the disease. The tremor has a characteristic frequency of 4–6 Hz and may begin in only one extremity and spread to the others. The distal joints of the limbs are preferentially affected. In the hand, the tremor is characteristic and involves the thumb and fingers rolling together. This is called a ‘pill-rolling’ tremor. The tremor is seen at rest and disappears during an intentional movement and during sleep. 2. Bradykinesia/akinesia Bradykinesia is a slowing of normal movement. In the advanced stages of the disease, the patient becomes akinetic and shows almost no motor initiative. There is reduced arm - swinging when walking, reduced blinking, and various daily simple or complex tasks (e.g. washing, brushing the teeth, dressing and writing) can be affected. There is a gradual loss of normal facial movement and expression. The speech is poorly articulated, and the voice is quiet and monotonous. Eating and swallowi ng become increasingly difficult. This may result in a tendency to drool (sialorrhoea). 3. rigidity Parkinsonian patients have increased muscle tone in flexor and extensor muscles and typically present resistance to passive movement of the limbs. The increased resistance to movement, combined with tremor, leads to the ‘cogwheel’ phenomenon. Manipulating the patient’s limbs feels like manipulating a lead pipe; hence the term ‘lead pipe’ rigidity. Other motor and non-motor manifestations of Parkinson’s disease 1. Abnormalities of posture and gait. The gait of a parkinsonian patient becomes slow and shuffling, and the posture is flexed. 2. The handwriting is small and indecipherable (micrographia). 3. Other autonomic abnormalities, such as urinary dysfunction (in particular, urinary incon- tinence due to bladder detrusor hyperreflexia), increased sweating and sexual dysfunction. 4. Memory impairment, confusion and disorientation, and other features of dementia. References: 1. Guyton and Hall textbook of medical physiology 13th edition unit XI , chapter 57, pages 730-734. 2. (Systems of the Body) Adina T. Michael-Titus, Patricia Revest, Peter Shortland - The Nervous System-Churchill Livingstone (2010)(1).pdf chapter 10 pages 181-185

text: L27:Neuroglia and Myelination D. SILVIA SAWIRES Assistant Professor OF HISTOLOGY AND CELL BIOLOGY Share in formation of blood–brain barrier (BBB Definition Components Functions of Astrocytes Blood brain barrier (BBB ) end feet of glial astrocytes do not touch the endothelial cells release factors that induce characteristics in the capillary endothelial cells (high transendothelial resistance) high transendothelial resistance due to length and complexity of tight junctions between endothelial cells. transcytosis is limited  very few pores , either small or large, that cross the endothelium, and. 2. Regulation of K + levels in EX medium around neurones 3. storage of glycogen that can be supplied to neurones , in the form of lactate, when required 4. controlling distribution of neurotransmitters released by neurones : by restricting diffusion by transporting neurotransmitters into the astrocyte, where they can be metabolized or recycled. Gap junctions between: adjacent astrocytes  stimulated by neurotransmitters, changes in intracellular levels of Ca2 + ions  spread between astrocytes as waves Astrocytes and neurons  modulate the behaviour of the neurones by allowing the passage of Ca2 + between them Ependymal cells simple epithelial cells with numerous microvilli and one or two cilia on their apical surface Their basolateral surface is in contact with astrocytic Processes line the ventricles are not connected by tight junctions. Microglial cells small cells with long spiny processes During development  act as macrophages release growth factors + removing debris produced by programmed cell death which occurs on a large scale at this time In adult  relatively inactive any type of injury to the nervous system  reactive revert to the role of phagocytotic macrophages Oligodendrocytes One of the neuroglia of the CNS large cells with few processes Important for the process of MYELINATION (wrap around the axons, forming multiple lipid bilayers, with their plasma membranes forming a myelin sheath. These membranes have a high lipid/ protein ratio, which makes them excellent insulators) Oligodendrocyte can myelinate more than one axon , and the cell body lies between them Schwann cells One of the neuroglia of the PNS They are flattened cells whose cytoplasm contains a flattened nucleus Functions : Important for the process of MYELINATION ( myelinate a single axon, and the cell body is closely apposed to the myelin sheath). Dear students & 2. role in regeneration of peripheral axons following injury . This stimulates mitosis in Schwann cell  extends processes towards growth cone of the axon. axon regrows at between 2 - 5 mm / day along Schwann cells, which remyelinate new axon in the CNS No regeneration because CNS glial cells release factors that specifically inhibit axon growth. Unmyelinated nerve fibers grey matter, which consists of cell bodies and unmyelinated axons Dendrites Summary or take-home message Glial cells are important component in both CNS and PNS which plays essential roles in their integrity Lecture notes Transfer Goal Recognition the other types of cells in the nervous system (neuroglia ) and study their importance Students’ learning outcomes At the end of this session, you have to : 1. Classify types of neuroglia according to their sites. 2. Distinguish the structural adaptation of each to its specific function. 3. Specify components of the blood brain barrier. 4. Differentiate between process of myelination in CNS & PNS. Neuroglia Supporting cells of the nervous system Make up about half the brain mass Functions:- 1- Structural and metabolic support 2- Immune functions 3- Electrical insulation of axons. A- In the CNS Astrocytes ependymal cells Microglia Oligodendrocytes B- In the PNS Schwan cell Types of Neuroglia Astrocytes most common glial cells in the CNS distinguished from neurones by the presence of glial fibrillary acidic protein . Precursors : radial glial cells during early development, span the cerebral cortex, forming a scaffolding for the migration of new nerve cells to their destinations. large, stellate cells. They have multiple radiating processes, that surround neurones , capillaries and the ependymal cells lining the ventricles Astrocytes Astrocytes Long unbranched processes found in the white matter of the brain. Many short branching processes found mainly in the grey matter.

text: Page 1 of 8 22 Brain Stem Anatomy ILOs At the end of this session, the student will be able to: 1. Correlate the external features of the brain stem to its internal structure. 2. Classify cranial nerves according to their function. 3. Differentiate between the deep origin of the different cranial nerves (nuclei), and their functional components. 4. Appraise the clinical importance of the different functional components of nuclei. Brain stem: It is a part of CNS present in posterior cranial fossa. Parts: Mid brain Pons Medulla Brainstem connected to cerebellum by 3 peduncles. Functions of the Brain Stem: 1. Pathway of tracts between cerebral cortex & spinal cord. 2. Site of origin of nuclei of cranial nerves (from 3rd to 12th). 3. Site of emergence of cranial nerves (from 3rd to 12th). 4. Contains reticular formation: control of level of consciousness, regulation of cardiovascular & respiratory systems. Cranial nerves: 1- Olfactory nerve 2- Optic nerve 3- Oculomotor nerve 4- Trochlear nerve 5- Trigeminal nerve 6- Abducens nerve 7- Facial nerve 8- Vestibulocochlear nerve 9- Glossopharyngeal nerve 10- Vagus nerve 11- Accessory nerve 12- Hypoglossal nerve Page 2 of 8 1- External Features of the Medulla Oblongata: A- ventral surface: - Anteromedian fissure: • Continuation of Anteromedian fissure of spinal cord. • Divides the medulla into 2 halves. • Its lower part is marked by decussation of pyramidal (corticospinal) Fibers. - Pyramid: • An elevation, lies on either (lateral) side of Anteromedian fissure • Produced by corticospinal tract (pyramidal tract) -Olive: • An elevation, lies lateral to the pyramid. • Produced by inferior olivary nucleus. Cranial nerves related to medulla (9-12): The groove between the pyramid and the olive is called anterolateral sulcus and it gives exit for the rootlets of the hypoglossal nerve. The groove lateral to the olive is called posterolateral sulcus. It gives exit to the rootlets of the glossopharyngeal, vagus and cranial accessory nerves. B- Dorsal surface: It is divided into: open medulla (cranial) closed medulla (caudal). The open and closed medulla , due to the emergence of the central canal from the spinal cord opening into the fourth ventricle. The point at which this occurs is called the Obex. Dorsal surface (closed medulla): form lower part of floor of fourth ventricle. Dorsal surface (closed medulla): Posterior median sulcus. Page 3 of 8 The longitudinal elevation lateral to the posteromedian sulcus is called gracile fasciculus as it overlies the gracile tract. The upper end of the gracile fasciculus expands to form the gracile tubercle which overlies the gracile nucleus. Elevation lateral to the gracile fasciculus is called cuneate fasciculus as it overlies the cuneate tract. The upper end of the cuneate fasciculus expands to form the cuneate tubercle which overlies the cuneate nucleus. The ridge lateral to the cuneate tubercle is the inferior cerebellar peduncle. 2 - External Features of the Pons: A. The ventral surface: It is convex from side to side Laterally it is continuous with the middle cerebellar peduncle. A median groove called basilar groove as it lodges the basilar artery. Cranial nerves related to pons (5-8): Trigeminal nerve: emerges from the middle part of the pons at its junction with the middle cerebellar peduncle. Abducent nerve: emerges at the lower border of the pons, between it and the pyramid. The facial and vestibulo-cochlear N: emerge at the lower border of the pons, between it and the medulla. Cranial nerves VII and VIII exit at the cerebellopontomedullary angle. Page 4 of 8 B. The dorsal surface: Separated from open medulla by an imaginary line Form the cranial 2/3rd of the floor of the 4th ventricle. 2- External Features of the midbrain The midbrain presents a narrow lumen called cerebral aqueduct (aqueduct of sylvius). A coronal plane passing through the cerebral aqueduct divides the midbrain into two divisions: A. Cerebral Peduncle B. Tectum A. The ventral surface presents the following features: Cerebral peduncles: formed of a large column of fibers (crus cerebri) on either side. interpeduncular fossa: depression between the 2 Cerebral peduncles. Occulomotor (3rd): emerge from medial aspect of Cerebral peduncles. B. The dorsal surface presents the following features: 4 elevations/colliculi: • Two superior colliculi: concerned with visual reflexes. • Two inferior colliculi: forms part of auditory reflexes. Page 5 of 8 Each colliculus gives rise to a brachium from its lateral side: • The superior brachium connects the superior colliculus with the lateral geniculate body. • The inferior brachium connects the inferior colliculus with the medial geniculate body. Dorsal surface marked by Trochlear (4th)Nerve: The only cranial nerve emerging from dorsal surface of brain stem. blood supply of brain stem: the entire brainstem derives its blood supply from the posterior - vertebral-basilar Medulla: two vertebral arteries Pons: the basilar artery. Midbrain: posterior cerebral arteries. Branches from the three main arteries, the vertebral, basilar and posterior cerebral, supply both the dorsal and ventral surfaces of the brainstem. Clinical correlation: 1- Brainstem death: In brainstem death, spontaneous breath ceases and there is a loss of reflexes. Cardiovascular function can be artificially maintained for a short while but will eventually deteriorate due to loss of function of the brainstem regulatory centers in the medulla. 2- Compression injuries of the brainstem by cerebellar or cortical herniation are often fatal. Page 6 of 8 Functional classification and deep origin of the cranial nerves Page 7 of 8 Cranial nerve nuclei of Occulomotor nerve: Oculomotor nucleus (GSE) Edinger-wesphal nucleus (GVE) Cranial nerve nuclei of Trochlear nerve: Trochlear nucleus (GSE). Cranial nerve nuclei of Trigeminal nerve Motor nucleus of trigeminal (SVE) Main sensory nucleus of trigeminal (GSA, touch) Spinal nucleus of trigeminal (GSA, pain & temperature) Mesencephalic nucleus (GSA, proprioception) Cranial nerve nuclei of Abducent nerve: Abducent nucleus (GSE) Cranial nerve nuclei of Facial nerve Motor facial nucleus (SVE) Superior salivary nucleus (GVE) Solitary nucleus (GVA, SVA) Cranial nerve nuclei of Vestibulocochlear nerve Cochlear nucleus (SSA) Vestibular nucleus (SSA) Cranial nerve nuclei of Glossopharyngeal nerve Nucleus ambiguus (SVE)+10+11 Inferior salivary nucleus (GVE) Solitary nucleus (GVA, SVA) Cranial nerve nuclei of Vagus nerve Nucleus ambiguus (SVE) Dorsal vagal nucleus (GVE) Solitary nucleus (GVA, SVA) Page 8 of 8 Cranial nerve nuclei of Accessory nerve: Cranial part: from nucleus ambiguus (SVE) Spinal part: from upper 5 or 6 spinal segments (GSE) Cranial nerve nuclei of Hypoglossal nerve: hypoglossal nucleus (GSE)

name: Physiology tutorial - Motor system
text: How Does the Brain Produce Movement? Tutorial section 2022-23 Extensor plantar responses (positive Babinski sign) Babinski sign is a part of the spinal withdrawal reflex which in normal subject is inhibited by the corticospinal tract. Plantar reflex Extensor Plantar Extensor Plantar response Babiniski sign can be elicited normally in infant ( Primitive reflexes ) This happens because the corticospinal pathways that run from the brain down the spinal cord are not fully myelinated at this age, so the reflex is not inhibited by the cerebral cortex . The extensor response disappears and gives way to the flexor response around 12 to 24 months of age. 5. Superficial reflexes as abdominal reflexes are lost Because superficial reflexes receive facilitatory influence from the pyramidal tract. Muscle status No or little Wasting. CASE-2 A patient presents with weakness of the right arm and hand, reduced muscle tone and depressed reflexes in the right arm and hand, and mild atrophy of the muscles of the right arm and hand. Where is the lesion? What is the cause of reduced muscle tone and reflexes? What is meant by muscle atrophy? LMN Lesion 1. Paralysis: same side- localized. 2. decreased tone (hypotonia) or flaccidity (cut of stretch reflex arc) 3. decreased or(absent) deep reflexes in the affected segment 4. Plantar reflex: Either normal or absent if the involved muscles are paralyzed. 5. Superficial reflexes: lost in the affected segment (if they involve contraction of the denervated muscle). 6. Muscle Wasting . Is marked because the muscle is deprived of its motor supply. Signs of muscle denervation as: Fasciculation: visible muscle twitches Fibrillation: muscle potentials detected by EMG CASE-2 An 18-year-old man is brought to the emergency center by the emergency medical service after being involved in a serious motor vehicle accident. The patient has severe agonizing pain and he cannot move both lower extremities. Physical examination revealed loss of sensation in both lower extremities, which are flaccid and without reflexes. Magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) reveals a fracture of the thoracic spine with significant swelling and injury to the spinal cord. images showing comminuted fracture of D12 vertebral body There is complete transection of distal thoracic cord at this level Comment on blood pressure and HR in this patient The patient may have Hypotension In spinal shock, there is loss of sympathetic vasomotor tone. Sympathetic motor neurons exit the spinal cord from the first thoracic segment [T1] to the second lumbar segment [L2]) The loss of this sympathetic stimulation can cause the systolic blood pressure to drop below 40 mmHg, thus decreasing blood flow to vital organs and putting the patient into shock. Which tracts are responsible for direct cortical control of spinal motor systems? What is the muscle response during the reverse myotatic reflex? What do group Ia afferents detect? Cortical control of motor neurons: By the lateral and ventral corticospinal tracts. Response during reverse myotatic reflex: Relaxation of muscle that had been strongly contracting. Group Ia afferents detect: Muscle stretch. Transection of spinal cord What are stages and signs of spinal cord transection Transections of the spinal cord have different effects on motor reflexes. When a transection takes place along the spinal cord, there is loss of voluntary movements and conscious proprioception sensation below the level of the transection on the same side. The muscles that are innervated below the lesion initially become flaccid and lose reflex responses during spinal shock. Depending on the location of the lesion, various other physical signs may be present, including urinary and/or fecal incontinence, decreased heart rate and pressure, and respiratory failure. Spasticity and hyperreflexia develop later during stage of recovery. text: Page 1 of 6 L7 Development of Head & Neck ILOs By the end of this lecture, students will be able to 1. Interpret the development & structure of branchial apparatus. 2. Differentiate between the derivatives of the branchial arches. 3. Correlate the nerve supply of different head& neck structures to their development. 4. Appraise the congenital anomalies affecting the head & neck relative to their development. BRANCHIAL (PHARYNGEAL) APPARATUS: The branchial arches are six arches, which develop in successive manner from above downward around the pharynx. Each arch contains: • a cartilaginous component, • a cranial nerve, • an artery, • muscular component. The artery supplying the fifth arch degenerates early, so the 5th arch itself degenerates too. 1st arch divides into small maxillary and large mandibular parts. Fig. 1: Embryo showing the pharyngeal arches from outside. A. Coronal section in the pharynx of an embryo. Page 2 of 6 What are the derivatives of each pharyngeal arch& its innervation? Ectodermal; Endodermal, and Mesodermal derivatives. ggggggggggg • Some of the components ossify; others disappear or become ligamentous. • The maxillary process and Meckel’s cartilage of the first arch are replaced by the maxilla and mandible, respectively, which develop by membranous ossification. • The cartilage of the 2nd arch is called Reichert's cartilage. Page 3 of 6 Skeletal derivatives of pharyngeal arches Endodermal derivatives of the pharyngeal pouches: 1st Pharyngeal Pouch: Primitive tympanic cavity& auditory tube 2 nd Pharyngeal Pouch: Palatine tonsil 3rd Pharyngeal Pouch: Forms 2 diverticula: dorsal and ventral. • dorsal: becomes the inf. Parathyroid gland. • ventral: becomes the thymus. 4th Pharyngeal Pouch: • Develops into dorsal and ventral diverticula. • The dorsal bud becomes the Sup. Parathyroid. • The ventral bud becomes the Ultimobranchial body which fuses with the thyroid gland to give the parafollicular C cells which produce calcitonin. Fig. 3: Endodermal derivatives of the pharyngeal pouches Fig. 2: Skeletal derivatives of pharyngeal arches Page 4 of 6 Ectodermal derivatives of pharyngeal clefts • The first cleft penetrates the underlying mesoderm to form the external auditory meatus. • The mesoderm of the second arch proliferates to form the operculum. • This operculum grows caudally to overlap the third and fourth clefts. • The operculum forms a space between it and the clefts called cervical sinus. • This sinus will disappear to give smooth contour of the neck. Abnormalities of Branchial Arches: 1. Ectopic thymus and parathyroid. 2. Branchial fistulas: occurs when pharyngeal pouch 2 and pharyngeal groove 2 persist, forming a patent opening from the internal tonsillar area to the external neck. It is found along the anterior border of the sternocleidomastoid muscle. 3. Branchial (cervical) cyst: occurs when parts of the pharyngeal grooves 2, 3, and 4 persist, thereby forming a cyst. Fig. 4: Ectodermal derivatives Fig. 5: Abnormalities Page 5 of 6 DEVELOPMENT OF THE FACE: The face is developed from five processes: 1. The maxillary processes (2 in number, originated from the first branchial arch). 2. The mandibular processes (2 in number, originated from the first branchial arch). 3. The frontonasal process formed by proliferation of the mesoderm ventral to the brain. • The ectoderm on both sides of the frontonasal process will form nasal placode. • The nasal placode invaginates the underlying structures& will transform into nasal pit. • The nasal pits divide the frontonasal process into lateral & medial nasal processes. ❖ The frontonasal process will form the bridge of the nose; ❖ The medial nasal processes will form the tip of nose and the filtrum of upper lip, ❖ The lateral nasal processes will form the alae of the nose. The maxillary processes increase in size and grow medially; they meet the medial nasal processes, and fuse with them. • The maxillary process will form the upper lip. • The lateral nasal process and the maxillary process are separated by deep groove called (nasolacrimal groove). • Canalization of this groove leads to formation of nasolacrimal duct. • The ectoderm of the maxillary processes and the lateral nasal processes will fuse together burring the nasolacrimal duct. • This fusion leads to the formation of the upper part of the cheek and the maxilla. Fig. 6: Development of the face Page 6 of 6 Nerve supply of the processes: 1. The frontonasal process: ophthalmic nerve. 2. The maxillary processes: maxillary nerve. 3. The mandibular processes: mandibular nerve. Abnormalities of the face: 1. Cleft upper lip (hare lip): Most common congenital anomaly, it is due to failure of fusion of the maxillary process and the medial nasal process. 2. Oblique facial cleft: Defect in the face extends from the medial angle of eye to upper lip. It is due to failure of fusion of lateral nasal process with the maxillary process. The nasolacrimal duct is exposed to the surface. 3. Median cleft lower lip It is a rare anomaly. It is due to failure of fusion of the 2 mandibular processes. Fig. 7: facial abnormalities

text: Demyelinating and neurodegenerative neurological disorders ILOs By the end of this lecture, students will be able to 1. Compare neurodegenerative diseases to demyelinating CNS disorders as regards etiology, pathogenesis, and morphology. 2. Correlate pathological changes of neurodegenerative diseases to the clinical presentation of Alzheimer disease and parkinsonism. 3. Correlate pathological characteristics of demyelinating brain disorders to the clinical presentation of multiple sclerosis and Guillian Barre disease. Demyelinating diseases These are group of disorders that lead to a loss of myelin, a disease of white matter. A loss of myelin can cause neurological deficits, such as vision changes, weakness, altered sensation, and behavioral or cognitive (thinking) problems. The natural history of demyelinating diseases is determined by the limited capacity of the CNS to regenerate normal myelin and by the degree of secondary damage to axons that occurs as the disease runs its course. Etiology; Demyelination is often caused by inflammation that attacks and destroys myelin. Inflammation usually occurs due to Immune-mediated, infectious, toxic\ metabolic, granulomatous, and myelin disorders. Classification according to etiology and site of affection by demyelination; A- Brain and Spinal Cord Diseases- Multiple sclerosis. B- Peripheral Nerve demyelination; Guillain-Barré syndrome. C- Deficiencies and Exposures – Vitamin B12 and Copper deficiency - demyelinating disease of the spine and peripheral neuropathy. (Prior history of gastric surgery, excessive intake of zinc, or malabsorption). Hypoxia, medications and toxins may induce demyelination. Multiple sclerosis (MS) Definition; MS is an autoimmune demyelinating disorder characterized by distinct episodes of neurologic deficits that are separated in time and are attributable to patchy white matter lesions that are separated in space. Pathogenesis There is a genetic predisposition linked to the DR2 HLA haplotype and an autoimmune reaction directed against myeline and initiated by CD4+ TH1 cells responding to myelin components. The resulting inflammatory infiltrate causes myelin destruction and the formation of demyelinated plaques, (loss of function with axon preservation) which undergo at some point axonal damage and neurodegeneration. Morphology • Gross: Lesions (plaques) are sharply defined areas of gray discoloration of white matter occurring especially around the ventricles but can be located anywhere in the CNS. • Microscopic: Active plaques show myelin breakdown, lipid -laden macrophages, and relative axonal preservation. Lymphocytes and mononuclear cells are prominent at plaque edges and around venules. Clinical Features Women are affected twice as frequently as men; peak onset is between childhood and age 50. The clinical course is variable but is characteristically relapsing and remitting with acute (days to weeks) deficit onset and slow, gradual partial remission. Relap se frequency tends to decrease over time, but most patients exhibit steady neurologic deterioration. Although neurologic manifestations can be diverse (depending on the site of demyelination), certain features are more common: • Unilateral vision impairment due to optic neuritis, cranial nerve signs, ataxia, nystagmus due to brainstem involvement. • Spinal cord lesions cause limb and trunk motor and sensory impairment, spasticity, and bladder dysfunction. Lab investigation; Examination of the CSF shows a mildly elevated protein level and increased IgG levels. Guillain‐Barre Syndrome Pathogenesis; an autoimmune condition after respiratory or GIT infectious disease in which the immune response generates antibodies that cross-react with gangliosides at nerve membranes. This autoimmune response results in nerve damage or functional blockade of nerve conduction. Clinical presentation; Ascending Paralysis begins in the lower limbs and distal extremities (toes and fingers first) that finishes with death from paralysis of the diaphragm. Outcome; Axonal damage and nerve death result, though recovery is possible from live neurons being remyelinated (some patients have residual weakness). Neurodegenerative Diseases These are gray matter diseases, characterized by progressive loss of specific neuron regions with secondary white matter tract changes . They are characterized by the presence of protein aggregates (intracellular inclusions) that are resistant to proteolytic degradation; eliciting a neuronal stress response and can be directly neurotoxic. Degenerative CNS disorders are grouped according to; 1 - the anatomic site of neuronal loss (and/or related clinical manifestations and 2- the nature of the associated inclusions or abnormal structures. Alzheimer Disease A progressive degenerative disease of the cerebral cortex caused by accumulation of abnormal proteins, demonstrable as plaques and tangles. Pathogenesis A. Genetic abnormalities; Point mutations in Amyloid precursor Protein (APP) gene and mutations in presenilin 1 and 2 genes that affects proteolytic cleavage or propensity to aggregate of the abnormal insoluble Amyloid β (a normal transmembrane protein) in specific brain regions. B. Defective autophagy with abnormal removal. C. Amyloid plaques deposit as extracellular aggregates of Amyloid β (Aβ) peptides in the neuropil. Aβ elicits an inflammatory response from microglia and astrocytes that can assist in aggregate clearance but can also stimulate the secretion of potentially deleterious mediators. D. Neurofibrillary tangles are another abnormal aggregate of the microtubule binding protein tau, which when hyperphosphorylated, a stress response is elicited. They develop intracellularly and then persist extracellularly after neuronal death. Both plaques and tangles appear to contribute to the neural dysfunction, through a pathogenesis that has yet to be fully unraveled. Basis for cognitive impairment: A large burden of plaques and tangles is highly associated with severe cognitive dysfunction. The degree of dementia also correlates with loss of choline acetyltransferase, synaptophysin immunoreactivity, and amyloid burden. Morphology • Gross: Cortical Atrophy especially in the frontal, temporal, and parietal lobes and brain stem. Widening of sulci (more space between gyri). Compensatory ventricular enlargement (hydrocephalus ex vacuo) . • Microscopic: There are NO unique pathognomonic findings in AD, the main features are: i) Senile neuritic plaque; extracellular, dilated, tortuous, neuritic processes surrounding a central Amyloid core (Aβ).Stains positive for Congo Red. ii) Neurofibrillary tangle ; intracellular, cytoplasmic, filamentous collection of neurofilaments and neurotubules within the cytoplasm of cortical pyramidal neurons. iii) Amyloid angiopathy is deposition of the same amyloid in the vessel wall which is deposited in the amyloid core of the plaque. Clinical Features AD is the most common dementing illness of the elderly, reaching a prevalence of >40% in the 85- to 89- year-old. It usually begins after age 50, with progressive, insidious impairment of higher intellectual function over the subsequent 5 to 10 years. Most cases are sporadic, although at least 5% to 10% of cases are familial. PARKINSONISM A chronic progressive disorder of motor function and is clinically characterized by tremors, rigidity and disordered gait and posture. Etiology, trauma, toxic agents, and drugs (dopamine antagonists). Pathogenesis; 1- Extensive and progressive loss of dopaminergic neurons with depigmentation of substantia nigra due to loss of neuromelanin pigment from neurons. 2- Accumulation of neuromelanin pigment in the glial cells. 3- Some of the residual neurons in these areas contain intracytoplasmic, eosinophilic, elongated inclusions called Lewy bodies.

They are present in CNS only . I. Functional Classification At the end of this lecture, students should know: 1. Morphologically: According to the number of their processes: 1- Multipolar 2- Pseudo-unipolar:  spinal ganglia. 3- Bipolar:  retina a- Pyramidal: present in cerebral cortex(brain) b- Purkinje cells in the cerebellar cortex 1- Multipolar Classified according to shape of the cell body 2- Pseudounipolar Present in the dorsal root ganglion (outside the CNS). Has a single process that divides into central & peripheral divisions 3- Bipolar neurons Present in the retina What is a synapse? It is the area of contact between two neurons or a neuron and an effector organ. Most of the synapses are chemical that depend on release of neurotransmitter. Others are electrical (gap junctions) Parts of a chemical synapse Types of synapses 1- Electrical Synapses (gap junctions) 2- Chemical Synapses (neurotransmitter) Parts of the chemical synapse Components of a chemical synapse: 1- Presynaptic neuron (axon terminal); abundant mitochondria, neurotransmitter vesicles. 2- Synaptic cleft 3- Post synaptic membrane; contains receptors for the released neurotransmitter. 1 2 3 Mitochondria Ultra structure of a chemical synapse 1- Presynaptic 2-Cleft 3-Post synaptic How do axons terminate? The axons end at a synapse by a nerve ending. Types of nerve endings: 1- Motor nerve ending: the axon terminals establish a synapse with an effector organ (muscle or gland). The nervous tissue is one of the four primary basic tissues. It consists of two types of cells: Neurons Neuroglia. Structural and functional unit Supportive cells How do axons terminate? Types of nerve endings: 2- Sensory nerve ending: The axon terminals end in the periphery of the body; skin, joints, muscle & some viscera. Transmit information from the periphery into the CNS. Summary or take-home message Neurons are structurally adapted to establish a communication network. Neurons are metabolically active cells that synthesize neurotransmitters and generate action potential. Textbook on Kortext Chapter 2; pages 32, 33 & 40. Lecture Notes Lecture PPT. text: 1 | Page Study Guide for course NMD2101: Neuroscience I Dr Course coordinator: Dr. Gehan Yassin Soliman Professor of Medical Physiology Contact information: gehanyassinsoliman@aast.edu 2 | Page INTRODUCTION TO MEDICAL PROFESSION YEAR 1 SEMESTER 1 STUDY GUIDE IN THIS Guide: • Welcome Note P. 3 • Educational Opportunities P.4-7 • Timetable link P. 8 -9 • Assessment P.10-11 • Learning Resources P. 12-13 3 | Page Dear students Welcome to Medical School. We hope you enjoy your 5 years' journey of becoming a physician. Here in the sixth course" Neurosciences I”, you will learn how to integrate smoothly between basic medical and clinical sciences, in a manner that will help you rationalize the clinical importance of the topics your study in the pre-clerkship phase. It consists of an extensive and in-depth study of the anatomical and functional aspects of central nervous system in order to understand the human brain & behavior. The aim of this course is to help you be acquainted with the gross and microscopic structural features of the brain, brain stem, basal ganglia and spinal cord. You will discover the miraculous physiology of synapses, neurotransmitters and mechanisms of neuronal excitation as well as the structure and functions of different receptors during neuronal excitation. You will discover the mechanisms and pathways of sensory inputs in the nervous system. You will explore the structure and functions of motor system and how can you maintain your posture. You will be surprised a lot about neuronal plasticity and memory types. You will realize the structure of skin and how you can feel pain. You will explore treatment of various cerebral dysfunctions such as Alzheimer's disease, Parkinson's disease and the uses of anti-seizure drugs in different clinical scenarios. We hope you enjoy your sixth block in your enjoyable long-life medical knowledge. 4 | Page IN THIS SECTION: • The different Course Themes • The Course Objectives • Different Teaching and Learning Methods EDUCATIONAL OPPORTUNITIES 5 | Page Through reviewing the following table, you will understand the Four major themes in Neuroscience I course and how these themes are related to the course objectives. You will also know which teaching method will be used to cover each theme. It is important for you to review the course objectives at the beginning of each week. Educational Strategy (Interactive Lecturing- Practical- Problem Based Learning- Tutorial- skills Sessions- self-directed learning- E-learning) Course Theme Course objectives Theme 1: General Organization of Head & Neck & CNS 1. Describe the different bones bounding the cranial cavity and the meninges. 2. Compare the basic organization of the peripheral and central nervous systems in relation to their primary functions. 3. Discriminate the activation and inhibition mechanism of action of different neurotransmitters on human body 4. Describe the triangles of the neck in relevance to their related structures, boundaries, and contents. 5. Appraise the anatomical-clinical importance of different structures of the neck. 6. Appraise the importance of identifying the level of termination of the spinal cord to different clinical disorders. 7 Appraise the congenital anomalies affecting the head & neck relative to their development. Theme 2: The Somatosensory System 8. Classify the receptors according to their structure and function with emphasis on skin structure and its receptors. 9. Appraise neurotransmission and the excitatory and inhibitory postsynaptic potential. 10.Differentiate sub-modalities of sensations in relation to somato-tropic map. EDUCATIONAL OPPORTUNITIES 6 | Page 11. Deduce types of pain, pathways for pain sensation and mechanisms of hypoalgesia and hyperalgesia. 12. Discuss spinal cord role in the gating of nociceptive transmission and the role of endorphins in central control of pain. 13. Determine principles of pain management, categories of analgesics and classification of opiate and non- opiate analgesics. Theme3: Motor Control: Cerebrum, Brain stem & Spinal cord 14. Appraise the functional and clinical correlation of different sulci & gyri and cortical areas. 15. Interpret the functional relation of different parts of the brain & spinal cord to its vascular supply. 16. Correlate microstructure of the cerebral cortex to its function 17. Define Brodmann areas for motor control and its clinical relevance to cortical injuries. 18. Deduce the causes and risk factors for different types of cerebral strokes and the patterns of brain damage caused by head injury. 19. Define the neuronal plasticity as a mechanism of memory, types of memory and the characteristics of each type. 20. Outline cortical areas for speech control and main types of aphasia. 21. Classify cranial nerves according to their function and clinical importance and the different functional components of their nuclei. 22. Delineate the neural pathways for monosynaptic& polysynaptic spinal cord reflexes. 23. Categorize neuronal circuits of spinal reflexes, types of motor units and the role of muscle tone in maintaining posture Theme 4: Motor Modulation: The Basal Ganglia 24. Distinguish between upper and lower motor neuron and the interconnections between them in health and disease. 25. Describe the organization, connections and neurotransmitters of the basal ganglia and its related clinical disorders. 28. Some of the components ossify; others disappear or become ligamentous. The maxillary process and Meckel’s cartilage of the first arch are replaced by the maxilla and mandible, respectively, which develop by membranous ossification. The cartilage of the 2nd arch is called Reichert's cartilage. Fate of the pharyngeal arch cartilages. Endodermal derivatives of the pharyngeal pouches 1st Pharyngeal Pouch: Primitive tympanic cavity& auditory tube 2 nd Pharyngeal Pouch: Palatine tonsil 3rd Pharyngeal Pouch: Forms 2 diverticula: dorsal and ventral. Endoderm of dorsal diverticulum: becomes the inf. Parathyroid gland. Endoderm of ventra l diverticulum: becomes the thymus. 4th Pharyngeal Pouch: Also develops dorsal and ventral diverticula. The dorsal bud becomes the Sup. Parathyroid. The ventral bud becomes the Ultimobranchial body. The ultimobranchial body fuses with the thyroid gland and disseminates within it to give the parafollicular C cells which produce calcitonin. Dear students & Endodermal derivatives of the pharyngeal pouches (cont.) The first cleft penetrates the underlying mesoderm to form the external auditory meatus. The mesoderm of the second arch proliferates to form the operculum . This operculum grows caudally to overlap the third and fourth clefts. The operculum forms a space between it and the clefts called cervical sinus . This sinus will disappear to give smooth contour of the neck. Ectodermal derivatives of pharyngeal clefts Abnormalities of Branchial Arches Ectopic thymus and parathyroid. Branchial fistulas : Occurs when pharyngeal pouch 2 and pharyngeal groove 2 persist, thereby forming a patent opening from the internal tonsillar area to the external neck. It is generally found along the anterior border of the sternocleidomastoid muscle. 3. Branchial (cervical) cyst: Occurs when parts of the pharyngeal grooves 2, 3, and 4 that are normally obliterated persist, thereby forming a cyst. Cervical Cyst “ Branchial Cyst” CLINICAL PROBLEM Branchial fistula Development of the face The face develops from five processes : The maxillary processes (2 in number, originated from the first branchial arch). 2. The mandibular processes (one on each side, originated from the first branchial arch). 3. Frontonasal process formed by proliferation of the mesoderm ventral to the brain. The ectoderm on both sides of the frontonasal process will form nasal placode . The nasal placode invaginates the underlying structures& will transform into nasal pit. Development of the face (cont.) The nasal pits divide the frontonasal process into lateral & medial nasal processes. The frontonasal process will form the bridge of the nose; the medial nasal processes will form the tip of nose and the filtrum of upper lip, while the lateral nasal processes will form the alae of the nose. The nasal pits excavated to form the nasal cavities. Development of the face (cont.) The maxillary processes increase in size and grow medially. They meet the medial nasal processes ; compress them towards the midline. Finally, the maxillary process fuses with the medial nasal process. The maxillary process will form the upper lip . Development of the face (cont.) Transfer Goal To appreciate the stages of Head& Neck development , and the related clinical conditions. The lateral nasal process and the maxillary process are separated by deep groove called ( nasolacrimal groove ). Canalization of this groove leads to formation of nasolacrimal duct . The ectoderm of the maxillary processes and the lateral nasal processes will fuse together burring the nasolacrimal duct. This fusion leads to the formation of the upper part of the cheek and the maxilla. Development of the face (cont.) Fusion of the maxillary and mandibular processes leads to formation of the lower part of the cheek. The two mandibular processes grow medially meet and fuse to form the lower lip and lower jaw. Development of the face (cont.) Nerve supply of the processes: Frontonasal process : Ophthalmic nerve. 2. Maxillary processes: Maxillary nerve. 3. Mandibular processes :Mandibular nerve. Abnormalities of the face: 1. Cleft upper lip (hare lip): Most common congenital anomaly, It is due to failure of fusion of the maxillary process and the medial nasal process. 2. Oblique facial cleft: Defect in the face extends from the medial angle of eye to upper lip. It is due to failure of fusion of lateral nasal process with the maxillary process .The nasolacrimal duct is exposed to the surface. 3. Median cleft lower lip It is a rare anomaly. It is due to failure of fusion of the 2 mandibular processes. Summary Understanding the developmental process of head& neck structures is essential for the proper diagnosis and management of their congenital malformations. Abnormal facial features indicates abnormal development of pharyngeal arches. Sadler, T. W., & Langman , J. (2012). Langman's medical embryology (13th ed.). text: Cranial cavity Prof. Dr. Abdelghany Hassan Abdelghany Professor of Anatomy and Embryology Faculty of Medicine Alexandria University Dear students & Transfer Goal • This lecture aims to explain the cranial cavity, meninges of the brain and dural folds with the related venous sinuses. Students’ learning outcomes •By the end of this lecture, students will be able to •1. Relate different bones bounding the cranial cavity to the important structures passing through. 2. Describe the different layers of the meninges and specify their related spaces. •3. Describe the dural folds and correlate them to common relevant clinical conditions. 4. Differentiate between the dural venous sinuses regarding their site and termination. Q: • A patient came to the ER complaining of sever headache, diplopia, redness and swelling of one eye. He told the physician that few days ago, he had a boil in the upper lip that became inflamed and septic. What is the most probable diagnosis? Skull anterior view posterior view side view Cranial cavity Anterior cranial fossa • It forms the roof of the nasal cavity and the 2 orbits. • The frontal bone shows frontal crest and foramen cecum lies behind it. • The cribriform plate of ethmoid bone shows the crista gali. • The lesser wing of sphenoid ends medially in the anterior clinoid process. • Medial to the process, lies the optic canal. Middle cranial fossa • It is formed by body of sphenoid, its greater wing and the petrous part of temporal bone. • The sella turcica is formed of tuberculum sellae, hypophyseal fossa and dorsum sellae that expands into the posterior clinoid processes. - It shows : superior orbital fissure, foramen rotundum, foramen ovale and foramen spinosum and foramen lacerum. Posterior cranial fossa • It shows the clivus and dorsum sellae. • The internal occipital crest extends from the protuberance. • Transverse sulcus continues as sigmoid sulcus. • Foramen magnum lies inferiorly with the hypoglossal canal, jugular foramen and internal acoustic meatus above it in order. Q: • Which foramen lies in the posterior cranial fossa? A. Foramen ovale. B. Foramen cecum. C. Jugular foramen. D. Foramen rotundum. Answer : C Brain 1- cerebrum. 2- cerebellum. 3- brain stem (midbrain, pons and medulla). Meninges • Outer layer; dura mater. • Middle layer; arachnoid mater. • Inner layer; pia mater. Dural folds •They project into the cranial cavity and partially subdivide it. They include the falx cerebri, tentorium cerebelli, falx cerebelli, and diaphragma sellae. -Diaphragma sellae overlies the pituitary gland and is pierced by the infundibulum. Dural folds • Falx cerebri : sickle-shaped, extends between the 2 cerebral hemispheres. - Falx cerebelli between the 2 cerebellar hemispheres. 1- Falx cerebri •It is a sickle-shaped fold between the two cerebral hemispheres. It is attached anteriorly to the crista galli and frontal crest. Posteriorly it is attached to the tentorium cerebelli. 2- Falx cerebelli •It is a midline fold attached posteriorly to the internal occipital crest and superiorly to the tentorium cerebelli. Its anterior edge lies between the two cerebellar hemispheres. 3- Diaphragmasellae •It is attached to the anterior and posterior clinoid processes overlying the pituitary gland. •It is pierced by the infundibulum, connecting the pituitary gland with the hypothalamus. Dural folds Tentorium cerebelli • A tent-shaped fold, extends between the 2 cerebral hemispheres and the 2 cerebellar hemispheres. • It has an outer attached border and an inner free border.

text: L 9 Histology of the skin & sensory nerve endings Dr Rehab Ahmed Abdel- Moneim Professor of histology & cell biology SL A- Keratinocytes: 5 strata desquamating cells Process of keratinization ►►takes 15-30 days ►►desquamation of the horny layer Deduce structural features of each layer in relation to its function 1-Stratum basal ; high rate of mitosis & responsible for renewal of other cell layers. 2- Stratum spinosum; thickest layer, polyhedral cells still undergo mitosis. It is the specialized sensory nerve ending of a sensory nerve fiber. Each type of sensory nerve ending has a special structure and pattern at its termination in a specific site (skin, muscle & others). Primary ( Ia ) afferent sensory axons that end by annulo spiral endings on all types of intra fusal fibers. Only group Ia fibers , however, respond to a change in the rate of stretching. a b c Innervation of the muscle spindle 2- Golgi tendon organs Site: junction between tendon & muscle. To spread over a wide surface area to perceive pain more efficiently. 2- Thermoreceptors; penetrate the basal lamina & also gives branches parallel to the dermal epidermal junction. Pathway of sensations transmitted from skin receptors 1- Sensory receptor Action potential is generated in the axon hillock close to the sensory nerve ending 2- Pseudounipolar neurons central process synapses with sensory neurons in the spinal cord 1 2 3 To sum up Keratinocytes are represented in 4-5 stages with structural differences. text: Eman Helmy Thabet MD PhD Lecturer of Medical Physiology Alexandria Faculty of Medicine Fulbright Scholar at UCSF-USA L18: Organization & function of motor & prefrontal cortex Flow of information 1 2 3 4 5 Flow of information 3 3 2 1 4 Primary motor cortex Early station Primary motor area????? (area 4) Supplementary motor area (medial area 6) Premotor area (area 6) Last station Front Left hemisphere Primary motor cortex Top view Somato- sensory cortex Right hemisphere Frontal lobe Central sulcus Parietal lobe Occipital lobe Back Location: Precentral gyrus Primary motor cortex 1- Primary motor cortex: MI Brodmann’s area 4 Characters : The motor cortex on each side of the brain primarily controls muscles on the opposite side of the body ( contralateral cotrol ). Has a topographical representation of the body surface, with the head, lips and hands represented laterally, and the legs and feet medially . The more complex the movement of a particular body part, the more motor cortex is devoted to it. Functions of the primary motor area Primary motor cortex, MI: The primary motor cortex is responsible for executing fine skilled movements. The MI cortex is involved in the voluntary control of movements, by carrying the motor command to the LMNs Damage to the motor cortex on the left side of the brain produces paralysis on the right side of the body, and the converse is also true . Premotor cortex 2- Premotor area (PM ) Brodmann’s area 6 Primary motor cortex Location: Site: located on the lateral surface of each hemisphere in front of the primary motor cortex, The premotor cortex is guided by sensory input processed by the posterior parietal cortex Premotor area ( PM) (Functions): The PM area is involved in planning movements that involve external sensory cues . It deals with learned motor activities of a complex/ gross and sequential nature , by coordinating contractions of specific groups of muscles; for example, it is active during writing (program bank). It is important in orienting the body and arms toward a specific target . - Together with basal ganglia it initiates automatic associated movements (simultaneous or sequential movements )(swinging of arms in walking ,face gesture) Site: Medial surface of frontal lobe in front of primary area 4 above are 6(mainly ) N:B Supplementary motor are is not a single area 3- Supplementary motor area,SMA (medial areaa6): Transfer goal To understand the functions of the different areas of the motor cortex and their relations to other areas of the brain and consequent effect of their damage. Supplementary motor area,SMA :Functions It plays a preparatory role in programming complex sequences of movement (internally guided movements) i:e not triggered by sensory stimuli) Produce complex patterns of movement , such as opening or closing the hand . The SMA is crucial for the performance of complicated tasks involving both sides of the body, e.g. two-handed tasks such as typing (bimanual tasks). Lesions here do not result in paralysis, but they do interfere with performance of more complex, useful integrated movements. Whereas the premotor cortex appears to be involved in selecting motor programs external sensory stimuli (based on visual stimuli or on abstract associations) , the supplementary motor area appears to be involved in selecting movements based on remembered sequences of movements (internally generated actions) What does damage to PM &SMA do? Difficulty in performing complex motor ,familiar , learned tasks such as brushing their hair, cleaning their teeth or dressing themselves . Difficulty in performing learned motor activity in absence of sensory or motor impairment , is called apraxia . Have you ever thought about what happens the moment you decide to throw a ball? The frontal eye field area ( Brodmann’s area 8 ) Site :It lies anterior to area 6 The frontal eye field (function) The frontal eye field region of the motor cortex controls voluntary scanning movements of the eyes, such as during reading (horizontal movement of both eyes to opposite direction . Stimulation of this region --  conjugate deviation of the eyes towards the opposite side to the cortical area stimuled What is meant with association (integrative) cortical areas multimodal association areas constitute (80 % of cortex) These areas receive and analyze signals from both motor and sensory cortex as well as from subcortical structures. They are not involved directly with sensory perception or performance of motor actions. Integrative (multimodal associative) areas ILOs 1 . Identify Brodmann areas for motor control. 2 . Understand the function of each area in motor function 3 . Recognize the different manifestation of lesions in cortical areas. 4 . Compare between motor cortex and premotor cortex in motor control 5 . Identify thalamo -cortical projection 6 . Describe the functions of the prefrontal association cortex. Association areas of the cerebral cortex The motor, sensory, and language areas account for only about half of the total cerebral cortex. The remaining areas, called association areas, are involved in higher functions. There are three association areas: (1) the prefrontal association cortex, (2) the parietal-temporal-occipital association cortex, a (3) the limbic association cortex 2 1 3 Please notice the effective convergence of these integrative (multimodal association) areas 1-The prefrontal cortex The prefrontal cortex is the region of the frontal lobe just anterior to the premotor cortex of the brain, also known as the " personality center". Pre-frontal association area(parts) 3 1 2 3 Prefrontal association area Ventromedial Prefrontal cortex ( orbitofrontal cortex) Dorsolateral Prefrontal cortex 15/10/24 prof.Hala Abdel Gawad Involved in controlling Behavior Involved in executive functions Multiple steps problem solving requiring temporary storage of information (working memory ) Prefrontal association area receives, analyses and integrates signals from both motor and sensory cortex as well as from subcortical structures. The prefrontal cortex This is the part of the brain that thinks, Functions: (1) planning for voluntary activity; (2) decision making (weighing consequences of future actions and choosing between different options for various social or physical situations). (3) creativity ( 4) personality traits. 5)the prefrontal cortex is the site of operation of working memory, where the brain temporarily stores and actively manipulates information used in reasoning and planning. deficits in this area change personality and social behavior . text: Lecture # 21 Cortical areas for speech physiology Eman Helmy Thabet MD PhD Lecturer of Medical Physiology Alexandria Faculty of Medicine Former Fulbright Scholar at UCSF-USA Areas involved in language processing Non-language areas important for language language areas Auditory areas 1.Primary auditory area 41, 42 2. Auditory association area 22 Visual areas 1.Primary visual area 17 2.Visual association area ( 18,19) 1-Wernicke's area 2- Inferior parietal lobule (area 39 and area 40) 3-Broca’s area (area 44,45) Areas involved in language processing For the spoken words (non language areas) Primary auditory area ( 41, 42 - temporal lobe ) where spoken words are perceived. Auditory association area ( area 22 ) preliminary understand the meaning of the perceived words. For the written words ( non language areas ) Primary visual area (area 17 ) present in the occipital cortex where written words are perceived. Visual association area (areas 18 and 19 ) to understand the meaning of the written words (visually presented words). After the interpretation of auditory or visually presented words , the word meanings are fed into a large area present in the posterior part of superior temporal gyrus , the Wernicke's area. 1- Wernicke’s area Word meanings Large area in “the posterior part of auditory association area” ( area 22 on the left hemisphere ) in the posterior part of the superior temporal gyrus. Wernicke’s area Responsible for (associate sound with concept) Understanding auditory and visual information (both spoken and written language). Word recognition Understanding thoughts Allows the choice of the suitable words to express different ideas (with other areas). Arrange words into coherent sentences. Analysis of sounds (associating sound with concept) for comprehension of words both spoken and written . involved in transforming the visual impression of letters ( graphemes ) into mental representations of speech sounds ( phonemes ). N:B.Phonemes are spoken sounds in the English language, while graphemes are written symbols that represent those sounds. تحويل الانطباع البصري للحروف الي تمثيلات ذهنيه لاصوات الكلام Graphemes into phonemes? 2- Angular and supramarginal area Somato sensory cortex Lateral sulcus Angular gyrus (area 39) Supramarginal gyrus (area 40) Location In the posterior parietal lobule (posterior to Wernick’s area and anterior to the visual occipital areas (areas 17, 18, and 19) Arches over the end of the Lateral sulcus adjacent to the inferior portion of the somatosensory cortex. Involved in Translation of written words into sounds, important in writing words that are not phonetic e.g circuit. involved in correlation of sounds and letters. Associating letters with sounds. Acts as short term auditory memory, to remember how to sound words . Lesion inability to understand written words only but comprehension of spoken words is retained. Transfer goal Identify the function of the cortical areas for speech control and their corresponding lesions. 3-Broc’s area (Inferior frontal gyrus ) Broca’s area:speech production Location frontal lobe immediately in front of the inferior end of the motor cortex ( Brodmann areas 44 and 45) Connection to Wernicke’s area by the arcuate faciculus . to the motor cortex (area 4) to initiate the necessary muscle movements via the pyramidal tracts. Importance Language production and grammar. Area 44 Located in posterior part of the inferior left frontal gyrus . It is part of a network used in combining sounds into words and words into sentences for language production . The information in this area is stored, and at needed times projected to the motor cortex to initiate the needed movements of muscles. Area 45 Located in anterior part of the left inferior frontal gyrus . It processes the grammatical structure of sentences and the proper use of grammatical vocabulary and verbs. It is not directly involved in meaning. Broca Basic circuit for understanding spoken &written language Different regions of the left cerebral cortex participate in the processes of (A) repeating a word that is heard and (B) speaking a written word. Basic circuit for understanding spoken language 1. When a person hears a sentence, this is transmitted via the auditory apparatus to the primary &secondary auditory cortex in the temporal lobe 2. This then connects to Wernicke’s area (in the temporal lobe), which decodes the language into meaning . 3 . If the sentence is to be repeated, or replied to, the information has to be transmitted forwards to Broca’s area (expressive speech ) in the frontal lobe (via the arcuate fasciculus). 4. Broca’s area then produces speech via the motor programes of the motor cortex, which activate the tongue and laryngeal muscles. Basic circuit for understanding written speech 1. Visual input is transmitted to the visual cortex (areas 17–19) in the occipital lobe. 2.Input from the visual association area is sent to the left angular gyrus, where the objects are recognized and named. 3.Input then goes to Wernicke’s area, where words are assembled into sentences, and the appropriate messages are sent via the arcuate and superior longitudinal fasciculi to Broca’s area . 4. Broca’s area activates motor programmes in the primary motor cortex that elicit speech via appropriate brainstem centres and muscles of the tongue and larynx ILOs 1. Identify cortical areas for speech control 2. Explain the role of each area in speech processing &Comprehension 3. Define aphasia 4. Categorize main types of aphasia Effects of damage to specific cortical speech centers Wernicke’s aphasia Receptive /fluent aphasia Lesion in this area results in: Difficulty in understanding language both spoken and written Impaired comprehension of sentences spoken by others. Speech production is effortless, at a normal rate, fluent well articulated. However it cannot be understood with frequent errors in the choice of words (word salad). Lesion in Broca’s area: Speech that is slow difficult to produce with effort, articulation is impaired. Comprehension is largely preserved for single words and grammatically simple sentences. Patients seem to comprehend (but cannot comprehend grammatically complex sentences due to defect in grammatical processing). Broca aphasia Expressive /affluent aphasia Wernick’s Aphasia Damage of Broca's area, (44 and 45). Patients seem to comprehend (but cannot comprehend grammatically complex sentences due to defect in grammatical processing). Speech is slow , difficult to produce (with effort), Non-fluent, articulation is impaired. Difficulty in repeating complex sentences. Damage to the left posterior STG. Difficulty in understanding language (spoken and written ) + impaired comprehension of sentences spoken by others. Speech production is effortless , fluent well articulated. There is an Impaired repetition of complex sentences. Broca’s aphasia Could understand language but not speak Could speak but not understand language Effects of damage to specific cortical areas Wernicke’s area : receptive aphasia —fluent meaningless speech with severely impaired speech understanding . Broca’s area : expressive aphasia —abbreviated, ungrammatical but meaningful speech, but speech understanding impaired where grammer conveys meaning. Arcuate fasciculus : conduction aphasia —speech deficiencies are similar to those in receptive aphasia, but because comprehension remains intact, the patient makes attempts to say the right words. Angular gyrus : alexia (inability to read) with agraphia (inability to write), but the patient can comprehend speech and speak normally. text: L 24 : Motor output-descending tracts By Seham Zakaria Nassar Associate Professor of Physiology- Alexandria Faculty of Medicine The pyramidal tract arises from the motor cortex and is essential for planning, initiating and directing voluntary movements . The extrapyramidal tracts arise from the brainstem. They play an important role in postural control Movements Fine and skilled movements Gross and postural movements Performed by muscles of axial and (girdle) proximal parts of limbs (extra pyramidal system ) Performed by muscles of distal parts of limbs (pyramidal system) The descending tracts (UMNs) The pyramidal pathway Arises in the motor cortex It provides for fine, precise skillful movements and voluntary control of distal muscle groups(digits). The Extra-pyramidal pathway Arise from the brain- stem. responsible for orientating the body, head and eyes in response to somatic, auditory, visual or vestibular stimuli . Regulating muscle tone. The medial brainstem pathways (axial muscles) Arise from cells in the reticular formation, the vestibular nuclei and the tectum . provide for reflex movements related to posture and balance. The Lateral brainstem pathways (distal muscles) Originates in the red nucleus. provides for voluntary movements of the arms but not the individual digits. Design of spinal motor neurons (topographic organization of ventral horn cells ) Proximal distal rule Pyramidal Tracts The pyramidal system comprises : The corticospinal tract (Body) (pyramidal tract proper) The corticobulbar tract. ( Head&neck )) Pyramidal tract ( Corticospinal & corticobulbar tracts) The descending tracts (UMNs) The pyramidal pathway Corticospinal tract Cotricobulbar tract The Extra-pyramidal pathway The medial brainstem pathways The Lateral brainstem pathways Pyramidal Tracts Origin: 30% in the primary motor cortex 30% from supplementary and premotor areas . 30% The somatosensory cortex 10% The posterior parietal cortex Internal capsule Posterior limb anterior limb Pyramidal Tracts Pathway: They pass through the internal capsule and descend in the ventral part of the brainstem, but they differ in their termination sites: Corticobulbar fibres terminate on LMNs in the brainstem and control facial movements . Corticospinal axons bypass the brainstem LMNs and terminate in the spinal cord, to control limb movements. Transfer Goal Explain the motor/ descending tracts and its clinical applications. Pyramidal Tracts why pyramidal ? Derive their name from the medullary pyramids of the medulla oblongata, which they pass through Pyramidal Tracts At the spinomedullary junction ( lower end of medulla oblogata ) 85% of the corticospinal axons decussate to form the lateral CST. The 15% of uncrossed fibres form the anterior CST. These decussate in the spinal cord at the same segmental level Both tracts are excitatory, and most of these axons synapse with spinal cord interneurones ; some synapse directly with ⍶ -motor neurones. Pyramidal Tracts(pathway ) 1- Cortical motor neurons 2-Coron radiata 3-Internal capsule 4-Upper medulla(pyramids 5-Lower medulla: -lateral cortico spinal tract - Anterior corticospinal tract 1 2 3 4 5 Pyramidal Tracts(functions ) (Fine skilled movement ) Essential for planning, initiating and directing voluntary movements and complex spatiotemporal sequences of movements. It provides fine, precise movement and voluntary control of distal muscle groups (flexors). Describe the interconnections between the upper motor neurones and the lower motor neurones. Name and describe the locations of the main descending motor pathways. Trace the pathway of the main descending motor pathways. -Automatic associated movement Facial expression (at rest),body gesture& arm swinging ,all are controlled by extra pyramidal system automatically The Lateral brainstem pathways : 1- The rubrospinal trat (origin &termination) Cervical motor neurons (short tract) mid brain contralateral pathway (crossed) that ends on interneurones in the spinal cord. It is short tract ,convey motor commands to cervical motor neurones for control of limb muscles (not digits). The majority of red nucleus axons do not project to the spinal cord but relay information to the motor cortex from the cerebellum . The Lateral brainstem pathways : The rubrospinal trat (pathway) The rubrospinal axons are intermingled with those of the lateral CST, so that the function of the rubrospinal tract has largely been taken over by the corticospinal tract (distal muscles not digits) . (The corticospinal and rubrospinal tracts together are called the lateral motor system of the cord ) The rubrospinal tract (functions) Convergence of different motor control pathways on the anterior motor neurons. Red nucleus acts a break system checking extensive activity of vestibulospinal system(extensor hypertonus) Red nucleus plays a role in decorticate posturing of the upper extremities which is typically seen in lesions above the red nucleus (will be explained later) Originates in the reticular formation in the brain stem. The reticulospinal tract (RST) has lateral and medial components : 1- Medial RST ( pontine ) originates from the pones and has a facilitatory effect 2- Lateral RST ( medullary ) originates from the medulla and has an inhibitory effect The Medial brainstem pathways : 1-The reticulo -spinal trat (RST) (origin ) Medial brainstem pathways : 1- The reticulospinal tract (function) The Medial ( pontine )RF t erminate on the motor neurons that excite the( antigravity muscles)axial muscles of the body, which support the body against gravity(, the muscles of the vertebral column and the extensor muscles of the limbs). The Lateral ( medullary ) RF transmit inhibitory signals to the same antigravity (extensors) anterior motor neurons. Pontine reticular formation ( facilitatory ) has an intrinsic activity, while the medullary reticular formation (inhibitory) has no intrinsic activity so it depends on higher centers for its activity (cortex, red nucleus and basal ganglia) How a coordinated motor movement is performed? Originates in the superior colliculus . Descends to the contralateral cervical spinal cord (short tract) . Terminates on the axial motor neurones of the neck on both sides of the cord.
