Increased tone (spasticity) Normally the cortical areas suppress the activity of the facilitatory reticular formation and vestibular nuclei in the brain stem. in UMNL there is release of the pontine reticular formation and vestibular nuclei from the inhibitory influence with more facilitatory discharge to the gamma motor neurons causing increased sensitivity of muscle spindle. N.B. Faciliatory RF discharges spontaneously, However, Inhibitory RF which decrease gamma efferent discharge does not discharge spontaneously but is facilitated by fibres from cerebral cortex . Clasp knife spasticity 3-Hyperactive myotatic reflexes: (especially in quadriceps and biceps) exaggerated patellar reflex 23/10/24 17 Prof.Hala Abdel Gawad Due to state of supraspinal facilitation that increase the activity of muscle spindle to stretch . 3. Plantar reflex Extensor Plantar Babiniski sign can be elicited normally in infant ? ( Primitive reflexes ) This happens because the corticospinal pathways that run from the brain down the spinal cord are not fully myelinated at this age, so the reflex is not inhibited by the cerebral cortex . The extensor response disappears and gives way to the flexor response around 12 to 24 months of age. Babinisk’s sign could be elicited normally in some conditions Lower motor neuron lesions (LMNL) CASE-2 A patient presents with weakness of the right arm and hand, reduced muscle tone and depressed reflexes in the right arm and hand, and mild atrophy of the muscles of the right arm and hand. text: L26- Effects of lesion to descending tracts at different levels By : Dr. Youssef Hatem Professor of Medical Physiology, Alexandria Faculty of Medicine 5 Mechanism of Clasp knife spasticity: Dr. Youssef Hatem 10 3. Exaggerated deep reflexes (Hyper- reflexia ): Dr. Youssef Hatem 11 - Clonus: may be found “Alternating regular rhythmic muscle contraction & relaxation that develops on sudden maintained stretch of a spastic paralyzed muscle” Dr. Youssef Hatem 12 * Mechanism: stretch reflex - inverse stretch reflex sequence Initial sudden stretch → nuclear bag intrafusal fs → muscle contraction → very high muscle tension → G.T.O → muscle relaxation → but the stretch is maintained → the process is repeated rhythmically * Pathological sign in UMNL due to hypertonia + + Dr. Youssef Hatem 13 4. Lost superficial reflexes e.g., abdominal & withdrawal reflexes because they receive facilitatory influence from the pyramidal tract Dr. Youssef Hatem 14 5- Plantar reflex shows + ve Babiniski’s sign: Dr. Youssef Hatem 15 + ve Babiniski’s sign: - Believed to be a flexor withdrawal reflex that is normally inhibited by the lateral corticospinal system - Its physiologic significance is unknown - It is of value in the localization of disease processes Dr. Youssef Hatem 16 Dr. Youssef Hatem 17 6 - Muscle status: No or little wasting due to hypertonia Dr. Youssef Hatem 18 A. Lower Motor Neuron Lesion (UMNL) Causes : Mainly poliomyelitis or trauma to peripheral nerves Dr. Youssef Hatem 19 Transfer Goal To correlate the functions and organization of the descending tracts to the lesions that might occur. Dr. Youssef Hatem 2 Manifestations: Paralysis : Ipsilateral (on the same side) & localized ↓ tone (Hypotonia) or flaccidity: (due to cut of stretch reflex arc) ↓ or (absent) deep reflexes (Hyporeflexia) : in the affected segment Plantar reflex : normal or absent if the involved muscles are paralyzed Lost Superficial reflexes: in the affected segment (if they involve contraction of the denervated muscle) Dr. Youssef Hatem 20 6. Muscle status: Marked wasting ( Atrophy ) (the muscle is deprived of its motor supply) Followed by Degeneration after 2 months 7. Signs of muscle denervation: Fasciculations (muscle twitches visible under the skin due to denervation of motor units) & Fibrillations (muscles potentials detected by electromyography in denervated muscles) Dr. Youssef Hatem 21 Spinal Cord Injury (SCI) Causes: Most commonly Trauma by penetrating injuries such as gun Shot or stab wounds, or by compression due to flexion/extension injuries of structures associated with the vertebral column May be uni - or bilateral → sensory ± motor ± sphincter dysfunction Dr. Youssef Hatem 22 Can either be: COMPLETE : → no voluntary movement or sensation below the level of the lesion on both sides INCOMPLETE : → a variable amount of function loss below the level of the lesion Dr. Youssef Hatem 23 Manifestations: Pain: early Motor dysfunction: early, → hypotonia, muscle wasting & paralysis Depending on the level of the lesion, there may be CVS, respiratory & autonomic (bladder, sweating & sexual) dysfunction + loss of protective functions such as pain & temperature Dr. Youssef Hatem 24 I. Complete transection of the spinal cord According to the level: U pper cervical region (above C3 ): Immediate death due to respiratory arrest as in hanging - L ower cervical region: Quadriplegia - T horacic region: Paraplegia Dr. Youssef Hatem 25 1- Stage of spinal shock: All spinal reflexes below the level of the transection are REDUCED Duration : Weeks to months Cause: Sudden withdrawal of tonic facilitatory influence from the brain Stages : Dr. Youssef Hatem 26 Manifestations: Loss of all sensations 2. Loss of all voluntary movements below the level of the lesion 3. Loss of cord reflexes as stretch reflex & flexor withdrawal reflex 4. loss of Bladder & bowl control (retention with overflow) Dr. Youssef Hatem 27 5. Loss of erection 6. Drop of ABP (due to block of the sympathetic activity) if the transection is at T1, but slight drop occurs if below L2 Dr. Youssef Hatem 28 N.B The spinal cord ends at the level of the base of L2 vertebra. Below this level the spinal canal is occupied by the lower nerve roots. → injuries to the spinal canal below vertebral level L2 → sensory loss in the region of the body innervated by the lower lumbar & sacral nerve roots + a LMN weakness & hyporeflexia in certain leg muscles Dr. Youssef Hatem 29 At the end of this session, you should be able to: 1. Describe clinical signs of different upper and lower motor neuron lesions and explain their pathophysiology. 2. Compare between such neuron lesions. 3. Interpret clinical scenarios based on understanding of different lesions. Students’ learning outcomes Dr. Youssef Hatem 3 2- Stage of recovery of spinal reflexes: Dr. Youssef Hatem 30 Manifestations: 1. Gradual recovery of spinal reflexes : as stretch reflex, they are often exaggerated 2. The spinal sympathetic vasoconstrictor centers below the level of the transection regain their activity → arterioles & veins regain tone 3. Micturition & defecation become automatic as in children with residual urine due to weakness of the reflex 4. M ass reflex: Stimulus: Application of a noxious stimulus to the skin Response: - Flexor withdrawal reflex : wide spreading flexor activity → flexor spasm of both lower extremities & contraction of the anterior abdominal wall - Impulses may irradiate to autonomic centers → sweating, pallor, swinging ABP, micturition, defecation Possible mechanism: Activation of great number of neuronal circuits that excite large areas of the cord at once ; Dr. Youssef Hatem 31 Mechanism : May be due to: - Denervation hypersensitivity to the mediators released by the remaining spinal excitatory endings - ↑ number of postsynaptic receptors & the sprouting of collaterals Increase number of receptors Decrease uptake of secreted NT Dr. Youssef Hatem 32 The long recovery period reflects the greater influence of descending input on spinal reflex circuits Complications as urinary tract infection, malnutrition & decubitus ulcers → ↑ duration of spinal shock or even failure of recovery occurs → Adequate management of paraplegic patients is very important Dr. Youssef Hatem 33 One side of the cord is transected → Brown- Séquard syndrome Caused commonly by : Penetrating trauma Ruptured disk II. Hemisection of the spinal cord Dr. Youssef Hatem 34 Manifestations: A) Below the hemisection : 1- On the same side: 1. UMNL paralysis due to interruption of the descending motor pathways. Some of the ventral facilitatory reticulospinal & vestibulospinal tracts are spared because the ventrolateral part of cord usually escapes injury → Spastic paralysis Dr. Youssef Hatem 35 2.Touch is impaired: - Fine touch is lost. - Crude touch is normal (carried by the opposite intact ventral spinothalamic tract) 3. Kinesthetic sensations & vibration sense , are lost. 4. Vasodilation (temporary) , dryness of the skin , constriction of the pupil (if in cervical region) 2- On the opposite side: Pain & temperature are lost (due to cut of lateral spino -thalamic tract from intact side) Dr. Youssef Hatem 36 B) Above the transection for 1 or 2 segments, on the same side: Cutaneous hyperesthesia (due to irritation of dorsal nerve roots, by the neighboring lesion) Dr. Youssef Hatem 37 C) At the level of the transection, on same side: 1. LMNL paralysis of muscles supplied by the damaged segments, i.e., no voluntary movements & no reflex contractions 2. Loss of all sensations (superficial & deep) from areas supplied by dorsal roots entering the cord in the damaged segments. text: L29; Basal ganglia A journey into the deep nuclei Dr. Seham Zakaria Nassar Assistant professor Physiology department Glu Basal ganglia circuits & neurotransmitters RED: Excitatory glutamatergic pathway , BLUE : Inhibitory GABAergic pathways , Magenta : Modulatory dopaminergic pathways What do the basal ganglia do? basal ganglia function with the ipsilateral CC of which controls contralateral muscles via two closed circuits : Making movement Not moving Maintain purposeful motor activity Inhibit unwanted movements Inhibit muscle tone Direct pathway (excitatory) Indirect pathway (inhibitory) What is meant by direct &indirect??? Motor cortex Thalamus (VA&VL) Muscle Globus Pallidus (int.) Striatum Caudate/ Putamen Substantia Nigra Subthalamic Nucleus Move Inhibition Excite GABA Inhibition Dopamine D1 Glutamate Move Inhibition Excite Direct pathway Brain stem/ Spinal cord VA/VL Striatum Direct pathway: facilitates movement * * tonically active~100 Hz GPe STN * Tonically inhibited Cortex GPi/SNr Excitation (glutamate) Inhibition (GABA) Direct to GPi Disinhibition 1 2 3 4 Cortex - Striatum ( glu ) Striatum - GPi / SNr (GABA) GPi / SNr - Thalamus (GABA) SNc – Striatum (Dopamine) Disinhibition of the thalamus The final function of the direct pathway of the basal ganglia is to excite the motor cortex or to increase the motor activity. 1 2 3 4 Nigro striate pathway Movement When movement start Dis-inhibition of the thalamus Enhancement of thalamo -cortical projection Facilitate movements Positive feedback Take off the brake Purpose To free the thalamus from tonic inhibition of GPIS and STPr . Dopamine acting on D1 receptors enhances activity of this circuit ( nigrostriate projections) 1- THE PUTAMEN CIRCUIT Premotor and supplementary motor cortex and in the somatosensory areas of the sensory cortex The putamen The globus pallidus ( int ) The ventroanterior and ventrolateral relay nuclei of the thalamus, Primary motor cortex, the premotor and supplementary cerebral areas For executing learned patterns of movement Is there any differences between caudate and putamen circuit? 19 Habits and skills development (procedural learning ) Transfer Goal Understanding the functions of the basal ganglia in motor movements and its clinical applications. 2- THE CAUDATE CIRCUIT The caudate nucleus extends into all lobes of the cerebrum. It receives large amounts of its input from the association areas of the cerebral cortex, areas that integrate the different types of sensory and motor information. COGNITIVE CONTROL OF SEQUENCES OF MOTOR PATTERNS 2- THE CAUDATE CIRCUIT The cerebral cortex Caudate nucleus The internal globus pallidus the ventroanterior and ventrolateral thalamus the prefrontal, premotor, and supplementary motor areas of the cerebral cortex, but with almost none of the returning signals passing directly to the primary motor cortex. COGNITIVE CONTROL OF SEQUENCES OF MOTOR PATTERNS Caudate circuit is Concerned with putting together sequential patterns of movement lasting 5 or more seconds instead of exciting individual muscle movements. Cognitive control of voluntary movements ?example (when you see fast motor car approaching you) 29/10/24 22 The basal ganglia will decide automatically: What muscle to be used for moving. The sequence and duration of contraction of each muscle(when &where to move). The amplitude , speed ,strength of movements. Basal ganglia converts thoughts into voluntary motor acts 29/10/24 23 Turning away from the bus, beginning to run, even jumping away from it The basal ganglia decide automatically: 29/10/24 24 Motor loop (putamen circuit): Concerned with learned movment . Executes skilled motor activities for example shooting a basketball & Cognitive loop (Caudate circuit): Concerned with cognitive control of sequences of motor pattern . Motor intentions Motor cortex Thalamus Muscle Globus Pallidus (int.) Striatum Substantia Nigra Subthalamic Nucleus Not moving Glutamate Excite Inhibition Globus Pallidus (ext.) D2 Dopamine Augment braking Movement Disinhibition To subthalamus Brain stem/ Spinal cord VA/VL Striatum * * tonically active ~100 Hz STN * Indirect pathway: Inhibits movement Cortex Indirect pathway GPe GPi/SNr + Excitation (glutamate) Inhibition (GABA) Indirect to GPi weak more GABA strong Thalamus inhibited  - + suppression of the extemporaneous movement . Disinhibition of subthalamus 1 2 3 4 5 5 6 Students’ learning outcomes At the end of this session, the student should be able to; Describe the organization of the basal ganglia and their connections with other central nervous system regions. Understand Circuits and neurotransmitters of basal ganglia Describe the role of the basal ganglia in the motor regulation Describe the main symptoms and diseases associated with dysfunction of the basal ganglia, and their pathophysiology. Indirect pathway: Inhibit movements Cerebral cortex Striatum inhibit GP ext. (GP ext. normally inhibit subthalamus) Release of subthalamus ( Disinhibition of subthalamus ) (it is normally activating GPIs) Activate GP int. Inhibition of thalamus-inhibit movement Negative feedback Augment braking Activates striatum An important pathway in the modulation of the direct and indirect pathways is the dopaminergic, nigrostriatal projection from the substantia nigra to the striatum. Stimulation of Dopamine (D1) receptors, depolarizes and stimulates direct pathway striatal neurons. stimulation of dopamine (D2) receptors, hyperpolarizes and inhibits the indirect pathway striatal neurons. The nigrostriatal pathway thus has the dual effect of exciting the direct pathway while inhibiting the indirect pathway. Substantia Nigra (kick starter) Through the direct and indirect pathways , the cortex can either increase (direct pathway) or decrease (indirect path- way) the excitatory thalamocortical projections . Functions of the basal ganglia I . Motor functions: They are involved in the planning of voluntary movement. (discharge before movement begins ) . Caudate circuits Executing pattern of learned acts. Putamen circuit . They inhibit and suppress unwanted motor activity through the indirect circuit. C. striatum share in learning and storing automatic subconscious movements Hypokinetic disorders (failure of initiation ) Weak direct pathway output Very strong indirect pathway output Hyperkinetic disorders(failure of suppression) .Very strong direct path w ay output . weak indirect path w ay output Motor behavior is determined by the balance between direct/indirect striatal outputs Disorders of movement in Basal ganglia disease 1. Hyperkinetic: Excessive abnormal movement i.e. chorea, athetosis, ballism. (excess direct pathway - insufficient indirect pathway ) 2. Hypokinetic: Slow movements i.e. akinesia, bradykinesia. text: 1 L-10 Physiological function of receptors & Sensory coding ILOs By the end of this lecture, students will be able to 1. Define sensory receptors and their functions 2. Classify receptor 3. Compare between receptor potential and action potential 4. Explain how the nervous system is adapted to determine the locality, modality, and intensity of stimulation. 5. Appraise the excitatory and inhibitory postsynaptic potential and their summation. SENSORY RECEPTORS The somatic part of the sensory system transmits sensory information from the receptors through peripheral nerves to multiple sensory areas in the spinal cord and the higher centers The sensory receptors are specialized structures at the peripheral ends of afferent neurons. They are excitable structures: they respond to various forms of stimuli & generating action potentials. Functions of receptors: 1- They act as detectors and transducers: They detect energy changes in both the external and internal environments and transform such changes into electrical form and generates action potentials in the nerve; they act as generators. 2- They can compress the huge increase in the stimulus intensity into a relative increase in frequency of action potential into the afferent nerve, they act as compressor. PROPERTIES OF SENSORY RECEPTORS: 1- Specificity (differential sensitivity) Each receptor is specifically respond to one type of stimulus, its adequate stimulus and produces a particular sensation. Some receptors can respond to other stimuli called inadequate stimuli. However, to produce a response. the threshold of such inadequate stimuli must be high, and they produce the same sensation for which the receptor is specialized “Mullers law” The adequate stimulus of the retinal receptors is light, but they can also be stimulated by mechanical pressure; a person often “sees stars,” because the mechanical pressure stimulates the photoreceptors. 2- Transduction of sensory stimulation into nerve impulses. “Local receptor potential” Whatever the stimulus that excites the receptor, its immediate effect is to change their membrane electrical potential. This change is called a receptor potential. 2 Mechanisms of Receptor Potentials: Application of stimulus changes the membrane permeability of the receptor, allows ions to diffuse through the membrane The magnitude of receptor potential is proportionate to intensity of stimulus § Relation of the Receptor Potential to Action Potentials. When the receptor potential rises above the threshold for eliciting action potentials in the attached nerve, then action potentials occur. § The more the receptor potential rises above the threshold level, the greater becomes the frequency of action potential. Properties (characteristics) of receptor potential: o It does not obey to all or none law, so it can be graded o It is not followed by absolute refractory period, and its duration is long (about 5 milliseconds) so it can be summated o It is not blocked by local anesthetic drugs 3- ADAPTATION OF RECEPTORS All sensory receptors adapt either partially or completely to constant stimulus after a period. On application of continuous stimulation, the receptor responds at a high impulse rate at first and then at a progressively slower rate until finally to none at all. Some receptors adapt rapidly, and some adapt very slowly Mechanisms of receptors adaptation: Each receptor adapts in his own way o Photoreceptors of the eye adapt by changing the concentrations of their light sensitive chemicals. o In the case of the mechanoreceptors: Pacinian corpuscle, Adaptation occurs in this receptor → (1) structural readjustment (redistribution) of fluid, (2) Na⁺ channel inactivation (accommodation). TYPES AND CLASSIFICATION OF RECEPTORS Basis Types Examples By Adequate Stimulus Mechanoreceptors Touch, pressure, vibration, baroreceptors Thermoreceptors Cold, warm receptors Osmoreceptors Hypothalamus (ECF solute conc.) Chemoreceptors Taste, smell, carotid/aortic bodies Nociceptors Pain (tissue damage) Photoreceptors Rods & cones By Location Exteroceptors Skin, vision, hearing, taste, smell Interoceptors Proprioceptors, visceroceptors (baro-, chemo-), hypothalamic receptors By Adaptation Slowly adapting (Tonic): They continue to transmit impulses to the brain as long as the stimulus is present to relay their Important information to the CNS Posture (muscle spindles), pain, baroreceptors Rapidly adapting (Phasic) They are stimulated only when the stimulus strength changes Pacinian corpuscles, vibration, touch 3 CODING OF SENSORY INFORMATION It is the ability of the nervous system to discriminate the modality, locality and intensity of various sensations, although all sensations are transmitted in the form of action potential. (1) MODALITY DISCRIMINATION - The “Labeled Line” Principle Each type of receptors is specifically stimulated by its adequate stimulus. Each nerve tract terminates at a specific point in the central nervous system, and the type of sensation felt when a nerve fiber is stimulated is determined by the point in the nervous system to which the fiber leads. This specificity of nerve fibers for transmitting only one modality of sensation is called the labeled line principle. each sensory pathway (from the receprors till the termination at the higher centres) is labeled for a specific sensation. (2) LOCALITY DISCRIMINATION The discrimination of the locality of a certain sensation also depends on the specific pathway of that sensation. When this pathway is stimulated anywhere along its course, the evoked sensation is projected to (i.e. referred to) the location of its receptors. This effect is called" law of projection ", and it is evident in patients whose limbs are amputated and still may feel severe pain in the phantom limb (i.e. the non-existing limb) due to irritation of the sensory nerves at the site of amputation. (3) INTENSITY DISCRIMINATION The discrimination of the intensity of sensation depends on the number of activated receptors and hence the frequency of discharge in the nerve fiber as well as on the state of nerve (if they are depressed e.g. due to oxygen lack or hypoglycemia, the sensations become dull and their intensity is decreased) ELECTRICAL EVENTS IN POSTSYNAPTIC NEURONS A single stimulus applied to the sensory nerves does not lead to the formation of a propagated action potential in the postsynaptic neuron. Instead, the stimulation produces either a transient partial depolarization or a transient hyperpolarization.The initial depolarizing response produced by a single stimulus to the proper input begins about 0.5 ms after the afferent impulse enters the spinal cord. During this potential, the excitability of the neuron to other stimuli is increased, and consequently the potential is called an excitatory postsynaptic potential (EPSP) The EPSP is produced by depolarization of the postsynaptic cell membrane immediately under the presynaptic ending. The excitatory transmitter opens Na+ or Ca2+ ion channels in the postsynaptic membrane, producing an inward current. The area of current flow thus created is so small that it does not drain off enough positive charge to depolarize the whole membrane. The EPSP due to activity in one synaptic knob is small, but the depolarizations produced by each of the active knobs summate. 4 However, stimulation of other inputs produces hyperpolarizing responses. During this potential, the excitability of the neuron to other stimuli is decreased, it is called an inhibitory postsynaptic potential (IPSP). An IPSP can be produced by a localized increase in Cl transport. When an inhibitory synaptic knob becomes active, the released transmitter triggers the opening of Cl– channels in the postsynaptic cell membrane. The net effect is the transfer of negative charge into the cell, so that the membrane potential increases. With decreased excitability, (hyperpolarization). IPSP can be produced by alterations in other ion channels in the neuron. For e

text: Page 1 of 5 11 Somatic Sensations- Ascending pathways ILOs By the end of this lecture, students will be able to 1. Differentiate different sub -modalities of sensations with their central termination of the pathways. 2. Describe the pathway of the main sensory pathways and its injury 3. Solve clinical scenarios based on understanding different levels of lesion SOMATIC SENSATIONS These are sensations from the skin and deeper structures (muscles, bones, tendons and joints). According to their nature, somatic sensations are classified into: A. Mechanoreceptive sensations: resulting from stimulation of mechanoreceptors and include: Tactile sensations: 1. Light touch: it is a touch sensation that is not sharply localized and results from stimulation of tactile receptors in the superficial layers of the skin. It is tested using a piece of cotton wool on different dermatomes. 2. Tactile discrimination (2-point discrimination): It is the ability to perceive, with closed eyes, two touch stimuli applied to the skin at the same time as two separate points of touch provided that the distance between the two points is more than a certain threshold variable in different areas of the body. 3. Pressure sensation: it is the ability to discriminate different weights results from stimulation of tactile receptors in deeper layers of the skin. 4. Vibration sense: it results from rapidly repetitive sensory signals from tactile receptors. 5. Proprioceptive ( kinaesthetic) sensations: Located in the muscles, tendons, and joints, they signal awareness of body position and movement. B. Thermoreceptive sensations: Cutaneous thermoreceptors are specialized free nerve endings, found with highest density in the skin of the hands and face. They monitor skin temperature not body temperature and detecting changes in external environmental temperature. They help to maintain constant body temperature despite changes in environmental temperature. Thermoreceptors include: Cold receptors are on dendritic endings of A  fibers and C fibers, whereas warmth (heat) receptors are on C fibers. Mapping experiments show that the skin has discrete cold-sensitive and heat-sensitive spots. There are 4 to 10 times as many cold -sensitive as heat -sensitive spots. The threshold for activation of warmth receptors is 30 °C, and they increase their firing rate up to 46 °C. Cold receptors are inactive at temperatures of 40 °C, but then steadily increase their firing rate as skin temperature falls to about 24 °C. As skin temperature further decreases, the firing rate of cold receptors decreases until the temperature reaches 10 °C. Below that temperature, they are inactive, and the cold becomes an effective local anaesthetic. Thermal nociceptors are activated by skin temperatures above 45 °C or by severe cold. C. Pain sensation: resulting from stimulation of nociceptors. Page 2 of 5 The somatosensory system Most activities of the nervous system are initiated by sensory experiences that excite sensory receptors, such as tactile receptors on the surface of the body, or other types of receptors. The somatosensory system includes many types of sensation from the body: touch, pressure, pain, temperature, and joint and muscle position sense (proprioception). These modalities may or may not reach consciousness. They travel in different ascending pathways that are in specific areas of the spinal cord white matter and terminate in specific areas of the brain. There are several ascending tracts, which travel to varying degrees in the spinal cord. Their names reflect where they originate and terminate in the nervous system. Almost all sensory information from the somatic segments of the body enters the spinal cord through the dorsal roots of the spinal nerves (for sensations from the body) and the trigeminal root (for sensations from the face), (figure 1). However, from the entry point into the cord and then to the brain, the sensory signals are carried through three important pathways that run the entire length of the spinal cord:(1) the dorsal column–medial lemniscal system; or (2) the ventrolateral system and (3) spinocerebellar systems. These main pathways share important common features: • Each pathway has 2-4 order neurons. The first order neuron for all sensations being the cell bodies in the dorsal root ganglia or the ganglia of cranial nerves. • Conscious sensations decussate (cross) to the contralateral side. • Crossing-over always occurs from the second-order neuron. In adults, the spinal cord extends to the L1–L2 level in the vertebral column. In the spinal cord, the gray matter is localized centrally and is surrounded by white matter. Gray matter contains the nerve cell bodies: motor neurons and interneuron circuits in the anterior horn and sensory neurons in the posterior horn. White matter is d ivided into three columns: the anterior, lateral, and posterior columns. THE DORSAL COLUMN MEDIAL LEMNISCUS (DCML) PATHWAY The dorsal column medial lemniscus (DCML) pathway conveys information about: • Discriminative touch- Fine touch—the ability to recognize the exact location of light touch, and the ability to perform two-point discrimination. • Conscious proprioception: the awareness of body position and awareness of body movements (kinaesthesia) • Vibration and the perception of pressure (weight discrimination). Texture is mediated by Aα and Aβ fibres and enables us to ‘read’ Braille letters or numbers (graphesthesia) or describe the shape and texture of an object without seeing it (Stereognosis). Pathway • First order neuron (dorsal root ganglion). The primary afferents Fibers enter the spinal cord and ascend ipsilaterally in the dorsal column to the medulla, on the same (ipsilateral) side of the cord. A key feature of this pathway is that it is somatotopically organized, such that afferents from the lower limbs and trunk travel more medially in the gracile funiculus, and afferents from the upper limb travel more laterally, in the cuneate fasciculus, to their respective nuclei in the medulla. Page 3 of 5 • Second order neuron (gracile and cuneate nuclei ). After synapsing in the dorsal column (or the analogous trigeminal) nuclei, the secondary neurons cross in the medulla and ascend as the medial lemniscus to the thalamus, where they synapse in the ventroposterior (VP) nucleus. In the VP nucleus, the head is represented medially and the rest of the body laterally. • Third order neuron (ventral posterolateral nucleus of the thalamus) Finally, information ascends from the thalamus via, to the primary somatosensory cortex (SI) in the postcentral gyrus. Lesions to the posterior columns is associated with: - loss of discriminative touch, vibration - Difficulty in identifying objects by touch (astereognosis) - Sensory ataxia (due to lack of proprioceptive feedback) - Positive Romberg sign : Patient sways or falls when eyes are closed (loss of proprioception) THE VENTROLATERAL SYSTEM: PAIN AND TEMPERATURE This system comprises several pathways that ascend in the ventrolateral part of the spinal cord. The Spinothalamic tract (STT) is the most important and conveys information about temperature and pain. These fibers can be divided into several different tracts. The majority of the fibers travels to the thalamus (spinothalamic tract). Other smaller tracts are involved in modulating these sensations and terminate in various targets in the brainstem and diencephalon. These targets include the midbrain (spinomesencephalic), reticular formation (spinoreticular), brainstem nuclei (spinobulbar) Spinothalamic tract: Fibers from nociceptors and thermoreceptors synapse on neurons in the dorsal horn. The synaptic transmitter secreted by afferent fibers subserving fast pain is glutamate, and the transmitter subserving slow severe pain is substance P . The axons from these neurons cross the midline and ascend in the ventrolateral quadrant of the spinal cord, where they form the ventrolateral spinothalamic tract. Fibers within

text: Page 1 of 5 11 Ascending pathways and somatosensory cortex ILOs By the end of this lecture, students will be able to 1. Describe the pathway of the main sensory pathways and its injury 2. Solve clinical scenarios based on understanding different levels of lesion 3. Recognize the lobes in the cerebral cortex with their different activities. 4. Identify somatotopic map 5. Discuss hemispheric lateralization SPINOCEREBELLAR TRACT (SCBT) PATHWAY The spinocerebellar tracts relay information about limb position and movement (proprioception) to the cerebellum. To do this effectively, proprioceptive information from muscles, tendons, and joints, and exteroceptive information from skin receptors are integrated to allow for a complete picture of the body in motion . These sensations are conveyed by Aα fibres and terminates in the cerebellum, which needs continuous feedback on what the muscles are doing. Posterior spinocerebellar tract Pathway: Fibers from the muscle spindles, joint receptors and from cutaneous receptors (exteroceptors) enter the spinal cord at their respective levels through the posterior root and synapse in the Second-order neuron Clarke nucleus, (nucleus dorsalis) located at the base of the dorsal horn of the spinal cord. From Clarke nucleus, fibers travel in the ipsilateral posterior spinocerebellar tract to the brainstem, where they enter the cerebellum through the inferior cerebellar peduncle and project mainly to the ipsilateral cerebellum . It gives the cerebellum feedback a nd information on the position and the movement of the lower limb. The posterior (dorsal) spinocerebellar tract carries proprioceptive and tactile information from the lower limb. The cuneocerebellar tract has functions analogous to the posterior spinocerebellar tract but carries information about the upper limb to the cerebellum. Ventral spinocerebellar tract The anterior (ventral) spinocerebellar tract has an anatomical organization and function somewhat different from those of the posterior spinocerebellar . ventral spinocerebellar tract is an ascending pathway that originates in the spinal cord and runs up the ventral margin of the cord with several synapses along the way, crosses twice; until it eventually terminates mainly in the ipsilateral cerebellum. The ventral spinocerebellar tracts receive much less information from the peripheral receptors. Instead, they are excited mainly by motor signals arriving in the anterior horns of the spinal cord. Thus, this ventral fiber pathway tells the cerebellum which motor signals have arrived at the anterior horns; this feedback is called the efference copy of the anterior horn motor drive. Page 2 of 5 Topographic organizations of the sensory tracts and clinical significance Fibres of the ascending tracts are very orderly, so that fibres and cells carrying information from one part of the peripheral surface maintain their positions relative to fibres and cells representing neighbouring parts of the receptive surface. Thus, different parts of the body are represented in an orderly sequence in the tracts and nuclei of the DCML system. This orderly arrangement of cells and fibres is called topographical organization. For the somatosensory system, it is usually called somatotopic o rganization. This is of clinical relevance when an injury or disease affects specific relay pathways. If the problem occurs within the spinal cord, such as in syringomyelia (central cavitation within the spinal cord originating at the central canal) which is common at the cervical spinal cord level. Thus, it interrupts the STT bilaterally, resulting in loss of pain and temperature sensation below the level of the lesion, particularly in the hands.) So, the cervical dermatomes will be affected first, and the lower body is less affected. Page 3 of 5 Topographic organizations of the dorsal column medial lemniscus (DCML), spinothalamic (STT) and corticospinal (CST) tracts in a hemi-cross-section of the spinal cord. C, cervical; T , thoracic; L, lumbar; S, sacral. SUMMARY The three main ascending somatosensory pathways each carry a specific modality of sensation associated with specific receptors. Each pathway is somatotopically organized, so that a complete representation of the body is reproduced in each relay nucleus along the pathway. Any sensory system going to the cerebral cortex will have to cross over at some point, because the cerebral cortex operates on a contralateral basis. The discriminative touch system crosses in the medulla and the pain system crosses in the spinal cord. The proprioceptive system ascends to the cerebellum and does not cross. There is some overlap of modalities between the ascending tracts: some light touch information travels in the STT , so that lesioning the dorsal column does not completely abolish touch and pressure sensation; similarly, visceral pain fibres travel in the dorsal columns and not the STT. CEREBRAL CORTEX The cerebral cortex covers the entire surface of the brain. In order to accommodate the vast number of neurons in the human cortex, the cortical surface area needs to be increased. Therefore, the cortex is highly folded, forming gyri and sulci. Each cerebral hemisphere can be divided into five lobes: the frontal, parietal, temporal, occipital, and limbic lobes. The forebrain comprises the largest part of the brain (80% by volume) and consists of the cerebral cortex, the limbic system, and the basal ganglia. The forebrain is concerned with perception, cognition, motivation, memory, emotion and control of higher motor functions. Functionally, it can also be divided into: I. Somatosensory areas. II. Motor areas. III. Prefrontal association area. IV . Language areas. Functions of the brain lobes Organization of the somatosensory cortex Page 4 of 5 Sensory areas of the brain (SI) The primary somatosensory cortex is composed of the postcentral gyrus of the parietal lobe on each side of the brain receives sensory input from the opposite side of the body, and include: • The (primary) somatosensory area I (S1) and the (secondary) somatosensory association area. 1. The (primary) somatosensory area I (S1) Characteristic of S1 - This area occupies the postcentral gyrus (Brodmann's areas 1,2 and 3). It receives fibers from the posteroventral nucleus of the thalamus via the sensory radiation. - It receives sensations from the opposite side of the body. - The body is represented in this area in an inverted manner, but the face is not inverted (foot and leg are represented medially and the trunk, chest, arm and hand are represented more lateral in the middle of the postcentral gyrus). - The face is represented in the lower half of the postcentral gyrus. - The different parts of the body are not equally represented, the size of the area of representation of different parts of the body is determined by the number of receptors of that part. The exaggerated size of the face, tongue, and hands indicates the high degree of sensory perception associated with these body parts. - This area shows modality separation of different sensations i.e. the cells of the somatosensory area I are organized functionally into columns with each column is specialized in the perception of a specific modality of sensation. Functions: SI cortex is necessary for the conscious awareness that a stimulus has occurred, and of its quality, location, intensity and duration.SI cortex sends information to other cortical areas. It is the site for initial cortical processing and perception of both somesthetic and proprioceptive input. The somatosensory cortex localizes the source of sensory input and perceives the level of intensity of the stimulus. It also is capable of spatial discrimination. The somatosensory cortex, in turn, projects this sensory input via white matter fibers to adjacent higher sensory areas for even further elaboration, analysis, and integration of sensory information. These higher areas are important in perceiving complex patterns

text: 1 12 Physiology of Pain ILOs By the end of this lecture, students will be able to 1. Identify types of pain and how it is perceived via pain receptors 2. Distinguish pathways for pain sensations 3. Describe the peripheral and central mechanisms of hyperalgesia 4. Discuss referred pain and its mechanism 5. Explain peripheral and central sensitization 6. Define neuropathic pain and its main causes Pain is defined as unpleasant sensory and emotional experience associated with actual or potential tissue damage. Pain is termed nociceptive and nociceptive means sensitive to noxious stimuli. Pain Receptors Nociceptors are sensory receptors that detect signals from damaged tissue. Nociceptive afferents do not have specialized receptors; they use free nerve endings and most are polymodal, i.e. they respond to more than one kind of stimulus, such as chemical, thermal or mechanical stimuli. Nociceptors are free (bare) nerve endings . They transduce a variety of noxious stimuli into receptor potentials, which in turn initiate action potential in the pain nerve fibers. Free nerve endings are found in all parts of the body except the interior of the bones and the brain itself. Pain receptors are divided into four categories based on function: 1. High threshold mechano-nociceptors or specific nociceptors: (mechanical stimulation such as pinching, cutting or stretching). 2. Thermal nociceptors, (thermal stimuli). 3. Chemical nociceptors, (chemical substances). 4. Polymodal nociceptors, which respond to high intensity stimuli such as mechanical, thermal and to chemical substances like the previous three types. Factors that Activate Nociceptors Nociceptors respond to a stimulus causes tissue damage. The damage of tissue results in a release of a variety of substances from lysed cells as well as from new substances synthesized at the site of the injury. These substances include: - Globulin and protein kinases: which are believed to be one of the most active pain - producing substances. - Arachidonic acid. Arachidonic acid is one of the chemicals released during tissue damage. It is then metabolized into prostaglandin (and cytokines). - Histamine. Tissue damage stimulates the mast cells to release histamine to the surrounding area. - Nerve growth factor (NGF). - Substance P (SP) and calcitonin gene-related peptide (CGRP) are released by injury. - Potassium - K+. Most tissue damage results in an increase in extracellular K+. 2 - Serotonin (5-HT), acetylcholine (ACh), low pH (acidic) solution, and ATP. - Lactic acid. When muscles are hyperactive or when blood flow to a muscle is blocked, lactic acid concentration increases, and pain is induced. CLASSIFICATION OF PAIN Pain is classified as fast and slow pain. A painful stimulus causes a “bright,” sharp, localized sensation (fast pain) followed by a dull, intense, diffuse, and unpleasant feeling (slow pain) .Fast pain is due to activity in the Aδ pain fibers, whereas slow pain is due to activity in the C pain fibers Pain Fibers, there are two types of pain fibers, A delta fiber (group III fibers) - 2-5 mm in diameter, - myelinated, - have a fast conduction velocity (5- 40 meters/sec), - and carry information mainly from the nociceptive-mechanical or mechano-thermal nociceptors. - Their receptive fields are small. Therefore, they provide precise localization of pain. C fibers (group IV fibers) - 0.4-1.2 mm in diameter - unmyelinated - have a slow conduction velocity (0.5-2.0 meters/sec) - activated by a variety of high-intensity mechanical, chemical and thermal stimulation and carry information from polymodal nociceptors - Their receptive fields are large, therefore, less precise for pain localization. Fig. 1: Pain fibers Types of pain Nociceptive (acute) pain is elicited by a brief noxious stimulus such as pinprick and induces a flexion withdrawal response to the stimulus. This type of pain is an adaptive sensation whose primary function is to protect the body from injury; it is an early warning alarm system. Acute pain is characterized by activation of nociceptors for a limited duration and is mediated mainly by A delta fibers . Nociceptive pain may result from activation of either superficial or deep nociceptors. 3 Chronic pain can be considered “bad pain” because it persists long after recovery from an injury and is often refractory to common analgesic agents, including nonsteroidal anti -inflammatory drugs (NSAIDs) and opiates. Chronic pain which results from nerve injury is known as neuropathic pain. Neuropathic pain: is defined as pain resulting from disease or damage to the peripheral or central nervous systems. Thus, it covers a wide range of conditions such as muscle and joint pain disorders such as fibromyalgia and back pain where there is no clear nerve damage and to pain in diseases such as diabetes, cancer and AIDS. The quality of pain sensations is distinct from that seen in acute pain (burning, stabbing) . May be associated with sympathetic nervous system dysfunctions, vasomotor and sudomotor (stimulation of sweat glands) changes. In neuropathic pain, the pain persists in the absence of the initial injury. Chronic pain often results from abnormal sensitivity of nociceptors and pathological changes in the nervous system. Sensitization of peripheral receptors Tissue damage and inflammation result in the release of inflammatory molecules which lower the activation threshold of nociceptors (sensitize peripheral nociceptors). When the response to a normally painful stimulus is heightened (more pain felt than usual), it is referred to as primary hyperalgesia, which include the expression of more Na + channels. Overexpression of Na + channels in clusters on the peripheral branches of the A  and C fibers can lead to spontaneous discharges and lower the threshold for signaling. Primary hyperalgesia occurs in the region of damaged skin and is a result of receptor sensitization. Therefore, Pain is heightened in response to normally painful stimuli (enhanced nociception) Secondary hyperalgesia , on the other hand, occurs in the skin immediately bordering the damaged tissues (in surrounding uninjured tissue), as pain spreads beyond the border of a burn or surgical incision. Although receptor sensitization may contribute to secondary hyperalgesia, there is central component as increased responsiveness of neurons in the dorsal horn of the spinal cord (Central sensitization) Central sensitization: changes in the synapses of the posterior horn of the spinal cord. Changes in glutamate receptor with insertion of more glutamate receptors in the postsynaptic second - order neuron led to increased excitability of this neuron and facilitated synaptic transmission. In addition, some nociceptor neurons can be converted to wide dynamic range neurons that now receive input from all types of sensory fibers which typically occurs following nerve injury. This will result in non-noxious stimuli being interpreted as pain light touch on sunburn (allodynia). Deep Pain Results from stimulation of nociceptors in the muscles or viscera. deep pain is poorly localized, due to a relative deficiency of A δ nerve fiber in deep structures, due to the lower innervation densities of these tissues, and is periodic , frequently associated with nausea, sweating and changes in blood pressure. Example of deep pain is pain resulting from prolonged muscle contraction with occluded blood supply to the muscle, contraction soon causes pain due to 4 accumulation of chemical agent (Lewis’s “P factor”) and lactic acid. The pain persists after the contraction until blood flow is reestablished, and this material is washed out. Fig. 2: Hyperalgesia- Sensitization Visceral pain Is poorly localized, unpleasant, and associated with nausea and autonomic symptoms, visceral pain often radiates or is referred to other areas. text: 1 13 Pain control mechanisms ILOs By the end of this lecture, students will be able to 1. Discuss spinal cord role in the gating of nociceptive transmission. 2. Interpret how nociceptive transmission can be modulated 3. Discuss role of endorphins versus other transmitters in central control of pain 4. Identify location and functions of the endogenous analgesic centers. The transmission of information from primary afferents to secondary neurones in the spinal cord is not only a passive process but is a dynamic process including excitation, inhibition and modulation. Neurones in the superficial dorsal horn are subject to modulation that GATES the flow of information to the CNS. These descending influences on posterior horn neurons can be both inhibitory and facilitatory. The balance between inhibition and facilitation can be altered to meet different behavioral, emotional, and pathophysiological needs . The CNS also contains a built-in pain-suppressing or analgesic system that suppresses transmission in the pain pathways as they enter the spinal cord. GATE CONTROL THEORY Proposed by Patrick Wall and Ronald Melzack. This theory states that pain is a function of the balance between the information traveling into the spinal cord through large (non -nociceptive) nerve fibres and information travelling into the spinal cord throug h small (nociceptive) nerve fibres. Without any stimulation, both sets of nerve fibres are inactive and the inhibitory neurone (I) blocks the signal in the projection neurone (P) that connects to the brain. The gate is ‘closed’, and therefore no pain is sensed. With non-painful stimulation, large nerve fibres are activated. This activates P, but it also activates I, which then blocks the signal in P, that connects to the brain. As the gate is ‘closed’, no stimulation is perceived by the brain. With noxiou s stimulation, nociceptive fibres become active. They activate P and, block I. Since activity of the inhibitory neurone is blocked, it cannot block the output of the projection neurone that connects with the brain. Therefore, if the relative amount of activity is greater in large nerve fibres, there should be little or no pain. However, if there is more activity in small nerve fibres, then pain takes place, because the gate is ‘open’. 2 Rubbing the head or shin stimulates the non -nociceptive afferents that send impulses into the spinal cord. This phenomenon can be explained by the gate theory, where the inhibitory interneurones are activated either directly or indirectly by stimulation of these afferents from the skin that would then block the projection neurone and therefore block the pain. This may explain why counter- stimulation techniques are sometimes effective at relieving pain. Fig. 1 Gate control theory Large-diameter Aβ fibers (touch): stimulate inhibitory interneurons → close the gate, reduce pain. Small-diameter Aδ and C fibers (pain): inhibit these interneurons → open the gate, facilitate pain. SUPRASPINAL (DESCENDING) ANALGESIA It is a mechanism by which the brain can reduce pain. It uses feedback loops that involve several different nuclei in the brainstem reticular formation. Areas of the brainstem that are involved in reducing pain are the periaqueductal gray (PAG), the nucleus raphe magnus (NRM) and the locus coeruleus (LC) . The PAG is very important in the control of pain. This region surrounds the cerebral aqueduct in the midbrain. Neurosurgeons can implant stimulating electrodes near the PAG of intractable pain patients . The PAG contains enkephalin-rich neurones that excite the NRM and/or LC neurones . This allows PAG (anti - nociceptor) neurones to excite the amine -containing cells in NRM and LC that in turn project to the spinal cord to block pain transmission by dorsal horn cells. 3 Stimulation of the raphe nuclei produces a powerful analgesia and it is thought that the 5 -HT released by this stimulation activates the inhibitory interneurones even more powerfully than noradrenaline (from LC) and thus blocks pain transmission. The descending serotonergic and noradrenergic axons induce release of enkephalin from certain dorsal horn interneurons as well as activating some GABAergic inhibitory interneurones . These interneurons can act both postsynaptically on projection cells by causing hyperpolarization and opening potassium channels or presynaptically via closing calcium channels and inhibition of neurotransmitter release from primary afferent terminals. These brainstem nuclei are tightly linked to the thalamus, limbic system, hypothalamus, and cortical areas that are part of the p ain control system Fig. 2. Supraspinal (descending) analgesia ENDOGENOUS OPIOID SYSTEM The endogenous opioid system provides a strong modulatory influence on pain processing. Opioid receptors can be found at all levels of the pain system. The powerful analgesic effect of opiate drugs is likely due to the fact that they influence the pain system at every level (mainly on peripheral nerves,at the site of an injury; in the dorsal horn and in the brain stem). Opioid receptors are physiologically activated by a group of endogenous molecules that comprise enkephalins, endorphins, and dynorphins.Three classes of opioid receptors have been identified: μ (mu), δ (delta), and κ (kappa). Activation of these receptors results in the inhibition of voltage -gated Ca2+ channels and/or the opening of K+ channels, which results in hyperpolarization and less neuronal Excitability. 4 Arousal (stress) analgesia Recent work has clarified the mechanisms involved in the analgesia seen during intense excitement or arousal. During arousal, the sympathetic nervous system is active in the body. Sympathetic fibres activate the slow pain pathways, whose axons ascend to activate noradrenergic cells in the locus coeruleus. Noradrenergic axons project back down to the spinal cord neurons which can block pain transmission through different inhibitory interneurons. Therefore, agents that increase noradrenergic transmission have analgesic potential. Additionally, activity from autonomic brain areas such as the hypothalamus or the amygdala stimulates the PAG to induce analgesia. This is involved in the fight or flight reaction that produces hypoalgesia in life -threatening situations, e.g. on battlefields. Fig. 3. The action of opiates at the synapse REFERENCES o Bear, M. F., Connors, B. W., & Paradiso, M. A. (2020). Neuroscience: Exploring the Brain (4th ed.). McGraw-Hill Education. o Brunton, L. et al. Goodman & Gilman's: The Pharmacological Basis of Therapeutics , 13th Edition o Hall, J. E. and Michael E. Hall. Guyton and Hall textbook of Medical Physiology (15 th ed.). Elsevier.

text: 1 Reflex action Definition of a reflex It is the involuntary response of an organ to a stimulus. It is the simplest motor response to sensory input, and it occurs in both the autonomic and somatic nervous systems. For example, the application of a painful stimulus to a limb leads to flexion and withdrawal of that limb (The flexion- withdrawal reflex). Reflex action refers to all the steps involved beginning with the application of the stimulus which is detected by a specific receptor that transforms it into nerve impulses transmitted in the afferent (sensory) nerve to reach the central nervous system. The afferent neuron synapses either directly or through interneurons with the motor neuron forming the center of the reflex. The motor neuron in turn sends nerve impulses to the effector organ which performs the response. Reflex arc refers to the reflex pathway beginning with the receptor and ending with the effector. Innate (Simple-basic) reflexes are built-in, inborn, unlearned and genetically determined e.g., the withdrawal reflex or contraction of the wall of the urinary bladder when it is filled with urine. Acquired (Conditioned) reflexes on the other hand, need training, previous experience, and an intact cerebral cortex e.g., increased heart rate in athletes on seeing the courtyard (anticipatory sympathetic response), the secretion of digestive juices on seeing or smelling the food or going silent when the lights dim in a cinema. The reflex may be monosynaptic if it consists of one sensory neuron and one motor neuron (with one synapse between the two neurons). The stretch reflex is the only example in the body. The reflex is called polysynaptic when two or more synapses are present in the reflex arc e.g., The withdrawal reflex. 23 SPINAL CORD REFLEXES ILOs By the end of this lecture, students will be able to 1. Delineate the neural pathways for monosynaptic & polysynaptic reflexes. 2. Specify the function of the muscle spindle and interpret its relation to the tendon-jerk reflex. 3. Interpret the significance of alpha-gamma co-activation. 4. List the functions and properties of the stretch reflex. 2 In spinal reflexes the center is present in the spinal cord, while in cranial reflexes it is present in the brain, including the hypothalamus (as those regulating body temperature, body water, or general metabolism), and the brain stem e.g., midbrain reflexes (as the pupillary light reflex and postural reflexes) , and medullary reflexes (as those regulating cardiovascular, respiratory, and digestive functions). In superficial reflexes, the stimulus is applied to the skin, while in deep reflexes, it is present in deep structures as the muscle or tendon. The stretch reflex (Myotatic reflex) Reflex skeletal muscle contraction in response to its passive stretch. It is a localized deep monosynaptic reflex; it is the simplest spinal reflex. Receptors is a small, encapsulated spindle like or fusiform shaped structure called the muscle spindle, located within the fleshy part of the muscle. The central part of the intrafusal fibers is the receptor area, which is sensitive to stretch, while the peripheral parts on both sides are contractile. Innervation of muscle spindle Each muscle spindle has three essential elements: (1) a group of specialized intrafusal muscle fibers with contractile polar ends and a noncontractile center, (2) large diameter myelinated afferent nerves ( types of Ia and II) originating in the central portion of the intrafusal fibers, and (3) small diameter myelinated efferent nerves supplying the polar contractile regions of the intrafusal fibers. I) Afferent Fibers: 3 - 1ry (Annulospiral) -group Ia endings -Rapidly adapting: Ia afferents detect the rate of change in muscle length during a stretch ( fast, dynamic change); thus, they provide information about the speed of movements and allow for quick corrective movements - 2ry (Flower spray) -group II endings- Slowly adapting provide information on steady state length of the muscle, i.e. detect static changes in muscle length. II) Efferent fibers (γ efferent): The spindles have a motor nerve supply of their own, originating in the ventral roots, and are called γ- motor neurons. They adjust the sensitivity of the muscle spindle so that it will respond appropriately during muscle contraction. There are two types of γ -motor neurons: Dynamic γ efferent fiber: which supply the dynamic nuclear bag fibers Static γ efferent fibers: which supply the static nuclear bag fibers and the nuclear chain fibers Center of stretch reflex: α motor neurons which receive impulses from 1ry and 2ry afferent endings. Efferent: Thick myelinated fibers supplying the extrafusal fibers of skeletal muscle which is the Effector Response: muscle contraction How the muscle spindle works Muscle spindle reflexes oppose (correct for) increases in muscle length (stretch). (1) Sensory information about muscle length is received by group Ia (velocity) and group II (static) afferent fibers. (2) When a muscle is stretched (lengthened), the muscle spindle is also stretched, stimulating group Ia and group II afferent fibers. (3) Stimulation of group Ia afferents stimulates α-motoneurons in the spinal cord. This stimulation in turn causes contraction and shortening of the muscle. Thus, the original stretch is opposed, and muscle length is maintained. 4 There are two types of stretch reflex based on different stimulus, receptors and response 1. Dynamic stretch reflex: Sudden strong passive stretch causes stretching of nuclear bag fibers leading to stimulation of 1ry endings. This results in rapid contraction followed by rapid relaxation (Which is the basis of the tendon jerks). The reflex functions to oppose sudden changes in muscle length. 2. Static stretch reflex: Maintained weak passive stretch causes stretching of nuclear chain fibers leading to stimulation of 2ry endings. This results in maintained sub-tetanic contraction (Which is the basis of the muscle tone). Higher (Supraspinal) control of the stretch reflex: Supraspinal facilitatory centers (Which are normally predominant during rest) and supraspinal inhibitory centers, through the descending tracts, affect the activity of γ motor neurons. Therefore, the threshold of the reflex is changed. This changes the tone of various muscles to keep the posture of the body. Supraspinal Facilitatory centers include: 1. Facilitatory reticular formation (FRF) through the medial reticulospinal tract. 2. Vestibular nucleus (in medulla oblongata) through the medial and lateral vestibulospinal tracts. 3. Olive nucleus (in medulla oblongata). Supraspinal inhibitory centers include: 1. Inhibitory reticular formation (IRF) through the lateral reticulospinal tract. Premotor cortex, paleocerebellum and Corpus striatum influences the stretch reflex through descending control of spinal motor circuits. gamma efferent discharge can also be increased by: Anxiety, cutaneous painful stimulation and hooking of fingers together or clenching of teeth while eliciting tendon jerks (Jendrassik maneuver). Co-activation of α and γ motor neurons: stimulation of γ motor neurons cause the contractile ends of the intrafusal fibers to shorten and therefore stretches the nuclear bag portion of the spindles and initiating impulses in the Ia fibers. This in turn can lead to reflex contraction of the muscle. Thus, muscle can be made to contract via stimulation 5 of the α-motor neurons that innervate the extrafusal fibers or the γ motor neurons that initiate contraction indirectly via the stretch reflex. Therefore, Increased γ-motor neuron activity led to increase in spindle sensitivity during stretch. Signals from the motor cortex, or other areas, to α motor neurons cause simultaneous stimulation of γ motor neurons “α–γ coactivation,” so that both extrafusal and intrafusal muscle fibers shorten at the same time without contradiction and the muscle spindles remain stretched throughout the period of muscle contraction. text: 1 Inverse Stretch Reflex (Lengthening Reaction) Up to a point, the harder a muscle is stretched, the stronger is the reflex contraction. However, when the tension becomes great enough, contraction suddenly ceases, and the muscle relaxes. This relaxation in response to strong stretch is called the inverse stretch reflex or autogenic inhibition. It is a protective di -synaptic reflex due to stimulation of the inhibitory tendon tension receptors “Golgi Tendon Organs, G.T.O” Neural Pathway of inverse stretch reflex Receptors are Golgi tendon organ (GTO) located in tendons they are sensitive to muscle tension or the force of contraction , not length and activated during strong muscle contraction. The fibers from the Golgi tendon organs make up the Ib group of myelinated, rapidly conducting sensory nerve fibers. The group Ib afferents stimulate inhibitory interneurons in the spinal cord. These interneurons inhibit α -motoneurons and cause relaxation of the muscle that was originally contracted (homonymous). In addition, they stimulate an excitatory interneuron which stimulates the α motor neuron of the antagonistic muscles. Function of the inverse stretch reflex: 1- Prevents further increases in tension. 2- Prevents muscle rupture. L-25 SPINAL CORD REFLEXES PART -2- THE MOTOR UNIT ILOs By the end of this lecture, students will be able to 1. Describe inverse stretch reflex 2. Discuss flexor withdrawal reflex 3. Categorize neuronal circuits of spinal reflexes. 4. Classify types of motor units. 5. Describe hierarchy of motor control 2 3- Protects the tendon from being injured by too much tension. 4- Switch off movement and allow the muscle to relax. Clasp-knife reflex, an exaggerated form of the Golgi tendon reflex, can occur with disease of the corticospinal tracts (hypertonicity or spasticity). For example, if the arm is hypertonic, the increased sensitivity of the muscle spindles in the extensor muscles (triceps) cau ses resistance to flexion of the arm. Eventually, tension in the triceps increases to the point at which it activates the Golgi tendon reflex, causing the triceps to relax and the arm to flex closed like a jackknife The withdrawal (Flexor-Withdrawal) Reflex: Application of an injurious stimulus to a limb leads to contraction of the ipsilateral limb flexors withdrawing it away from the stimulus and extension on the contralateral side. This crossed extensor response is properly part of the withdrawal reflex; it is used to compensate for the extra load imposed by limb withdrawal on the antigravity extensor muscles of the opposite leg. Characteristics: It is a basic, protective, polysynaptic, superficial spinal reflex. It shows irradiation, a weak noxious stimulus to one foot evokes a minimal flexion response; stronger stimuli produce greater and greater flexion as the stimulus irradiates to more and more of the motor neuron pool supplying the muscles of the limb. Stronger stimuli also cause a more prolonged response. This prolonged response is due to prolonged, repeated firing of the motor neurons. The repeated firing is called after-discharge and is due to continued activation of motor neurons by impulses arriving by complicated and circuitous polysynaptic paths. 3 UPPER & LOWER MOTOR NEURONS Two groups of motor neurons are related to the performance of a motor act: Lower Motor Neurons (LMNs) and Upper Motor Neurons (UMNs). A) Lower Motor Neurons (LMNs): Those whose axons terminate on skeletal muscles: -Anterior horn cells (AHCs, anterior motor neurons) of the spinal cord and neurons in the cranial nerves motor nuclei. - They elicit coordinated & graded patterns of muscular contractions in both voluntary and involuntary movements. Their activity is modulated by UMNs. B) Upper Motor Neurons (UMNs): Neurons in cerebral cortex and brainstem with their axons. They rely on brain stem motor nuclei and spinal cord neurons; chiefly of the opposite side (They never innervate muscles directly). THE MOTOR UNIT It refers to one motor neuron and all the muscle fibers it innervates. It is considered as the smallest functional component of the motor system. Innervation ratio: The number of muscle fibers in each motor unit which ranges from 3 – 2000. In the antigravity muscles of the leg each motor unit tends to be quite large, with an innervation ratio of more than 1000 muscle fibers per single alpha motor neuron. In contrast, the smaller muscles that control the movement of the fingers and the rotation of the eyes are characterized by much smaller innervation ratios, as few as three muscle fibers per alpha motor neuron. 4 Types of the motor unit: The types of the motor unit can be distinguished by the properties of the muscle fiber and the firing characteristics of its LMN. Accordingly, motor units can be classified into: Recruitment of motor units: It means increasing the number of active motor units. The more motor units that are recruited, the greater the muscle force will be. During a voluntary movement, smallest ones are activated first, then fast fatigue-resistant and finally the fast fatigue units (The size principle). Recruiting an increased number of motor units generates the desired increased force of contraction. Motor pool The collection of alpha motor neurons that innervates a single muscle (e.g., the biceps brachii) is called a motor neuron pool There are two types of LMNs in the same motor pool: -⍺ -Motor neurons: larger and innervate the (extrafusal) muscles that generate the forces needed for movement and postural balance. -𝛾 -Motor neurons: Smaller and innervate the muscle spindle sensory receptors (intrafusal fibers). Their function is to regulate the tension of the muscle spindle. a- Large motor units: b- Small motor units: Large motoneurons. Small motoneurons. Innervate many muscle fibers. Innervate a few muscle fibers. -Have the highest thresholds. -Have the lowest thresholds. -Fire last. -Fire first. -Generate the largest force. -Generate the smallest force. 5 HIERARCHY OF MOTOR CONTROL Refers to the levels of the nervous system that cooperate to plan, initiate, and execute movement. Each level has a distinct role, but they interact continuously through feedback loops. Highest Level (Strategy / Planning) Middle Level (Tactics) Lowest Level (Execution) Structures involved: - Association cortex (prefrontal cortex, posterior parietal cortex) - Basal ganglia - Motor cortex (primary motor area, premotor cortex, supplementary motor area) - Cerebellum Brainstem motor centers (vestibular nuclei, reticular formation, red nucleus, tectum) Spinal cord (local circuits, motor neurons) Functions: -Decide what movement to make and why -Integration of sensory information with experience and motivation. -Selection of the best motor plan (e.g., reaching for a glass vs. waving). -Translate goals into tactics, the sequence, timing, and coordination of muscles. -Motor programs are generated (specific patterns of movement). -Cerebellum adjusts for accuracy, smoothness, and coordination -Direct activation of motor neurons. -Execution of refined movement programs. - Reflex integration and posture control. - Adjustment of force, speed, and muscle tone. References 1- Systems of the body, second edition- The nervous system 2- Hall JE. Guyton and Hall Textbook of Medical Physiology, 14th. Ed. Elsevier Saunders; 2021, Chapter 55. 3- Barrett K.E., & Barman S.M., & Brooks H.L., & Yuan J.J.(Eds.), Ganong's Review of Medical Physiology, (27th ed.). McGraw-Hill Education.

section: PBL 2 - Theme 3: Motor Control: Cerebrum, Brain Stem & Spinal Cord
name: L-26 NOTE 25/26
text: 1 The motor system is responsible for the initiation, control, and execution of voluntary movements. It consists of two major types of motor neurons: Upper and lowe r Motor Neurons. Each level of the nervous system, when affected by a lesion, gives rise to specific patterns of neurological deficits. Recognizing these distinct features is crucial for clinical diagnosis and determining the exact site of pathology. I- Upper Motor Neuron Lesions (UMNL) Damage to motor neurons originating in the motor cortex or descending tracts above the anterior horn cell (spinal cord) or cranial nerve motor nuclei (brainstem) • Causes: Mainly vascular, trauma, tumor and degenerative diseases. The most common site of the lesions is internal capsule commonly caused by vascular disorders. • Manifestations: Paralysis or muscle weakness - Usually on the opposite side of the lesion (due to crossing of the motor tracts). Usually widespread (pyramidal fibers form a compact bundle which occupies a small area). L-26 NERVOUS LESION ILOs By the end of this lecture, students will be able to 1. Explain the pathophysiological mechanisms underlying upper and lower motor neuron lesions 2. Identify characteristic clinical features of lesions at different levels 3. Define and classify spinal cord injury (SCI) 4. Recognize the clinical features of SCI at different levels 5. Localize a nervous system lesion based on clinical signs and symptoms 6. Interpret clinical scenarios based on understanding of different lesions. 2 Spasticity (increased muscle tone-clasp knife spasticity): Cause of spasticity: It is due to decreased inhibitory discharge from the inhibitory reticular formation (IRF) on the gamma efferent while the facilitatory discharge continues from the facilitatory reticular formation (FRF). Normally the FRF discharges spontaneously, possibly in response to afferent input like the reticular activating system, the IRF does not discharge spontaneously but is driven instead by fibers from the cerebral cortex. In UMNL there is interruption of the cortical discharge to the IRF which decreases its activity. Hence the balance between inhibition and facilitation shifts towards facilitation and the gamma efferent discharge is increased. Furthermore, the vestibulospinal tracts remain intact and they also have a facilitator y effect on muscle tone. 3. Increased (exaggerated) deep reflexes (Hyperreflexia): Due to the state of supraspinal facilitation that increases the activity of muscle spindle to stretch. 4. Clonus: (Ankle or knee clonus) This sign may be elicited. It means alternating regular rhythmic contractions and relaxations of a of spastic paralyzed muscle in response to sudden sustained stretch. Mechanism: It is the result of a stretch reflex - inverse stretch reflex sequence. When a muscle (e.g., ankle dorsiflexors) is suddenly stretched, muscle spindles are activated, leading to muscle contraction. The examiner’s-maintained pressure led to increased muscle tension and stimulation of GTO with relaxation of the muscle (inverse stretch reflex). As stretch is maintained a new stretch reflex occurs (helped by the state of excessive spinal facilitation). 5. Lost superficial reflexes: Superficial reflexes as the abdominal and cremasteric reflexes are lost because superficial reflexes receive facilitatory influence from the pyramidal tract. 3 5-Plantar reflex shows a positive Babinski sign : On eliciting the planter reflex, dorsiflexion of the big toe and fanning of the other toes occur. Babinski sign is a part of the spinal withdrawal reflex which in normal subject is inhibited by the corticospinal tract. 6 - Muscle status: There is no or little wasting in the affected muscles due to hypertonia. II- Lower Motor Neuron Lesions (LMNL) Lesions or damage to the lower motor neurons in the spinal ventral horns or to the corresponding motor nuclei of cranial nerves in the brain stem, or to their axons. Occurs mainly due to poliomyelitis or trauma to peripheral nerves. • Manifestations: -Paralysis: On the same side of the lesion which is localized. -Decreased tone ( hypotonia) or flaccidity of the affected muscles, due to cut of the stretch reflex arc. -Decreased or (absent) deep reflexes in the affected segment. -Plantar reflex: either normal or absent if the involved muscles are paralyzed. -Superficial reflexes: Lost in the affected segment (if they involve contraction of the denervated muscle). -Muscle status: There is marked wasting because the muscle is deprived of its motor supply. Signs of muscle denervation could be detected as Fasciculations (muscle twitches visible under the skin due to denervation of motor units) and Fibrillations (muscle potentials detected by electromyography in denervated muscles). Feature UMN Lesion LMN Lesion Weakness Muscle groups Individual muscles Tone ↑ (spastic) ↓ (flaccid) Reflexes ↑ (hyperreflexia, clonus) ↓ or absent Pathological reflexes Present (Babinski +) Absent Superficial reflexes Absent Absent Atrophy Mild (disuse) Severe (denervation) Fasciculations Absent Present 4 Spinal Cord Injury (SCI) Spinal cord injury is due to trauma, ischemia, infection, tumor, or degenerative disease. Trauma injuries are the most common. The clinical features depend on the level and extent of injury, leading to motor, sensory, and autonomic dysfunction. Types of Spinal Cord Injury Complete Cord Transection or incomplete as Hemisection of Cord (Brown -Séquard Syndrome) Complete transection of the spinal cord -Upper cervical region lesions (Above the level of C3) leads to immediate death due to respiratory arrest as in hanging. -Lower cervical lesions result in quadriplegia i.e., paralysis of the four limbs. Thoracic region lesions result in paraplegia i.e., paralysis of both lower limbs. Thoracic region lesions result in paraplegia i.e., paralysis of both lower limbs. • Stages: A- Spinal shock: When the transection is complete there is usually a period after the accident when all spinal reflexes below the level of the transection are reduced. This condition is known as spinal shock mainly due to Sudden withdrawal of tonic facilitatory influence from the brain. The duration of spinal shock is proportionate to the degree of encephalization of motor function in the various species, in dogs and cats it lasts for 1 to 2 h : and in humans it usually lasts for a minimum of 2 w eeks in the absence of any complications, but if complications are present, it is much longer. B- Stage of recovery: During this stage, spinal reflexes gradually return, often greatly exaggerated compared with normal which is described as stage of recovery. If complications are present the duration of spinal shock is much longer or even failure of recovery occurs. Complications 5 include urinary tract infection, malnutrition and decubitus ulcers. Therefore, adequate management of the paraplegic patient is very important to prevent the occurrence of complications. A- Stage of spinal shock • Manifestations: - Flaccid paralysis, areflexia, loss of all sensations below the lesion, loss of Bladder and bowl control (retention with overflow) and Loss of erection. - Drop of the arterial blood pressure if the transection is at the level of first thoracic segment, but slight drop occurs if the lesion is below the second lumber segment, due to block of the sympathetic activity. B- Stage of recovery • Manifestations: 1. Recovery of spinal reflexes as stretch reflex, they are often exaggerated compared with normal. 2. The spinal sympathetic vasoconstrictor centers in the lateral horn below the level of the transection regain their activity and send their impulses to the arterioles and veins, which regain tone. 3. Micturition and defecation become automatic as in children with residual urine due to weakness of the reflex. 4.
