name: L-24 NOTE 25/26
text: 1 L-24 MOTOR-OUTPUT & DESCENDING TRACT By the end of this lecture, students will be able to: • Deﬁne the terms upper motor neuron and lower motor neuron. • Name and describe the loca8ons and pathway of the main descending motor pathways. • Describe the mechanisms underlying decor8cate and decerebrate rigidity posturing. Movement is a composite of voluntary and involuntary motor ac8vity. Voluntary movement is mostly directed at the distal muscle groups, such as the complex movements of the hand. Involuntary movement involves mainly proximal and truncal muscle groups and is cri8cal for postural stability. The descending tracts are the pathways by which motor signals are sent from the brain to lower motor neurones. The lower motor neurones then directly innervate muscles to produce movement. The motor tracts can be func8onally divided into two major groups: • Pyramidal tracts – These tracts originate in the cerebral cortex, carrying motor ﬁbres to the spinal cord and brain stem. They are responsible for the voluntary control of the musculature of the body and face. • Extrapyramidal tracts – These tracts originate in the brain stem, carrying motor ﬁbres to the spinal cord. They are responsible for the involuntary and automa8c control of all musculatures, such as muscle tone, balance, posture and locomo8on At the termina8on of the descending tracts, the neurones synapse with a lower motor neurone. Thus, all the neurones within the descending motor system are classed as upper motor neurones. Their cell bodies are found in the cerebral cortex or the brain stem, with their axons remaining within the CNS. Fig 1 – Schema=c of the motor nervous system. 2 PYRAMIDAL TRACTS The pyramidal tracts derive their name from the medullary pyramids of the medulla oblongata, which they pass through. These pathways are responsible for the voluntary control of the musculature of the body and face. Func8onally, these tracts can be subdivided into two: • Cor=cospinal tracts – supplies the musculature of the body. • Cor=cobulbar tracts – supplies the musculature of the head and neck. Cor=cospinal Tracts The cor8cospinal tracts begin in the cerebral cortex, from which they receive a range of inputs: • Primary motor cortex • Premotor cortex • Supplementary motor area They also receive nerve ﬁbres from the somatosensory area, which play a role in regula8ng the ac8vity of the ascending tracts. -AMer origina8ng from the cortex, the neurones converge and descend through the internal capsule (a white maOer pathway, located between the thalamus and the basal ganglia). This is clinically important, as the internal capsule is par8cularly suscep8ble to compression from haemorrhagic bleeds, and vulnerable to stroke. Such an event could cause a lesion of the descending tracts. -AMer the internal capsule, the neurones pass through the crus cerebri of the midbrain, the pons and into the medulla. In the most inferior (caudal) part of the medulla, the tract divides into two: -The ﬁbres within the lateral cor=cospinal tract decussate (cross over to the other side of the CNS). They then descend into the spinal cord, termina8ng in the ventral horn (at all segmental levels). -The anterior cor=cospinal tract remains ipsilateral, descending into the spinal cord. They then then most of the ﬁbres decussate and terminate in the ventral horn of LMNs controlling trunk and proximal musculature. The innerva8on from the anterior cor8cospinal tract is oMen bilateral, that is, to both sides of the body Func=on: 1. The lateral cor8cospinal tract innervates LMN within the anterior horn. They are responsible for the innerva8on of the distal muscle groups for precise skilled movements. 2. The anterior cor8cospinal tract is important for ipsilateral postural adjustments when voluntary movements are performed with the contralateral extremity. 3 Cor=cobulbar Tracts - The cor8cobulbar tracts arise from the lateral aspect of the primary motor cortex. They receive the same inputs as the cor8cospinal tracts. The ﬁbres converge and pass through the internal capsule to the brainstem. -The neurones terminate on the motor nuclei of the cranial nerves. Here, they synapse with lower motor neurones, which carry the motor signals to the muscles of the face and neck. Many of these ﬁbres innervate the motor cranial nerve nuclei bilaterally, so, if one hemisphere is damaged, the other can s8ll provide some func8on. Excep8ons to this rule (mostly unilateral innerva8on):is Lower face muscles (lower half of facial nucleus) and hypoglossal nucleus. EXTRAPYRAMIDAL TRACTS The extrapyramidal tracts originate in the brainstem, carrying motor ﬁbres to the spinal cord. They are responsible for the involuntary and automa=c control of all musculatures, such as muscle tone, balance, posture and locomo8on. There are four tracts in total. The ves=bulospinal and re=culospinal tracts do not decussate, providing ipsilateral innerva8on. The rubrospinal and tectospinal tracts do decussate and therefore provide contralateral innerva8on. The medial brainstem pathways Ves=bulospinal Tracts There are two ves8bulospinal pathways; medial and lateral. They arise from the ves=bular nuclei, which receive input from the organs of balance. The tracts convey this balance informa8on to the spinal cord, where it remains ipsilateral. Fibres in this pathway control balance and posture by innerva8ng the ‘an8gravity’ muscles (ﬂexors of the arm, and extensors of the leg), via lower motor neurones. The Medial VST descends to the cervical and upper thoracic spinal cord and acts on interneurons that facilitate ac8vity in neck muscles and is responsible for stabilizing the head as we move our bodies The Lateral VST arises from the lateral ves8bular nucleus in the medulla and descends in the ventral funiculus to all levels of the spinal cord. Maintain balance by ac8ng on the extensor motor neurones to keep the centre of gravity between the feet. 4 Re=culospinal Tracts The pon8ne and medullary re8culospinal tracts project to all spinal levels, they descend mainly ipsilaterally to the spinal cord. They are involved in the maintenance of posture and in modula8ng muscle tone, especially via an input to γ -motor neurons. Pon8ne re8culospinal tract is primarily excitatory while medullary re8culospinal tract is primarily inhibitory. It also contains network of ﬁbers which comprise the emo8onal motor system that mediates the expression of emo8on. For example, an individual with depression will exhibit posture and body language diﬀerent from those of someone who is happy. Tectospinal Tracts This pathway begins at the superior colliculus of the midbrain. The superior colliculus is a structure that receives input from the op=c nerves. The neurones then quickly decussate and enter the spinal cord. They terminate at the cervical levels of the spinal cord. The tectospinal tract coordinates movements of the head in rela8on to vision, auditory and soma=c s=muli. Cross sec=on of the spinal cord showing pyramidal and extrapyramidal tracts The Lateral brainstem pathways: Rubrospinal Tracts The rubrospinal tract originates from the red nucleus, a midbrain structure. As the ﬁbres emerge, they decussate and descend into the spinal cord. Thus, they have a contralateral innerva8on. They inﬂuence motor neurons that control distal limb muscles, excites arm ﬂexors. In humans, the func8on of the rubrospinal tract is outweighed by the cor8cospinal pathway. Posturing in the Comatose Pa=ent In a comatose pa8ent, abnormal posturing is common because of the ac8vity of descending motor tracts. The type of posturing can give an indica8on of the loca8on of the lesion or the extent of the brain damage. text: 1 | Page Study Guide for course NMD2101: Neuroscience I Dr Course coordinator: Dr. Gehan Yassin Soliman Professor of Medical Physiology Contact information: gehanyassinsoliman@aast.edu 2 | Page INTRODUCTION TO MEDICAL PROFESSION YEAR 1 SEMESTER 1 STUDY GUIDE IN THIS Guide: • Welcome Note P. 3 • Educational Opportunities P.4-7 • Timetable link P. 8 -9 • Assessment P.10-11 • Learning Resources P. 12-13 3 | Page ! Dear students Welcome to Medical School. We hope you enjoy your 5 years' journey of becoming a physician. Here in the sixth course" Neurosciences I”, you will learn how to integrate smoothly between basic medical and clinical sciences, in a manner that will help you rationalize the clinical importance of the topics your study in the pre-clerkship phase. It consists of an extensive and in-depth study of the anatomical and functional aspects of central nervous system in order to understand the human brain & behavior. The aim of this course is to help you be acquainted with the gross and microscopic structural features of the brain, brain stem, basal ganglia and spinal cord. You will discover the miraculous physiology of synapses, neurotransmitters and mechanisms of neuronal excitation as well as the structure and functions of different receptors during neuronal excitation. You will discover the mechanisms and pathways of sensory inputs in the nervous system. You will explore the structure and functions of motor system and how can you maintain your posture. You will be surprised a lot about neuronal plasticity and memory types. You will realize the structure of skin and how you can feel pain. You will explore treatment of various cerebral dysfunctions such as Alzheimer's disease, Parkinson's disease and the uses of anti-seizure drugs in different clinical scenarios. We hope you enjoy your sixth block in your enjoyable long-life medical knowledge. 4 | Page IN THIS SECTION: • The different Course Themes • The Course Objectives • Different Teaching and Learning Methods EDUCATIONAL OPPORTUNITIES 5 | Page Through reviewing the following table, you will understand the Four major themes in Neuroscience I course and how these themes are related to the course objectives. You will also know which teaching method will be used to cover each theme. It is important for you to review the course objectives at the beginning of each week. Educational Strategy (Interactive Lecturing- Practical- Problem Based Learning- Tutorial- skills Sessions- self-directed learning- E-learning) Course Theme Course objectives Theme 1: General Organization of Head & Neck & CNS 1. Describe the different bones bounding the cranial cavity and the meninges. 2. Compare the basic organization of the peripheral and central nervous systems in relation to their primary functions. 3. Discriminate the activation and inhibition mechanism of action of different neurotransmitters on human body 4. Describe the triangles of the neck in relevance to their related structures, boundaries, and contents. 5. Appraise the anatomical-clinical importance of different structures of the neck. 6. Appraise the importance of identifying the level of termination of the spinal cord to different clinical disorders. 7 Appraise the congenital anomalies affecting the head & neck relative to their development. Theme 2: The Somatosensory System 8. Classify the receptors according to their structure and function with emphasis on skin structure and its receptors. 9. Appraise neurotransmission and the excitatory and inhibitory postsynaptic potential. 10.Differentiate sub-modalities of sensations in relation to somato-tropic map. EDUCATIONAL OPPORTUNITIES 6 | Page 11. Deduce types of pain, pathways for pain sensation and mechanisms of hypoalgesia and hyperalgesia. 12. Discuss spinal cord role in the gating of nociceptive transmission and the role of endorphins in central control of pain. 13. Determine principles of pain management, categories of analgesics and classification of opiate and non- opiate analgesics. Theme3: Motor Control: Cerebrum, Brain stem & Spinal cord 14. Appraise the functional and clinical correlation of different sulci & gyri and cortical areas. 15. Interpret the functional relation of different parts of the brain & spinal cord to its vascular supply. 16. Correlate microstructure of the cerebral cortex to its function 17. Define Brodmann areas for motor control and its clinical relevance to cortical injuries. 18. Deduce the causes and risk factors for different types of cerebral strokes and the patterns of brain damage caused by head injury. 19. Define the neuronal plasticity as a mechanism of memory, types of memory and the characteristics of each type. 20. Outline cortical areas for speech control and main types of aphasia. 21. Classify cranial nerves according to their function and clinical importance and the different functional components of their nuclei. 22. Delineate the neural pathways for monosynaptic& polysynaptic spinal cord reflexes. 23. Categorize neuronal circuits of spinal reflexes, types of motor units and the role of muscle tone in maintaining posture Theme 4: Motor Modulation: The Basal Ganglia 24. Distinguish between upper and lower motor neuron and the interconnections between them in health and disease. 25. Classify types of neuroglia according to their sites and function and components of the blood brain barrier. 26. Differentiate between types of white matter of the brain, the importance of internal capsule and relevant clinical conditions. 7 | Page 27. Describe the organization, connections and neurotransmitters of the basal ganglia and its related clinical disorders. 28. Compare neurodegenerative diseases to demyelinating CNS disorders (Alzheimer disease and multiple sclerosis) as regards etiology, pathogenesis, and clinical presentation 29. Deduce the treatment of various cerebral dysfunction such as Alzheimer's and Parkinson's diseases, chronic pain and anti-seizure drugs. 30. Appraise the importance of micro and macro nutrients to neuronal function in health and disease. Practical 31. Identify the anatomical structure of the skull, cranial cavity, triangles of the neck, vertebrae, brain, dural folds and spinal cord.) 32. Identify microscopically the layers of cerebrum, types of neurons, the skin and skin appendages. 33. text: L 9 Histology of the skin & sensory nerve endings Dr Rehab Ahmed Abdel- Moneim Professor of histology & cell biology SL A- Keratinocytes: 5 strata desquamating cells Process of keratinization ►►takes 15-30 days ►►desquamation of the horny layer Deduce structural features of each layer in relation to its function 1-Stratum basal ; high rate of mitosis & responsible for renewal of other cell layers. 2- Stratum spinosum; thickest layer, polyhedral cells still undergo mitosis. Keratin synthesis increases. Cells contain lamellated granules (membrane coating granules). Cells are interconnected by desmosomes (mechanical stability). A- Keratinocytes 3-Stratum granulosum (2 types of granules) ; Flat cells that contain: 1- K eratohyaline granules (packing of keratin filaments) and 2- L amellar granules (exocytosis of contents to form sheets of lipid rich material; ( water-proof barrier ). 4- Stratum Lucidum Only in thick skin. Cells lack organelles & nuclei; contain only keratin. 5- Stratum Corneum Flat dead cells that contain keratin only. Undergoes desquamation(fall out). A- Keratinocytes Non capable of keratin synthesis. Not attached to keratinocytes. 1- Melanocytes 2- Langerhans’ cells 3- Merkel cells Non-Keratinocytes 1- MELANOCYTES Site: In st. basale Function: Synthesis of melanin pigment. Melanin granules are injected into surrounding keratinocytes Between cell of stratum spinosum Multiple processes that extend to St granulosum. Motile cell Function Antigen presenting Role in hypersensitivity reactions 2-Langerhan cells Non-Keratinocytes 3- MERKEL CELLS In basal layer Large Attached to keratinocytes Function Sensory nerve ending contact basal surface of Merkel’s cell; Merkel cell neurite The neurite functions as a Receptor to light touch Non-Keratinocytes Sensory Nerve Endings What is a receptor? It is the specialized sensory nerve ending of a sensory nerve fiber. Each type of sensory nerve ending has a special structure and pattern at its termination in a specific site (skin, muscle & others). Classification of receptors Functionally Mechanoreceptors; Ex; Pacinian’s corpuscles, Meissner’s corpuscle, muscle spindle & Golgi tendon organs. Thermoreceptors Nociceptors (pain) Others rods & cones in the retina, gustatory cells in the taste bud & olfactory epithelium in the nose. What is the result of receptor stimulation? Generation of action potential along the sensory axon. Olfactory cells Gustatory cells Olfactory epithelium Taste Buds 1.Differentiate between microstructure of the skin layers 2. Classify sensory nerve endings on histological basis. 3. Correlate structure & site of different skin sensory nerve endings to their specific function. 4. Correlate microstructure of the muscle spindle & Golgi tendon organs to their functions. At the end of this lecture, the students should be able to: Structurally: 1- Encapsulated ; covered by a CT capsule 2- Non encapsulated; free nerve endings, Merkel’s disks Site Muscle spindle Golgi tendon organs Between skeletal muscle fibers near the tendon At junction between tendon & muscle Core Intrafusal muscle fibers Collagen fibers Function Stretch receptor ; monitors degree of muscle stretch (length) & induces reflex contraction Tension receptor; monitors force of contraction; induces reflex relaxation Encapsulated mechanoreceptors in the skeletal muscle 1- Muscle spindle 2- Golgi tendon organs 1- Structure of the muscle spindle 1- CT capsule ; separating it from the skeletal muscle fibers (extra fusal fibers) 2- Content; intrafusal fibers (modified muscle fibers) of two types: A- Nuclear chain ; cylindrical, uniform, nuclei are arranged in one row B- Nuclear bag (dynamic & static); swollen middle part that contains randomly oriented nuclei Both types lack myofibrils at their central (non contractile central parts) Peripheral portions contain myofibrils and are contractile CT cap Nuclear Bag Nuclear Chain 3- Innervation of the muscle spindle Gamma efferent Motor axons to peripheral zones of intrafusal fibers; to maintain them stretched and sensitive. Primary ( Ia ) afferent sensory axons that end by annulo spiral endings on all types of intra fusal fibers. Secondary II afferent sensory axons that end by flower spray endings on static type of nuclear bag fibers & nuclear chain Functional variation : Group Ia and group II fibers both respond to a stretching of the muscle at a constant rate. Only group Ia fibers , however, respond to a change in the rate of stretching. a b c Innervation of the muscle spindle 2- Golgi tendon organs Site: junction between tendon & muscle. Structure ; CT capsule, wavy collagen fibers (role of collagen). Innervation : sensory afferent axons only. B. Nail. C. Sebaceous glands. D. Sweat glands. To spread over a wide surface area to perceive pain more efficiently. 2- Thermoreceptors; penetrate the basal lamina & also gives branches parallel to the dermal epidermal junction. Pathway of sensations transmitted from skin receptors 1- Sensory receptor Action potential is generated in the axon hillock close to the sensory nerve ending 2- Pseudounipolar neurons central process synapses with sensory neurons in the spinal cord 1 2 3 To sum up Keratinocytes are represented in 4-5 stages with structural differences. text: Cranial cavity Prof. Dr. Abdelghany Hassan Abdelghany Professor of Anatomy and Embryology Faculty of Medicine Alexandria University Middle cranial fossa It is formed by body of sphenoid, its greater wing and the petrous part of temporal bone. The sella turcica is formed of tuberculum sellae , hypophyseal fossa and dorsum sellae that expands into the posterior clinoid processes. It shows : superior orbital fissure, foramen rotundum , foramen ovale and foramen spinosum and foramen lacerum . Posterior cranial fossa It shows the clivus and dorsum sellae . The internal occipital crest extends from the internal occipital protuberance. Transverse sulcus continues as sigmoid sulcus. Foramen magnum lies inferiorly with the hypoglossal canal, jugular foramen and internal acoustic meatus above it in order. Q: Which foramen lies in the posterior cranial fossa? Foramen ovale . Foramen cecum. Jugular foramen. Foramen rotundum . Answer : C Cranial cavity Brain 1- cerebrum. 2- cerebellum. 3- brain stem (midbrain, pons and medulla). Meninges Outer layer; dura mater. Middle layer; arachnoid mater . Inner layer; pia mater. Meninges 1- Extradural (epidural) space : outside the dura mater. 2- subdural space : deep to the dura mater . 3- subarachnoid space : deep to the arachnoid mater . It contains CSF. Dural folds They project into the cranial cavity and partially subdivide it. They include the falx cerebri , tentorium cerebelli , falx cerebelli , and diaphragma sellae . Cranial cavity Falx cerebri A sickle-shaped dural fold, extends between the 2 cerebral hemispheres. It is attached anteriorly to the crist gali and frontal crest and posteriorly to the tentorium cerebelli . Dear students & Falx cerebelli It lies between the 2 cerebellar hemispheres. It is attached to the internal occipital crest and superiorly to the tentorium cerebelli . Tentorium cerebelli A tent-shaped fold, extends between the 2 cerebral hemispheres and the 2 cerebellar hemispheres. It has an outer attached border and an inner free border. Tentorium cerebelli Attached border : to posterior clinoid processes, dorsum sellae , upper border of petrous bone, transverse sulci and internal occipital protuberance. Tentorium cerebelli Free border : is attached to anterior clinoid processes. It bounds the tentorial notch through which the midbrain passes. Q: To which structure is the free border of tentorium cerebelli attached? Anterior clinoid process. Transverse sulcus. Posterior clinoid process. Internal occipital protuberance. Answer : A Diaphragma sellae - It is attached to the anterior and posterior clinoid processes. - It overlies the pituitary gland and is pierced by the infundibulum. Dural venous sinuses Single Paired Superior sagittal Sphenoparietal Inferior sagittal Cavernous Straight Superior petrosal Occipital Inferior petrosal Intercavernous Transverse Sigmoid Superior sagittal sinus It begins at foramen cecum (receives an emissary vein through foramen cecum). It passes along the upper border of falx cerebri . It ends as right transverse sinus. Inferior sagittal sinus It passes along the lower border of falx cerebri It joins the great cerebral vein to form the straight sinus. straight sinus It lies in the line of junction of falx cerebri and tentorium cerebelli . At the internal occipital protuberance, it ends as left transverse sinus. Transfer Goal This lecture aims to explain the cranial cavity, meninges of the brain and dural folds with the related venous sinuses. Transverse sinus Right transverse sinus is larger than the left. It runs along the transverse sulcus in the attached margin of tentorium cerebelli . - It continues as sigmoid sinus. Sigmoid sinus A continuation of the transverse sinus. It runs in the sigmoid sulcus and continues through jugular foramen as internal jugular vein. Superior petrosal sinus It lies along the upper border of the petrous part of temporal bone in the attached margin of tentorium cerebelli . It begins at the cavernous sinus. It ends in the corresponding transverse sinus. Inferior petrosal sinus It lies along the lower border of the petrous part of temporal bone. It begins at the cavernous sinus. It passes through jugular foramen to end in the internal jugular vein. Sphenoparietal sinus It lies along the lesser wing of sphenoid. It ends in the cavernous sinus. Cavernous sinus Site : on either side of the sella turcica . Tributaries : veins from the cerebrum, orbit, face, sphenoparietal sinus. Drainage : into the superior and inferior petrosal sinuses. Cavernous sinus Connections : 1- orbit . 2- face . 3- opposite cavernous sinus by intercavenous sinuses. Therefore, extracranial infections may pass to the cranial cavity through these connections. Cavernous sinus Structures inside the sinus : internal carotid artery and abducent (6 th cranial) nerve. Structures in the lateral wall : 1- occulomotor (3 rd cranial) nerve. 2- trochlear (4 th cranial ) nerve. 3- ophthalmic (branch of 5 th cranial ) nerve. 4- maxillary (branch of 5 th cranial) nerve . Cavernous sinus Cavernous sinus thrombosis : Due to infection of the face or eye. Patients complain of swelling and redness of the eye, double vision and sever headache. Q: Which structure continues as the right transverse sinus? Straight sinus. Superior sagittal sinus. Inferior sagittal sinus. Superior petrosal sinus. Answer : B Students’ learning outcomes By the end of this lecture, students will be able to 1. Relate different bones bounding the cranial cavity to the important structures passing through. 2. Describe the different layers of the meninges and specify their related spaces. 3. Describe the dural folds and correlate them to common relevant clinical conditions. 4. Differentiate between the dural venous sinuses regarding their site and termination. Summary or take-home message The cranial cavity overlies the nasal cavity and the two orbits and its floor has anterior, middle and posterior cranial fossae. The meninges are the coverings of the brain and the outer layer ( dura mater) gives dural fold that separate the cranial cavity into compartments. The dural venous sinuses drain the brain. There are single and paired sinuses that eventually end in the internal jugular vein. The cavernous sinus is connected with the orbit and face so that extracranial infections may be transmitted to the cranial cavity. Lecture notes. Gray’s Anatomy for Students. Dear Student: Don’t forget to complete your KWL chart And reflect on your learning experience by writing down what do you learnt from the lecture (3 points at least) Q: A patient came to the ER complaining of sever headache, diplopia, redness and swelling of one eye. He told the physician that few days ago, he had a boil in the upper lip that became inflamed and septic. What is the most probable diagnosis? Skull a nterior view posterior view side view Cranial cavity Anterior cranial fossa It forms the roof of the nasal cavity and the 2 orbits. It is formed by : Anterior : cribriform plate of ethmoid in the middle and orbital plate of frontal bone on each side. Posterior : body of sphenoid in the middle and lesser wing of sphenoid on each side. orbital plate of frontal bone forms the roof of the orbit. Anterior cranial fossa The frontal bone shows frontal crest and foramen cecum lies behind it. The cribriform plate of ethmoid bone shows the crista gali . The lesser wing of sphenoid ends medially in the anterior clinoid process. Medial to the process, lies the optic canal. orbital plate of frontal bone forms the roof of the orbit.

name: PPT: L 10- 2026-  PPT SENSORY RECEPTORS
text: SENSORY NERVOUS SYSTEM SENSORY RECEPTORS BY GEHAN YASSIN SOLIMAN-ABEER ELEMAM PROFESSOR OF MEDICAL PHYSIOLOGY- ALEXANDRIA UNIVERSITY, EGYPT INTENDED LEARNING OBJECTIVES (ILOS): 1. Classify receptor by sensory modality 2. Describe principle of neurotransmission 3. Appraise the excitatory and inhibitory postsynaptic potential and their summation 4. Explain how the nervous system is adapted to determine the locality, modality, and intensity of stimulation. 5. Compare between receptor potential and action potential THE SENSORY RECEPTORS • Specialized structures at the peripheral ends of sensory neurons, and they may be a part of it or a separate organ. • Excitable structures FUNCTIONS OF RECEPTORS: detectors transducers maintain homeostasis. compressors PROPERTIES OF SENSORY RECEPTORS: • Differential sensitivity (SPECIFICITY) • Transduction of sensory stimulation into nerve impulses. Local electrical current at the nerve endings- receptor potentials: (EXCITABILITY) • ADAPTATION PROPERTIES OF SENSORY RECEPTORS: 1- DIFFERENTIAL SENSTIVITY : ➢Each respond to adequate stimulus to particular sensation. ➢But can respond to inadequate stimuli and give the same sensation MULLER'S LAW: Each receptor is most sensitive to one specific type of stimulus called its adequate stimulus giving rise to one type of sensation regardless of the method of stimulation because the sensation perceived depends on the area in the brain ultimately activated. (specific projection). PROPERTIES OF SENSORY RECEPTORS: 2- RECEPTOR POTENTIALS : PROPERTIES OF SENSORY RECEPTORS: 2- RECEPTOR POTENTIALS : PROPERTIES OF SENSORY RECEPTORS: 2- PROPERTIES (CHARACTERISTICS) OF RECEPTOR POTENTIALS : It does NOT obey to all or none law, so it can be graded It is NOT followed by ARP and its duration is long (about 5 milliseconds) so it can be summated It is NOT blocked by local anesthetic drugs PROPERTIES OF SENSORY RECEPTORS: 3- RECEPTOR ADAPTATION : when a continuous sensory stimulus is applied, the receptor responds at a high impulse rate at first and then at a progressively slower rate until finally the rate of action potentials decreases to very few or often to none at all. In all receptors PROPERTIES OF SENSORY RECEPTORS: 3- RECEPTOR ADAPTATION MECHANISM: o by changing the concentrations of their lightsensitive chemicals e.g.cones and rods. In the Pacinian corpuscle: o Readjustment in the structure of the receptor itself' after its initial distortion o Slowly by accommodation of the nerve fiber, due to progressive “inactivation” of the sodium channels in the nerve fiber membrane ACCORDING TO THEIR ADEQUATE STIMULUS: • Mechanoreceptors • Touch, pressure and vibration receptors • Proprioceptors • Baroreceptors • Stretch receptors. • Thermoreceptors • Osmoreceptors. • Chemoreceptors. • Nociceptors, or pain receptors • Photoreceptors • Some sensations are compound sensations “wetness receptor.” TYPES AND CLASSIFICATION OF RECEPTORS TYPES AND CLASSIFICATION OF RECEPTORS ACCORDING TO LOCALITY • Exteroceptors: o Cutaneous receptors o Vision, hearing, taste and smell • Interceptors oProprioceptors oVisceroceptors: baroreceptors, chemoreceptors, visceral stretch receptors & pain oHypothalamic receptors: glucoreceptors, Osmoreceptors, hypothalamic thermoreceptors TYPES AND CLASSIFICATION OF RECEPTORS ACCORDING TO RATE OF ADAPTATION: • Slowly Adapting “Tonic” Receptors. • Slowly adapting receptors continue to transmit impulses to the brain as long as the stimulus is present • muscle stretch receptors, • receptors of the vestibular apparatus, • pain receptors • baroreceptors • chemoreceptors Rapidly Adapting “Phasic Receptors.” Receptors that adapt rapidly • they are stimulated only when the stimulus strength changes. • EX: Pacinian corpuscle, CODING OF SENSORY INFORMATION This is the ability of the nervous system to discriminate the modality,locality and intensity of various sensations, although all sensations are transmitted to the higher centers in the same form of action potentials. CODING OF SENSORY INFORMATION MODALITY DISCRIMINATIO N - THE “LABELED LINE” PRINCIPLE • Each nerve tract terminates at a specific point in the CNS, where a specific type of sensation is percieved what ever the type of stimulation • modality of sensation is called the labeled line principle. Each sensory pathway (from the receprors till the termination at the higher centres) is labeled for a specific sensation CODING OF SENSORY INFORMATION LOCALLITY DISCRIMINATIO N - THE “LAW OF PROJECTION” • It depends on the spceifie pathway of that sensation. When this pathway is stimulated any where along its course, the evoked sensation is projected to (i.e. referred to) the location of its receptors. (phantom limb).

text: By Abeer El-Emam Professor of Physiology- Alexandria Faculty of Medicine L12: Physiology of Pain STUDENTS’ LEARNING OUTCOMES At the end of this session, the student should be able to; 1. Identify types of pain and how it is perceived via pain receptors 2. Distinguish pathways for pain sensations 3. Describe the peripheral and central mechanisms of hyperalgesia 4. Discuss referred pain and its mechanism 5. Explain peripheral and central sensitization 6. Define neuropathic pain and its main causes 9/26/2025 2 WHAT IS PAIN? Pain could be defined as ( unpleasant sensory and emotional experience associated with actual or potential tissue damage ) Pain from poena --- > Latin means punishment . It is uniquely experienced by each individual ; it cannot be adequately defined, identified, or measured by an observer . 9/26/2025 3 Pain threshold and P ain tolerance The pain threshold: Is the point at which a stimulus is perceived as pain. The pain tolerance: Is expressed as duration of time or the intensity of pain that an individual can sustain before initiation of pain responses. 9/26/2025 4 • Pain tolerance is generally decreased : - with repeated exposure to pain, - by fatigue, anger, sleep deprivation • Tolerance to pain may be increased : - by alcohol consumption, medication, hypnosis, - distracting activities, - strong beliefs or faith Pain tolerance varies greatly among people and in the same person over time. A decrease in pain tolerance is also evident in the elderly, and women appear to be more tolerant to pain than men . Pain threshold and p ain tolerance 9/26/2025 5 A. Transduction of Pain B. Conduction & Transmission of Pain C. Perception of Pain D. Modulation of Pain STAGES & STEPS OF PAIN SIGNALING & PROCESSING Nocicepto r 9/26/2025 6 PAIN RECEPTORS 9/26/2025 7 Pain is termed nociceptive (nocer – to injure or to hurt in Latin), and nociceptive means sensitive to noxious stimuli. Nociceptors are sensory receptors that detect signals from damaged tissue and also respond to chemicals released from the damaged tissue. Nociceptors are free (bare) nerve endings found in the skin, muscle, joints, bone and viscera. They transduce a variety of noxious stimuli into receptor potentials, which in turn initiate action potential in the pain nerve fibers. No nociceptors are found inside the CNS. Pain Receptors 9/26/2025 8 ➢ Divided into four categories based on function: 1. High threshold mechano-nociceptors or specific nociceptors. (mechanical stimulation such as pinching, cutting or stretching). 2. Thermal nociceptors, (thermal stimuli). 3. Chemical nociceptors, (chemical substances). 4. Polymodal nociceptors, which respond to high intensity stimuli such as mechanical, thermal and to chemical substances like the previous three types. Pain Receptors 9/26/2025 9 Factors that Activate Nociceptors Nociceptors respond when a stimulus causes tissue damage. The damage of tissue results in a release of a variety of substances from lysed cells as well as from new substances synthesized at the site of the injury. These substances include: - Globulin and protein kinases: which are believed to be one of the most active pain-producing substances. - Arachidonic acid. Arachidonic acid is one of the chemicals released during tissue damage. It is then metabolized into prostaglandin (and cytokines). - Histamine. Tissue damage stimulates the mast cells to release histamine to the surrounding area. 9/26/2025 10 - Nerve growth factor (NGF)). - Substance P (SP) and calcitonin gene-related peptide (CGRP) are released by injury. - Potassium - K+. Most tissue damage results in an increase in extracellular K+. - Serotonin (5-HT), acetylcholine (ACh), low pH (acidic) solution, and ATP. - Muscle spasm and lactic acid. When muscles are hyperactive or when blood flow to a muscle is blocked, lactic acid concentration increases, and pain is induced. 9/26/2025 11 • pain producing substance 9/26/2025 12 Therefore, Non-steroidal anti-inflammatories, are effective in minimizing pain because they minimize the effects of these substances released, especially prostaglandins (blocking cyclo- oxygenase enzyme COX). 9/26/2025 13 Pain Fibers A delta fibers (group III fibers) 2-5 mm in diameter, myelinated, have a fast conduction velocity (5- 40 meters/sec), and carry information mainly from the nociceptive-mechanical or mechano-thermal nociceptors. Their receptive fields are small. Therefore, they provide precise localization of pain.. C fibers (group IV fibers) 0.4-1.2 mm in diameter unmyelinated have a slow conduction velocity (0.5-2.0 meters/sec) activated by a variety of high- intensity mechanical, chemical and thermal stimulation and carry information from polymodal nociceptors Their receptive fields are large . Therefore, less precise for pain localization. 9/26/2025 14 9/26/2025 15 Double pain sensations Pricking-fast pain ❑ caused by a needle, pin prick, skin cut, ❑ sharp, pricking quality, ❑ carried fast by the A delta fibers ❑ transmitted along rapidly conducting thin myelinated A-δ fibers, ❑ short duration, ❑ precisely localized. ❑ Carried by neo-spinothalamic tract Slow-Burning-soreness pain ❑ caused by inflammation, burned skin, ❑ It is an annoying pain and intolerable pain, ❑ transmitted by the slowly conducting unmyelinated C-fibres ❑ long duration, ❑ poorly localized, diffuse ❑ transmitted by the paleo-spinothalamic tract, ❑ arises mainly from the viscera and somatic deep structures. 9/26/2025 16 TYPES OF PAIN 1. Nociceptive (acute pain) 2. Chronic pain 3. Neuropathic 9/26/2025 17 • Elicited by a brief noxious stimulus such as pin-prick • Induces a flexion withdrawal response to the stimulus • Protect the body from injury • Of limited duration, mediated mainly by A delta fibers • Caused by damage to muscle, bone, joint • Superficial or deep Nociceptive pain 9/26/2025 18 • Considered “bad pain” because it persists long after recovery from an injury • often refractory to common analgesic agents, • Chronic pain which results from nerve injury is known as neuropathic pain. Chronic pain 9/26/2025 19 • Longer duration than acute pain • Resistant to treatment • In prolonged pain (e.g. sunburn) injury to the body has already occurred and the biological function of pain is to prevent further damage, assist healing and tissue repair. • It does this by the development of areas of hypersensitivity in and around the injury site, which are the result of a decreased activation threshold of nociceptors–a phenomenon called peripheral sensitization. • The pain recedes once healing has occurred. Chronic pain 9/26/2025 20

name: PPT: 2026 L 13-   Pain control
text: By Abeer El-Emam Professor of Physiology- Alexandria Faculty of Medicine L13- Pain Control mechanisms By the end of this lecture, you should be able to: 1. Discuss spinal cord role in the gating of nociceptive transmission. 2. Interpret how nociceptive transmission can be modulated 3. Discuss role of endorphins versus other transmitters in central control of pain 4. Identify location and functions of the endogenous analgesic centers. PAIN MODULATION The transmission of information from pain afferents to secondary neurons in the spinal cord is NOT A PASSIVE process but is dynamic involving excitation, inhibition and modulation. Neurons in the dorsal horn are subject to modulation that gates the flow of information to the CNS. Modulation occurs at different levels, Local—’segmental antinociception’ regulated by primary afferent inputs. - at the spinal cord level at a higher level using the descending pathways from the brainstem PAIN CONTROL MECHANISM AT THE LEVEL OF SPINAL CORD GATE CONTROL THEORY Ronald Melzack, a Canadian researcher 1965; (gate theory for pain control) asserts that; non-painful input closes the "gates" to painful input, which prevents pain sensation from traveling to the CNS. Therefore, stimulation by non-noxious input is able to suppress pain. Without any stimulation, both sets of nerve fibres are inactive, and the inhibitory neurone (I) blocks the signal in the projection neurone (P). The gate is ‘closed’ Normal somatosensory input happens when there is more large-fiber stimulation (or only large-fiber stimulation). both the inhibitory neuron and the projection neuron are stimulated, but the inhibitory neuron prevents the projection neuron from sending signals to the brain (gate is closed). Nociception (pain reception) happens when there is more small-fiber stimulation or only small-fiber stimulation. They activate P and inactivates the inhibitory neuron. Therefore, the projection neuron sends signals to the brain informing it of pain (gate is open). gate opened gate closed IN OTHER WORDS Certain neurons of the dorsal horn, which project an axon up the spinothalamic tract, are excited by both large diameter sensory axon and unmyelinated pain axons. The projection neuron is also inhibited by an interneuron. The interneuron is both excited by the large sensory axon and inhibited by the pain axon. Therefore, activity in the pain axon alone maximally excites the projection neuron, allowing nociceptive signals to rise to the brain. However, if the large mechanoreceptive axon fires concurrently, it activates the interneurons and suppresses nociceptive signals. COUNTER-STIMULATION ANALGESIA •Trauma elicits acute pain. However, if the injury site is rubbed, the pain immediately subsides, and it feels better. •RUBBING stimulates the non- nociceptive afferents that send impulses into the spinal cord. •According to the gate theory, inhibitory interneurons are activated either directly or indirectly by stimulation of these afferents from the skin that would then block the projection neuron and therefore block the pain. • Acupuncture • gentle rubbing • Massage • electrical stimulation Supraspinal (descending) analgesia Brain regions that are involved in pain modulation project back to the brainstem and spinal cord and can change or modify information that is coming to the brain. This is one way that the brain can reduce pain ENKEPHALIN NE SEROTONIN ENKEPHALIN Analgesic system at the level of the brain - Periaqueductal gray matter (PAG) surrounding the cerebral aqueduct in the midbrain (enkephalinergic neuron) - Nucleus raphe magnus (NRM), in lower pons and upper medulla (serotonergic neuron) - Dorsal raphe (DR), caudate nucleus (CN), septal nucleus (Spt) - Periventricular nuclei in hypothalamus (endorphin neurons) - locus coeruleus (LC) (NE) They can exert this inhibition by different mechanisms: Direct presynaptic inhibition of neurotransmitter release from primary afferent terminals. This works by activating G protein- linked receptors that cause closing of calcium channels, thus reducing transmitter release Direct postsynaptic inhibition of projection cells causing hyperpolarization of the membrane due to activation of G protein-linked receptors that cause opening of potassium channels it seems likely that opiate drugs may act by mimicking the activity of the interneurones of lamina II. • Provides a strong modulatory influence on pain processing. • Opioid receptors can be found at all levels of the pain system. • The powerful analgesic effect of opiate drugs is likely due to the fact that they influence the pain system at every level (mainly on peripheral nerves,at the site of an injury; in the dorsal horn and in the brain stem). Endogenous Opioids Opioid receptors μ-mu β-endorphins δ-delta enkephalins κ-kappa. dynorphins Endogenous Opioids Opioidergic neurotransmission is found throughout the brain and spinal cord. Activation of these receptors results in inhibition of voltage-gated Ca2+ channels and/or the opening of K+ channels, which results in hyperpolarization and less neuronal Excitability. Analgesia may be produced in certain stressful situations. Exposure to a variety of painful or stressful events produces an analgesic reaction. For example, soldiers wounded in battle or athletes injured in sports events sometimes report that they do not feel pain during the battle or game; however, they will experience the pain later after the battle or game has ended. It has been suggested that endogenous opiates are released in response to stress and inhibit pain by activating the midbrain descending system. Stress-Induced Analgesia (SIA)

text: L11: Somatic Sensations- Ascending pathways-1 Dr. Eman Helmy Thabet - Dr. Norhan Sobhy Medical Physiology department - Alexandria Faculty of Medicine ILOs 1. Differentiate different sub-modalities of sensations with their central termination of the pathways. 2. Describe the pathway of the main sensory pathways and its injury 3. Solve clinical scenarios based on understanding different levels of lesion Somatic sensations These are sensations from the skin and deeper structures (muscles, bones, tendons and joints). • According to their nature, somatic sensations are classified into: A. Mechanoreceptive sensations B. Thermoreceptive sensations C. Pain sensations A. Mechanoreceptive sensations • Results from stimulation of mechanoreceptors and include: 1. Light touch 2. Tactile discrimination 3. Pressure sensation 4. Vibration sense 5. Proprioceptive sensations B. Thermoreceptive sensations • Cutaneous thermoreceptors are specialized free nerve endings, found with highest density in the skin of the hands and face. • They help to maintain constant body temperature despite changes in environmental temperature. • They monitor skin temperature not body temperature and detect changes in external environmental temperature. B. Thermoreceptive sensations • Thermoreceptors include: ✓Cold receptors ✓warmth (heat) receptors Thermal nociceptors are activated by skin temperatures above 45 °C or by severe cold. Cold receptors Warmth receptors A delta fibers and C fibers C fibers more less Sensitive to temperatures between 10° and 35°C and are normally silent above 40°C. The threshold for activation of warmth receptors is 30 °C N.B. Below that temperature, they are inactive, and the cold becomes an effective local anaesthetic C. Pain sensation: • Resulting from stimulation of nociceptors. The somatosensory system • These modalities may or may not reach consciousness. They travel in different ascending pathways that are located in specific areas of the spinal cord white matter and terminate in specific areas of the brain. • There are three important pathways that run the entire length of the spinal cord The somatosensory system pathway consists of four neurons. cross to the contralateral side: Decussate .Point of decussation is important. Runner 1 Runner 2 Neuron 1 Neuron 2 /Brainstem Runner 2 Runner 3 Neuron 1 Neuron 2 Neuron 3 Thalamus Cortex Neuron 4 The dorsal column medial lemniscus (DCML) pathway • Sensation conveyed: 1. Touch (discriminative-light touch) 2. The perception of vibration and perception of pressure(weight discrimination) 3. Enables us to ‘read’ Braille letters or numbers GRAPHESTHESIA, and describe the shape and texture of an object without seeing it STEREOGNOSIS. 4. Conscious Proprioception • Somatotopically organized. • Nerve fibres : mediated by Aa/B fibres The dorsal column medial lemniscus (DCML) pathway First order neuron (dorsal root ganglion): The primary afferents Fibers enter the spinal cord and ascend ipsilaterally in the dorsal column to the medulla, on the same (ipsilateral) side of the cord. Somatotopic organization • Afferents from the lower limbs and trunk travel more medially in the gracile funiculus, and afferents from the upper limb travel more laterally, in the cuneate fasciculus, to their respective nuclei in the medulla. The extent to which a body part is represented in SI is related to its sensory acuity, not to its size. Somatotopic organization Second order neuron (gracile and cuneate nuclei): After synapsing in the dorsal column nuclei, the secondary neurons cross in the medulla and ascend as the medial lemniscus to the thalamus, where they synapse in the ventroposterior (VP) nucleus. In the VP nucleus, the head is represented medially and the rest of the body laterally. The dorsal column medial lemniscus (DCML) pathway Third order neuron (ventral posterolateral nucleus of the thalamus): Finally, information ascends from the thalamus to the primary somatosensory cortex (SI) in the postcentral gyrus The dorsal column medial lemniscus (DCML) pathway Lesions to the posterior columns is associated with: 1. loss of discriminative touch, vibration 2. Difficulty in identifying objects by touch (astereognosis) 3. Sensory ataxia (due to lack of proprioceptive feedback) 4. Positive Romberg sign: Patient sways or falls when eyes are closed (loss of proprioception) The ventrolateral system: pain and temperature ➢This system comprises several pathways that ascend in the ventrolateral part of the spinal cord and relay information to: • Thalamus: spinothalamic tract. • midbrain: spinomesencephalic tract. • reticular formation: spinoreticular tract. • Brain stem nuclei: spinobulbar tract.

text: L11 : Ascending pathways and somatosensory cortex Eman Helmy Thabet MD PhD Lecturer of Medical Physiology Alexandria Faculty of Medicine Fulbright Scholar at UCSF-USA modified by Dr. Abeer Abed Ahmed Professor of Physiology- axons responsible for the unconscious proprioception leave the white matter and synapse in Clarke’s nucleus (nucleus dorsalis 1 st order neurons 2 nd order neurons Enter the dorsal SCBT on the lateral edge of the cord. Ascends WITHOUT crossing to the cerebellum and is also somatotopically organized. terminate on Purkinje cells--  relay the information --  deep cerebellar nuclei---  other motor areas of the thalamus, brainstem and basal ganglia. Clarke’s column only extends from T1 to L1, it only carries information from the lower body and trunk. 3rd order neurons Topographic organizations of the sensory tracts and clinical significance The dorsal column medial lemniscus (DCML) system is very orderly, fibers and cells carrying information from one part of the peripheral receptive surface maintain their positions relative to fibers and cells representing neighboring parts of the receptive surface. Thus, different parts of the body are represented in an orderly sequence in the tracts and nuclei of the DCML system. Topographic organizations of the sensory tracts and clinical significance This orderly arrangement of cells and fibers is called topographical organization. For the somatosensory system, it is usually called somatotopic organization. precise spatial arrangement whereby neurons in a sensory receptor surface (e.g., retina, cochlea, or skin) connect to corresponding neurons in central nervous system structures, preserving neighborhood relationships. Topographic organizations of the sensory tracts and clinical significance This is of clinical relevance when an injury or disease affects specific relay pathways If the problem occurs within the spinal cord, such as in syringomyelia (central cavitation within the spinal cord originating at the central canal) syringomyelia it is common at the cervical spinal cord level. it interrupts the STT bilaterally resulting in loss of pain and temperature sensation below the level of the lesion, particularly in the hands.) the cervical dermatomes will be affected first, and the lower body is less affected. Summary of somatosensory pathways The three main ascending somatosensory pathways each carry a specific modality of sensation associated with specific receptors. Each pathway is somatotopically organized , so that a complete representation of the body is reproduced in each relay nucleus along the pathway. Any sensory system going to the cerebral cortex will have to cross over at some point, because the cerebral cortex operates on a contralateral basis. Summary of somatosensory pathways The discriminative touch system crosses in the medulla, and the pain system crosses in the spinal cord. The proprioceptive system ascends to the cerebellum and does not cross. There is some overlap of modalities between the ascending tracts: some light touch information travels in the STT, so that lesion in the dorsal column does not completely abolish touch and pressure sensation; similarly, visceral pain fibers travel in the dorsal columns and not the STT. The cortex can also be divided into areas that have a single function, such as touch, vision, hearing, taste and smell or the production of movement. These are called primary areas . Their function is to receive and start the initial processing of information. The rest of the cortex is association cortex, which provides higher-order processing of sensory and motor information. The forebrain comprises the largest part of the brain (80% by volume) and consists of the cerebral cortex, the limbic system, and the basal ganglia. Functionally it is divided into: I. Somatosensory areas. II. Motor areas. III. Prefrontal association area. IV. Language areas. CEREBRAL CORTEX Somatosensory cortex (sensory areas of the brain ) The primary somatosensory cortex is composed of the postcentral gyrus of the parietal lobe on each side of the brain it includes: 1- The (primary) somatosensory area I (S1) 2-The (secondary) somatosensory association area. Transfer goal To understand how sensation gets transmitted , perceived, and analyzed from the peripheral system to the CNS via ascending sensory pathways. Characteristic of S1 location :in the postcentral gyrus (Brodmann's areas 1,2 and 3). Body representation of S 1. 1-Crossed 2-Inverted but the face is not inverted 3-Foot and leg are represented medially, and the trunk, chest, arm and hand are represented more lateral in the middle of the postcentral gyrus. 4-The face is represented in the lower half of the postcentral gyrus. Characteristic of S1 The different parts of the body are not equally represented, the size of the area of representation is determined by the number of receptors of that part. The exaggerated size of the face, tongue, and hands indicates the high degree of sensory perception associated with these body parts. This area shows modality separation of different sensations Somatotopic maps in the SI cortex The extent to which a body part is represented in SI is related to its sensory acuity, not to its size. Somatosensory acuity 1- it is the ability to distinguish fine detail by touch 2-directly related to the amount of neural tissue devoted to the representation of a body Part 3-the greater the peripheral innervation density, the smaller the receptive fields of the innervating neurons, and the larger the volume of the cortex representing that region. , The ability to perform point localization two-point discrimination Is best face (around the lips), hands(fingertips) feet (toes). function of SI cortex I Responsible for Conscious awareness that a stimulus has occurred, and of its quality, location, intensity and duration. Responsible for initial cortical processing and perception of both somesthetic and proprioceptive input. localizes the source of sensory input and perceives the level of intensity of the stimulus. It also is capable of spatial discrimination. projects this sensory input to adjacent higher sensory areas( posterior parietal association cortex ) for further elaboration, analysis, and integration of sensory information. ( areas that give meaning to the received stimulus.) SI cortex is somatotopically organized. Somatotopic maps in the SI cortex Brodmann’s areas 1, 2, 3a and 3b Area 3b :mostly receives cutaneous input (from slowly and rapidly adapting receptors) Area 3a receives input from proprioceptors in muscles Area 2:process both tactile and proprioceptive stimuli. and is thought to be important for stereognosis), Area 1 receives information from rapidly adapting cutaneous mechanoreceptors. Lesion Unilateral destruction of SI produces severe deficits in all aspects of discriminative touch and proprioception on the contralesional side of the body. The secondary Somatosensory association area ( Brodmann’s areas 5 and 7) Site: it is located in the superior parietal lobe behind the sensory area I in the parietal lobe (posterior parietal cortex). connection :It receives efferent fibers from the primary somatic sensory areas as well as from the thalamic association nuclei. It also receives input from the visual system. This area combines the various sensory information received from the primary somatic sensory areas to recognize objects (stereognosis). It integrates tactile and proprioceptive information from the hand before performing a voluntary movement. Important for spatial awareness and perception of the different parts of the body . The secondary Somatosensory association area ( Brodmann’s areas 5 and 7) Functions: They provide a higher level of interpretation of sensory experiences. Understanding and giving meaning to them, so it is important for stereognosis. text: Tutorial # 1 Physiology of the sensory system Department of Medical Physiology Hala abdel Gawad Locality depends on specific pathway from each receptor to the sensory cortex . text: L 24 : Motor output- descending tracts By Seham Zakaria Nassar Associate Professor of Physiology- Alexandria Faculty of Medicine Students’ learning outcomes At the end of this session, the student should be able to; • Define the terms upper motor neurone and lower motor neurone. • Describe the interconnections between the lower motor neurones, and upper motor neurones. • Name and describe the locations of the main descending motor pathways. • Trace the pathway of the main descending motor pathways Upper motor neurons (UMNs) Lower motor neurons (LMNs) Neuronal system in the control of the voluntary movements Upper motor neurons ❑ Motor cells of cerebral cortex and their axons ❑ terminate at the brain stem and spinal cord lower motor neurons ❑ Motor nuclei of cranial nerves and their axons ❑ Anterior horn cells of the spinal cord and their axons. circuits involved in motor function 1. The lower motor neurones (LMNs) of the spinal cord and brain stem. 2. The upper motor neurones (UMNs), whose cell bodies lie in the cortex and brainstem. 3. The cerebellum 4. The basal ganglia 1 2 3 4 Movements Fine and skilled movements Gross and postural movements Performed by muscles of axial and (girdle) proximal parts of limbs (extrapyramidal ) Performed by muscles of distal parts of limbs (pyramidal system) The descending tracts (UMNs) ❑Descending tracts are the pathways by which motor signals are sent from the brain to the spinal cord. ❑They are also called motor tracts, due to their involvement in movement coordination. ❑There are two functionally distinct pathways. 1- Pyramidal and 2- Extrapyramidal The descending tracts (UMNs) The pyramidal pathway • Arises in the motor cortex • Essential for planning, initiating and directing voluntary movements and complex spatiotemporal sequences of movements. • It provides for fine, precise movement and voluntary control of distal muscle groups. The Extra-pyramidal pathway • Arise from the brainstem. • responsible for orientating the body, head and eyes in response to somatic, auditory, visual or vestibular stimuli . • Regulating muscle tone. The medial brainstem pathways • Arise from cells in the reticular formation, the vestibular nuclei and the tectum. • provide for reflex movements related to posture and balance. The Lateral brainstem pathways • Originates in the red nucleus. • provides for voluntary movements of the arms but not the individual digits. text: L26: Effects of lesion to descending tracts at different levels Prof. Abeer Elemam Dr. Eman Helmy Medical Physiology Department ILOs • Explain the pathophysiological mechanisms underlying upper and lower motor neuron lesions • Identify characteristic clinical features of lesions at different levels • Define and classify spinal cord injury (SCI) • Recognize the clinical features of SCI at different levels • Localize a nervous system lesion based on clinical signs and symptoms • Interpret clinical scenarios based on understanding of different lesions. Motor neuron lesions • Upper motor neuron lesion (UMNL) • Lower motor neuron lesion (LMNL) Upper motor neuron lesion (UMNL) • lesions which affect the cortical motor areas or the pathways of the descending tracts in the brain or spinal cord. Causes: 1. Mainly vascular. 2. Trauma 3. Tumor 4. Degenerative diseases. The most common lesions are lesions of the internal capsule commonly caused by vascular disorders. Manifestations of UMNL 1. Paralysis: •- Opposite side (due to crossing of the motor tract) •- Widespread (pyramidal fibers form a compact bundle which occupies a small area) 2. Spasticity (increased muscle tone): Decrease of the inhibitory discharge (from the IRF) on the gamma efferent while the facilitatory discharge continues ( from the FRF) Cause of spasticity: ➢Normally the facilitatory reticular formation discharges spontaneously, possibly in response to afferent input like the reticular activating system. ➢The inhibitory reticular formation does not discharge spontaneously but is driven instead by fibers from the cerebral cortex. ➢In UMNL there is interruption of the cortical discharge to the inhibitory reticular formation which decreases its activity. ➢ Hence the balance between inhibition and facilitation shifts towards facilitation and the gamma efferent discharge is increased. ➢ Furthermore, the vestibulospinal tracts remain intact and they also have a facilitatory effect on muscle tone. 3. Increased (exaggerated) deep reflexes and may be clonus Due to state of supraspinal facilitation that increases the activity of muscle spindle to stretch. 4. clonus Alternating regular rhythmic contractions and relaxations of a of spastic paralyzed muscle in response to sudden sustained stretch. Mechanism of clonus: • Clonus is the result of a stretch reflex - inverse stretch reflex sequence. • Sudden stretch of the muscle (nuclear bag) • Its contraction through the stretch reflex. • Stimulation of the GTOs • Initiation of an inverse stretch reflex • Relaxation • As stretch is maintained a new stretch reflex occurs (helped by the state of excessive spinal facilitation). 5. Superficial reflexes Superficial reflexes as abdominal and withdrawal reflexes are lost because superficial reflexes receive facilitatory influence from the pyramidal tract. Plantar reflex Abnormal response: + Babinski sign Dorsiflexion of the big toe with fanning of the other toes. • Manifestations: • 1 - Paralysis: • 2. Spasticity (increased muscle tone): • 3 - Increased (exaggerated) deep reflexes and may be clonus. • 4- Superficial reflexes. • 5- Plantar reflex. • 6 - Muscle status • There is no or little wasting. Upper motor neuron lesion (UMNL) Lower motor neuron lesion (LMNL) ➢ Definition: Lower motor neuron lesion (LMNL) means lesion or damage to the lower motor neurons in the spinal ventral horns (or motor nerve or damage to the muscle) or the corresponding motor nuclei of cranial nerves in the brain stem. ➢Causes: Mainly poliomyelitis or trauma to peripheral nerves. ▪ Damage of A.H.C. Poliomyelitis ▪ Damage of ventral Root ▪ Damage of peripheral nerves. ▪ e.g. alpha compression of median nerve at wrist or Polyneuritis. ▪ Damage of muscle or neuromuscular junction as in Myasthenia Gravis. Manifestations: 1. Paralysis: On the same side and localized. 2. Decreased tone (hypotonia) or flaccidity due to cut of stretch reflex arc. 3. Decreased or (absent) deep reflexes in the affected segment. 4. Plantar reflex: either normal or absent if the involved muscles are paralyzed. 5. Superficial reflexes: Lost in the affected segment (if they involve contraction of the denervated muscle). 6. Muscle status: There is marked wasting because the muscle is deprived of its motor supply. • N.B. signs of muscle denervation could be elicited as fasciculation (muscle twitches visible under the skin due to denervation of motor units)and fibrillations (muscles potentials detected by electromyography in denervated muscles). Lower motor neuron lesion (LMNL) SPINAL CORD INJURIES ❑COMPLETE spinal cord transection ❑INCOMPLETE- (Hemi-section of the cord) I. Complete transection of the spinal cord causes: ▪ Trauma. ▪ Tumour. ▪ Ischemia ▪ Demyelinating diseases. According to the level of lesion: o Above the level of C3, breathing could be affected. o Lower cervical region results in quadriplegia i.e. paralysis of the four limbs. o Thoracic region results in paraplegia i.e. paralysis of both lower limbs. Spinal shock : When the transection is complete there is usually a period after the accident when all spinal reflexes below the level of the transection are REDUCED .This condition is known as spinal shock. Stage of recovery During the course of weeks and months spinal reflexes GRADUALL Y RETURN, often greatly exaggerated compared with normal which is described as stage of recovery. If complications are present the duration of spinal shock is much longer or even failure of recovery occurs. Complication could be urinary tract infection, malnutrition and decubitus ulcers. Therefore, adequate management of the paraplegic patient is very important to prevent occurrence of complications I. Complete transection of the spinal cord Stage of spinal shock • Manifestations: • 1. Loss of all sensations. • 2. Loss of all voluntary movements below the level of the lesion. • 3. Loss of cord reflexes as stretch reflex and flexor withdrawal reflex etc… • 4. loss of Bladder and bowl control (retention with overflow) • 5. Loss of erection • 6. Drop of the arterial blood pressure if the transection is at the level of first thoracic segment, but slight drop occurs if the lesion is below the second lumber segment, due to block of the sympathetic activity. Autonomic Motor Sensory • Duration: • The duration of spinal shock is much shorter in animals than in human (in animals it lasts for minutes up to hours or day). The long recovery period for humans reflects the greater influence of descending input on spinal reflex circuits. • Cause: • Spinal shock is due to sudden withdrawal of tonic facilitatory influence from the brain Stage of spinal shock

text: L18: Organization & function of motor & prefrontal cortex Eman Helmy Thabet MD PhD Lecturer of Medical Physiology Alexandria Faculty of Medicine Fulbright Scholar at UCSF-USA II. Premotor area Site: This area lies anterior to the primary motor area; anterior to the precentral gyrus, on the lateral and medial cortical surface. It occupies the part of Brodmann area 6 Generating a plan for movement Functions of the premotor cortex The PM area is involved in planning movements that involve external sensory cues . (arrange red box to right) Cells are active when there is an intention to make a movement rather than during the movement. Nerve signals generated in the premotor area cause much more complex “patterns” of movement than the discrete patterns generated in the primary motor cortex. It deals with learned motor activities of a complex/gross and sequential nature, by coordinating contractions of specific groups of muscles; for example, it is active during writing . Functions of PMA (area 6):- This region may be concerned with setting posture at the start of a planned movement and with getting the individual prepared to move. It is most involved in control of proximal limb muscles needed to orient the body for movement. Supplementary motor area (SMA) Site: Small area lies anterior and superior to area 6 on the medial surface of the frontal lobe. programs complex motor sequences and is active during “mental rehearsal” for a movement. Functions of the SMA Supplementary motor area ,SMA : The SMA is also involved in planning movements but is concerned with internally generated commands or cues. Dealing with spontaneously well learned action that not depend on external cues The SMA is crucial for the performance of complicated tasks involving both sides of the body, e.g. two-handed tasks such as typing, piano playing . Cells are active while an intended movement is being thought about. Selection of movements based on incoming sensory information In general, this area functions in concert with the premotor area to provide body-wide attitudinal movements, fixation movements of the different segments of the body, positional movements of the head and eyes, as background for the finer motor control of the arms and hands by the premotor area and primary motor cortex. Functions of the SMA What does damage to PM &SMA do? Difficulty in performing complex motor ,familiar , learned tasks such as brushing their hair, cleaning their teeth or dressing themselves in the absence of sensory or motor impairment, it is known as apraxia. The frontal eye field The frontal eye field region of the motor cortex controls voluntary scanning movements of the eyes, such as during reading. Connections with the superior colliculus and the gaze centres located in the paramedian pontine reticular formation. Stimulation of this region --  conjugate deviation of the eyes towards the opposite side to the stimulation, Damage to this region---  a transient conjugate deviation of the eyes towards the side of the lesion. I. Pre-frontal association area Site: This area is located in the anterior part of the frontal lobe, in front of the premotor area. They are Brodmann’s areas 9,10,11,12,13,14 ILOs 1. Identify Brodmann areas for motor control. 2. Understand the function of each area in motor function 3. Recognize the different manifestation of lesions in cortical areas. 4. Compare between motor cortex and premotor cortex in motor control 5. Identify thalamo -cortical projection 6. Describe the functions of the prefrontal association cortex. The prefrontal cortex Prefrontal association area receives, analyses and integrates signals from both motor and sensory cortex as well as from subcortical structures. It is divided into the dorsolateral prefrontal cortex ( Executive functions ) and the ventromedial prefrontal cortex (orbitofrontal cortex) (Controlling behavior). Functions of the dorsolateral prefrontal cortex Shares with the motor cortex in planning complex pattern of voluntary movements. Provides the ability to concentrate and promotes attention . Mediates working memory. Controls the ability to follow and obey rules . Controls creativity and learning. Functions of ventromedial prefrontal cortex Plays a role in motivation. Regulates emotions and impulsive behavior. Involved in social decision making . What does this tell you about the function of prefrontal cortex in different animals ? Thalamo -cortical projection The thalamus is a sensory relay station and is important in motor control. Deep within the brain is the diencephalon, a midline structure that forms the walls of the third ventricular cavity, one of the spaces through which CSF flows. The diencephalon consists of two main parts, the thalamus and the hypothalamus Thalamo -cortical projection The thalamus serves as a “relay station” for preliminary processing of sensory input. All sensory input synapses in the thalamus on its way to the cortex. The thalamus screens out insignificant signals and routes the important sensory impulses to appropriate areas of the somatosensory cortex, as well as to other regions of the brain. The thalamus also plays an important role in motor control Guyton and Hall Textbook of Medical Physiology 14 th edition – Adina T. Michael-Titus, et al. Systems of the body-second edition- The nervous system Lecture Notes Cerebral cortex is the largest portion of the nervous system Cerebral Cortex Introduction Most “voluntary” movements initiated by the cerebral cortex are achieved when the cortex activates “patterns” of function stored in lower brain areas—the cord, brain stem, basal ganglia, and cerebellum. These lower centers, in turn, send specific control signals to the muscles. Motor areas Primary motor area (area 4/ MI) Secondary association areas: Premotor area (area 6/ PM) Supplementary motor area ( SMA ) PYRAMIDAL TRACTS I. The primary motor area (area 4) Located in the precentral gyrus in the frontal lobe. It controls muscle activity in the opposite half of the body (The body is represented in inverted manner. head, lips and hands represented laterally, and the legs and feet medially The more complex the movement of a particular body part, the more motor cortex is devoted to it. Contains large pyramidal cells (Betz cells)-give origin to pyramidal tract. Functions of the motor cortex Primary motor cortex, MI: Movement execution Functions of the motor cortex Primary motor cortex, MI: The MI cortex is involved in the voluntary distal control of movements, by carrying the motor command to the LMNs. Excitation of a single motor cortex neuron usually excites a specific movement rather than one specific muscle. To do this, it excites a “pattern” of separate muscles, each of which contributes its own direction and strength of muscle movement. II. Premotor area

text: L29; BASAL GANGLIA A JOURNEY INTO THE DEEP NUCLEI Dr. Seham Zakaria Nassar Assistant professor Physiology department STUDENTS’ LEARNING OUTCOMES At the end of this session, the student should be able to; ➢Describe the organization of the basal ganglia and their connections with other central nervous system regions. ➢Understand Circuits and neurotransmitters of basal ganglia ➢Describe the role of the basal ganglia in the motor regulation ➢Describe the main symptoms and diseases associated with dysfunction of the basal ganglia, and their pathophysiology. PARTS OF THE BASAL GANGLIA consist of: ➢ The caudate nucleus ➢Putamen ➢Globus pallidus (GPint & GPext) ➢ Substantia nigra ➢ Subthalamic nucleus. (Receiving center ) (pars compacta and the pars reticulata). (Discharging center) CIRCUITS AND NEUROTRANSMITTERS What do the basal ganglia do? basal ganglia function with the ipsilateral CC of which controls contralateral muscles via two closed circuits : • Making movement • Not moving Direct pathway (excitatory) Indirect pathway (inhibitory) ➢Maintain purposeful motor activity ➢Inhibit unwanted movements ➢Inhibit muscle tone Motor cortex ThalamusGlobus Pallidus (int.) Striatum Caudate/ Putamen Substantia Nigra Subthalamic Nucleus Inhibition Excite Inhibition Dopamine D1 Move Inhibition Excite Direct pathway When movement start cortex Stimulate striatum Inhibit GP int Dis-inhibition of the thalamus Enhancement of thalamo-cortical projection Facilitate movements Positive feedback Take off the brake Purpose To free the thalamus from tonic inhibition of GPIS and STPr. Dopamine acting on D1 receptors enhances activity of this circuit THE PUTAMEN CIRCUIT Premotor and supplementary motor cortex and in the somatosensory areas of the sensory cortex. The putamen The globus pallidus (int) The ventroanterior and ventrolateral relay nuclei of the thalamus, Primary motor cortex, the premotor and supplementary cerebral areas For executing learned patterns of movement THE CAUDATE CIRCUIT ❑ The caudate nucleus extends into all lobes of the cerebrum. ❑ It receives large amounts of its input from the association areas of the cerebral cortex, areas that integrate the different types of sensory and motor information. COGNITIVE CONTROL OF SEQUENCES OF MOTOR PATTERNS THE CAUDATE CIRCUIT The cerebral cortex Caudate nucleus The internal globus pallidus the ventroanterior and ventrolateral thalamus the prefrontal, premotor, and supplementary motor areas of the cerebral cortex, but with almost none of the returning signals passing directly to the primary motor cortex. COGNITIVE CONTROL OF SEQUENCES OF MOTOR PATTERNS Concerned with putting together sequential patterns of movement lasting 5 or more seconds instead of exciting individual muscle movements. Motor cortex ThalamusGlobus Pallidus (int.) Striatum Substantia Nigra Subthalamic Nucleus Not moving Excite Inhibition Globus Pallidus (ext.)D2 Dopamine Augment braking Indirect pathway Indirect pathway: Inhibit movements Cerebral cortex Striatum inhibit GP ext. (GP ext. normally inhibit subthalamus) Release of subthalamus (it is normally activating GPIs) Activate GP int. Inhibition of thalamus-inhibit movement Negative feedback Augment braking Activates striatum suppression of the spontaneous movement. An important pathway in the modulation of the direct and indirect pathways is the dopaminergic, nigrostriatal projection from the substantia nigra to the striatum. Stimulation of Dopamine (D1) receptors, depolarizes and stimulates direct pathway striatal neurons. stimulation of dopamine (D2) receptors, hyperpolarizes and inhibits the indirect pathway striatal neurons. The nigrostriatal pathway thus has the dual effect of exciting the direct pathway while inhibiting the indirect pathway. Substantia Nigra (kick starter) Through these two pathways, the cortex can either increase (direct pathway) or decrease (indirect path- way) the excitatory thalamocortical projections. FUNCTIONS OF THE BASAL GANGLIA I. Motor functions: 1. They are involved in the planning of voluntary movement. (discharge before movement begins ). Caudate circuits 2. Executing pattern of learned acts (walking, typing, writing) Putamen circuit. 3. They inhibit and suppress unwanted motor activity through the indirect circuit. 4. C. striatum share in learning and storing automatic subconscious movements 5. Scales amplitude and velocity of movements (decides how big or fast a movement should be 6. Regulates muscle tone and posture. Cognitive and Associative Functions ▪Involved in planning and sequencing of motor acts and problem-solving. ▪Participates in working memory. ▪Filters and directs attention to relevant stimuli, suppressing distractions. ▪Helps switch between tasks or mental sets efficiently (mental flexibilty) FUNCTIONS OF THE BASAL GANGLIA
