text: 1 29 Basal ganglia: A journey into the deep nuclei ILOs: By the end of this lecture, students will be able to 1. Describe the organization of the basal ganglia and their connections with other central nervous system regions. 2. Understand Circuits and neurotransmitters of basal ganglia 3. Describe the main symptoms and diseases associated with dysfunction of the basal ganglia, and their pathophysiology. 4. Describe the role of the basal ganglia in the motor regulation The basal ganglia: structure and organization The basal ganglia consist of five subcortical interconnected nuclei that are involved in the initiation and execution of movement. This system receives inputs from wide areas of the cerebral cortex and returns it, via the thalamus, to the cortex . The caudate nucleus, The putamen nucleus The caudate nucleus and the putamen are two nuclei that are interconnected and form the striatum. The striatum receives afferents from the neocortex, the thalamus and the substantia nigra. The globus pallidus. The globus pallidus has an internal (or medial) and an external (or lateral) division. It receives projections from the striatum and the subthalamic nucleus. It is the discharging center of the Basal ganglia. The major output of the basal ganglia projects from the globus pallidus (internal division) to thalamic nuclei (in particular, the ventral anterior, ventral lateral nuclei), which project to motor and prefrontal cortical areas. The subthalamic nucleus The substantia nigra The substantia nigra can be subdivided into substantia nigra pars compacta and substantia nigra pars reticulata. The pars compacta contain dopaminergic neurons that project to the striatum. Figure 2; Basal ganglia nuclei 2 Circuits and neurotransmitters One of the principal roles of the basal ganglia in motor control is to function in association with the corticospinal system to control complex patterns of motor activity. 1. the direct pathway: The direct pathway starts from the cortex and projects to the striatum (caudate nucleus and putamen) with excitatory glutamatergic (glu) neurons. The neurons from the striatum, which are inhibitory GABAergic, send their axons to the medial (internal) globus pallidus and substantia nigra, pars reticulata (SNr). The neurons from the internal globus pallidus and SNr send their axons to the thalamus, and they are also inhibitory. 2. The indirect pathway: This pathway begins (like the direct pathway) from the cortex, projecting to the striatum. Instead of sending axons directly to the GPi, they inhibit the external globus pallidus. The neurons from the GPe send inhibitory fibers to the subthalamic nucleus that causes disinhibition of the subthalamus. From the subthalamic nucleus, neurons excite the GPi/SNr and then continue as the direct pathway with GA BAergic inhibitory neurons to the thalamus and glutamate excitatory efferents to the cortex. The final result of this pathway is a decreased activity of the cortical motor neurons and consequential suppression of the extemporaneous movement. In summary, when a given motor pattern is computed by the cerebral cortex, it is first conveyed to the basal ganglia via glutamatergic projections to the striatum, with the purpose of releasing the intended movement and suppressing the unintended ones. Figure 2; circuits connecting the motor cortex with the basal ganglia green arrows: excitatory; red arrows: inhibitory Substantia Nigra An important pathway in the modulation of the direct and indirect pathways is the dopaminergic, nigrostriatal projection from the substantia nigra to the striatum. Stimulation of Dopamine (D1) receptors, depolarizes and stimulates direct pathway striatal neurons. 3 While, stimulation of dopamine (D2) receptors, hyperpolarizes and inhibits the indirect pathway striatal neurons. The nigrostriatal pathway thus has the dual effect of exciting the direct pathway while inhibiting the indirect pathway. Functions of the basal ganglia Motor functions: 1. They are involved in the planning of voluntary movement. (Discharge before movement begins- Converts an intention to move into actual motor action.) Caudate circuits 2. Initiation and execution of voluntary movement — especially automatic, learned, and skilled movements (e.g., walking, typing, writing ) Putamen circuit) . Therefore, inactivate caudate – cannot learn new sequences. While inactivate putamen – cannot execute previously learned sequences 3. They inhibit and suppress unwanted motor activity through the indirect circuit. 4. Scales amplitude and velocity of movements (decides how big or fast a movement should be 5. Suppresses unwanted movements and refines desired ones. 6. Regulates muscle tone and posture. Automatic Behavior and Habit Formation 1. Converts repeated voluntary actions into automatic routines (habit learning). Cognitive and Associative Functions 1. Involved in planning and sequencing of motor acts and problem-solving. 2. Participates in working memory. 3. Filters and directs attention to relevant stimuli, suppressing distractions. 4. Helps switch between tasks or mental sets efficiently (mental flexibilty) Disorders of movement in Basal ganglia disease 1. Hyperkinetic: Excessive abnormal movement i.e. chorea, athetosis, ballism. (excess direct- insufficient indirect) 2. Hypokinetic: Slow movements (akinesia, bradykinesia) (insufficient direct-excessive indirect) Effects of Lesions in Different Parts of the Basal Ganglia: Lesion in the globus pallidus frequently → spontaneous and often continuous slow writhing movements of a hand, an arm, the neck, or the face. called athetosis. Lesion in the subthalamus → sudden flailing intense and violent movements of an entire limb, called hemiballismus. Multiple small lesions in the putamen → Rapid involuntary “dancing” movements called chorea. 4 Lesions of the substantia nigra → the common and extremely severe disease of rigidity, akinesia, and tremors known as Parkinson’s disease. Parkinson’s disease Pathophysiology: The pathological hallmark of PD is the degeneration of the nigrostriatal dopaminergic pathway. Nigrostriatal dopaminergic neurons are tonically active and exert a modulatory influence on the striatum and the striatonigral and striatopallidal efferent pathways, through D1 and D2 receptors, respectively. Symptoms: 1. Tremor The most prominent symptom is the resting tremor of the extremities that almost always accompanies the disease. The tremor has a characteristic frequency of 4–6 Hz and may begin in only one extremity and spread to the others. The distal joints of the limbs are preferentially affected. In the hand, the tremor is characteristic and involves the thumb and fingers rolling together. This is called a ‘pill-rolling’ tremor. The tremor is seen at rest and disappears during an intentional movement and during sleep. 2. Bradykinesia/akinesia Bradykinesia is a slowing of normal movement. In the advanced stages of the disease, the patient becomes akinetic and shows almost no motor initiative. There is reduced arm swinging when walking, reduced blinking, and various daily simple or complex tasks (e.g. washing, brushing the teeth, dressing and writing) can be affected. There is a gradual loss of normal facial movement and expression. The speech is poorly articulated, and the voice is quiet and monotonous. Eating and swallowing become increasingly d ifficult. This may result in a tendency to drool (sialorrhea). 3. Rigidity Parkinsonian patients have increased muscle tone in flexor and extensor muscles and typically present resistance to passive movement of the limbs. The increased resistance to movement, combined with tremor, leads to the ‘cogwheel’ phenomenon. Manipulating the patient’s limbs feels like manipulating a lead pipe; hence the term ‘lead pipe’ rigidity. Other motor and non-motor manifestations of Parkinson’s disease 1. Abnormalities of posture and gait. The gait of a parkinsonian patient becomes slow and shuffling, and the posture is flexed.

Specify the function of muscle spindle and interpret its related tendon- jerk reflex. 3.Interpret the significance of alpha-gamma co-activation. 4. List the functions and properties of stretch reflex. prof.Hala Abdel Gawad 4 Do you remember the last time you have experienced this behavior? prof.Hala Abdel Gawad 5 Stretch reflex and human civilization The stretch reflex is a fundamental, involuntary biological mechanism that helps maintain balance and stability, which is crucial for human civilization's development and continued functioning, particularly in areas like locomotion and tool use. prof.Hala Abdel Gawad 6 Gravity tends to double us up and pull us down (passively stretching our muscles) The stretch reflexes making us resist this stretching and maintain us stand upright stretch reflex in a very simple way prof.Hala Abdel Gawad 7 prof.Hala Abdel Gawad 8 What is the aim of the stretch reflex To keep constant length of the muscle and resist any trials to change this length with the aim of maintaining posture Reflex is the involuntary response of an organ to a stimulus. Reflex is the functional unit in the nervous system , it is the simplest motor response. Reflex action : All the steps involved since application of stimulus detected by specific receptor transforming it into nerve impulse transmitted in afferent nerve which synapse with motor neuron .The motor neuron in turn sends these impulses to effector organ to perform its final response. Important basic definitions prof.Hala Abdel Gawad 9 Reflex pathway ( reflex arc) Reflex arc : it is the reflex pathway through which reflex action occurs, beginning with receptor and ending at effector organ. prof.Hala Abdel Gawad 10 Reflexes could be classified in many ways Processing center (SC, brain stem ,hypothalamus ,cortex) Receptor site (superficial &deep) Effector organ (somatic &autonomic) Developmental Innate :flexor withdrawal Acquired: conditioned reflex Complexity (Synapse) (monosynaptic &polysynaptic) prof.Hala Abdel Gawad 11 Methods of Classifying Reflexes 12 prof.Hala Abdel Gawad It is reflex contraction of the innervated skeletal muscle in response to passive stretch Stretch reflex is the only monosynaptic reflex in our body. What is the stretch(myotatic) reflex? prof.Hala Abdel Gawad 13 prof.Hala Abdel Gawad 14 Skeletal muscles consists of 2 types of muscle fibers Extrfusal muscle fibers Intrafusal muscle fibers (muscle spindle) majority of the muscle & are responsible for its contractile function Small spinel cells found deep to the extrafusal muscle fibers (receptor organs) prof.Hala Abdel Gawad 15 Muscle spindle consists of specialized small muscle fibers called intrafusal fibers which are distributed paralleled throughout the fleshy part of the muscle. Intrafusal fibers Extrafusal fibers prof.Hala Abdel Gawad 16 Intrafusal muscle fibers Intrafusal fibers has both peripheral contractile part & central (receptor area)non contractile part (stretchable) Nuclear bag (detect rate of change in muscle length) Nuclear chain (detect actual length of the muscle ) prof.Hala Abdel Gawad 17 Capsule a-Nuclear chain fibre b-Nuclear bag fibre Structure of muscle spindle Intrafusal fibers Extrafusal fibers prof.Hala Abdel Gawad 18 Types of intrafusal fibers Nuclear bag Nuclear chain It is longer-thicker with centrally located nuclei arranged like a bag. Stimulated while stretch is going on (dynamic) Thinner , s horter -with nuclei arranged like a chain attached to the sides of nuclear bag fibers. S timulated while the stretch `is maintained ( s tatic) prof.Hala Abdel Gawad 19 Innervations of the muscle spindle Afferent fibers(sensory) (around the central part) Efferent fibers (gamma fibers-motor) (to peripheral parts ) prof.Hala Abdel Gawad 20 Innervation of muscle spindle Afferent fibers (supply central part ) Efferent fibers (supply peripheral parts) Gamma motor fibers??? Primary ending ( Anulo spiral) type 1a fibers (n. bag & n.chain ) Rapidly adapting (rate of change in length) (Dynamic stretch) S econdary ending (Flower spray) Type II fibers (n. chain only) S lowly adapting (steady state of length) ( S tatic stretch) prof.Hala Abdel Gawad 21 Innervation of muscle spindle Afferent nerves Efferent nerves prof.Hala Abdel Gawad 22 prof.Hala Abdel Gawad 23 Nuclear chain fiber Nuclear bag fiber Annulospiral endings Gamma motoneurons Secondary (II) afferent fibers Primary ( Ia ) afferent fibers Flower spray endings Static gamma motor fibers Dynamic gamma moor fibers Receptors: muscle spindle. Afferent: DRG (dorsal root ganglia) Through rapidly conducting fibers 1a (Aα) and 11 (AB) fibers. Center: AHC (anterior horn cells = α motor neuron). Efferent : axons of the AHC (nerve supply to the muscle) Effector: skeletal muscle contraction ( extrafusal muscle fibers). Response : muscle contraction( ms. shortening to its original length prof.Hala Abdel Gawad 26 Components of the stretch reflex prof.Hala Abdel Gawad 27 Please do not get confused with efferent innervation for stretch reflex and efferent innervation for the muscle spindle . Sudden stretch Maintained stretch Stretch of the muscle spindle ,is the stimulus for stretch reflex? Dynamic response (example) static response (example) prof.Hala Abdel Gawad 28 Tendon jerk Muscle tone Stimulus Mechanism of stimulation of muscle spindle (How can we stimulate muscle spindle?) Stretching of whole muscle . Two types of resposes with two types of stretch (dynamic vs static responses) prof.Hala Abdel Gawad 35 Types of Stretch reflex Dynamic stretch reflex (mediated by group 1a fibers) Static stretch reflex (mediated by group II fibers) It is responsible for monitoring the rate (speed) of change in the muscle length (How fast the muscle has to be flexed or extended) It monitors the absolute length of the muscle, (How short or long the muscle is now) It is the base of tendon jerk It is the base of muscle tone prof.Hala Abdel Gawad 36 prof.Hala Abdel Gawad 37 Muscle spindle &Golgi tendon organs both are your muscle GPS Dynamic (tendon jerk) Static (muscle tone) Stimulus Sudden stretch of muscle Maintained stretch Receptor Nuclear bag Nuclear chain Afferent Ia fibers ( annulospiral ) 1a fibers ( annulospiral )&II fibers (flower-spray) Center α motor neurons α motor neurons Efferent axons of α motor neurons axons of α motor neurons Effector organ Extrafusal muscle fibers Extrafusal muscle fibers Response Rapid contraction followed by rapid relaxation Sustained contraction Types of stretch reflex prof.Hala Abdel Gawad 38 Dynamic Stretch Reflex 2 1 prof.Hala Abdel Gawad 39 Reciprocal innwevation Static stretch reflex prof.Hala Abdel Gawad 40 What is the role played by gamma motor neurons prof.Hala Abdel Gawad 41 14 micron Where is the gamma motor neurons arise from? Peripheral parts of the intrafusal muscle fibers Extrafusal muscle fibers (+) γ motor neurons (+) γ axons Contraction of peripheral contractile part of intrafusal fibers Stretch of central receptor area Of muscle spindle Increase sensitivity of muscle to stretch Reflex muscle contraction Function of γ motor neurons: Gamma fibers arises from gamma motor neurons present in the anterior horn cells that supply the muscle spindle. Gamma motor neurons cause reflex muscle contraction &stimulate muscle spindle peripheral contractile parts leading to stretch of its central part. Gamma motor neurons are controlled through supraspinal higher mechanism. Gamma motor neurons allows higher centers to be always in duty always informed about changes in muscle length, keeping muscle spindle always active even during muscle contraction i.e no tension unloading prof.Hala Abdel Gawad 45 prof.Hala Abdel Gawad 46 Thinking point How muscle spindle be sensitive during muscle shorting? Thanks to gamma motor neurons Extrafusal fibers Muscle spindle Relaxed muscle; spindle fiber sensitive to stretch of muscle Contracted muscle in hypothetical situation of no spindle coactivation; slackened spindle fiber not sensitive to stretch of muscle Contracted muscle in normal situation of spindle coactivation; contracted spindle fiber sensitive to stretch of muscle How muscle spindle be sensitive during muscle shorting? Thanks to gamma motor neurons How gamma motor neuron are regulated (supra-spinal control of muscle spindle) prof.Hala Abdel Gawad 50 Supra -spinal control of gamma motor neurons Supra spinal inhibitory centers Facilitatory (pontine) reticular formation through medial reticulospinal tract Vestibular nucleus(medial &lateral vestibulospinal tract) Olive nucleus prof.Hala Abdel Gawad 52 Supra spinal faciliatory centers Inhibitory(medullary ) reticular formation through lateral reticulospinal tract Premotor cortex Paleocerebellum Corpus striatum More dominant Is there any other factors affecting gamma motor discharge Anxiety ,cutaneous painful stimuli , Gendrassik’s maneuver prof.Hala Abdel Gawad 53 What do we mean with alpha gamma coactivation &what about its significance prof.Hala Abdel Gawad 54 prof.Hala Abdel Gawad 55 During muscle contraction higher brain centers produce simultaneous activation of both alpha &gamma motor neurons thus keeping spindle sensitivity throughout muscle contraction and provide the alpha motor neurons with effective source of presynaptic excitatory input (indirect stimulation of alpha motor neurons). what is meant by alpha gamma coactivation? Co- activation of α and γ motor neurons Supraspinal centers (Descending tracts) α motor neurons γ motor neurons Contraction of intrafusal muscle fibers (reflex contraction of extrafusal fibers) Contraction of extrafusal muscle fibers During active contraction α - γ linkage Muscle spindles remain stretched throughout the contraction Both extrafusal & intrafusal muscle fibers contract at the same time without contradiction prof.Hala Abdel Gawad 57 Co- activation of α and γ motor neurons α - γ linkage Shortening of the extrafusal fibers by the alpha motor neurons would cause slack in the muscle spindle making it a non- effective sensory organ. Therefore ,as soon as the alpha motor neurons discharge and the muscle shortened the gamma motor neurons are also co-activated causing stretching of the spindle , thus keeping it sensitive during contraction. This co-activation of gamma motor neurons along with the activation of alpha motor neurons is called the ( alpha-gamma linkage). The gamma motor neurons adjust the length of muscle spindles so that the spindles do not lose their sensitivity during the period of muscle contraction ,insure that the spindle is at its appropriate length. When muscle spindles are relaxed ,they are relatively insensitive to stretch ,but when already tense ,they sense stretch rapidly. 18/10/25 prof.Hala Abdel Gawad Properties of the stretch reflex: think why ? It is deep monosynaptic reflex. Total reflex time is short. (fastest reflex in the body ) Localized. No after discharge. No fatigue. It shows reciprocal innervation . prof.Hala Abdel Gawad 60 Functions of the stretch reflex Maintain muscle length constant. Control postures. Maintain balance during walking and standing. Tendon jerks are very important clinical tool to assess integrity of nervous system as well as its degree of higher control. prof.Hala Abdel Gawad 61 It is mild maintained sub tetanic alternating reflex contraction of the skeletal muscle at rest . It results from the continuous muscle stretch (gravity-anatomical position in the body.) Mechanism: It is an example to the static stretch reflex . functions : 1-Maintainance of body posture against gravity. 2-Helps in the regulation of body temperature. 3-Helps the venous return and lymph flow. 4-keeps the viscera in its position. 5-Background for voluntary movements Muscle tone prof.Hala Abdel Gawad 62 Distribution: In all muscles most marked in antigravity muscles( flexors of upper limb, extensors of lower limbs ,muscles of back and neck and jaw elevators) Changes in muscle tone is a very important diagnostic criteria during clinical examination prof.Hala Abdel Gawad 63 Summary or take-home message Reflex is the involuntary response of an organ to a stimulus Stretch reflex is a deep monosynaptic spinal reflex It is elicited by applying stretch to a muscle resulting in contraction of that ms Muscle spindles are receptors within the muscle fibers which detect the length and rate of change of length of muscle Sensory fibers arising from muscle spindles are of 2 types: 1)- Annulospiral from nuclear bag and chain (sense velocity & length) 2)-Flower spray from nuclear chain (sense ms length) prof.Hala Abdel Gawad 64 Stretch reflex is of two types: dynamic and static Gamma fibers are motor fibers arising from γ motor neurons and supply the peripheral contractile part of muscle spindle Knee jerk is an example of dynamic stretch reflex Muscle tone is an example of static stretch reflex Stretch reflex is controlled by supraspinal (facilitatory & inhibitory) centers through descending pathways It affects the activity of γ & α motor neurons ( mainly γ) prof.Hala Abdel Gawad 65 1-Systems of the body-second edition- The nervous system (chapter ). 2- Lauralee S. Human Physiology: from Cells to Systems. - Hall JE. Ed. McGraw-Hill Education. prof.Hala Abdel Gawad 66 prof.Hala Abdel Gawad 67

text: L16 Blood Supply of CNS ILOs By the end of this lecture, students will be able to Differentiate between the anatomy of circle of Willis and the vertebrobasilar system. Interpret the blood supply of different parts of the brain & spinal cord in relation to their function. Appraise the importance of anterior and posterior circulations in maintaining blood flow in cases of occlusion. Correlate the clinical picture of cerebrovascular accidents with the distribution of different vessels. Anterior & posterior circulation of the central nervous system (Fig. 1) Blood is supplied to the brain via the anterior (circle of Willis) and posterior ( vertebrobasilar system) circulations. The anterior circulation supplies supratentorial structures (the cortex and diencephalon). The posterior circulation supplies the structures in the posterior fossa (cerebellum and brainstem). The posterior circulation enters the skull cavity through the foramen magnum . The anterior circulation enters through the foramen lacerum. CAROTID SYSTEM (anterior circulation) It consists of the intracranial part of the internal carotid artery and its two terminal branches; (the anterior and middle cerebral arteries). Internal carotid artery (intracranial part): It enters the brain cavity through the carotid canal to emerge on its interior surface via the foramen lacerum . It makes a series of stepwise turns, passing through the cavernous sinus, before emerging, on each side, next to the optic chiasma, where they divide into their major branches, the middle cerebral artery (MCA) and anterior cerebral artery (ACA). Branches of internal carotid artery (ICA): (Fig. 2) Ophthalmic Artery Anterior Cerebral Artery Middle Cerebral Artery Anterior Choroidal Artery Posterior Communicating Artery Fig. 2: Branches of ICA Fig. 2: Branches of ICA Fig. 1: Anterior & posterior circulation Fig. 1: Anterior & posterior circulation Middle cerebral artery (MCA): (Fig. 3) It is the largest and most important branch of the ICA. It receives 80% of the carotid blood flow. Its proximal part gives off deep branches; the lateral and medial striate arteries supply the striatum and the internal capsule. The more distal part of the MCA travels laterally through the lateral fissure to supply most of the lateral side of the brain. Occlusion of these deep arteries is the chief cause of classic stroke. Anterior cerebral artery (ACA): (Fig. 4) It winds around the genu of corpus callosum before dividing into two main terminal branches. It supplies the medial side of the frontal and parietal lobes as far back as the parieto-occipital sulcus, and overlaps onto the orbital and lateral surfaces of the brain. • It gives: Cortical branches Central branches Occlusion of this artery is rare but can cause ‘clumsy hand’ syndrome, with contralateral weakness of the arm and face. Fig. 3: Distribution of MCA Fig. 3: Distribution of MCA Fig. 4: Distribution of ACA Fig. 4: Distribution of ACA Vertebro-basilar system (posterior circulation): (Fig. 5) It consists of: 1. Two vertebral arteries. 2. Basilar artery (single). 3. Posterior cerebral artery (two). Vertebral artery: Origin: In the neck from 1st part of subclavian artery. Course & relations: it passes through the transverse foraminae of the C1–C6 vertebrae before entering the skull cavity via the foramen magnum to travel along the ventral surface of the brainstem. Branches: (Fig. 6) 1. Anterior spinal artery; the 2 Ars unite together to form a single trunk which runs in the anterior median fissure of the spinal cord. 2. Posterior spinal artery; two arteries, each one arises from the corresponding vertebral artery. Each artery divides into two longitudinal branches which descend on each side of the posterior root of the spinal nerves. 3. Posterior inferior cerebellar artery (PICA) is a tortuous artery and is the largest branch of the vertebral artery. 4. Medullary branches; to supply the medulla oblongata. Fig. 6: Branches of vertebral & basilar arteries Fig. 6: Branches of vertebral & basilar arteries Fig. 5: Vertebro-basilar system Fig. 5: Vertebro-basilar system Basilar artery (Fig. 6) Origin: at the lower border of pons by the union of the 2 vertebral arteries. Course & relations: it passes on the front of the pons in the midline (pontine sulcus, groove for basilar artery). Termination: at the upper border of pons by bifurcation into the 2 posterior cerebral arteries. Branches: 1. Anterior inferior cerebellar artery, supplies also the cerebellar tonsil. 2. Superior cerebellar artery 3. Pontine branches 4. Labyrinthine (internal auditory) artery 5. Posterior cerebral artery (terminal branches) Posterior cerebral artery (PCA) (Fig. 7) Origin: at the upper border of pons as the 2 terminal branches of the basilar artery. Course & relations: it passes around the midbrain to reach the occipital pole of the cerebrum. It passes inside the calcarine sulcus. Termination: it terminates by dividing into its terminal cortical branches. Branches: 1- Central: Supply thalamus, hypothalamus, globus pallidus, midbrain and geniculate bodies. 2- Cortical: • Superolateral surface; occipital lobe + lowermost 1 finger breadth of this surface. • Inferior surface; the whole tentorial surface except temporal pole. • Medial surface; occipital lobe. CIRCULUS ARTERIOSUS (CIRCLE OF WILLIS): (Fig. 5&6) It is formed at the base of the brain by the interconnecting vertebrobasilar and internal carotid systems of vessels. This anastomotic interconnection is formed by: • An anterior communicating artery connecting the left and right anterior cerebral arteries to each other. • Two posterior communicating arteries, one on each side, connecting the internal carotid artery with the posterior cerebral artery. CEREBRAL VEINS: (Fig. 8) External Cerebral Veins The superior cerebral veins empty into the superior sagittal sinus. The superficial middle cerebral vein drains the lateral surface of the cerebral hemisphere; empties into the cavernous sinus. The basal vein ultimately joins the great cerebral vein, which in turn drains into the straight sinus. Internal Cerebral Veins : two veins unite beneath the splenium of the corpus callosum to form the great cerebral vein. Fig. 7: PCA Fig. 7: PCA Fig. 8: Cerebral veins Fig. 8: Cerebral veins

text: Lecture 9 Somatosensory system & receptors Dr Rehab Ahmed Abdel- Moneim Professor in histology & cell biology Distribution: the cell body and dendrites. Other organelles; well developed Golgi complex (only in the perikaryon). NB: neurotransmitter vesicles are formed in the perikaryon and transported along the axon. rER Ribosomes Neurotransmitters  proteins required for impulse transport Cytoskeleton(cytosolic proteins) Nissl granules (EM) Cytoskeleton of the neuron It plays an essential role in axonal transport It includes three types: 1- Microtubules (MT). 2-Neurofilaments;(intermediate filaments). 3- Microfilaments (actin). Axonal transport 1- Anterograde 2- Retrograde Cytoskeleton Anterograde; mitochondria & neurotransmitter vesicles. In association with motor protein Kinesin. Retrograde; molecules for recycling (receptors). In association with motor protein Dyenin . Neuron processes (neurites) Axon Dendrites Cytoplasm axoplasm Plasma membrane axolemma Axon 1- Origin: Arises from axon hillock (what is its functional significance?) ; first area for generation of action potential. 2- Function : Conduct impulses away from the perikaryon. 3- Number : Always single Length : Long or short Axon hillock Axon Branching : collaterals & terminal arborizations Organelles: few Neurofibrils , mitochondria , vesicles No Nissl Coverings: Myelin and/or neurilemma. Dendrite Origin : arise from any part of the cell Function : Conduct impulses toward Number : Single /multiple Length: short Shape : Highly branching The axon The dendrite Origin Arises from axon hillock Arises from any part of the cell Direction of the impulse. conducts nerve impulse away from the cell body . conducts nerve impulse toward the cell body Number Always single Usually multiple (in multipolar neurons). It may be single ( in bipolar neurons) Length Long Short Branching Limited numerous Organelles present Contains few organelles ( neurofibrils , vesicles and mitochondria . Nissl granules are absent. Contains most of the organelles as in the perikaryon except Golgi. Nissl granules are present Surrounding structures It may be surrounded by sheaths. It is not surrounded by sheaths Distribution of nerve cell bodies & axons: 1- IN CNS (central nervous system) 2- In PNS ( peripheral NS) Cell bodies are only in ganglia CNS (Grey matter) PNS (Ganglia) c lassification of neuron I- Functionally 1-Sensory neurons : where impulses are carried from receptors to the CNS . 2-Motor neurons : where impulses are carried from CNS to the effector organs e.g. muscle or gland . 3-Interneurons: act as a link between sensory and motor neurons. They are present in CNS only . At the end of this lecture, students should know: Correlate structure of different parts of the neuron to its role in nerve impulse transmission. Identify types of neurons on morphological basis. Appraise the functional classification of receptors. Correlate structure & site of different skin sensory nerve endings to their specific function. Correlate microstructure of the muscle spindle & Golgi tendon organs to their functions. II. Morphologically: According to the number of their processes: 1- Multipolar 2- Pseudo-unipolar:  spinal ganglia. 3- Bipolar:  retina a- Pyramidal: present in cerebral cortex(brain) b- Purkinje cells in the cerebellar cortex 1- Multipolar 2- Pseudounipolar Present in the dorsal root ganglion (outside the CNS). Has a single process that divides into central & peripheral divisions 3- Bipolar neurons Present in the retina What is a synapse? It is the area of contact between two neurons or a neuron and an effector organ. Most of the synapses are chemical that depend on release of neurotransmitter. Others are electrical (gap junctions) Parts of a chemical synapse Types of synapses Cell structures & organelles involved in chemical synaptic transmission Mitochondria Ultra structure of a chemical synapse 1- Presynaptic 2-Cleft 3-Post synaptic How do axons terminate? The axons end at a synapse by a nerve ending. Types of nerve endings: 1- Motor nerve ending: the axon terminals establish a synapse with an effector organ (muscle or gland). How do axons terminate? Types of nerve endings: 2- Sensory nerve ending: The axon terminals end in the periphery of the body; skin, joints, muscle & some viscera. Transmit information from the periphery into the CNS. The nervous tissue is one of the four primary basic tissues. It consists of two types of cells: Neurons Neuroglia. Structural and functional unit Supportive cells Sensory Nerve Endings What is a receptor? It is the specialized sensory nerve ending of a sensory nerve fiber. Each type of sensory nerve ending has a special structure and pattern at its termination in a specific site (skin, muscle & others). Classification of receptors Functionally Mechanoreceptors; Ex; Pacinian’s corpuscles, Meissner’s corpuscle, muscle spindle & Golgi tendon organs. Thermoreceptors Nociceptors (pain) Others rods & cones in the retina, gustatory cells in the taste bud & olfactory epithelium in the nose. What is the result of receptor stimulation? Generation of action potential along the sensory axon. Olfactory cells Gustatory cells Olfactory epithelium Taste Buds Structurally: 1- Encapsulated ; covered by a CT capsule 2- Non encapsulated; free nerve endings, Merkel’s disks Site Muscle spindle Golgi tendon organs Between skeletal muscle fibers near the tendon At junction between tendon & muscle Core Intrafusal muscle fibers Collagen fibers Function Stretch receptor ; monitors degree of muscle stretch (length) & induces reflex contraction Tension receptor; monitors force of contraction; induces reflex relaxation Encapsulated mechanoreceptors in the skeletal muscle 1- Muscle spindle 2- Golgi tendon organs 1- Structure of the muscle spindle 1- CT capsule ; separating it from the skeletal muscle fibers (extra fusal fibers) 2- Content; intrafusal fibers (modified muscle fibers) of two types: A- Nuclear chain ; cylindrical, uniform, nuclei are arranged in one row B- Nuclear bag (dynamic & static); swollen middle part that contains randomly oriented nuclei Both types lack myofibrils at their central (non contractile central parts) Peripheral portions contain myofibrils and are contractile CT cap Nuclear Bag Nuclear Chain 3- Innervation of the muscle spindle Gamma efferent Motor axons to peripheral zones of intrafusal fibers; to maintain them stretched and sensitive. Primary ( Ia ) afferent sensory axons that end by annulo spiral endings on all types of intra fusal fibers. Secondary II afferent sensory axons that end by flower spray endings on static type of nuclear bag fibers & nuclear chain Functional variation : Group Ia and group II fibers both respond to a stretching of the muscle at a constant rate. Only group Ia fibers , however, respond to a change in the rate of stretching. a b c Innervation of the muscle spindle 2- Golgi tendon organs Site: junction between tendon & muscle. Structure ; CT capsule, wavy collagen fibers (role of collagen). Innervation : sensory afferent axons only. Excitability as they respond to environmental changes by generation of action potential or nerve impulse. Conductivity as they are capable of propagation of nerve impulse to other neurons, or to effector organs that produce an action (muscles and glands.) text: Page 1 of 9 L 1 Cranial cavity ILOs By the end of this lecture, students will be able to 1. Know the overall structure of the skull and define the different bones bounding the cranial cavity. 2. Describe the different layers of the meninges and their related spaces with their clinical significance. 3. Describe the dural folds dividing the cranial cavity. 4. Differentiate between the dural venous sinuses regarding their site and termination. 5. Relate some clinical conditions to their anatomical basis. CLINICAL PROBLEM A patient came to the ER complaining of sever headache, diplopia, redness and swelling of one eye. He told the physician that few days ago, he had a boil in the upper lip that became inflamed and septic. What is the most probable diagnosis? - Cranial cavity : The cranial cavity lodges the brain and its coverings, cranial nerves and supplying vessels. Its floor is divided into anterior, middle, and posterior cranial fossae. (Fig. 1) Figure 1. Cranial cavity. - Anterior cranial fossa : (Fig. 2) The anterior cranial fossa lies above the nasal cavity and the two orbits. The frontal bone shows the frontal crest with foramen cecum behind the crest. The floor of the anterior cranial fossa is formed of : 1- Anteriorly : the cribriform plate of ethmoid bone that presents the crista galli and on each side, the orbital plate of the frontal bone. 2- Posteriorly : the body of sphenoid and the lesser wing of the sphenoid on each side. The lesser wing ends as the anterior clinoid process and the optic canal lies medial to the process. Page 2 of 9 The cribriform plate of ethmoid and body of sphenoid roof the nasal cavity while the orbital plate of frontal bone and lesser wing of sphenoid roof the orbit. Figure 2. (A) anterior cranial fossa. (B) anterior view of skull - Middle cranial fossa : (Fig. 3) The floor of the middle cranial fossa is formed by the body of the sphenoid in the middle with the greater wing of the sphenoid and the petrous part of temporal bone on each side. Sella turcica The body of sphenoid shows the sella turcica which is composed of : 1- hypophyseal fossa that lodges the pituitary gland. 2- tuberculum sellae that forms the anterior wall of the sella turcica. 3- dorsum sellae that forms the posterior wall of the sella turcica. Its upper border shows the posterior clinoid processes. The middle cranial fossa shows the following foramina arranged from before backwards : superior orbital fissure, foramen rotundum, foramen ovale and foramen spinosum. At the apex of the petrous part of temporal bone, foramen lacerum lies. A B Figure 3. Middle cranial fossa. Page 3 of 9 - Posterior cranial fossa : (Fig. 4) It contains the brainstem (midbrain, pons, and medulla) and the cerebellum. Anteriorly, it is bounded by the dorsum sellae and the clivus that slopes downwards till foramen magnum. Posteriorly, the occipital bone shows the internal occipital protuberance with the internal occipital crest extending downwards. On each side of the protuberance, the transverse sulcus extends and continues as the sigmoid sulcus that ends at the jugular foramen. Above the jugular foramen, lies the internal acoustic meatus while below the foramen, the hypoglossal canal is present. Figure 4. posterior cranial fossa. - Meninges : (Fig. 5) The brain, as well as the spinal cord, is surrounded by three layers of membranes (meninges) : - an outer layer; the dura mater. - a middle layer; the arachnoid mater. - an inner layer; the pia mater. 1- Dura mater : (Fig. 5,6) It is the tough outer covering of the brain in close contact with the arachnoid mater. Figure 5. Meninges. dorsum sellae Page 4 of 9 - Dural folds (partitions) : They project into the cranial cavity and partially subdivide it into compartments for the parts of the brain. They include the falx cerebri, tentorium cerebelli, falx cerebelli, and diaphragma sellae. Figure 6 (A&B). Dural folds and spaces of the meninges. 1- Falx cerebri : (Fig. 6,7) It is a sickle-shaped fold between the two cerebral hemispheres. It is attached anteriorly to the crista galli and frontal crest. Posteriorly it is attached to the tentorium cerebelli. 2- Falx cerebelli : (Fig. 6,7) It is a midline fold attached posteriorly to the internal occipital crest and superiorly to the tentorium cerebelli. Its anterior edge lies between the two cerebellar hemispheres. A B Page 5 of 9 Figure 7 (A&B). Dural folds. 3- Diaphragma sellae : (Fig. 6,7) It is attached to the anterior and posterior clinoid processes overlying the pituitary gland. It is pierced by the infundibulum, connecting the pituitary gland with the hypothalamus. 4- Tentorium cerebelli : (Fig. 7,8) It is a tent-shaped fold that separates the cerebellum in the posterior cranial fossa from the cerebral hemispheres. It has an outer border attached to the internal occipital protuberance, transverse sulci, upper borders of the petrous parts of temporal bones, dorsum sellae and the posterior clinoid processes. A B Page 6 of 9 Its inner border is free attached anteriorly to the anterior clinoid processes bounding an opening (tentorial notch), through which the midbrain passes. 2- Arachnoid mater : (Fig. 5,6) It lines the inner layer of the dura mater. It does not follow the grooves of the brain, except for the longitudinal fissure between the two cerebral hemispheres. 3- Pia mater : (Fig. 5,6) It closely invests the surface of the brain. It follows the grooves of the brain, and is closely applied to the cranial nerves at their origins. - Dural venous sinuses : Veins draining the brain empty into dural venous sinuses that eventually lead to the internal jugular veins. The dural venous sinuses receive also emissary veins which connect extracranial veins to the dural venous sinuses. The sinuses may be single or paired. Single sinuses Paired sinuses Superior sagittal. Spheno-parietal sinuses. Inferior sagittal. Cavernous sinuses. Straight sinus. Superior petrosal sinuses. Occipital sinus. Inferior petrosal sinuses. Intercavernous sinuses. Transverse sinuses. Sigmoid sinuses. 1- Superior sagittal sinus : (Fig. 6,7,9,10) It lies in the upper border of the falx cerebri. It begins anteriorly at foramen cecum, where it may receive an emissary vein from the nasal cavity and ends posteriorly at the internal occipital protuberance where it continues as the right transverse sinus. Figure 8. Tentorium cerebelli. Page 7 of 9 Figure 9 (A&B). Dural venous sinuses. 2- Inferior sagittal sinus : (Fig. 6,7,9,10) It lies in the lower border of the falx cerebri. Posteriorly, it is joined by the great cerebral vein to form the straight sinus. 3- Straight sinus : (Fig. 6,7,9,10) It passes posteriorly along the junction of the falx cerebri and the tentorium cerebelli to the internal occipital protuberance where it continues as the left transverse sinus. 4- Transverse sinus : (Fig. 9,10) It lies in the transverse sulcus along the attached margin of the tentorium cerebelli and continues as the sigmoid sinus. The right transverse sinus (a continuation of the superior sagittal sinus) is larger in size than the left (a continuation of the smaller straight sinus). 5- Sigmoid sinus : (Fig. 9,10) It lies in the sigmoid sulcus. It passes through the jugular foramen and it continues as the internal jugular vein. 6- Occipital sinus : (Fig. 6,10) It lies along the attached margin of the falx cerebelli. 7- Spheno-parietal sinus : (Fig. 10) It runs along the lesser wing of sphenoid to end in the cavernous sinus. 8- Cavernous sinus : - Site : lateral side of the body of the sphenoid on either side of the sella turcica. (Fig. 9) - Tributaries : The cavernous sinus receives blood from : (Fig. 10) a. cerebral veins. b. spheno-parietal sinus. c. veins of the orbit. d. veins from the face. A B Page 8 of 9 Figure 10. Dural venous sinuses. - Drainage : by the superior and inferior petrosal sinuses. (Fig. 9,10) - Connections : it is connected with : a. the orbit. b. the face. c. opposite cavernous sinus by intercavenous sinuses ar

text: Cranial cavity Prof. Dr. Abdelghany Hassan Abdelghany Professor of Anatomy and Embryology Faculty of Medicine Alexandria University Posterior cranial fossa It shows the clivus and dorsum sellae . The internal occipital crest extends from the protuberance. Transverse sulcus continues as sigmoid sulcus. Foramen magnum lies inferiorly with the hypoglossal canal, jugular foramen and internal acoustic meatus above it in order. Q: Which foramen lies in the posterior cranial fossa? Foramen ovale . Foramen cecum. Jugular foramen. Foramen rotundum . Answer : C Brain 1- cerebrum. 2- cerebellum. 3- brain stem (midbrain, pons and medulla). Meninges Outer layer; dura mater. Middle layer; arachnoid mater. Inner layer; pia mater. Dural folds They project into the cranial cavity and partially subdivide it. They include the falx cerebri , tentorium cerebelli , falx cerebelli , and diaphragma sellae . - Diaphragma sellae overlies the pituitary gland and is pierced by the infundibulum. Dural folds Falx cerebri : sickle-shaped, extends between the 2 cerebral hemispheres. - Falx cerebelli between the 2 cerebellar hemispheres. Falx cerebri It is a sickle-shaped fold between the two cerebral hemispheres. Anteriorly, it is attached to the crista galli and frontal crest . Posteriorly, it is attached to the tentorium cerebelli . Falx cerebelli It is a dural fold that lies between the two cerebellar hemispheres. It is attached posteriorly to the internal occipital crest and superiorly to the tentorium cerebelli . Diaphragma sellae It overlies the pituitary gland. It is attached to the anterior and posterior clinoid processes . It is pierced by the infundibu­lum , connecting the pituitary gland with the hypothalamus. Dural folds Dear students & Tentorium cerebelli A tent-shaped fold, extends between the 2 cerebral hemispheres and the 2 cerebellar hemispheres. It has an outer attached border and an inner free border. Tentorium cerebelli The outer border is attached to the internal occipital protuberance, transverse sulci, upper borders of the petrous parts of temporal bones, dorsum sellae and the posterior clinoid processes. The inner border is free and is attached anteriorly to the anterior clinoid processes bounding an opening (tentorial notch), through which the midbrain passes. Q: To which structure is the free border of the tentorium cerebelli attached? Anterior clinoid process. Transverse sulcus. Posterior clinoid process. Internal occipital protuberance. Answer : A Dural venous sinuses Single Paired Superior sagittal Sphenoparietal Inferior sagittal Cavernous Straight Superior petrosal Occipital Inferior petrosal Intercavernous Transverse Sigmoid Paired Superior sagittal sinus It begins at foramen cecum. It passes along the upper border of falx cerebri It ends as right transverse sinus. Inferior sagittal sinus It passes along the lower border of falx cerebri It joins the great cerebral vein to form the straight sinus that ends as left transverse sinus. Transverse and sigmoid sinuses Right transverse sinus is larger than the left. Transverse sinus continues as sigmoid sinus that continues as internal jugular vein. Superior and inferior petrosal siuses They lies along the upper and lower border of the petrous part of temporal bone. They begin at the cavernous sinus. The superior sinus ends in the corresponding transverse sinus. The inferior sinus passes through the jugular foramen to end in the internal jugular vein. Sphenoparietal sinus It lies along the lesser wing of sphenoid. It ends in the cavernous sinus. Transfer Goal This lecture aims to explain the cranial cavity, meninges of the brain and dural folds with the related venous sinuses. Cavernous sinus Site : on either side of the sella turcica . Tributaries : veins from the cerebrum, orbit, face, sphenoparietal sinus. It drains into the superior and inferior petrosal sinuses. - It communicates with the opposite cavernous sinus by intercavenous sinuses. Cavernous sinus Structures inside the sinus : internal carotid artery and abducent (6 th cranial) nerve. Structures in the lateral wall : 1- occulomotor (3 rd cranial) nerve. 2- trochlear (4 th cranial) nerve. 3- ophthalmic (branch of 5 th cranial) nerve. 4- maxillary (branch of 5 th cranial) nerve. Clinical points Emissary veins connect extracranial veins with intracranial sinuses and are important clinically because they may transmit extracranial infections to the cranial cavity as they have no valves . Cavernous sinus thrombosis Due to infection of the face or eye. Patients complain of swelling and redness of the eye, double vision and sever headache . Q: Which structure continues as the right transverse sinus? Straight sinus. Superior sagittal sinus. Inferior sagittal sinus. Superior petrosal sinus. Answer : B Summary or take-home message The cranial cavity overlies the nasal cavity and the two orbits and its floor has anterior, middle and posterior cranial fossae. The meninges are the coverings of the brain and the outer layer ( dura mater) gives dural fold that separate the cranial cavity into compartments. The dural venous sinuses drain the brain. There are single and paired sinuses that eventually end in the internal jugular vein. The cavernous sinus is connected with the orbit and face so that extracranial infections may be transmitted to the cranial cavity. Lecture notes. Gray’s Anatomy for Students. Dear Student: Don’t forget to complete your KWL chart And reflect on your learning experience by writing down what do you learnt from the lecture (3 points at least) Students’ learning outcomes By the end of this lecture, students will be able to 1. Relate different bones bounding the cranial cavity to the important structures passing through. 2. Describe the different layers of the meninges and specify their related spaces. 3. Describe the dural folds and correlate them to common relevant clinical conditions. 4. Differentiate between the dural venous sinuses regarding their site and termination. He told the physician that few days ago, he had a boil in the upper lip that became inflamed and septic. What is the most probable diagnosis? The frontal bone shows frontal crest and foramen cecum lies behind it. The cribriform plate of ethmoid bone shows the crista gali . The lesser wing of sphenoid ends medially in the anterior clinoid process. Medial to the process, lies the optic canal. Middle cranial fossa It is formed by body of sphenoid, its greater wing and the petrous part of temporal bone. The sella turcica is formed of tuberculum sellae , hypophyseal fossa and dorsum sellae that expands into the posterior clinoid processes. It shows : superior orbital fissure, foramen rotundum , foramen ovale and foramen spinosum and foramen lacerum .

text: 14 ANALGESICS ILOs By the end of this lecture, students will be able to Categori ze analgesics based on their mechanism of action & clinical indications. Classify opiate analgesics into subtypes & select their use priorities. Appraise their acute risks versus their chronic abuse and addiction. Determine non - opiate analgesics acting on descending tracts PRE-REQUISITS: Terminologies linked to pai n, its incidence, types, nature, etiology , distribution ascending pathways to perception and descending inhibitory facilitatory modulation. Different approaches to induce analgesia with final stress on pharmacotherapeutic modulation by narcotic opioid analgesics, non-narcotic analgesics & others as α 2 adrenergic agonists NARCOTICS OPIOID ANALGESICS Opioid Receptors: mu [ ] [MOR] ; Supraspinal / delta [ ]; Supraspinal / kappa [ ]; Spinal . CLASSIFICATION of OPIOIDs [Acting on different opioid receptors] Depending On Their Source: Endogenous Opioids; in our body as Endorphins, Dynorphins, Enkephalins Exogenous opioids; Natural: extracted from opium [ poppy plant ] . These are opiates as M orphine Semisynthetic: naturally mod ified: C odeine Synthetic; Manufactured: Meperidine , Heroin, Methadone, Fentanyl , T ramadol Depending On Their Action Agonists; Morphine, Meperidine, Methadone, Fentanyl, Tramadol Agonist / Antagonists ; buprenorphine . NB. : Antagonists ; are not analgesics but are used as antidotes in acute narcotic toxicities . MECHANISM OF OPIOID ACTION In Induction of Analgesia: Inhibit Pain Transduction : By attenuating pain stimuli via activation of MOR to excitation of peripheral nociceptive afferent neurons Reduce Pain Transmission & Supraspinal Processing & Perception : Whether along ascending supraspinal pathways or at cortex, thalamus & limbic system. So nociceptive sensation even if perceived is no longer unpleasant or threatening . By Direct Presynaptic Inhibition via b ind ing to MOR [a Gi GPCR] that – ve AC & cAMP Ca 2+ influx via closing Ca 2 + channels excitatory transmitter release; Glutamate & SP in ascending pathways By Direct Postsynaptic Inhibition via binding to MOR , so K + efflux via opening of K + channels neuronal membrane hyperpolarization generation of action potential at postsynaptic fibers . Facilitate Descending Pain Inhibitory Modulation : By facilitating the inhibitory inputs at PAG to RM & LC th rough inhibition of GABA- ergic release by activation of MOR . This will exert a modulatory action via the supraspinal descending inhibitory serotonergic & noradrenergic axons . That indirectly will activate the inhibitory MOR interneurons at dorsal horn cells suppressing pain signaling . In Inducing Euphoria: Dopamine is dominating the reward pathway that gives rise to pleasurable sensation & happiness. This is checked by higher central control , specially from the frontal lobe to keep a balanced mood and to prevent over excitement and euphoria. Such higher check signals are dominated by GABA- ergic inhibitory transmission. H owever, opioids through MOR activation can disinhibit such GABA- ergic signals leaving dopamine unrestrained to fully activate the reward centres with development of intense pleasure excitement & euphoria . In Development of Withdrawal Manifestations: As MOR belong to GPCR of the Gi type, so continuous opioid occupancy in addicts will always exert suppress ion on adenyl cyclase (AC) . As an adaptive process, cell s will begin to synthesize more and more adenyl cyclase as a compensation . But with the maintenance of opioid occupancy, cAMP production remains at a low pace. Once opioids are withdrawn, cAMP production shoots up secondary to the overexpressed AC already present. Such cAMP shooting is responsible for the withdrawal manifestation that peaks immediately on withdrawal and takes days to way off. _________________ _________________________________________ INDIVIDUAL OPIOID ANALGESICS Morphine Commonest rout e of administration is IM every 4 hours but can be given subcutaneous or with dose adjustment IV to prevent adverse effects . It i s now rarely taken orally as it undergoes e xtensive 1 st pass metabolism and has low bioavailability. Intrathecal o r epidural is given by anesthetist in smaller doses. It is indicated in : Control of p ain; after trauma, severe burns, cancer pain, visceral pain (not renal/biliary colic, acute pancreatitis) < neuropathic < musculoskeletal . In distressful c onditions ; even if are not painful ; acute pulmonary edema , AMI, acute HF… In pre-anesthetic medication and in post-operative pain control . It produces less respiratory depression and possesses atropine-like (anticholinergic) properties. It is used for obstetric analgesia because of its relatively limited respiratory depressant effect, as well as for severe visceral pain and renal or biliary colic, where its anticholinergic action may provide additional benefit. It also has a favourable pre-anaesthetic profile. Toxicity is more likely to occur in patients with renal impairment due to accumulation of its active metabolite. Toxicity may manifest as anticholinergic effects, including tremors, hyperthermia, hypotension, mydriasis, blurred vision, dry mouth, and urinary retention. Tramadol It is a centrally acting analgesic indicated for the management of moderate pain. It exerts its analgesic effects through a dual mechanism: weak agonism at μ-opioid receptors and inhibition of norepinephrine and serotonin synaptic reuptake, thereby enhancing descending inhibitory pain pathways. Compared with full μ-opioid agonists, it generally produces less respiratory depression and has a lower potential for abuse and dependence. text: 31 Therapeutic s for Cerebral Dysfunction ILOs By the end of this lecture, students will be able to Identify the rational of treatment of various cerebral dysfunction as Alzheimer's, Parkinson's diseases, stroke, and chronic pain . Categorize different anticonvulsant drugs according to their mechanism of action and miscellaneous clinical use. Segregate the different use precautions of drugs used in chronic pain. Select appropriate drug/drug group in different clinical scenarios. The diseases of the nervous system represent one of the most important challenges in modern medicine. The main therapeutic strategy depends significantly on the integrated pathophysiological knowledge for each disease. Unfortunately, many of these diseases still represent an unresolved medical challenge. That's why understanding the therapeutic strategic plan to treat these diseases is remarkably warranted. In this context, cerebral dysfunction can be exceptionally classified according to the causative underlying neurotransmitters deficiency , electrolytes or metabolic disturbance s , inflammatory, autoimmune, infectious , or neoplastic disorders , …. As examples of the commonest cerebral dysfunction are the stroke , epilepsy, multiple sclerosis, Alzheimer's disease, Parkinson's disease, chronic pain , among others. A brief demonstration of the therapeutic strategic plan for some of these diseases will be addressed based on their studied pathophysiological background . Stroke A stroke or cerebrovascular accident is characterized by a temporary, or permanent, loss of function of brain tissue caused by interruption of the vascular supply . It is s a serious medical condition that requires emergency care as it is a common cause of death and disability . Primarily, it is important to identify the type of stroke whether ischemic or haemorrhagic , minimize its size and evaluate what treatment options are available to maximize recovery of function and/or prevent the problem from reoccurring . For ischemic stroke : Atherosclerosis is the most important cause of ischaemic stroke that leads commonly to cerebral arterial thrombosis or sometimes stenosis. Every effort should be taken to reduce the stroke onset to emergency department (ED) arrival time (onset to door time ≤ 3 hours) to rescue the patient life and maximize recovery of function . After establishment of the diagnosis and exclusion of haemorrhagic stroke through prompt clinical examination and investigations, every attempt should be implemented to recanalization of the occluded artery . This can be done for eligible patients by either: Mechanical thrombectomy (removal of the blood clot by catheterization ) or Pharmacological thrombolysis using drugs to lyse the already formed thrombus. They are more efficacious on recently formed than older thrombi (having extensively polymerized fibrin resistant to lysis ) making their success cure rates depending on time of administration with a therapeutic window ranging from ≈ 6 hours post - insult. Fibrin-Specific Thrombolytics are more efficacious and safer. ( Refer to thrombolytic therapy in CVS ) Reduction of atherothrombotic events following a recent stroke (secondary stroke prevention) by using antiplatelet drugs ( aspirin & / or clopidogrel ) or oral a nticoagulant ( warfarin ) according to the cause. Treatment of associated events, e.g., epileptic fits using anticonvulsants (benzodiazepines as diazepam during the attack or other antiepileptic drugs in chronic epilepsy). Treatment of the associated risk factors, e.g., hypertension using antihypertensive drugs, hyperlipidaemia using antihyperlipidemic drugs as statins , …. Alzheimer's disease (AD) A lzheimer dementia is associated with a complex pattern of neuronal degeneration that mainly involves the cholinergic nuclei leading to neuronal loss in the basal forebrain. Besides, there are significant dysregulation s in other neurotransmitter systems, such as glutamatergic systems. Nowadays, no available medications can halt the progression of the disease pathology. The therapeutic strategy based on the disease pathogenesis include the following: Potentiation of central cholinergic transmission: Inhibition of the central acetylcholinesterase ( AChE ) activity would activate acetylcholine ( A C h ) and potentiate the failing cholinergic signal without modification of the disease process or progression . For example, donepezil is a non-competitive, reversible inhibitor of AChE , whose long half-life makes possible once-daily dosing. In patients with moderate to severe AD, donepezil leads to improved cognition and daily functioning. Control the dysregulated glutamatergic transmission: Memantine is an uncompetitive NMDA receptor antagonist. Because of its voltage dependency and fast kinetics, memantine does not interfere with normal glutamatergic transmission, but blocks increased transmission under chronic conditions. M emantine significantly slows down the rate of cognitive and functional decline . In addition , it has a positive synergistic effect with cholinesterase inhibitors such as donepezil, without adding to the burden of adverse effects. Neuroprotective agents especially antioxidants may reduce oxidative stress and free radical-induced neuronal damage, e.g., vitamin E . Reduction of the risk factors , e.g., hyperlipidaemia as t here is a possible link between cholesterol and Alzheimer's diseases. Treatment of other comorbid symptoms with dementia , such as psychosis, aggression, or depression . Parkinson' disease (PD) PD is a common neurodegenerative disease characterized by massive loss of nigrostriatal dopaminergic melanized cells . This shortage of dopamine leads to an imbalance in striatal output pathways. Drugs that block dopamine action in the nigrostriatal pathway in the basal ganglia can induce a Parkinson-like syndrome, for example the dopamine antagonist phenothiazines, e.g., haloperidol (antipsychotic) & metoclopramide (antiemetic). The pharmacological treatment of PD attempts to compensate for the loss of nigral dopaminergic cells and the input imbalance created in the striatum. Dopamine replacement therapy has been the major treatment for PD for decades. Since d opamine does not cross the blood–brain barrier (BBB), so direct systemic supplementation with dopamine is not therapeutically useful. This was overcome using either indirect and/ or direct dopaminergic agents and sometimes non-dopaminergic agents . Indirect dopaminergic agents include Precursor in the biosynthetic pathway of dopamine: L-DOPA (levodopa) can be administered to increase dopamine concentrations in the dopamine-deficient areas of the brain. It is the most efficacious antiparkinsonian drug and provides the greatest improvement in patients’ quality of life, despite its wide range of adverse effects. Therefore, it is generally not used as the initial treatment for mild-to-moderate Parkinson’s disease . Inhibition of endogenous dopamine degradation, e.g., MAO B or COMT inhibitors . Direct dopaminergic agents , e.g., pramipexole , that directly stimulate various dopaminergic receptors. Non-dopaminergic (antimuscarinic) agents, e.g., benztropine , can help restore the dopamine–acetylcholine balance in the striatum that is disrupted in Parkinson’s disease. They are particularly effective in alleviating tremor and rigidity but have limited efficacy against bradykinesia and are therefore less effective than L-DOPA. Consequently, they are mainly used in younger patients, in whom tremor and rigidity are often prominent features. Chronic pain Chronic pain is defined as pain that persists beyond normal healing time . Usually, pain is considered chronic when it lasts for more than 3 months. It is a frequent condition that is highly debilitating and presents a major medical challenge due to its obscure etiopathogenesis and poor response to therapy (opioid analgesics, NSAIDs) . Chronic pain should receive greater attention to improve patients’ quality of life

text: 6 Anatomy of Vertebrae and spinal cord ILOs At the end of this session, the student will be able to: 1. Correlate the structure of the vertebrae and ligaments attached to vertebral column to its stability and function . 2. Define the structure of the intervertebral disc and its clinical significance . 3. Appraise the importance of identifying the level of termination of the spinal cord and its covering meninges relevant to its clinical correlation . Vertebral Column : Mid line structure formed by series of 33 vertebrae separated by intervertebral discs . The vertebral column supports the body, protects spinal cord and helps in transmission of body weight. These 33 bones are divided into five regions: Cervical 7 Thoracic 12 Lumbar 5 Sacral 5 Coccygeal 4 The v ertebral column has several curves, these curves are important for balance, flexibility and stress absorption. Anatomy of the vertebrae : All vertebrae share a basic common structure. Anteriorly: vertebral body Posteriorly: vertebral arch Vertebral Body : Anterior part of the vertebrae. It is the weight-bearing component . I ts size increases as the vertebral column descends (to support increasing amounts of weight) . Vertebral Arch: The lateral and posterior parts of the vertebrae . With the vertebral body, the vertebral arch forms an enclosed hole called a vertebral foramen. -The foramina of the all vertebrae line up to form the vertebral canal which encloses the spinal cord . Side view of vertebra: Intervertebral Discs: They l ie in between the bodies of vertebrae. They add to the flexibility of the spine and act as shock absorbers. It is formed of: Annulus fibrosus (peripheral part) Nucleus pulposus (central gelatinous part) Clinical correlation: Intervertebral Disc Herniation: Occurs when the nucleus pulposus ruptures , breaking through the annulus fibrosus. The rupture usually occurs in a posterior-lateral direction. The nucleus pulpos u s can irritate nearby spinal nerves – resulting in a variety of neurological and muscular symptoms. Joints between adjacent vertebrae: Intervertebral joint Facet (zygapophyseal joint) Ligaments between adjacent vertebrae: Body: Anterior longitudinal ligament along the front of the vertebral bodies P osterior longitudinal ligament along the back of the vertebral bodies Lamina: ligamentu m flavum - Spinous process : Interspin o us ligament Supraspinous ligament - Transverse process : Inter transverse ligament Sacroiliac joint: The sacroiliac joints are large joints. Very little movement takes place at the sacroiliac joint . It provide s rotation between the ilium and the sacrum during normal gait. Clinical correlate: The sacroiliac joint is well innervated, and can be a source of pain (in the groin) in inflammatory and non-inflammatory conditions. muscles that act to move the lumbar spine: 1.Psoas major muscle 2. Quadratus lumborum posterior muscles of the spine: Multifidus Erector Spinae 1- PSOAS MAJOR MUSCLE : Origin: from the bodies and transverse processes of the lumbar vertebrae. Insertion: into the lesser trochanter of the femur . Action: flexion of the hip joint and flexion of the trunk . 2. QUADRATUS LUMBORUM MUSCLE: A broad, flat muscle that attaches to the iliac crest, lumbar vertebrae and last rib . Action: lateral flexion of the lumbar region and fixation of the last rib during resiration . The posterior muscles of the spine ( multifidus and erector spinae ) help to extend the spin e . 3. Multifidus: The most medial and largest group. It is attached to the spinous processes and sacrum. 4 . ERECTOR SPINAE Lateral to the multifidus . Clinical correlate: Scoliosis Lateral deviation of the vertebral column Kyphosis Thoracic curve is more convex backwards. Scoliosis Scoliosis Kyph osis Kyph osis Spinal Cord It is a part from Central Nervous System (CNS) . It connect s the brain and peripheral nervous system. It is s urrounded by the meninges and cerebrospinal fluid (CSF). Length of the spinal cord: about 46cm long . Beginning: starts at foramen magnum . Termination: at the lower border of L2 vertebra. Occupies the upper 2/3 of the vertebral canal Its lower tapering end is called conus medullaris S pinal nerve s descending below the end of spinal cord fan out, resembling a horse’s tail (cauda equina) - S pinal cord is differentiated into 31 segments not demarcated externally: 8 cervical 12 thoracic 5 lumbar 5 sacral 1 coccygeal - The spinal cord presents two enlargements: Cervical enlargement: corresponds to the nerves of the brachial plexus. Lumbosacral enlargement: corresponds to nerves of the lumbar and sacral plexuses. External features of spinal cord The spinal cord is incompletely divided into two equal parts. Anteriorly: anterior median fissure Posteriorly: posterior median sulcus. Cross Section o f Spinal Cord: grey matter in the centre surrounded by white matter. Central canal in the middle . SPINAL NERVES : Each spinal nerve arises as: Dorsal (posterior) root Ventral (anterior) root Two roots join to form the spinal nerve. Dorsal root has a dorsal root ganglion (sensory) that contains the cell bodies of the sensory neurons . Each spinal nerve then divides into a smaller dorsal and a larger ventral ramus . GREY MATTER : It resembles the shape of the letter H. Having: two posterior , two anterior and two lateral horns. Relation if the spinal and vertebral segments: 3 rd month of intra-uterine life: The spinal cord occupies the whole length of the vertebral canal. A t birth: (differential growth) the spinal cord ends at the level of L3 vertebra. In adults: the lower end of the cord lies opposite L 2 vertebra. So spinal segments do not lie opposite the corresponding vertebrae. Covering of spinal cord: Three layers of meninges from outside to inside: 1- Dura mater 2- Arachnoid mater 3- Pia mater Dura mater: It is the outermost layer of the three meninges. It extends from the foramen magnum to the 2 nd sacral segment . E xtradural (or epidural) space: The space outside the dura, between it and the periosteum of the vertebral canal. S ubdural space: The space deep to the dura, between it and the arachnoid mater. The arachnoid mater: It is a delicate sheath , It ends at the level S2. It is separated from the pia mater by the subarachnoid space which is filled with the cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) . The lower part of the subarachnoid space which contains the cauda equina and the filum terminale is called the lumbar cistern . Pia mater: It is a delicate sheath intimately adherent to the spinal cord. The pia mater gives laterally 21-teeth like processes to the dura mater called ligamenta denticulata fix ing the spinal cord to the dura mater . At the lower end of the spinal cord, the pia mater is prolonged to form the filum terminale . The filum terminale pierces the lower end of the arachnoid and dura where it extends to be attached to the first piece of coccyx . Factors of fixing the spinal cord in position : The ligamenta denticulata. The filum terminale . spinal nerve s Blood supply of the spinal cord : A. Arterial supply: Anterior spinal artery: arises from both vertebral arteries. supply the Anterior third of the cord Two posterior spinal arteries: each one arises from vertebral artery. ( Posterior two -thirds of the cord) Radicular arteries: branches of the body wall arteries. B. Venous drainage: 6 veins: - Anterior spinal vein. - Posterior spinal vein. - Anterolateral spinal veins (two) - Posterolateral spinal veins (two) Clinical correlate: Lumbar puncture: Lumbar puncture is performed with the patient lying on their side or leaning forward with their lower back flexed . (ligamentum flavum is stretched and the vertebral laminae and spinous processes are separated apart ) . T he needle is inserted between the L3 and L4 or L4 and L5 vertebrae T he needle punctures the dura and arachnoid mater to enter the subarachnoid space. cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) normally drips out. Indications for lumbar puncture: 1- retrieval of CSF is an important diagnostic

text: 1 | Page Study Guide for course NMD2101: Neuroscience I Dr Course coordinator: Dr. Gehan Yassin Soliman Professor of Medical Physiology Contact information: gehanyassinsoliman@aast.edu 2 | Page STUDY GUIDE IN THIS Guide: • Welcome Note P. 3 • Educational Opportunities P.4-7 • Timetable link P. 8 -9 • Assessment P.10-12 • Learning Resources P. 13-14 3 | Page Dear students Welcome to Medical School. We hope you enjoy your 5 years' journey of becoming a physician. Here in the sixth course" Neurosciences I”, you will learn how to integrate smoothly between basic medical and clinical sciences, in a manner that will help you rationalize the clinical importance of the topics your study in the pre-clerkship phase. It consists of an extensive and in-depth study of the anatomical and functional aspects of central nervous system in order to understand the human brain & behavior. The aim of this course is to help you be acquainted with the gross and microscopic structural features of the brain, brain stem, basal ganglia and spinal cord. You will discover the miraculous physiology of synapses, neurotransmitters and mechanisms of neuronal excitation as well as the structure and functions of different receptors during neuronal excitation. You will discover the mechanisms and pathways of sensory inputs in the nervous system. You will explore the structure and functions of motor system and how can you maintain your posture. You will be surprised a lot about neuronal plasticity and memory types. You will realize the structure of skin and how you can feel pain. You will explore treatment of various cerebral dysfunctions such as Alzheimer's disease, Parkinson's disease and the uses of anti-seizure drugs in different clinical scenarios. We hope you enjoy your sixth block in your enjoyable long-life medical knowledge. 4 | Page IN THIS SECTION: • The different Course Themes • The Course Objectives • Different Teaching and Learning Methods EDUCATIONAL OPPORTUNITIES 5 | Page Through reviewing the following table, you will understand the Four major themes in Neuroscience I course and how these themes are related to the course objectives. text: Page 1 of 5 L 28 White Matter& Internal Capsule ILOs By the end of this lecture, students will be able to 1. Differentiate between the different types of white matter of the brain. 2. Relate the different parts of corpus callosum to their location. 3. Appraise the importance of internal capsule relative to its contents. 4. Correlate the anatomy of corpus callosum & internal capsule to relevant clinical conditions. The white matter of the brain is divided into: Association fibers; Commissural fibers; Projection fibers I.Association fibers: (Fig. 1) Connect 2 areas on the same cerebral hemisphere, includes: A. Short association fibers: connecting adjacent gyri together. B. Long association fibers : connecting gyri away from one another. II. Commissural fibers: (Fig. 2) These connect same areas on different cerebral hemispheres. The brain houses two minds, not one, but they only orchestrate into a single personality if the two cerebral hemispheres communicate& exchange information, as by commissural fibers. Thus, consciousness is controlled by both hemispheres, and there is a crossing over of functions so that one never normally experiences a dissociation of information. Fig. 1: Association fibers Fig. 2: Commissural fibers Page 2 of 5 Types of Commissural Fibers: 1. Anterior commissure: It connects olfactory structures of both hemispheres (olfactory bulb; anterior perforated substance). (Fig. 3) 2. Posterior commissure: it is present just above the upper end of the cerebral aqueduct. It connects visual structures on both hemispheres. (Fig. 3) 3. Hippocampal commissure (or commissure of the fornix): these fibers connect the hippocampus with its fellow of the opposite side. (Fig. 4) 4. Corpus callosum: It is the largest commissure. It is divided into: ❑ Rostrum, is the thin part of the anterior end of the corpus callosum, ❑ Genu, the curved anterior end of the corpus callosum, ❑ Body, arches posteriorly and ends as the splenium. ❑ Splenium, posterior end of the corpus callosum. Parts of Corpus Callosum: (Fig. 5 A& B) • Rostrum: Connects the orbital surface of the frontal lobes on both sides. • Genu: Connects the anterior part of the frontal lobes on both sides. The fibers of the genu radiate forwards towards the frontal poles forming the forceps minor. • Body: Connects the posterior part of the frontal lobe and anterior part of the parietal lobe on both sides. • Splenium: Connects the posterior part of the parietal lobe, temporal lobe and occipital lobe on both sides. These fibers pass either: • Lateral to the posterior horn of the lateral ventricle and are called tapetum. • Medial to the posterior horn of the lateral ventricle and are called forceps major. Fig. 3: Anterior & Posterior commissures Fig. 4: Hippocampal commissure Page 3 of 5 Split-brain’ syndrome: (Fig. 6) ‘Splitting’ the brain, by sectioning the corpus callosum, and thereby disconnecting the hemispheres, was used by surgeons to treat chronic intractable forms of epilepsy. To the casual observer, the split-brain patients appeared normal, and their seizures disappeared. However, psychological testing revealed that if the patient held up an object like a comb in the left hand, they could not say what it was. When it was transferred to the right hand, the patient had no trouble at all to identity it. The same happened with words. If a card with a printed word like ‘ring’ was visible only in the patient’s left visual field, they could not read it, yet vision in the left eye was fine. When the word was in the right field, the patient immediately recognized it. Fig 5; A: Parts of corpus callosum in sagittal section Fig 5; B: Parts of corpus callosum in horizontal section Fig.6: Split- brain’ syndrome Page 4 of 5 III. Projection fibers: These are fibers passing from or to the cerebral cortex; thus, they are subdivided into: A. Ascending fibers B. Descending fibers e.g. for the projection fibers is the Internal Capsule. (Fig. 7: A, B, C) INTERNAL CAPSULE: (Fig. 7: A) The internal capsule is composed of all the fibers, afferent and efferent, which go to, or come from, the cerebral cortex. It has anterior limb, genu, & posterior limb (Fig. 7: B) Fibers of the internal capsule: (Fig. 7: C) A. Anterior limb: 1. Frontopontine fibers. 2. Anterior thalamic radiation. B. Genu: Corticobulbar fibers. C. Posterior limb: Subdivided into: I. Thalamolentiform part: Lies between the lentiform nucleus and the thalamus; contains: 1. Parietopontine fibers. 2. Superior thalamic radiation. 3. Corticospinal tract. 4. Corticorubral. 5. Corticostriate. II. Retrolentifrom part: Extends caudally behind the lentiform nucleus; contains: 1. Occipitopontine fibers. 2. Posterior thalamic radiation including optic radiation. III. Sublentifrom part: Passing beneath the lentiform nucleus; contains: 1. Tempropontine fibers. 2. Inferior thalamic radiation including auditory radiation. Fig. 7: A Fig. 7: B Fig. 7: C Page 5 of 5 Blood supply of Internal Capsule: Both anterior and posterior limbs are supplied primarily by branches of the middle cerebral artery. In addition, each part of the internal capsule receives another arterial branch: • The anterior cerebral artery supplies the anteromedial parts of the anterior limb. • The genu receives direct branches from the internal carotid artery. • The ventral portion of the posterior limb and its entire retrolenticular part are supplied by branches of the anterior choroid artery. CLINICAL CORRELATION: Infarction of the internal capsule: (Fig. 8) Most frequently results from occlusion of the lenticulostriate branches of the middle cerebral artery and results in the following contralateral conditions: • Anesthesia • Hemiparesis (with the Babinski sign) • Lower facial weakness Fig. 8: Infarction of the internal capsule
