text: Objective 1 14. A 46-year-old patient suffering from severe bradychardia , receives a drug that inhibits adenosine receptors and subsequently becomes more alert as a side effect. The clinician explains that adenosine normally has an effect in the CNS. Which description of adenosine explains this side effect? a. Primarily excitatory in the CNS b. Largely inhibitory in the CNS c. A spinal inhibitory amino acid d. A catecholamine e. A neuropeptide Correct answer: b. Largely inhibitory in the CNS 19. A 36-year-old patient has a disorder involving a neurotransmitter that is not stored in vesicles and is synthesized by nitric oxide synthase from arginine. The molecule acts through a second messenger involving GMP. Which chemical category best describes this transmitter? a. Amino acid b. Monoamine c. Soluble gas d. Neuropeptide e. Purine Correct answer: c. Soluble gas Objective 2 38. A patient has impaired removal of a neuropeptide from the synaptic region. Unlike catecholamines , the peptide is not normally cleared by a specific uptake pathway. Which process is the major route of neuropeptide disposal? a. Presynaptic reuptake b. Simple diffusion followed by extracellular peptidase cleavage c. Acetylcholinesterase cleavage d. COMT-mediated methylation e. Conversion to glutamine Correct answer: b. Simple diffusion followed by extracellular peptidase cleavage 39. A patient receives a medication that blocks reuptake of a neurotransmitter. The pharmacologist explains that interfering with uptake can be therapeutically useful because the transmitter remains in the synaptic space longer. Which general consequence is expected? a. Lower synaptic concentration b. Higher synaptic concentration c. Immediate transmitter synthesis failure d. Loss of all receptors e. Failure of action-potential generation Correct answer: b. Higher synaptic concentration 32. A patient receives a drug that prolongs acetylcholine action in the synaptic cleft. The drug works by preventing the major enzyme that normally breaks down ACh after secretion. Which enzyme is inhibited? a. Choline acetyltransferase b. Acetylcholinesterase c. Monoamine oxidase d. COMT e. Nitric oxide synthase Correct answer: b. Acetylcholinesterase Objective 3 46. A patient suffers a major cerebral stroke and subsequently develops neuronal injury. The physician explains that extracellular glutamate increases after stroke because of damaged cells and impaired glutamate uptake. Which mechanism best explains the resulting neurotoxicity? a. Excess glutamate-mediated excitotoxicity b. Loss of VIP diffusion c. Excess ACh degradation d. Reduced dopamine metabolism e. Histamine receptor blockade Correct answer: a. Excess glutamate-mediated excitotoxicity 48. A patient with a neurodegenerative disorder has excessive NO formation. The neurologist explains that NO normally acts as a signaling molecule and causes vasodlation but can have harmful effects. Which statement best characterizes NO in this context? a. Excessive formation of NO may be neurotoxic b. It is always an inhibitory peptide causing CNS depression c. It is stored in synaptic vesicles d. It competes with GABA for inhibition of CNS e. It is degraded slowly causing neurotoxicity Correct answer: a. It can have physiological roles but excessive formation may be neurotoxic 56. A patient with a mood disorder has symptoms associated with altered monoamine neurotransmission. The physician discusses serotonin and norepinephrine as monoamine systems with broad effects on brain function. Which statement best fits the mentioned neuroransmitters ? a. Can modulate overall brain functions such as mood and arousal b. They are exclusively spinal inhibitory transmitters c. They are all neuropeptides d. Both are stored only in adrenal glands e. Monoamines act only at skeletal muscle Correct answer: a. Monoamines can modulate overall brain functions such as mood and arousal Objective 4 62. A patient is treated with a barbiturate for a neurologic condition. The pharmacologist explains that, unlike benzodiazepines, barbiturates can stimulate the GABA receptor directly even in the absence of endogenous GABA. Why is overdose particularly dangerous? a. They are more likely to cause toxic side effects b. They cannot interact with GABA receptors c. They block all serotonin synthesis d. They inhibit glutamate recycling e. They prevent ACh synthesis Correct answer: a. They are more likely to cause toxic side effects 65. A patient with reduced cholinergic transmission is treated with a drug that inhibits the enzyme responsible for cleaving acetylcholine. The treatment aims to prolong the action of endogenous acetylcholine. Which enzyme is the drug targeting? a. Acetylcholinesterase b. Choline acetyltransferase c. COMT d. MAO e. Glutamate decarboxylase 73. A patient with depression is prescribed selective chatecolamine reuptake inhibitor that blocks presynaptic uptake of catecholamines . The clinician explains that uptake is a major route of catecholamine removal from the synaptic space. Which change should occur? a. Prolonged/increased catecholamine availability in the synaptic space b. Immediate loss of catecholamine receptors c . Reduced extracellular catecholamine concentration d. Increased conversion to GABA e. Complete inhibition of catecholamine synthesis Correct answer: a. Prolonged/increased catecholamine availability in the synaptic space Objective 5 82. A patient exposed to an organophosphate develops excessive cholinergic activity. The emergency team explains that acetylcholine is normally broken down after secretion by a specific enzyme.What is the direct biochemical consequence of organophosphate toxicity? a. Accumulation/prolongation of acetylcholine action b. Reduced acetylcholine concentration c. Failure of acetylcholine synthesis d. Conversion of ACh to dopamine e. Increased GABA degradation Correct answer: a. Accumulation/prolongation of acetylcholine action 92. A patient is brought in after severe pesticide exposure. The clinician explains that acetylcholinesterase normally cleaves acetylcholine in the synaptic cleft, so inhibition causes persistence of the transmitter. Which synaptic change is expected? a. Increased acetylcholine concentration/action in the cleft b. Reduced acetylcholine concentration/action c. Increased degradation of ACh d . Reduced cholinergic receptor stimulation e. Increased conversion of ACh into GABA Correct answer: a. Increased acetylcholine concentration/action in the cleft 96. A patient with a severe neurotoxic exposure develops convulsions because inhibitory neurotransmission has been blocked. The clinician compares this with GABA deficiency, which can also predispose to seizures. Which shared physiological principle explains both conditions? a. Loss of inhibitory neurotransmission permits excessive neuronal/motor activity b. Loss of excitation causes uncontrolled motor activity c. Increased peptide diffusion causes seizures d. Reduced dopamine always causes convulsions e. ACh breakdown always causes epilepsy Correct answer: a. Loss of inhibitory neurotransmission permits excessive neuronal/motor activity

name: L3 Notes 26/27
text: 1 3 Neurotransmitters ILOs By the end of this lecture, students will be able to 1. Classify the major human neurotransmitters into their distinct chemical categories (amino acids, monoamines, soluble gases, and neuropeptides), distinguishing between their primary excitatory or inhibitory physiological roles in the nervous system. 2. Explain the biochemical synthesis and degradation pathways of key neurotransmitters identifying the specific rate-limiting enzymes that serve as major targets for pharmacological intervention. 3. Analyze the pathophysiological consequences of localized neurotransmitter depletion or excess, correlating a loss of dopaminergic pathways with Parkinson's disease and imbalances in serotonin/norepinephrine with Major Depressive Disorder. 4. Differentiate between the mechanisms of action of major clinical drug classes that modulate neurotransmitter availability, explaining how selective serotonin reuptake inhibitors (SSRIs), monoamine oxidase inhibitors (MAOIs), and acetylcholinesterase inhibitors alleviate clinical symptoms. 5. Evaluate the acute neurotoxic effects of substances that disrupt neurotransmitter clearance or receptor binding (such as organophosphates inhibiting acetylcholinesterase or tetanospasmin blocking inhibitory GABA/glycine release), justifying the immediate physiological presentation and emergency clinical management. 6. DEFINITION OF A NEUROTRANSMITTER Neurotransmitters are molecules that act as chemical signals between nerve cells Traditionally, for a molecule to be labeled as a neurotransmitter, a number of criteria have to be met: • Synthesis of the molecule occurs within the neuron, i.e. all biosynthetic enzymes, substrates, cofactors, etc., must be present for de novo synthesis • Storage of the molecule occurs within the nerve ending prior to release, e.g. in synaptic vesicles. • Release of the molecule from the presynaptic ending occurs in response to an appropriate stimulus such as an action potential. • There is binding and recognition of the putative neurotransmitter molecule on the postsynaptic target cell. • Mechanisms exist for the inactivation and termination of the biological activity of the neurotransmitter. Rigorous adherence to the above criteria means that some molecules that are involved in the cross-talk between neurons are not in the strict sense classified as neurotransmitters. 2 Thus, nitric oxide (NO), adenosine, neurosteroids, polyamines, etc., are often termed neuromodulators rather than neurotransmitters. N.B.Several transmitters may be found in one nerve Furthermore, different transmitters may have a different timescale of action. CLASSIFICATION OF NEUROTRANSMITTERS A classification of neurotransmitters based on chemical composition is shown in table 1. Many are derived from simple compounds, such as amino acids but peptides are also now known to be extremely important. The principal transmitters in the peripheral nervous system are norepinephrine and acetylcholine (Ach) REGULATION OF NEUROTRANSMITTERS The action of transmitters must be halted by their removal from the synaptic cleft.This can be achieved through: 1. Simple diffusion is probably the major mechanism of removal of neuropeptides. 2. Enzymes such as acetylcholinesterase, which cleaves A cetyl choline, may destroy any remaining transmitter. 3. Surplus transmitters may also be taken back up into the presynaptic neuron for reuse, and this is a major route of removal for catecholamines and amino acids. Interference with uptake causes an increase in the concentration of transmitter in the synaptic space; this often has useful therapeutic consequences. CLASSES OF NEUROTRANSMITTERS (Table 1) I)Amino acids 1)Glutamate • Glutamate is the most important excitatory transmitter in the CNS • Glutamate acts on both ionotropic and metabotropic receptors. It acts on receptors called NMDA (N-methyl-D-aspartate).Glutamate is recycled by high -affinity transporters into both neurons and glial cells. The glial cells convert it into glutamine, Table 1 3 which then diffuses back into the neuron. Mitochondrial glutaminase in the neuron regenerates glutamate for reuse. Glutamate and excitotoxicity Extracellular glutamate concentration is increased after trauma and stroke, during severe convulsions, and in some organic brain diseases such as Huntington’s chorea, AIDS- related dementia, and Parkinson’s disease. This is because of release of glutamate from damaged cells and damage to the glutamate uptake pathways. Excess glutamate is toxic to nerve cells.The activation of NMDA receptor allows calcium entry into cells. This activates various proteases, which in turn initiate the pathway of apoptosis . 2)Glycine Glycine is primarily found in inhibitory interneurons in the spinal cord, where it blocks impulses traveling down the cord in motor neurons to stimulate skeletal muscle. The glycine receptor on motor neurons is ionotropic and is blocked by strychnine; motor impulses can then be passed without negative control, which accounts for the rigidity and convulsions caused by this toxin. II)Aminoacid derivatives 1)γ-Amino butyric acid (GABA) • GABA is synthesized from glutamate by the enzyme glutamate decarboxylase which utilizes vitamin B6 as a cofactor • GABA is the major inhibitory transmitter in the brain. There are two known GABA receptors: the GABA -A receptor is ionotropic and the GABA -B receptor is metabotropic. • Benzodiazepines bind to GABA -A and cause a potentiation of the response to endogenous GABA; these drugs reduce anxiety and also cause muscle relaxation. Barbiturates also bind to the GABA receptor and stimulate it directly in the absence of GABA; because of this lack of dependence on endogenous ligand, they are more likely to cause toxic side effects in overdose. • Deficiency in GABA may lead to convulsions and epilepsy 4 2)Catecholamines Norepinephrine, epinephrine, and dopamine, known as catecholamines, are all derived from the amino acid tyrosine .In common with other compounds containing amino groups, such as serotonin, they are also known as biogenic amines. These compounds are believed to have a general modulatory effect on overall brain functions such as mood and arousal. Catecholamines are metabolized through the enzyme s Monoamine oxidase (MAO) and catecholamine O -methyl transferase (COMT) (Figure 1) i)Norepinephrine and epinephrine • Norepinephrine (also known as noradrenaline) is a major transmitter in the sympathetic nervous system • Sympathetic nerves arise in the spinal cord and run to ganglia situated close to the cord, from which postganglionic nerves run to the target tissues. Norepinephrine is the transmitter for these postganglionic nerves, whereas the transmitter at the intermediate ganglia is ACh. • Stimulation of these nerves is responsible for various features of the ‘fight or flight’ response, such as stimulation of the heart rate, sweating, vasoconstriction in the skin, and bronchodilation. • There are also norepinephrine -containing neurons in the CNS, largely in the brainstem. Their axons extend in a wide network throughout the cortex and alter the overall state of alertness or attention. The stimulatory effects of amphetamines are caused by their close chemical similarity to catecholamines. • Epinephrine (also known as adrenaline) is produced by the adrenal medulla under the influence of ACh-containing nerves, analogous to the sympathetic preganglionic nerves • The end product of catecholamine metabolism, vanillylmandelic acid can be measured in the urine as indices of the function of the adrenal medulla. It is particularly increased in patients who have the tumor of the adrenal medulla known as pheochromocytoma. This tumor causes hypertension because of the vasoconstrictor action of the catecholamines it produces. ii)Dopamine 5 • Dopamine is both an intermediate in the synthesis of norepinephrine and a neurotransmitter.It is also derived from the aminoacid tyrosine. • It is a major transmitter in

text: L17: Histological Features of Cerebral Cortex D. SILVIA SAWIRES ASSOCIATE PROFESSOR OF HISTOLOGY AND CELL BIOLOGY 3.Fusiform cells : usually placed in deepest cortical layer. dendrite projects towards cortical surface, axon project to thalamus . 4.Horizontal cells of Cajal : ar small, spindle-shaped , oriented parallel to surface only seen in the most superficial part of the cortex one axon and one dendrite, both of them synapsing locally 5.Cells of Martinotti : multipolar neurons most located within the deepest layer of the cortex. numerous axons and dendrites course towards the surface of the cortex. Layers of cerebral cortex neurons of cerebral cortex have a laminar alignment. organized in layers, or laminas, parallel to the surface of the brain layers are differentiated between each other by the size and shape of the neuronal bodies . In a typical histological section of the motor area, six layers can be identified arranged from surface inwards Layers of cerebral cortex The molecular layer ( plexiform layer): This is the most superficial layer, lying directly under the pia mater very poor with cellular component(few horizontal cells of Cajal ). The major portion  processes of the neurons lying within the deeper layers and their synapses. Layers of cerebral cortex II. The external granular layer: consists mostly of stellate cells. small cells in this layer gives that “granular” appearance to this layer, hence its name. III. The external pyramidal cell layer: small & medium-sized pyramidal cells which increase in size and decrease in number in the deeper parts of this layer. Layers of cerebral cortex IV. The internal granular layer: Consists mostly of stellate cells similar to layer V. The internal pyramidal cell layer (ganglionic layer): medium-sized & large-sized pyramidal cells. giant pyramidal cells (Betz cells) constitute the projection neurons of the motor cortex. They are the upper motor neurons with their axons form the pyramidal tracts descending in the brainstem and spinal cord. Layers of cerebral cortex VI. The polymorphic layer (multiform layer ): Deepest and broadest layer in the cortex . Cells of this layer have variable sizes and shapes (fusiform, triangular and ovoid). How does the cerebral cortex adapt to its function? 1- Motor area (precentral gyrus): It is Agranular type : F ew granule cells. W ell developed pyramidal cell layers (Betz cells in the internal pyramidal layer). 2- Sensory area (post central gyrus): It is Granular type : W ell developed granular layers . I ll defined pyramidal layers(few & small pyramidal cells) A neurosurgical biopsy from the most superficial layer of the cerebral cortex reveals sparse cell bodies. Which cell type is most likely to be isolated in this layer? Multipolar Martinotti cells Thalamic-projecting fusiform cells Large output pyramidal cells Horizontal cells of Cajal Densely packed stellate cells Dear students & A patient presenting with severe paresthesia and sensory loss following a thalamic infarct is evaluated. Which structural characteristic is the most prominent in this specific affected cortical area in relation to the mentioned clinical picture? giant Betz cells polymorphic layer external pyramidal layer molecular layer internal granular layer A neuropathologist compares brain tissue from the precentral gyrus and postcentral gyrus . Which defining cytoarchitectonic feature best distinguishes favors the precentral motor cortex? Predominance of horizontal cells of Cajal Granular structure with prominent layer IV Thickened molecular layer devoid of axons Complete absence of layer V pyramidal neurons Agranular structure with reduced granular layers During neurosurgery, stimulation of the superficial cortical layer produces minimal response. Which feature explains this? A. Rich in pyramidal cells B. Contains giant Betz cells C. Poor in cellular components D. Contains fusiform cells E. Contains Martinotti cells Summary or take-home message The cerebral cortex has a unique histological structure in order to be able to perform higher functions. Lecture notes Portal resources: PDF Transfer Goal To study the microstructure of the cerebral cotrex Students’ learning outcomes At the end of this session, you have to : Analyze the Role of the Cortical Neuropil in Ischemic and Metabolic Brain Injury Differentiate Neuronal Morphologies to Understand Cortical Output Disorders Map the Six Histological Cortical Layers to Structural Function Evaluate the Histology of Upper Motor Neurons and Pyramidal Tract Pathology Compare Granular and Agranular Cortical Types in Diagnostic Regional Localization CEREBRUM Structurally, it consists of: 1- An outer grey matter (cortex): has a large surface area provided by convoluted gyri separated by sulci. 2- A central white matter: which contains collection of nerve cell bodies called basal ganglia . The cerebral cortex It is formed of: 1- Cell bodies of neurons: arranged in layers 2- Neuroglia. 3-Capillaries. 4-Neuropil: LM (H&E): pale & homogenoue . EM: network formed by cell bodies and processes of astrocytes & processes of neurons , enclosed intercellular spaces containing tissue fluid . This arrangement permits diffusion of nutrients & oxygen between capillaries and neurons. Types of neurons The cerebral cortex consists of the hundreds of billions of neurons all of them are different variations of only three morphological shapes: pyramidal cells , fusiform cells and stellate (granular cells). Other types of cells seen in the cortex are a modification one of those three .( horizontal cells of Cajal and cells of Martinotti .) Types of neurons 1.Pyramidal cells: 75 % of the cellular component of the cortex vary in size, going from small to gigantic. one thick apical dendrite that courses towards the surface of the cortex, and multiple basal dendrites one long axon arises from middle of base that leaves cortex and enters the subcortical white matter. 2.Stellate (granular) cells: small and densely-packed giving a granular appearance . numerous branching dendrites and a single short axon present in all cortical laminae .

text: L27:Neuroglia and Myelination D. SILVIA SAWIRES Associate Professor OF HISTOLOGY AND CELL BIOLOGY Share in formation of blood–brain barrier (BBB Definition Components Functions of Astrocytes Blood brain barrier (BBB ) end feet of glial astrocytes do not touch the endothelial cells release factors that induce characteristics in the capillary endothelial cells (high transendothelial resistance) high transendothelial resistance due to length and complexity of tight junctions between endothelial cells. transcytosis is limited  very few pores , either small or large, that cross the endothelium, and. 2. Regulation of K + levels in EX medium around neurones 3. storage of glycogen that can be supplied to neurones , in the form of lactate, when required 4. controlling distribution of neurotransmitters released by neurones : by restricting diffusion by transporting neurotransmitters into the astrocyte, where they can be metabolized or recycled. Gap junctions between: adjacent astrocytes  stimulated by neurotransmitters, changes in intracellular levels of Ca2 + ions  spread between astrocytes as waves Astrocytes and neurons  modulate the behaviour of the neurones by allowing the passage of Ca2 + between them Ependymal cells simple epithelial cells with numerous microvilli and one or two cilia on their apical surface Their basolateral surface is in contact with astrocytic Processes line the ventricles are not connected by tight junctions. Microglial cells small cells with long spiny processes During development  act as macrophages release growth factors + removing debris produced by programmed cell death which occurs on a large scale at this time In adult  relatively inactive any type of injury to the nervous system  reactive revert to the role of phagocytotic macrophages Oligodendrocytes One of the neuroglia of the CNS large cells with few processes Important for the process of MYELINATION (wrap around the axons, forming multiple lipid bilayers, with their plasma membranes forming a myelin sheath. These membranes have a high lipid/ protein ratio, which makes them excellent insulators) Oligodendrocyte can myelinate more than one axon , and the cell body lies between them Schwann cells One of the neuroglia of the PNS They are flattened cells whose cytoplasm contains a flattened nucleus Functions: Important for the process of MYELINATION ( myelinate a single axon, and the cell body is closely apposed to the myelin sheath). Dear students & 2. role in regeneration of peripheral axons following injury . This stimulates mitosis in Schwann cell  extends processes towards growth cone of the axon. axon regrows at between 2 - 5 mm / day along Schwann cells, which remyelinate new axon in the CNS No regeneration because CNS glial cells release factors that specifically inhibit axon growth. Unmyelinated nerve fibers grey matter, which consists of cell bodies and unmyelinated axons Dendrites A 45-year-old man presents with progressive weakness and loss of coordination. MRI shows multiple demyelinating plaques in the CNS. Which glial cell is primarily responsible this type of myelination? Astrocyte Oligodendrocyte Microglia Ependymal cell Schwann cell A neonate has congenital infection leading to impaired CSF flow. Pathology shows defective ciliated cells lining ventricles. Astrocyte Oligodendrocyte Microglia Ependymal cell Schwann cell Transfer Goal Recognition the other types of cells in the nervous system (neuroglia ) and study their importance Summary or take-home message Glial cells are important component in both CNS and PNS which plays essential roles in their integrity Lecture notes Students’ learning outcomes At the end of this session, you have to : Evaluate the integrity and clinical consequences of Blood-Brain Barrier (BBB) breakdown. Compare the pathophysiology and clinical features of CNS vs. PNS demyelinating diseases. Assess the role of reactive microglia in CNS pathology and neuroinflammation . Explain the cellular basis of peripheral nerve regeneration and central failure. Correlate astrocytic homeostatic functions with neurotoxicity and metabolic support. Neuroglia Supporting cells of the nervous system Make up about half the brain mass Functions:- 1- Structural and metabolic support 2- Immune functions 3- Electrical insulation of axons. A- In the CNS Astrocytes ependymal cells Microglia Oligodendrocytes B- In the PNS Schwan cell Types of Neuroglia Astrocytes most common glial cells in the CNS distinguished from neurones by the presence of glial fibrillary acidic protein . Precursors : radial glial cells during early development, span the cerebral cortex, forming a scaffolding for the migration of new nerve cells to their destinations. large, stellate cells. They have multiple radiating processes, that surround neurones , capillaries and the ependymal cells lining the ventricles Astrocytes Astrocytes Long unbranched processes found in the white matter of the brain. text: L19: Stroke Dr. Marwa Abd ElAziz, MD PhD Lecturer of Pathology Alexandria Faculty of Medicine Dear students & marwaabdelaziz@adj.aast.edu 2 Transfer Goal To provide an overview of the etiopathogenesis of cerebral stroke and head injury. marwaabdelaziz@adj.aast.edu 3 Students’ learning outcomes At the end of this session, the student will be able to: Discuss the causes and risk factors for different types of cerebral strokes Classify cerebral stroke according to etiopathogenesis with specific relation to vascular disorders marwaabdelaziz@adj.aast.edu 4 What is stroke? marwaabdelaziz@adj.aast.edu 5 Rupture of vessels Direct tissue damage Secondary ischemic injury Artery is blocked Blood supply to brain is interrupted marwaabdelaziz@adj.aast.edu 6 marwaabdelaziz@adj.aast.edu 7 Severe systemic hypotension, systolic blood pressure is < 50 mmHg. < marwaabdelaziz@adj.aast.edu 8 Morphology Functional alteration REVERSIBLE INJURY Distended cells, are swollen, pale The cytoplasm eosinophilic: due to loss of RNA. marwaabdelaziz@adj.aast.edu Mechanisms of cell injury in ischemic stroke Glutamate activating NMDA Channels Ca2+ influx Inflammation Mechanisms of cell injury in ischemic stroke marwaabdelaziz@adj.aast.edu 10 Increased intracranial pressure Compression on cerebral vessels More ischemic injury Mechanisms of cell injury in ischemic stroke marwaabdelaziz@adj.aast.edu 11 Ischemic core: Hypoxia is most severe and brain tissue rapidly dies Ischemic penumbra: residual blood flow The cell damage may be reversible Latin paene ‘almost’ + umbra ‘shadow’ penumbra Clinically: marwaabdelaziz@adj.aast.edu 12 Transient ischemic attack Progression of neurological defects over 24–48h, suggesting an ongoing infarct Infarction is complete, and the neurological deficits do not increase further. Most common Signs include: Contralateral flaccid hemiplegia: D rooping arm, leg or eyelid D ribbling mouth [dysphagia] S lurred speech [dysarthria] Incontinence Contralateral hemisensory loss marwaabdelaziz@adj.aast.edu 13 Signs include: Homonymous hemianopsia Global aphasia (dominant hemisphere) Gait apraxia marwaabdelaziz@adj.aast.edu 14 Right –sided homonymous hemianopia/ Hemianopsia marwaabdelaziz@adj.aast.edu 15 1. Lacunar stroke : occlusion of the deep brain ( thalamostriate ) arteries: small (0.5–10mm) infarcts. Effects of stroke: according to occluded vessel Morphology: global ischemia Swollen brain, wide gyri & narrow sulci. marwaabdelaziz@adj.aast.edu 16 Morphology of cell injury marwaabdelaziz@adj.aast.edu Membrane damage Nuclear changes Local inflammation marwaabdelaziz@adj.aast.edu Morphology 0-12hours => no gross or microscopic changes 12-24hours => oedema red neurons - hypereosinophilic - with pyknotic nuclei 19 12-24 hours: red neurons marwaabdelaziz@adj.aast.edu Morphology 24-48hours => neutrophilic infiltration Grossly: Brain is swollen with no gray/white matter demarcation . marwaabdelaziz@adj.aast.edu 20 24-48 hours: neutrophilic infiltration Morphology 2-10days => Histiocytic infiltration. Grossly: gelatinous and friable brain tissue, more distinct boundary between normal and abnormal tissue (edema resolves in adjacent viable tissue. 21 2-10 days: histiocytic infiltration marwaabdelaziz@adj.aast.edu Morphology 2-3weeks => Liquefactive necrosis 3weeks-months => foamy macrophages (phagocytose lipid-rich necrotic brain tissue). Grossly: fluid-filled cavity marwaabdelaziz@adj.aast.edu 22 3 weeks -months Morphology Years => Gliosis surrounds and fills the cyst often giving a honeycomb morphology marwaabdelaziz@adj.aast.edu 23 Rupture of vessels Direct tissue damage Secondary ischemic injury Artery is blocked Blood supply to brain is interrupted marwaabdelaziz@adj.aast.edu 24 marwaabdelaziz@adj.aast.edu 25 marwaabdelaziz@adj.aast.edu 26 Most common cause of hemorrhagic stroke Hypertension: in the basal ganglia, thalamus, pons, and cerebellum Lacunar infarcts Amyloid deposition in vessel wall (cerebral amyloid angiopathy). in the lobes of the cerebral cortex (lobar hemorrhages: symptomatic small (<1mm) cortical hemorrhages (microhemorrhages). marwaabdelaziz@adj.aast.edu 27 Are most common in mid to late adult life (60 years of age). Rupture of a small intraparenchymal vessel. Hemorrhagic stroke Intraventricular haemorrhage Intraventricular haemorrhage is the most common neurological complication in about 40% of premature babies (<1.5kg body weight). The hypoxic pressure exerted on the baby’s head during delivery can cause haemorrhage . marwaabdelaziz@adj.aast.edu 28 Hemorrhagic stroke Intracerebral hemorrhage: fate In acute intracerebral hemorrhage, the extravasated blood compresses the adjacent parenchyma which shows oedema and hypoxic injury . The cellular events then follow the same time course observed after cerebral infarction. With time, hemorrhages are converted to a cavity with a brown, discolored rim. marwaabdelaziz@adj.aast.edu 29 Spontaneous subarachnoid hemorrhage Rupture of a blood vessel on the surface of the brain into the subarachnoid space due to: Vascular malformation: Ruptured berry aneurysm or arteriovenous malformation Rupture of an intracerebral hemorrhage into the ventricular system Coagulopathies Tumors marwaabdelaziz@adj.aast.edu 30 Hemorrhagic stroke Most frequent cause of clinically significant spontaneous subarachnoid hemorrhage is rupture of a saccular (berry) aneurysm Saccular (berry) aneurysms: Anterior circulation near major branch points. May be multiple . Not present at birth but develops over time A thin-walled outpouching of an artery due to defective media & intimal elastic lamina. marwaabdelaziz@adj.aast.edu 31 Berry aneurysm Saccular (berry) aneurysms: Ruptures at the apex of the sac , releasing blood into the subarachnoid space, the brain parenchyma, or both Ruptures at the time of an acute increase in intracranial pressure [straining at stool]. Healing and meningeal fibrosis may obstruct CSF flow or disrupt CSF resorption, leading to hydrocephalus. marwaabdelaziz@adj.aast.edu 32 Arteriovenous Malformations Congenital: defective communications between arteries and veins without intervening capillaries. Involve subarachnoid vessels extending into brain parenchyma or occur exclusively within the brain. Commonly manifest at 10 - 30 years old with an intracerebral or a subarachnoid hemorrhage. Grossly : network of wormlike vascular channels that may be atrophied (prone to rupture). Rapid shunting of blood produces ischemia in neighboring parts of the brain resulting in infarction or seizure activity. marwaabdelaziz@adj.aast.edu 33 Clinical presentation of hemorrhagic stroke Onset is sudden while the patient is awake. Manifestations depend on the site of hemorrhage (Basal ganglia/ Lobar/SA space). Hypertensive hemorrhage: headache, loss of consciousness and sensorimotor disturbances. Ruptured aneurysm: sudden, severe headache, neck stiffness and vomiting , and loss of consciousness +/- focal neurological signs. marwaabdelaziz@adj.aast.edu 34 Morphology of hemorrhagic infarcts Multiple, sometimes confluent, petechial hemorrhages. The microscopic picture and evolution of hemorrhagic infarction parallel those of ischemic infarction, with the addition of blood extravasation and resorption. In coagulopathies, hemorrhagic infarcts may be associated with extensive intracerebral hematomas. marwaabdelaziz@adj.aast.edu 35 Outcome of hemorrhagic stroke Massive haemorrhages may rupture brain tissue and leak into the ventricles, resulting in blood in the CSF. A fatal outcome occurs when brain herniation occurs due to the mass effect of the oedema and haematoma . marwaabdelaziz@adj.aast.edu 36 Can you deduce risk factors for stroke??? marwaabdelaziz@adj.aast.edu 37 Contraceptive pills Genetic Haematological disorders: Thrombocytosis Polycythemia Sickle cell disease Haemophilia Hyperuricaemia Vasculitis: SLE Male gender Old age Previous transient ischaemic attack (TIA) 20% of patients with TIA will go on to have a full-blown stroke Family history Alcohol consumption Summary or take-home message Stroke can be either ischemic or hemorrhagic . Ischemic stroke can be due to global ischemia or focal ischemia due to embolism or thrombosis. Hemorrhagic stroke is most commonly due to ruptured intracerebral artery due to longstanding hypertension or ruptured berry aneurysm. Pathological changes in both types follow a similar course in both types of stroke. The clinical presentation varies according to occluded artery or site of hemorrhage. marwaabdelaziz@adj.aast.edu 38 39 A 68‑year‑old man with hypertension and smoking history presents with sudden right arm weakness and slurred speech. GROSSLY- Plaques have a grey-tan appearance, instead of the white of unaffected white matter . The Morphology of MS Active plaques show regions of demyelination (MS plaques) around the fourth ventricle lack the normal blue staining of myelin ( Luxol fast blue periodic acid–Schiff stain). The Morphology of MS Inflammatory reaction ; lipid-laden macrophages, and relative axonal preservation. Lymphocytes and mononuclear cells are prominent at plaque edges and around venules. Chronic inflammation. Demyelination Gliosis lately, Axon Damage, Neuronal loss Disease history ACUTE ONSET Guillain-Barré syndrome; Cross reacting autoimmune reaction against gangliosides. Target is Schwann cells , and myelin of peripheral nerves. POST-INFECTIOUS; Follow campylobacter infection, ZIKA,CoVID-19 Guillain-Barré syndrome is an immunologically mediated demyelinating peripheral neuropathy that may lead to life-threatening respiratory paralysis. [ NOT brain OR spinal cord] Prognosis is usually good. Schwann cells or Schwann cell precursors proliferate and initiate repair through the formation of new myelin sheaths, but these again tend to be shorter and thinner than the original ones. R espiratory muscles that control breathing. Slowly progressing Ascending weakness\paralysis that begins in both feet and arms within a few days 2- Neurodegenerative disorders Group of disorders that are characterized by progressive loss of selectively vulnerable populations of neurons, which often have shared functions because of metabolic or toxic disorders. HALLMARK ; is protein abnormalities with the presence of protein aggregates (intracellular inclusions) that are resistant to proteolytic degradation; eliciting a neuronal stress response and can be directly neurotoxic. The different diseases tend to involve particular neural systems and have stereotypic presenting signs and symptoms. Dear students & CLASSIFICATION; 1- The anatomic site of neuronal loss (and/or related clinical manifestations) 2- The nature of the associated inclusions or abnormal structures. Alzheimer Disease A progressive neurodegenerative disease of the cerebral cortex which has been attributed to extracellular aggregates of amyloid β (Aβ) plaques and intracellular neurofibrillary tangles made of hyperphosphorylated τau -protein in cortical and limbic areas of the human brain. Pathogenesis of Alzheimer disease Point mutations in Amyloid precursor Protein (APP) gene Mutations in presenilin 1 and 2 genes Pathogenesis of Alzheimer disease Morphology of Alzheimer disease Amyloid plaques deposit as extracellular aggregates of Amyloid β ( Aβ) peptides in the neuropil. Aβ elicits an inflammatory response from microglia and astrocytes that can assist in aggregate clearance but can also stimulate the secretion of potentially deleterious mediators. B. Neurofibrillary tangles are another abnormal aggregate of the microtubule binding protein tau , which when becomes hyperphosphorylated, a stress response is elicited. They develop intracellularly and then persist extracellularly after neuronal death. Parkinson Disease (PD) is a neurodegenerative disease marked by motor syndrome that manifests as rigidity, tremors, and bradykinesia . It is caused by loss of dopaminergic neurons from the substantia nigra this results in a decrease in dopamine levels, especially in the post-commissural putamen and other regions of the basal ganglia . PD typically responds to levodopa therapy . Parkinson Disease (PD) These symptoms can also result from other neurodegenerative disorders, as well as specific brain lesions, head trauma, medications, metabolic conditions, and toxin exposure. Parkinsonism A chronic progressive disorder of motor function that is clinically characterized by tremors, rigidity and disordered gait and posture. text: L 4 Anterior Triangle of The Neck ILOs By the end of this lecture, students will be able to Differentiate between the triangles of the neck in relevance to the related structures. C orrelate the boundaries and contents of the anterior triangle of the neck to its clinical importance. Appraise the structures forming the roof and floor of the anterior triangle . Relate the anatomy of the different muscles sharing in the anterior triangle to their clinical importance . The neck is divided into anterior and posterior triangle by the sternocleidomastoid muscle: 1- Anterior triangle 2- Posterior triangle The anterior triangle of the neck is outlined by the anterior border of the sternocleidomastoid muscle laterally , the inferior border of the mandible superiorly , and the midline of the neck medially . It is further subdivided into several smaller triangles as follows: Borders and subdivisions of the anterior triangle of the neck Submandibular (digastric) triangle is outlined by the inferior border of the mandible superiorly and the anterior and posterior bellies of the digastric muscle inferiorly; Submental triangle is outlined by the hyoid bone inferiorly, the anterior belly of the digastric muscle laterally, and the midline; Muscular triangle is outlined by the hyoid bone superiorly, the superior belly of the omohyoid muscle, and the anterior border of the sternocleidomastoid muscle laterally, and the midline; Carotid triangle is outlined by the superior belly of the omohyoid muscle anteroinferiorly , the stylohyoid muscle and posterior belly of the digastric superiorly, and the anterior border of the sternocleidomastoid muscle posteriorly. The muscles in the anterior triangle of the neck can be grouped according to their location relative to the hyoid bone: A muscles superior to the hyoid are classified as suprahyoid muscles and include the stylohyoid, digastric, mylohyoid . m uscles inferior to the hyoid are infrahyoid muscles and include the omohyoid, sternohyoid, thyrohyoid, and sternothyroid. They pass in a superior direction from the hyoid bone to the skull or mandible and raise the hyoid, as occurs during swallowing. The infrahyoid muscles are in the muscular triangle . They attach the hyoid bone to inferior structures and depress the hyoid bone. Because of their appearance, they are sometimes referred to as the ' strap muscles ' . All infrahyoi d muscles are supplied by ansa cervicalis ( C1- C3) except thyrohyoid which is supplied by C1. Suprahyoid muscles. A. Lateral view. B. Inferior view infrahyoid muscles Contents of the anterior triangle: Submental triangle: Submental lymph nodes. Submental vessels. Muscular triangle: Infrahyoid muscles which are: Superficial: Sternohyoid muscle. Omohyoid muscle. Deep: Sternothyroid muscle. Thyrohyoid muscle. Carotid triangle: Carotid sheath. External carotid artery. Internal jugular vein. Common, internal carotid arteries. Sympathetic trunk. Parts of vagus (X), spinal accessory (XI), hypoglossal (XII) and ansa cervicalis . Digastric triangle: Submandibular gland. Hypoglossal nerve. Facial artery. Submandibular lymph nodes Vessels of the neck: Passing through the anterior triangle of the neck are the common carotid arteries and their branches, the external and internal carotid arteries. These vessels supply all structures of the head and neck. Associated with this arterial system are the internal jugular vein and its tributaries. These vessels receive blood from all structures of the head and neck. Both right and left common carotid arteries ascend through the neck, just lateral to the trachea and esophagus, within a fascial compartment (the carotid sheath). They give off no branches as they pass through the neck. Near the superior edge of the thyroid cartilage each common carotid artery divides into its two terminal branches-the external and internal carotid arteries in the carotid triangle. Branches of external carotid artery: Superior thyroid artery arises from the anterior surface of the external carotid artery and passes downward to the thyroid gland. Lingual artery arises from the anterior surface of the external carotid artery to the tongue. Facial artery arises just above the lingual artery, passes to the face. Ascending pharyngeal artery arises from the posterior aspect of the external carotid artery and ascends to the pharynx. Occipital artery arises from the posterior surface of the external carotid artery, to the posterior aspect of the scalp. Posterior auricular arises from the posterior surface of the external carotid artery, and passes posterior to the auricle. text: By Abeer El- Emam Professor of Physiology- Alexandria Faculty of Medicine L13- Pain Control mechanisms 9/26/26 Prof.Hala Abdel Gawad 10 The transmission of information from pain afferents to secondary neurons in the spinal cord is NOT A PASSIVE process but is dynamic involving excitation, inhibition and modulation Pain Modulation Neurons in the dorsal horn are subject to modulation that gates the flow of information to the CNS. PAIN CONTROL MECHANISM AT THE LEVEL OF SPINAL CORD Pain evoked by activity in the nociceptors can be reduced (modulated) by simultaneous activity in the mechanoreceptor (Aβ fibers). This is explained by the gate theory of pain . The projection neuron is inhibited by an interneuron (tonically active). A β fibers Large, myelinated, fast — carry touch, pressure, vibration (non-painful) A δ / C fibers Small, thinly/unmyelinated, slow — carry pain (nociceptive) Projection neuron (2nd order) Sends the signal up to the brain — the "output" of the gate Inhibitory interneuron Located in the dorsal horn — can suppress the projection neuron Gate Control Theory of Pain Non-painful input (e.g., rubbing the skin) activates A β fibers that excite inhibitory interneurons in the dorsal horn Gate Control Theory of Pain Gate OPEN (pain transmitted) A δ/ C fibers activate the projection neuron and inhibit the inhibitory interneuron . ↓ projection neuron fires ↓ pain signal ascends to brain. "Gate is open." Gate CLOSED (pain reduced) A β fibers activate the inhibitory interneuron. ↓ The inhibitory interneuron releases GABA/enkephalins onto the projection neuron. ↓ projection neuron is suppressed ↓ less/no pain signal ascends. "Gate is closed." Projection neuron The gate control theory of pain (Gate is closed) The gate control theory of pain (Gate is opened) The gate control theory of pain (Gate is closed) Without any stimulation, both sets of nerve fibres are inactive and the inhibitory neurone (I) blocks the signal in the projection neurone (P). The gate is ‘closed’ 1-when there is no stimulation Normal somatosensory input happens when there is more large- fiber stimulation (or only large- fiber stimulation). both the inhibitory neuron and the projection neuron are stimulated, but the inhibitory neuron prevents the projection neuron from sending signals to the brain (gate is closed). Nociception (pain reception) happens when there is more small- fiber stimulation or only small- fiber stimulation. They activate P and inactivates the inhibitory neuron. Therefore, the projection neuron sends signals to the brain informing it of pain (gate is open). Understand the pain control mechanism at its different levels and correlate some of its applications. Transfer goal Gate Control Theory The interneuron is both excited by the large sensory axon and inhibited by the pain axon. Trauma elicits acute pain. However, if the injury site is rubbed, the pain immediately subsides and it feels better. This reaction can be explained by the gate control theory. Rubbing the head or shin stimulates the non-nociceptive afferents that send impulses into the spinal cord. According to the gate theory, lamina II inhibitory interneurons are activated either directly or indirectly by stimulation of these afferents from the skin that would then block the projection neuron and therefore block the pain. This may explain why ‘counter- stimulation’ Counter stimulation analgesia 9/26/26 Prof.Hala Abdel Gawad 22 Spinal mechanism (Pain Control by Rubbing) Painful stimuli A beta fibers Rubbing of the skin after injury Pain C fiber Acupuncture Massage 9/26/26 Prof.Hala Abdel Gawad 23 Trans cutaneous electric nerve stimulation (TENS) IN OTHER WORDS The projection neuron is inhibited by an interneuron. The interneuron is both excited by the large sensory axon and inhibited by the pain axon. Therefore, activity in the pain axon alone maximally excites the projection neuron, allowing nociceptive signals to rise to the brain . However, if the large mechanoreceptive axon fires concurrently, it activates the interneurons and suppresses nociceptive signals. Supraspinal (descending) analgesia Endogens opioid system Brain regions that are involved in pain modulation project back to the brainstem and spinal cord and can change or modify information that is coming to the brain. This is one way that the brain can reduce pain Supraspinal (descending) analgesia Endogens opioid system Special areas in the brain & spinal cord where endogenous opioid peptides (endorphin, enkephalin & dynerphins ) & opiate receptors are highly concentrated Activation of this system can greatly reduce or even completely abolish pain sensation (morphine like analgesic action) These endogenous opiates bind with opiate receptors on the afferent pain fiber terminals(central branches ) inhibiting the release of substance P, thereby blocking further transmission of pain signals. Opioid receptors μ-mu β-endorphins δ-delta enkephalins κ-kappa. dynorphins Endogenous Opioids Opioidergic neurotransmission is found throughout the brain and spinal cord. P rovides a strong modulatory influence on pain processing. Opioid receptors can be found at all levels of the pain system. The powerful analgesic effect of opiate drugs is likely due to the fact that they influence the pain system at every level (mainly on peripheral nerves,at the site of an injury; in the dorsal horn and in the brain stem). Endogenous Opioids PAIN CONTROL AT THE LEVEL OF BRAIN periaqueductal - gray matter ( PAG ) in mid brain ( enkephalinergic neuron) Raphe magnus nucleus in lower pons and upper medulla (serotonergic neuron) Locus ceruleus which secretes catecholamines Opioid control system Midbrain Medulla By the end of this lecture, you should be able to: Analyze how the balance between large-diameter non-nociceptive and small-diameter nociceptive afferent activity determines whether the spinal “gate” is closed or open and how this influences pain perception. Apply the gate control theory to predict the effect of non-painful counter-stimulation, such as rubbing the skin, on nociceptive transmission and pain perception. Integrate the PAG–nucleus raphe magnus–locus coeruleus descending pathways with spinal inhibitory interneurons to explain how supraspinal mechanisms suppress pain transmission. Predict how activation of endogenous opioid receptors alters presynaptic and postsynaptic neuronal activity to produce analgesia through inhibition of Ca² ⁺ channels and opening of K ⁺ channels. Evaluate how emotional arousal, stress, and autonomic activation can engage descending analgesic mechanisms through the hypothalamus, amygdala, PAG, and locus coeruleus to produce stress-induced hypoalgesia. Cortex-Amygdala-Hypothalamus Enkephalin Serotonin NE Enkephalin Supraspinal (descending) analgesia Endoephin Sympathetic stimulation activate Locus cereulus ,which activate inhibitory interneurons Main areas for brain(endogenous) opioid system - Periventricular nuclei in hypothalamus → (endorphin neurons) - Periaqueductal gray matter ( PAG ) surrounding the cerebral aqueduct in the midbrain → (enkephalinergic neurons) locus coeruleus (LC)in the pons → (Norepinephrine) Nucleus raphe magnus (NRM), in lower pons and upper medulla → (serotonergic neurons) PAIN CONTROL AT THE LEVEL OF BRAIN presynaptic inhibition of neurotransmitter release from primary afferent terminals. This works by activating G protein-linked receptors that cause closing of calcium channels, thus reducing transmitter release postsynaptic inhibition of projection cells causing hyperpolarization of the membrane due to activation of G protein-linked receptors that cause opening of potassium channels resulting in IPSP Enkephalin produces pre and post synaptic inhibition at PIC: Presynaptic Post synaptic Enkephalin produces pre synaptic inhibition at dorsal horn: Spinal inhibitory interneurons at dorsal horn can exert this inhibition by 2 different mechanisms: Direct presynaptic inhibition of neurotransmitter release f

text: L12: Physiology of Pain By Abeer El- Emam Professor of Physiology- Alexandria Faculty of Medicine Pain Receptors Divided into four categories based on function: High threshold mechano- nociceptors or specific nociceptors. (mechanical stimulation such as pinching, cutting or stretching). Thermal nociceptors, (thermal stimuli). Chemical nociceptors, (chemical substances). Polymodal nociceptors, which respond to high intensity stimuli such as mechanical, thermal and to chemical substances like the previous three types. Factors that Activate Nociceptors Nociceptors respond when a stimulus causes tissue damage. The damage of tissue results in a release of a variety of substances from lysed cells as well as from new substances synthesized at the site of the injury. These substances include: which are believed to be one of the most active Globulin and protein kinases pain- producing substances. Arachidonic acid Arachidonic acid is one of the chemicals released during tissue damage. It is then metabolized into prostaglandin (and cytokines). Histamine. Tissue damage stimulates the mast cells to release histamine to the surrounding area. Nerve growth factor (NGF)). Substance P (SP) and calcitonin gene-related peptide (CGRP) are released by injury. Potassium - K+. Most tissue damage results in an increase in extracellular K + . Serotonin (5-HT), acetylcholine (ACh), low pH (acidic ) solution, and ATP. Muscle spasm and lactic acid. When muscles are hyperactive or when blood flow to a muscle is blocked, lactic acid concentration increases, and pain is induced. Therefore, Non- steroidal anti- inflammatories, are effective in minimizing pain because they minimize the effects of these substances released, especially prostaglandins (blocking cyclo- oxygenase enzyme COX). Pain Fibers A delta fibers (group III fibers) 2- 5 mm in diameter, myelinated, have a fast conduction velocity (5- 40 meters/sec), and carry information mainly from the nociceptive- mechanical or mechano- thermal nociceptors. Their receptive fields are small. Therefore, they provide precise localization of pain.. C fibers (group IV fibers) 0.4- 1.2 mm in diameter unmyelinated have a slow conduction velocity (0.5- 2.0 meters/sec) activated by a variety of high- intensity mechanical, chemical and thermal stimulation and carry information from polymodal nociceptors Their receptive fields are large . 9/26/2025 14 Therefore, less precise for pain localization. Double pain sensations Pricking- fast pain caused by a needle, pin prick, skin cut, sharp, pricking quality, carried fast by the A delta fibers transmitted along rapidly conducting thin myelinated A- δ fibers, short duration, precisely localized. Carried by neo- spinothalamic tract Slow- Burning- soreness pain caused by inflammation, burned skin, It is an annoying pain and intolerable pain, transmitted by the slowly conducting unmyelinated C- fibres long duration, poorly localized, diffuse transmitted by the paleo-spinothalamic tract, arises mainly from the somatic deep s t r u c t u 9 / r 2 e 6 / 2 s 0 2 . 5 viscera and 16 TYPES OF PAIN Nociceptive (acute pain) Chronic pain Neuropathic Nociceptive pain Elicited by a brief noxious stimulus such as pin-prick Induces a flexion withdrawal response to the stimulus Protect the body from injury Of limited duration, mediated mainly by A delta fibers Caused by damage to muscle, bone, joint Superficial or deep STUDENTS’ LEARNING OUTCOMES At the end of this session, the student should be able to; Identify types of pain and how it is perceived via pain receptors Distinguish pathways for pain sensations Describe the peripheral and central mechanisms of hyperalgesia Discuss referred pain and its mechanism Explain peripheral and central sensitization Define neuropathic pain and its main causes Chronic pain Considered “bad pain” because it persists long after recovery from an injury often refractory to common analgesic agents, Chronic pain which results from nerve injury is known as neuropathic pain. Chronic pain Longer duration than acute pain Resistant to treatment In prolonged pain (e.g. sunburn) injury to the body has already occurred and the biological function of pain is to prevent further damage , assist healing and tissue repair. It does this by the development of areas of hypersensitivity in and around the injury site, which are the result of a decreased activation threshold of nociceptors– a phenomenon called peripheral sensitization. The pain recedes once healing has occurred. 9/26/2025 20 Persists even in the absence of the initial injury Defined as ‘ pain resulting from disease or damage to the peripheral or central nervous systems. E.g. pain in irritable bowel syndrome, fibromyalgia and back pain, Herpes zoster infection, pain in diseases such as diabetes, cancer and AIDS. Difficult to treat. Pain qualities include burning or, "pins and needles" sensations. May be associated with ssympathetic nervous system dysfunctions, vasomotor and sudomotor (stimulation of sweat glands) changes. often results from abnormal sensitivity of nociceptors with ectopic impulse generation and abnormal somatosensory processing and spontaneous firing without a peripheral stimulus Chronic (Neuropathic) pain Peripheral Mechanism After a peripheral nerve lesion, aberrant regeneration may occur. • Neurons become unusually sensitive and develop spontaneous pathological activity, abnormal excitability, Heightened sensitivity to chemical, thermal and mechanical stimuli. This phenomenon is called " PERIPHERAL SENSITIZATION” Peripheral sensitization. Occur as a result of inflammation . Chemical mediators of inflammation (such as prostaglandins) and neuropeptide (Substance P) are released following tissue damage can stimulate the nociceptive receptors and sensitize them (bringing the membrane potential closer to the depolarization threshold). Receptors are sensitized by up- regulation of the ion- channels which makes them more sensitive to chemical mediators. This results in a lowered activation threshold (more sensitive to the same quantity of chemical mediators) and results in peripheral sensitization. CENTRAL SENSITIZATION Increased excitability of second- order neurons in the spinal cord. Enhanced responsiveness to both painful (noxious) and non-painful stimuli Insertion of more glutamate receptors in the postsynaptic second-order neuron led to increased excitability of this neuron and facilitated synaptic transmission. . Hypoactivity of the descending anti- nociceptive systems or loss of descending inhibition Stimuli that are normally non- painful (like light touch) are perceived as painful (allodynia). Painful stimuli are felt as more intense than usual (hyperalgesia). 9/26/2025 25 HYPERALGESIA . Increased painful sensation in response to additional noxious stimuli . The threshold for pain in the area surrounding an inflamed or injured site is LOWERED. Sensitized nociceptors. If one pricks normal skin with a sharp probe, it will elicit sharp pain followed by reddened skin. The reddened skin is an area of hyperalgesia. 9/26/2025 26 Feature Primary Hyperalgesia Secondary Hyperalgesia Location At the site of injury Surrounding or remote from the injury Cause/Mechanism Peripheral sensitization of nociceptors by inflammatory mediators) Central sensitization of dorsal horn neurons in the spinal cord Pain Trigger Directly injured tissue Intact tissue near the injury Clinical Example Burned skin is extremely sensitive at the burn site Skin around a burn becomes painful to mild touch 9/26/2025 27 Allodynia Pain resulting from a stimulus that does not normally produce pain. For example, light touch to sunburned skin produces pain WHAT IS PAIN? Pain could be defined as (unpleasant sensory and emotional experience associated with actual or potential tissue damage ) Pain from poena -- - > Latin means punishment. It is uniquely experienced by each individual ; it cannot be adequately defined, identified, or measured by an observer. 9/26/2

text: L11 : Ascending pathways and somatosensory cortex Eman Helmy Thabet MD PhD Lecturer of Medical Physiology Alexandria Faculty of Medicine Fulbright Scholar at UCSF-USA modified by Dr. Abeer Abed Ahmed Professor of Physiology- axons responsible for the unconscious proprioception leave the white matter and synapse in Clarke’s nucleus (nucleus dorsalis 1 st order neurons 2 nd order neurons Enter the dorsal SCBT on the lateral edge of the cord. Ascends WITHOUT crossing to the cerebellum and is also somatotopically organized. terminate on Purkinje cells--  relay the information --  deep cerebellar nuclei---  other motor areas of the thalamus, brainstem and basal ganglia. Clarke’s column only extends from T1 to L1, it only carries information from the lower body and trunk. 3rd order neurons Topographic organizations of the sensory tracts and clinical significance The dorsal column medial lemniscus (DCML) system is very orderly, fibers and cells carrying information from one part of the peripheral receptive surface maintain their positions relative to fibers and cells representing neighboring parts of the receptive surface. Thus, different parts of the body are represented in an orderly sequence in the tracts and nuclei of the DCML system. Topographic organizations of the sensory tracts and clinical significance This orderly arrangement of cells and fibers is called topographical organization. For the somatosensory system, it is usually called somatotopic organization. precise spatial arrangement whereby neurons in a sensory receptor surface (e.g., retina, cochlea, or skin) connect to corresponding neurons in central nervous system structures, preserving neighborhood relationships. Topographic organizations of the sensory tracts and clinical significance This is of clinical relevance when an injury or disease affects specific relay pathways If the problem occurs within the spinal cord, such as in syringomyelia (central cavitation within the spinal cord originating at the central canal) syringomyelia it is common at the cervical spinal cord level. it interrupts the STT bilaterally resulting in loss of pain and temperature sensation below the level of the lesion, particularly in the hands.) the cervical dermatomes will be affected first, and the lower body is less affected. Summary of somatosensory pathways The three main ascending somatosensory pathways each carry a specific modality of sensation associated with specific receptors. Each pathway is somatotopically organized , so that a complete representation of the body is reproduced in each relay nucleus along the pathway. Any sensory system going to the cerebral cortex will have to cross over at some point, because the cerebral cortex operates on a contralateral basis. Summary of somatosensory pathways The discriminative touch system crosses in the medulla, and the pain system crosses in the spinal cord. The proprioceptive system ascends to the cerebellum and does not cross. There is some overlap of modalities between the ascending tracts: some light touch information travels in the STT, so that lesion in the dorsal column does not completely abolish touch and pressure sensation; similarly, visceral pain fibers travel in the dorsal columns and not the STT. The cortex can also be divided into areas that have a single function, such as touch, vision, hearing, taste and smell or the production of movement. These are called primary areas . Their function is to receive and start the initial processing of information. The rest of the cortex is association cortex, which provides higher-order processing of sensory and motor information. The forebrain comprises the largest part of the brain (80% by volume) and consists of the cerebral cortex, the limbic system, and the basal ganglia. Functionally it is divided into: I. Somatosensory areas. II. Motor areas. III. Prefrontal association area. IV. Language areas. CEREBRAL CORTEX Somatosensory cortex (sensory areas of the brain ) The primary somatosensory cortex is composed of the postcentral gyrus of the parietal lobe on each side of the brain it includes: 1- The (primary) somatosensory area I (S1) 2-The (secondary) somatosensory association area. Transfer goal To understand how sensation gets transmitted , perceived, and analyzed from the peripheral system to the CNS via ascending sensory pathways. Characteristic of S1 location :in the postcentral gyrus (Brodmann's areas 1,2 and 3). Body representation of S 1. 1-Crossed 2-Inverted but the face is not inverted 3-Foot and leg are represented medially, and the trunk, chest, arm and hand are represented more lateral in the middle of the postcentral gyrus. 4-The face is represented in the lower half of the postcentral gyrus. Characteristic of S1 The different parts of the body are not equally represented, the size of the area of representation is determined by the number of receptors of that part. The exaggerated size of the face, tongue, and hands indicates the high degree of sensory perception associated with these body parts. This area shows modality separation of different sensations Somatotopic maps in the SI cortex The extent to which a body part is represented in SI is related to its sensory acuity, not to its size. Somatosensory acuity 1- it is the ability to distinguish fine detail by touch 2-directly related to the amount of neural tissue devoted to the representation of a body Part 3-the greater the peripheral innervation density, the smaller the receptive fields of the innervating neurons, and the larger the volume of the cortex representing that region. , The ability to perform point localization two-point discrimination Is best face (around the lips), hands(fingertips) feet (toes). function of SI cortex I Responsible for Conscious awareness that a stimulus has occurred, and of its quality, location, intensity and duration. Responsible for initial cortical processing and perception of both somesthetic and proprioceptive input. localizes the source of sensory input and perceives the level of intensity of the stimulus. It also is capable of spatial discrimination. projects this sensory input to adjacent higher sensory areas( posterior parietal association cortex ) for further elaboration, analysis, and integration of sensory information. ( areas that give meaning to the received stimulus.) SI cortex is somatotopically organized. Somatotopic maps in the SI cortex Brodmann’s areas 1, 2, 3a and 3b Area 3b :mostly receives cutaneous input (from slowly and rapidly adapting receptors) Area 3a receives input from proprioceptors in muscles Area 2:process both tactile and proprioceptive stimuli. and is thought to be important for stereognosis), Area 1 receives information from rapidly adapting cutaneous mechanoreceptors. Lesion Unilateral destruction of SI produces severe deficits in all aspects of discriminative touch and proprioception on the contralesional side of the body. The secondary Somatosensory association area ( Brodmann’s areas 5 and 7) Site: it is located in the superior parietal lobe behind the sensory area I in the parietal lobe (posterior parietal cortex). connection :It receives efferent fibers from the primary somatic sensory areas as well as from the thalamic association nuclei. It also receives input from the visual system. This area combines the various sensory information received from the primary somatic sensory areas to recognize objects (stereognosis). It integrates tactile and proprioceptive information from the hand before performing a voluntary movement. Important for spatial awareness and perception of the different parts of the body . The secondary Somatosensory association area ( Brodmann’s areas 5 and 7) Functions: They provide a higher level of interpretation of sensory experiences. Understanding and giving meaning to them, so it is important for stereognosis. text: L11 -A : Somatic Sensations- Ascending pathways- 1 Dr. Eman Helmy Thabet , Dr. Norhan Sobhy Prof Gehan Yassin Soliman Medical Physiology department - Alexandria Faculty of Medicine Ascending pathways T here names are based on their origin and destination in NS S ensory sensations enter the CNS via dorsal roots from body & the trigeminal root from facial. Common Features: Consist of a chain of 2–4 order neurons , T he first-order cell bodies are in the dorsal root ganglia or cranial nerve ganglia. Pathways for conscious sensation cross to the contralateral side. Decussation always occurs at the level of the second-order neuron . Ascending pathways Runner 1 Runner 2 Neuron 1 Neuron 2 /Brainstem Runner 2 Runner 3 Neuron 1 Neuron 2 Neuron 3 Thalamus Cortex Neuron 4 3 Major Ascending Pathways: Dorsal column–medial lemniscal system Ventrolateral system Spinocerebellar systems Ascending pathways 1- T he dorsal colimn medial lemniscuss pathway (DCML) it carries: Touch (discriminative- Fine touch) V ibration P ressure Conscious Proprioception (sense of position and movements): kinaesthesia GRAPHESTHESIA , and STEREOGNOSIS . Nerve fibres : Aa/B fibres The dorsal column medial lemniscus (DCML) pathway The dorsal column medial lemniscus (DCML) pathway It is Somato -topically organized. The extent of a body part in SI is related to its sensory acuity , not to its size. 1 st order neuron (dorsal root ganglion): ascend ipsilaterally in DC to the medulla 2 nd order neuron (gracile and cuneate nuclei ): of the medulla cross in the medulla and ascend as the medial lemniscus to the ventro -posterior lateral (VPL) nucleus of the thalamus . the head is represented medially and the rest of the body laterally. 3 rd order neuron (VPL nucleus of the thalamus): ascends to the primary somatosensory cortex ( SI) The dorsal column medial lemniscus (DCML) pathway ILOs: By the end of this lecture, students can Analyze the organization and functional roles of the major ascending somatosensory pathways. Differentiate the DCML, spinothalamic, and spinocerebellar pathways according to modality, course, decussation, and destination. Apply knowledge of decussation and somatotopy to predict the laterality and distribution of sensory deficits following neurological lesions. Lesions to the posterior columns → loss of discriminative touch, vibration Difficulty in identifying objects by touch (astereognosis) Sensory ataxia (due to lack of proprioceptive feedback) Positive Romberg sign: Patient sways or falls when eyes are closed (loss of proprioception) THE VENTROLATERAL SYSTEM It comprises several pathways , ascend in the ventrolateral spinal cord to: Thalamus: spinothalamic tract. midbrain: spinomesencephalic . reticular formation: spinoreticular . Brain stem nuclei: spinobulbar it carries: Pain (tissue damage) & temperature & some touch Receptors: free nerve endings Nerve fibres : A-delta and C fibres . The synaptic transmitter for fast pain is glutamate. slow severe pain is substance P. Spinothalamic tract (STT) 1 st order neuron (dorsal root ganglion): synapse in the dorsal horn 2 nd order neuron cross in the spinal cord and ascend as the lateral lemniscus to the the thalamus . 3 rd order neuron Spinothalamic tract (STT) → 3 rd order neuron 1- discriminative aspect of pain” location, severity & duration neospinothalamic tract (lateral pathway) → (VPL nucleus ): → SI 2- the motivational-affective component of pain = the “second” pain= the dull, throbbing poorly localized the paleospinothalamic tract (medial pathway) → the non-specific intralaminar nuclei, & the autonomic centres of the RF → reticular activating system → all brain →the arousal effects Lesions to the spinothalamic tract loss of pain and temperature on the opposite side to the injury, beginning a few levels below or above the level of the injury Other ventrolateral pathways Spinotectal tract Spino- olivary tract Spinotectal tract I t integrates visual inputs to mediates reflexes in response to touch → turning the eyes/head or body towards a tactile stimulus. This pathway runs medially alongside the STT, from the cervical spinal cord → cross → superior colliculus of midbrain Spino- olivary tract M ay play a role in modifying movements when a moving body part encounters an unexpected obstacle. Associated to motor learning From proprioceptors → inferior olivary nucleus (ION) in the medulla → contralateral cerebellum Somatic sensations These sensations come from the skin and deeper structures (muscles, bones, tendons, and joints). According to their nature (Modality) , somatic sensations are : Mechanoreceptive sensations Thermoreceptive sensations Pain sensations Somatic s ensation from the face Trigeminal pathway 1 st order neuron is the trigeminal ganglion. 2 nd order neuron: trigeminal nuclei. The pain & temperature → spinal trigeminal nucleus Proprioceptors → mesencephalic nucleus Touch → main sensory nucleus 3 rd order neuron → trigeminal lemniscus → SI EXAMINE YOUR-SELF A patient with a lesion involving the left spinothalamic tract reports that he cannot feel a painful pinprick applied to the right leg. Which structure normally serves as the major relay for these ascending sensory signals before they reach the cerebral cortex? A. Caudate nucleus B. Lateral geniculate nucleus C. Ventral posterior nucleus of the thalamus D. Substantia nigra E. Hippocampus Answer: C. A 54-year-old patient underwent neurological testing after a spinal cord injury. The physician tested vibration using a tuning fork, pain using a pinprick, and proprioception by moving the patient's great toe. Which combination correctly identifies the major pathways involved? A. Vibration—spinothalamic; pain—DCML; proprioception—spinocerebellar B. Vibration—DCML; pain—spinothalamic; proprioception—DCML C. Vibration—spinocerebellar; pain—DCML; proprioception—spinothalamic D. Vibration—spinothalamic; pain—spinocerebellar; proprioception—DCML E. Vibration—DCML; pain—spinocerebellar; proprioception—spinothalamic Answer: B. A 48-year-old woman developed a lesion involving the anterior white mattar at the cervical spinal cord. She developed bilateral loss of pain and temperature sensation over the shoulders and upper limbs, while vibration and proprioception remained intact. Which condition most closely produces? A. Syringomyelia B. Multiple sclerosis affecting the medial lemniscus C. Complete spinal cord transection D. Posterior column degeneration E. Cerebellar infarction Answer: A.
